A security administrator wants to implement a logon script that will prevent MITM attacks on the local LAN. Which of the following commands should the security administrator implement within the script to accomplish this task?
A. arp - s 192.168.1.1 00-3a-d1-fa-b1-06
B. dig - x@192.168.1.1 mypc.comptia.com
C. nmap - A - T4 192.168.1.1
D. tcpdump - lnv host 192.168.1.1 or either 00:3a:d1:fa:b1:06
cards.why: A static ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) entry binds the gateway IP address to its real MAC (Media Access Control) address, so forged ARP replies from a MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attacker are ignored.

whyNot.B: The dig command performs a reverse DNS (Domain Name System) lookup and does nothing to stop ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) spoofing.
whyNot.C: The nmap command scans and fingerprints hosts, which is reconnaissance and does not prevent a MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attack.
whyNot.D: The tcpdump command only captures and displays packets, so it can observe traffic but cannot block a MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attack.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the BEST reason for salting a password hash before it is stored in a database?
A. To prevent duplicate values from being stored
B. To make the password retrieval process very slow
C. To protect passwords from being saved in readable format
D. To prevent users from using simple passwords for their access credentials
cards.back: A. To prevent duplicate values from being stored
cards.why: Salting adds a unique random value to each password before hashing, so two users with the same password get different hashes and no duplicate hash values are stored.

whyNot.B: Deliberately slowing hashing is the job of key stretching functions such as bcrypt, not of salting.
whyNot.C: Hashing alone already keeps passwords out of readable form, and salting does not add that protection.
whyNot.D: Salting happens after the user picks a password and has no effect on password complexity choices.

cards.front:
An actor downloads and runs a program against a corporate login page. The program imports a list of usernames and passwords, looking for a successful attempt. Which of the following terms BEST describes the actor in this situation?
A. Script kiddie
B. Hacktivist
C. Cryptologist
D. Security auditor
cards.why: A script kiddie is an unskilled attacker who runs prebuilt tools, such as a credential-stuffing program with an imported username and password list, without understanding how it works.

whyNot.B: A hacktivist is motivated by a political or social cause, and nothing in the scenario suggests that motive.
whyNot.C: A cryptologist studies and designs ciphers and is not an attacker running a credential-guessing tool.
whyNot.D: A security auditor is authorized to assess controls, while this actor is attacking a login page without permission.

cards.front:
An organization wants to utilize a common, Internet-based third-party provider for authorization and authentication. The provider uses a technology based on OAuth 2.0 to provide required services. To which of the following technologies is the provider referring?
A. OpenID Connect
B. SAML
C. XACML
D. LDAP
cards.why: OpenID Connect is an identity layer built on top of OAuth (Open Authorization) 2.0 that provides authentication, and it is widely offered by Internet-based third-party providers.

whyNot.B: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) is an XML (Extensible Markup Language) based federation standard and is not built on OAuth (Open Authorization) 2.0.
whyNot.C: XACML (eXtensible Access Control Markup Language) defines access control policies and is not built on OAuth (Open Authorization) 2.0.
whyNot.D: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a directory access protocol and is not based on OAuth (Open Authorization) 2.0.

cards.front:
A penetration tester harvests potential usernames from a social networking site. The penetration tester then uses social engineering to attempt to obtain associated passwords to gain unauthorized access to shares on a network server. Which of the following methods is the penetration tester MOST likely using?
A. Escalation of privilege
B. SQL injection
C. Active reconnaissance
D. Proxy server
cards.why: Harvesting usernames from social sites and contacting people through social engineering involves direct interaction with the target, which is active reconnaissance used to gather access information.

whyNot.A: Escalation of privilege means gaining higher rights after access is obtained, but this scenario describes gathering information to gain initial access.
whyNot.B: SQL (Structured Query Language) injection exploits unvalidated input in database queries, which is not what the tester is doing.
whyNot.D: A proxy server relays traffic for clients and is not an attack method for harvesting usernames or passwords.

cards.front:
Which of the following could occur when both strong and weak ciphers are configured on a VPN concentrator? (Select TWO)
A. An attacker could potentially perform a downgrade attack.
B. The connection is vulnerable to resource exhaustion.
C. The integrity of the data could be at risk.
D. The VPN concentrator could revert to L2TP.
E. The IPSec payload reverted to 16-bit sequence numbers.
cards.back:
A. An attacker could potentially perform a downgrade attack.
E. The IPSec payload reverted to 16-bit sequence numbers.
cards.why: Supporting weak ciphers alongside strong ones lets an attacker force negotiation down to the weak option, which is a downgrade attack, and the keyed answer also lists reverted 16-bit sequence numbers.

whyNot.B: Resource exhaustion comes from excessive load or connection floods, not from having mixed cipher strengths configured.
whyNot.C: Data integrity risk from weak algorithms is plausible, but the key does not select it as an expected result here.
whyNot.D: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) concentrator does not automatically fall back to L2TP (Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol) because of cipher configuration.

cards.keyDoubt: C: weak ciphers or hashes negotiated on an IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) VPN (Virtual Private Network) put data integrity at risk, while 16-bit sequence numbers are not a known cipher downgrade result.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the BEST choice for a security control that represents a preventive and corrective logical control at the same time?
A. Security awareness training
B. Antivirus
C. Firewalls
D. Intrusion detection system
cards.why: Antivirus software is a logical control that prevents malware from running and also corrects infections by quarantining or removing malicious files, so it is both preventive and corrective.

whyNot.A: Security awareness training is an administrative control, not a logical control.
whyNot.C: A firewall is a logical preventive control that blocks traffic but does not correct an infection after it occurs.
whyNot.D: An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) is a detective control that alerts on activity and neither prevents nor corrects.

cards.front:
A web developers improves client access to the company's REST API. Authentication needs to be tokenized but not expose the client's password. Which of the following methods would BEST meet the developer's requirements?
A. SAML
B. LDAP
C. OAuth
D. Shibboleth
cards.why: The keyed answer is SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language), which issues signed assertions as tokens so clients authenticate without exposing their passwords to the service.

whyNot.B: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a directory protocol that typically passes credentials in binds and does not issue tokens.
whyNot.C: OAuth (Open Authorization) is the other tokenized option and is listed as wrong in this key.
whyNot.D: Shibboleth is a federated identity system built on SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) and is aimed at web single sign-on, not API (Application Programming Interface) access.

cards.keyDoubt: C: OAuth (Open Authorization) issues access tokens for API (Application Programming Interface) access without exposing the client's password, which fits a tokenized REST (Representational State Transfer) API better than SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language).

cards.front:
A vulnerability scan is being conducted against a desktop system. The scan is looking for files, versions, and registry values known to be associated with system vulnerabilities. Which of the following BEST describes the type of scan being performed?
A. Non-intrusive
B. Authenticated
C. Credentialed
D. Active
cards.why: A credentialed scan logs into the system with valid credentials so it can inspect files, installed versions, and registry values that a scan from outside cannot see.

whyNot.A: A non-intrusive scan avoids disruptive tests, but that describes scan impact and not the ability to read files and registry values.
whyNot.B: An authenticated scan is a synonym for credentialed, so it is loosely correct but is not the term the key selects.
whyNot.D: An active scan sends probes to the target, but that does not by itself give access to files and registry values.

cards.front:
A security analyst is updating a BIA document. The security analyst notices the support vendor's time to replace a server hard drive went from eight hours to two hours. Given these new metrics, which of the following can be concluded? (Select TWO)
A. The MTTR is faster.
B. The MTTR is slower.
C. The RTO has increased.
D. The RTO has decreased.
E. The MTTF has increased.
F. The MTTF has decreased.
cards.back:
A. The MTTR is faster.
D. The RTO has decreased.
cards.why: Replacing a drive in two hours instead of eight lowers the MTTR (Mean Time To Repair), meaning repairs are faster, and the shorter recovery supports a lower RTO (Recovery Time Objective).

whyNot.B: The MTTR (Mean Time To Repair) fell from eight hours to two hours, so repairs are faster and not slower.
whyNot.C: A faster replacement shortens the possible recovery time, so the RTO (Recovery Time Objective) does not increase.
whyNot.E: MTTF (Mean Time To Failure) measures how long a component runs before failing, which repair time does not change.
whyNot.F: MTTF (Mean Time To Failure) measures time until failure, and repair speed has no effect on it.

cards.front:
Which of the following could help detect trespassers in a secure facility? (Select TWO)
A. Faraday cages
B. Motion-detection sensors
C. Tall, chain-link fencing
D. Security guards
E. Smart cards
cards.back:
B. Motion-detection sensors
D. Security guards
cards.why: Motion-detection sensors alert when movement occurs in a protected area, and security guards can observe and respond to intruders, so both detect trespassers.

whyNot.A: A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic signals and does not detect people.
whyNot.C: Tall chain-link fencing is a deterrent and barrier that does not detect intruders.
whyNot.E: Smart cards authenticate authorized people for entry and do not detect trespassers.

cards.front:
The IT department is deploying new computers. To ease the transition, users will be allowed to access their old and new systems. The help desk is receive reports that users are experiencing the following error when attempting to log in to their previous system: Logon Failure: Access Denied Which of the following can cause this issue?
A. Permission issues
B. Access violations
C. Certificate issues
D. Misconfigured devices
cards.why: Users who can access both old and new systems may present a certificate tied to the new system, and the old system rejects it, causing a Logon Failure: Access Denied error from a certificate issue.

whyNot.A: Permission issues would typically affect resource access after a successful logon rather than cause a logon failure for many users after a migration.
whyNot.B: Access violations describe a program or process attempting illegal memory or resource access, not user logon failures.
whyNot.D: Misconfigured devices would more likely cause connectivity or configuration errors than an access denied logon failure tied to the migration.

cards.front:
A third-party penetration testing company was able to successfully use an ARP cache poison technique to gain root access on a server. The tester successfully moved to another server that was not in the original network. Which of the following is the MOST likely method used to gain access to the other host?
A. Backdoor
B. Pivoting
C. Persistance
D. Logic bomp
cards.why: Pivoting means using a compromised host as a foothold to attack other systems, including those on networks the tester could not reach directly.

whyNot.A: A backdoor is a hidden access method into a system and does not describe moving from one server to another.
whyNot.C: Persistence means keeping access across reboots or logouts, not reaching a different host.
whyNot.D: A logic bomb is malicious code that triggers on a condition and is not a lateral movement method.

cards.front:
Ann, a security administrator, wants to ensure credentials are encrypted in transit when implementing a RADIUS server for SSO. Which of the following are needed given these requirements? (Select TWO)
A. Public key
B. Shared key
C. Elliptic curve
D. MD5
E. Private key
F. DES
cards.back:
A. Public key
E. Private key
cards.why: Encrypting credentials in transit uses asymmetric cryptography, where the public key encrypts data and the matching private key decrypts it, so both keys are needed.

whyNot.B: A shared key is symmetric and is used between the RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) client and server, not for the public and private key pair this question asks for.
whyNot.C: Elliptic curve is a type of algorithm and not a key component that is needed here.
whyNot.D: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is a hashing algorithm and does not encrypt credentials.
whyNot.F: DES (Data Encryption Standard) is a weak, outdated symmetric cipher and is not what this key requires.

cards.front:
The POODLE attack is a MITM exploit that affects:
A. TLS1.0 with CBC mode cipher.
B. SSLv2.0 with CBC mode cipher,
C. SSLv3.0 with CBC mode cipher.
D. SSLv3.0 with ECB mode cipher.
cards.back: C. SSLv3.0 with CBC mode cipher.
cards.why: POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption) forces a downgrade to SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) 3.0 and exploits its CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) padding to decrypt data in a MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) position.

whyNot.A: The original POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption) attack targets SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) 3.0, not TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.0.
whyNot.B: POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption) targets SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) 3.0, not version 2.0.
whyNot.D: The attack relies on the padding in CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode, not ECB (Electronic Codebook) mode.

cards.front:
To determine the ALE of a particular risk, which of the following must be calculated? (Select TWO).
A. ARO
B. ROI
C. RPO
D. SLE
E. RTO
cards.why: ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) is calculated as SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) multiplied by ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence), so both of those values are required.

whyNot.B: ROI (Return on Investment) measures the financial benefit of a control, not an input to calculating ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy).
whyNot.C: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines acceptable data loss in time, which is a business continuity metric and not part of the ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) formula.
whyNot.E: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) defines how quickly a system must be restored, which is not an input to ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy).

cards.front:
Which of the following are used to increase the computing time it takes to brute force a password using an offline attack? (Select TWO)
A. XOR
B. PBKDF2
C. bcrypt
D. HMAC
E. RIPEMD
cards.why: PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) and bcrypt both use salting and many iterations or a cost factor, deliberately slowing each guess and so increasing offline brute force time.

whyNot.A: XOR (Exclusive OR) is a simple bitwise operation that adds no meaningful computational cost against password guessing.
whyNot.D: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) provides message integrity and authentication, and it is fast rather than deliberately slow.
whyNot.E: RIPEMD (RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest) is a fast general-purpose hash that does not stretch keys or slow brute force attempts.

cards.front:
Users in a corporation currently authenticate with a username and password. A security administrator wishes to implement two-factor authentication to improve security. Which of the following authentication methods should be deployed to achieve this goal?
A. PIN
B. Security question
C. Smart card
D. Passphrase
E. CAPTCHA
cards.why: A smart card is a something-you-have factor, which combined with the existing password (something you know) provides true two-factor authentication.

whyNot.A: A PIN (Personal Identification Number) is another something-you-know factor, so pairing it with a password is not two-factor authentication.
whyNot.B: A security question is knowledge-based, the same factor type as a password, so it does not add a second factor.
whyNot.D: A passphrase is a longer password and is still something you know, so it adds no second factor.
whyNot.E: A CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) distinguishes humans from bots and is not an authentication factor.

cards.front:
A security administrator needs to address the following audit recommendations for a public-facing SFTP server: Users should be restricted to upload and download files to their own home directories only. Users should not be allowed to use interactive shell login. Which of the following configuration parameters should be implemented? (Select TWO).
A. PermitTunnel
B. ChrootDirectory
C. PermitTTY
D. AllowTcpForwarding
E. IgnoreRhosts
cards.why: ChrootDirectory confines each SFTP (Secure File Transfer Protocol) user to their own home directory, and disabling PermitTTY (Pseudo-Terminal allocation) blocks interactive shell sessions.

whyNot.A: PermitTunnel controls whether SSH (Secure Shell) tun device forwarding is allowed, which does not restrict directories or shell access.
whyNot.D: AllowTcpForwarding controls TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port forwarding over SSH (Secure Shell), not directory restriction or shell login.
whyNot.E: IgnoreRhosts controls whether legacy rhosts files are honored for authentication, which does not confine users or block interactive shells.

cards.front:
An organization recently moved its custom web applications to the cloud, and it is obtaining managed services of the back-end environment as part of its subscription. Which of the following types of services is this company now using?
A. SaaS
B. CASB
C. IaaS
D. PaaS
cards.back:
B. CASB

Security Broker (CASB) gives you both visibility into your entire cloud stack and the security automation tool your IT team needs.
cards.why: The company runs its own custom web applications while the provider manages the back-end environment such as the operating system and runtime, which matches PaaS (Platform as a Service). The key lists CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker), which is not a service model.

whyNot.A: SaaS (Software as a Service) delivers finished applications, but this company runs its own custom web applications rather than consuming vendor software.
whyNot.C: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) leaves the customer managing the operating system and back-end, whereas here the provider manages the back-end.
whyNot.D: PaaS (Platform as a Service) is the best fit, so this is the option the key should have selected rather than a wrong answer.

cards.keyDoubt: D. The scenario describes custom applications on a provider-managed back-end, which is PaaS (Platform as a Service), while a CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) is a security control and not a service type.

cards.front:
Which of the following is commonly done as part of a vulnerability scan?
A. Exploiting misconfigured applications
B. Cracking employee passwords
C. Sending phishing emails to employees
D. Identifying unpatched workstations
cards.why: A vulnerability scan passively or actively checks systems for known weaknesses, such as missing patches, without exploiting them, so identifying unpatched workstations is a standard result.

whyNot.A: Exploiting misconfigured applications is penetration testing activity, whereas a vulnerability scan only identifies weaknesses.
whyNot.B: Cracking employee passwords is a password auditing or attack activity and not part of a vulnerability scan.
whyNot.C: Sending phishing emails to employees is a social engineering simulation, which is separate from vulnerability scanning.

cards.front:
A company is evaluating cloud providers to reduce the cost of its internal IT operations. The company's aging systems are unable to keep up with customer demand. Which of the following cloud models will the company MOST likely select?
A. PaaS
B. SaaS
C. IaaS
D. BaaS
cards.why: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) replaces aging servers with rented, scalable compute, storage, and networking, which directly addresses hardware that cannot keep up with demand while cutting costs.

whyNot.A: PaaS (Platform as a Service) provides a managed application platform, which is more than the company needs to simply replace aging hardware.
whyNot.B: SaaS (Software as a Service) delivers finished applications and does not replace the company's own aging systems and workloads.
whyNot.D: BaaS (Backend as a Service) supplies prebuilt backend functions for app developers and does not provide general replacement infrastructure.

cards.front:
After a security incident, management is meeting with involved employees to document the incident and its aftermath. Which of the following BEST describes this phase of the incident response process?
A. Lessons learned
B. Recovery
C. Identification
D. Preparation
cards.why: Meeting with involved staff after an incident to document what happened and how it was handled is the lessons learned phase, which aims to improve future response.

whyNot.B: Recovery restores affected systems to normal operation and is not a review meeting to document the incident.
whyNot.C: Identification detects and confirms that an incident has occurred, which happens before this post-incident review.
whyNot.D: Preparation builds plans, tools, and training before any incident occurs, not after one.

cards.front:
After an identified security breach, an analyst is tasked to initiate the IR process. Which of the following is the NEXT step the analyst should take?
A. Recovery
B. Identification
C. Preparation
D. Documentation
E. Escalation
cards.why: After a breach is identified, the IR (Incident Response) process begins with verifying and scoping the incident, so Identification is the step the analyst should take next.

whyNot.A: Recovery occurs late in the IR (Incident Response) process, after the incident is contained and eradicated.
whyNot.C: Preparation happens before incidents, so it is already complete when the IR (Incident Response) process is initiated.
whyNot.D: Documentation is ongoing throughout the IR (Incident Response) process and is not a discrete next phase.
whyNot.E: Escalation may follow once the incident is confirmed and scoped, but the incident must first be identified and assessed.

cards.keyDoubt: E. The question says a breach has already been identified, so the analyst's next step is escalation, although the key of Identification is also defensible depending on the IR (Incident Response) model.

cards.front:
A user needs to send sensitive information to a colleague using PKI. Which of the following concepts apply when a sender encrypts the message hash with the sender's private key? (Select TWO)
A. Non-repudiation
B. Email content encryption
C. Steganography
D. Transport security
E. Message integrity
cards.why: Encrypting a hash with the sender's private key creates a digital signature, which provides non-repudiation because only the sender could produce it, and message integrity because any change alters the hash.

whyNot.B: Email content encryption uses the recipient's public key to protect confidentiality, whereas signing a hash does not hide the message content.
whyNot.C: Steganography hides data inside other media and has nothing to do with signing a hash.
whyNot.D: Transport security such as TLS (Transport Layer Security) protects data in transit between systems and is not what a digital signature on a message provides.

cards.front:
A technician suspects that a system has been compromised. The technician reviews the following log entry: WARNING - hash mismatch: C:\Window\SysWOW64\user32.dll WARNING - hash mismatch: C:\Window\SysWOW64\kernel32.dll Based solely on the above information, which of the following types of malware is MOST likely installed on the system?
A. Rootkit
B. Ransomware
C. Trojan
D. Backdoor
cards.why: Hash mismatches on core operating system files such as user32.dll and kernel32.dll indicate the system files were altered, which is characteristic of a rootkit hiding itself at a low level.

whyNot.B: Ransomware encrypts user data and shows a ransom demand, and modified system DLL (Dynamic Link Library) hashes alone do not indicate that.
whyNot.C: A Trojan is malware disguised as legitimate software, and the log gives no sign of such a disguised program.
whyNot.D: A backdoor provides covert remote access, and the log shows no evidence of remote access, only modified system files.

cards.front:
As part of a new BYOD rollout, a security analyst has been asked to find a way to securely store company data on personal devices. Which of the following would BEST help to accomplish this?
A. Require the use of an eight-character PIN.
B. Implement containerization of company data.
C. Require annual AUP sign-off.
D. Use geofencing tools to unlock devices while on the premises.
cards.back: B. Implement containerization of company data.
cards.why: Containerization separates company data into a managed, encrypted workspace on a personal device, so the organization can protect or wipe it without touching personal content.

whyNot.A: An eight-character PIN (Personal Identification Number) only protects device unlock and does not separate or secure company data.
whyNot.C: An AUP (Acceptable Use Policy) sign-off is an administrative control that does not technically protect stored data.
whyNot.D: Geofencing unlocks or restricts devices by location, which does not securely isolate company data on a personal device.

cards.front:
A web server, which is configured to use TLS with AES-GCM-256, SHA-384, and ECDSA, recently suffered an information loss breach. Which of the following is MOST likely the cause?
A. Insufficient key bit length
B. Weak cipher suite
C. Unauthenticated encryption method
D. Poor implementation
cards.why: AES-GCM-256 (Advanced Encryption Standard Galois/Counter Mode), SHA-384 (Secure Hash Algorithm), and ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) are all strong, so the breach most likely stems from poor implementation or configuration.

whyNot.A: A 256-bit key length is strong and is not an insufficient key size.
whyNot.B: This cipher suite is modern and strong, so it is not a weak cipher suite.
whyNot.C: AES-GCM (Advanced Encryption Standard Galois/Counter Mode) is an authenticated encryption mode, so the encryption is not unauthenticated.

cards.front:
An incident involving a workstation that is potentially infected with a virus has occurred. The workstation may have sent confidential data to an unknown internet server. Which of the following should a security analyst do FIRST?
A. Make a copy of everything in memory on the workstation.
B. Turn off the workstation.
C. Consult the information security policy.
D. Run a virus scan.
cards.back: A. Make a copy of everything in memory on the workstation.
cards.why: Memory is volatile and may hold evidence such as malware, connections, and exfiltrated data, so following the order of volatility the analyst should capture memory first before anything changes it.

whyNot.B: Turning off the workstation destroys volatile memory contents, losing valuable forensic evidence.
whyNot.C: Consulting the information security policy is reasonable but delays evidence capture while volatile data may be lost.
whyNot.D: Running a virus scan alters system state and memory, which can overwrite or destroy evidence.

cards.front:
Which of the following BEST describes an important security advantage yielded by implementing vendor diversity?
A. Sustainability
B. Homogeneity
C. Resiliency
D. Configurability
cards.why: Vendor diversity avoids dependence on a single vendor, so a flaw or outage in one vendor's product does not affect everything, which improves resiliency.

whyNot.A: Sustainability concerns long-term environmental or operational viability and is not the main security advantage of vendor diversity.
whyNot.B: Homogeneity means using the same products everywhere, which is the opposite of vendor diversity and increases shared risk.
whyNot.D: Configurability describes how adjustable a product is, which is not a benefit gained from using multiple vendors.

cards.front:
A dumpster diver recovers several hard drives from a company and is able to obtain confidential data from one of the hard drives. The company then discovers its information is posted online. Which of the following methods would have MOST likely prevented the data from being exposed?
A. Removing the hard drive from its enclosure
B. Using software to repeatedly rewrite over the disk space
C. Using Blowfish encryption on the hard drives
D. Using magnetic fields to erase the data
cards.back: D. Using magnetic fields to erase the data
cards.why: Degaussing uses strong magnetic fields to destroy the magnetic data on a hard drive, making recovery from discarded drives effectively impossible before they reach the dumpster.

whyNot.A: Removing a drive from its enclosure does nothing to the data, which is still fully readable on the platters.
whyNot.B: Repeated overwriting can sanitize a drive, but it is less reliable than degaussing for drives that may have failed or have unreachable sectors.
whyNot.C: Blowfish is an encryption cipher; the question asks about disposal, and encryption alone does not destroy data or prove the key was protected.

cards.front:
A manager wants to distribute a report to several other managers with the company. Some of them reside in remote locations that are not connected to the domain but have a local server. Because there is sensitive data within the report and the size of the report is beyond the limit of the email attachment size, emailing the report is not an option. Which of the following protocols should be implemented to distribute the report securely? (Select THREE)
A. S/MIME
B. SSH
C. SNMPv3
D. FTPS
E. SRTP
F. HTTPS
G. LDAPS
cards.back:
B. SSH
D. FTPS
F. HTTPS
cards.why: SSH (Secure Shell) with its file copy tools, FTPS (File Transfer Protocol Secure), and HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) each move large files securely over an encrypted channel to remote servers outside the domain.

whyNot.A: S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) secures email, but the question rules out email because of the attachment size limit.
whyNot.C: SNMPv3 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 3) manages and monitors network devices and is not designed for distributing reports.
whyNot.E: SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) secures voice and video streams, not file transfers.
whyNot.G: LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol Secure) secures directory queries and authentication, not report distribution.

cards.front:
A vice president at a manufacturing organization is concerned about desktops being connected to the network. Employees need to log onto the desktops' local account to verify that a product is being created within specifications; otherwise, the desktops should be as isolated as possible. Which of the following is the BEST way to accomplish this?
A. Put the desktops in the DMZ.
B. Create a separate VLAN for the desktops.
C. Air gap the desktops.
D. Join the desktops to an ad-hoc network.
cards.why: An air gap physically isolates the desktops from every network, so employees can still log on locally while the machines remain as isolated as possible from network-based threats.

whyNot.A: A DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) hosts public-facing servers and is still connected to the network, so it does not isolate desktops.
whyNot.B: A VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) separates traffic logically, but the desktops remain network-connected and reachable through routing or misconfiguration.
whyNot.D: An ad-hoc network is a peer-to-peer wireless connection, which still connects the desktops and adds exposure instead of isolating them.

cards.front:
An in-house penetration tester has been asked to evade a new DLP system. The tester plans to exfiltrate data through steganography. Discovery of which of the following would help catch the tester in the act?
A. Abnormally high numbers of outgoing instant messages that contain obfuscated text
B. Large-capacity USB drives on the tester's desk with encrypted zip files
C. Outgoing emails containing unusually large image files
D. Unusual SFTP connections to a consumer IP address
cards.back: C. Outgoing emails containing unusually large image files
cards.why: Steganography hides data inside carrier files such as images, so outgoing emails with unusually large image files are a sign that data may be hidden and leaving the network.

whyNot.A: Obfuscated instant messages suggest encoding or encryption, but not steganography, which hides data inside other files.
whyNot.B: Encrypted zip files on USB (Universal Serial Bus) drives indicate encryption and removable media, not data hidden inside a carrier file.
whyNot.D: Unusual SFTP (Secure File Transfer Protocol) connections indicate a covert file transfer channel, not steganography.

cards.front:
A member of the admins group reports being unable to modify the "changes" file on a server. The permissions on the file are as follows: Permissions User Group File -rwxrw-r--+ Admins Admins changes Based on the output above, which of the following BEST explains why the user is unable to modify the "changes" file?
A. The SELinux mode on the server is set to "enforcing."
B. The SELinux mode on the server is set to "permissive."
C. An FACL has been added to the permissions for the file.
D. The admins group does not have adequate permissions to access the file.
cards.back: C. An FACL has been added to the permissions for the file.
cards.why: The plus sign at the end of the permission string means an FACL (File Access Control List) is attached, and its extra entries can override the basic permissions and deny the Admins group modify access.

whyNot.A: SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux) enforcing mode is not shown in the permission output, and nothing here points to it.
whyNot.B: SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux) permissive mode only logs violations and does not block access, so it could not cause this denial.
whyNot.D: The group permissions shown, rw-, would allow modification, so the basic permissions are not the reason; the FACL (File Access Control List) is.

cards.front:
A penetration tester is conducting an assessment on Comptia.org and runs the following command from a coffee shop while connected to the public Internet: c:\nslookup -querytype=MX comptia.org Server: Unknown Address: 198.51.100.45 comptia.org MX preference=10, mail exchanger = 92.68.102.33 comptia.org MX preference=20, mail exchanger = exchg1.comptia.org exchg1.comptia.org internet address = 192.168.102.67 Which of the following should the penetration tester conclude about the command output?
A. The public/private views on the Comptia.org DNS servers are misconfigured.
B. Comptia.org is running an older mail server, which may be vulnerable to exploits.
C. The DNS SPF records have not been updated for Comptia.org.
D. 192.168.102.67 is a backup mail server that may be more vulnerable to attack.
cards.back: D. 192.168.102.67 is a backup mail server that may be more vulnerable to attack.
cards.why: The 192.168.102.67 address is the lower-priority MX (Mail Exchanger) record with preference 20, so it acts as a backup mail server, and backup systems are often less hardened and patched than primary ones.

whyNot.A: Private and public DNS (Domain Name System) views are not shown to be misconfigured, since the output reflects normal MX (Mail Exchanger) records.
whyNot.B: The output shows no mail server software or version, so nothing indicates an older, vulnerable mail server.
whyNot.C: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) records are TXT records and were not queried; an MX (Mail Exchanger) lookup says nothing about them.

cards.front:
A security analyst is inspecting the results of a recent internal vulnerability scan that was performed against intranet services. The scan reports include the following critical-rated vulnerability: Title: Remote Command Execution vulnerability in web server Rating: Critical (CVSS 10.0) Threat actor: any remote user of the web server Confidence: certain Recommendation: apply vendor patches Which of the following actions should the security analyst perform FIRST?
A. Escalate the issue to senior management.
B. Apply organizational context to the risk rating.
C. Organize for urgent out-of-cycle patching.
D. Exploit the server to check whether it is a false positive.
cards.back: B. Apply organizational context to the risk rating.
cards.why: Applying organizational context to the CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) rating comes first, because the analyst must consider asset criticality, exposure, and compensating controls before deciding on escalation or patching.

whyNot.A: Escalating to senior management before assessing the risk in the organization's own context is premature and may be unnecessary.
whyNot.C: Urgent out-of-cycle patching may follow, but it should be decided after the risk is put in organizational context.
whyNot.D: Exploiting a production intranet server is risky and unnecessary, because the scan already reports certain confidence.

cards.front:
Company A agrees to provide perimeter protection, power, and environmental support with measurable goals for Company B, but will not be responsible for user authentication or patching of operating systems within the perimeter. Which of the following is being described?
A. Service level agreement
B. Memorandum of understanding
C. Business partner agreement
D. Interoperability agreement
cards.why: An SLA (Service Level Agreement) defines the services a provider delivers, such as perimeter protection and power, with measurable goals and clear limits on what the provider is not responsible for.

whyNot.B: An MOU (Memorandum of Understanding) is a general statement of intent and does not usually define measurable service goals.
whyNot.C: A BPA (Business Partner Agreement) covers the broader relationship between partners, such as profit sharing and responsibilities, not measurable service levels.
whyNot.D: An interoperability agreement addresses technical compatibility between systems, not measurable service delivery or responsibilities.

cards.front:
A company is deploying smartphones for its mobile salesforce. These devices are for personal and business use but are owned by the company. Sales personnel will save new customer data via a custom application developed for the company. This application will integrate with the contact information stored in the smartphones and will populate new customer records onto it. The customer application's data is encrypted at rest, and the application's connection to the back office system is considered secure. The Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) has concerns that customer contact information may be accidentally leaked due to the limited security capabilities of the devices and the planned controls. Which of the following will be the MOST efficient security control to implement to lower this risk?
A. Implement a mobile data loss agent on the devices to prevent any user manipulation with the contact information.
B. Restrict screen capture features on the devices when using the custom application and the contact information.
C. Restrict contact information storage data flow so it is only shared with the customer application.
D. Require complex passwords for authentication when accessing the contact information.
cards.back: C. Restrict contact information storage data flow so it is only shared with the customer application.
cards.why: Restricting the storage data flow so contact information is shared only with the custom application is a simple, efficient control that prevents accidental leakage to other apps on the device, using built-in data separation.

whyNot.A: A mobile data loss agent that blocks all user manipulation of contacts is heavy-handed and would break normal personal use of the company-owned phone.
whyNot.B: Blocking screen capture covers only one leak path and does not stop contact data from being shared with other applications.
whyNot.D: Complex passwords protect against unauthorized access, but do not stop accidental leakage of contact information by an authorized user.

cards.front:
The Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) is asking for ways to protect against zero-day exploits. The CISO is concerned that an unrecognized threat could compromise corporate data and result in regulatory fines as well as poor corporate publicity. The network is mostly flat, with split staff/guest wireless functionality. Which of the following equipment MUST be deployed to guard against unknown threats?
A. Cloud-based antivirus solution, running as local admin, with push technology for definition updates
B. Implementation of an off-site datacenter hosting all company data, as well as deployment of VDI for all client computing needs
C. Host-based heuristic IPS, segregated on a management VLAN, with direct control of the perimeter firewall ACLs
D. Behavior-based IPS with a communication link to a cloud-based vulnerability and threat feed
cards.back: D. Behavior-based IPS with a communication link to a cloud-based vulnerability and threat feed
cards.why: A behavior-based IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) detects unknown threats by watching for abnormal activity instead of known signatures, and a cloud threat feed adds fresh intelligence on emerging zero-day attacks.

whyNot.A: Antivirus running as local administrator relies mostly on known definitions and gives attackers elevated privileges if it is compromised.
whyNot.B: Moving data off-site and using VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure) changes where data lives but does not detect or block unknown threats.
whyNot.C: A host-based heuristic IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) with direct control of perimeter ACLs (Access Control Lists) gives one host excessive authority and does not cover the flat network.

cards.front:
An organization has several production-critical SCADA supervisory systems that cannot follow the normal 30- day patching policy. Which of the following BEST maximizes the protection of these systems from malicious software?
A. Configure a firewall with deep packet inspection that restricts traffic to the systems.
B. Configure a separate zone for the systems and restrict access to known ports.
C. Configure the systems to ensure only necessary applications are able to run.
D. Configure the host firewall to ensure only the necessary applications have listening ports.
cards.back: A. Configure a firewall with deep packet inspection that restricts traffic to the systems.
cards.why: A firewall with DPI (Deep Packet Inspection) in front of the SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) systems inspects and filters traffic content, shielding unpatched systems from malicious software without changing the fragile hosts.

whyNot.B: Zoning and restricting known ports controls where traffic goes but does not inspect content, so malware over allowed ports still gets through.
whyNot.C: Application whitelisting is an alternative, but it is a host-level change on production-critical SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) systems that cannot be easily modified.
whyNot.D: A host firewall limiting listening ports reduces exposure but does not inspect traffic for malicious content and requires changes on the sensitive hosts.

cards.keyDoubt: C: Application whitelisting allows only approved programs to run, which directly blocks malicious software on unpatched SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) hosts regardless of the exploited vulnerability.

cards.front:
An organization identifies a number of hosts making outbound connections to a known malicious IP over port TCP 80. The organization wants to identify the data being transmitted and prevent future connections to this IP. Which of the following should the organization do to achieve this outcome?
A. Use a protocol analyzer to reconstruct the data and implement a web-proxy.
B. Deploy a web-proxy and then blacklist the IP on the firewall.
C. Deploy a web-proxy and implement IPS at the network edge.
D. Use a protocol analyzer to reconstruct the data and blacklist the IP on the firewall.
cards.back: D. Use a protocol analyzer to reconstruct the data and blacklist the IP on the firewall.
cards.why: A protocol analyzer can capture and reconstruct the data sent over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 80 to identify what was exfiltrated, and blacklisting the malicious IP (Internet Protocol) address on the firewall blocks future connections.

whyNot.A: A web proxy does not by itself block the known malicious IP (Internet Protocol) address, and the data is already identifiable with an analyzer.
whyNot.B: A web proxy and firewall blacklist would block future connections, but nothing here reconstructs the already transmitted data.
whyNot.C: A web proxy and an IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) at the edge are broader than needed and do not reconstruct the data already sent.

cards.front:
Legal authorities notify a company that its network has been compromised for the second time in two years. The investigation shows the attackers were able to use the same vulnerability on different systems in both attacks. Which of the following would have allowed the security team to use historical information to protect against the second attack?
A. Key risk indicators
B. Lessons learned
C. Recovery point objectives
D. Tabletop exercise
cards.why: A lessons learned review after the first incident documents the exploited vulnerability and the response, giving the security team historical information to fix the weakness before the same attack succeeds again.

whyNot.A: KRIs (Key Risk Indicators) measure ongoing risk levels, but do not capture the specifics of a past incident or its remediation.
whyNot.C: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines the acceptable amount of data loss measured in time, and does not prevent repeat attacks.
whyNot.D: A tabletop exercise simulates incidents to test the response plan, but does not analyze a real past breach to prevent its recurrence.

cards.front:
A small company's Chief Executive Officer (CEO) has asked its Chief Security Officer (CSO) to improve the company's security posture quickly with regard to targeted attacks. Which of the following should the CSO conduct FIRST?
A. Survey threat feeds from services inside the same industry.
B. Purchase multiple threat feeds to ensure diversity and implement blocks for malicious traffic.
C. Conduct an internal audit against industry best practices to perform a qualitative analysis.
D. Deploy a UTM solution that receives frequent updates from a trusted industry vendor.
cards.back: A. Survey threat feeds from services inside the same industry.
cards.why: Surveying threat feeds from services in the same industry first identifies the targeted attacks that peers face, so the CSO (Chief Security Officer) can choose cost-effective, relevant protections quickly.

whyNot.B: Buying multiple feeds and blocking traffic before learning which threats are relevant wastes money and risks blocking legitimate traffic.
whyNot.C: An internal audit with qualitative analysis is slow and does not quickly address targeted attacks, which the CEO (Chief Executive Officer) wants.
whyNot.D: Deploying a UTM (Unified Threat Management) appliance is a purchase made before understanding which targeted threats the company faces.

cards.front:
During a routine vulnerability assessment, the following command was successful: echo "vrfy 'perl -e 'print "hi" x 500 ' ' " | nc www.company.com 25 Which of the following vulnerabilities is being exploited?
A. Buffer overflow directed at a specific host MTA
B. SQL injection directed at a web server
C. Cross-site scripting directed at www.company.com
D. Race condition in a UNIX shell script
cards.back: A. Buffer overflow directed at a specific host MTA
cards.why: The command sends an extremely long string (500 repeated characters) to the SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) VRFY (Verify) command on port 25, a classic buffer overflow attempt against the host's MTA (Mail Transfer Agent).

whyNot.B: SQL (Structured Query Language) injection targets database queries through a web application, and port 25 is a mail service, not a web server.
whyNot.C: Cross-site scripting injects script into web pages viewed by users, which does not apply to a raw mail protocol session.
whyNot.D: A race condition exploits timing between operations in a script, but this command only sends oversized input to a service.

cards.front:
A forensic investigator has run into difficulty recovering usable files from a SAN drive. Which of the following SAN features might have caused the problem?
A. Storage multipaths
B. Deduplication
C. iSCSI initiator encryption
D. Data snapshots
cards.why: Deduplication on a SAN (Storage Area Network) stores identical blocks once and replaces copies with pointers, so file fragments are scattered and carving usable files during forensic recovery becomes difficult.

whyNot.A: Storage multipaths provide redundant SAN (Storage Area Network) connections for availability and do not alter how file data is laid out on disk.
whyNot.C: iSCSI (Internet Small Computer System Interface) initiator encryption protects data in transit, and the investigator can still read data once the authorized session is established.
whyNot.D: Data snapshots on a SAN (Storage Area Network) preserve point-in-time copies, which usually help forensic recovery rather than hinder it.

cards.front:
A company offers SaaS, maintaining all customers' credentials and authenticating locally. Many large customers have requested the company offer some form of federation with their existing authentication infrastructures. Which of the following would allow customers to manage authentication and authorizations from within their existing organizations?
A. Implement SAML so the company's services may accept assertions from the customers' authentication servers.
B. Provide customers with a constrained interface to manage only their users' accounts in the company's active directory server.
C. Provide a system for customers to replicate their users' passwords from their authentication service to the company's.
D. Use SOAP calls to support authentication between the company's product and the customers' authentication servers.
cards.back: A. Implement SAML so the company's services may accept assertions from the customers' authentication servers.
cards.why: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) enables federation, letting the SaaS (Software as a Service) provider trust assertions from each customer's own identity provider so customers manage authentication and authorization themselves.

whyNot.B: Letting customers manage accounts in the company's Active Directory server keeps authentication with the company and does not federate with the customers' existing infrastructure.
whyNot.C: Replicating passwords to the company's system copies credentials outside the customer's control, which defeats federation and increases exposure.
whyNot.D: SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) is only a messaging format and does not by itself provide a federated trust model for authentication assertions.

cards.front:
A software development manager is taking over an existing software development project. The team currently suffers from poor communication due to a long delay between requirements documentation and feature delivery. This gap is resulting in an above average number of security-related bugs making it into production. Which of the following development methodologies is the team MOST likely using now?
A. Agile
B. Waterfall
C. Scrum
D. Spiral
cards.why: The Waterfall methodology completes requirements documentation before development and delivery, creating long gaps between requirements and delivered features, which lets security-related bugs slip through to production.

whyNot.A: Agile uses short iterations with frequent feedback, which would shorten the gap between requirements and delivery rather than lengthen it.
whyNot.C: Scrum is an Agile framework with short sprints and regular reviews, so it would not produce long delays between requirements and delivery.
whyNot.D: The Spiral model repeats planning, risk analysis, and prototyping in cycles, so it does not produce one long requirements-to-delivery gap.

cards.front:
Following the successful response to a data-leakage incident, the incident team lead facilitates an exercise that focuses on continuous improvement of the organization's incident response capabilities. Which of the following activities has the incident team lead executed?
A. Lessons learned review
B. Root cause analysis
C. Incident audit
D. Corrective action exercise
cards.why: A lessons learned review, held after an incident is resolved, examines what worked and what did not so the organization can continuously improve its incident response capabilities.

whyNot.B: Root cause analysis identifies why a specific incident occurred, rather than reviewing overall response performance for continuous improvement.
whyNot.C: An incident audit checks compliance with policy or controls, and is not a facilitated improvement exercise after the response.
whyNot.D: Corrective action exercise is not a standard post-incident phase; corrective actions are outputs of the lessons learned review.

cards.front:
A security analyst is attempting to break into a client's secure network. The analyst was not given prior information about the client, except for a block of public IP addresses that are currently in use. After network enumeration, the analyst's NEXT step is to perform:
A. a gray-box penetration test.
B. a risk analysis.
C. a vulnerability assessment.
D. an external security audit.
E. a red team exercise.
cards.why: The key selects gray-box, but the analyst began with only public IP (Internet Protocol) addresses, which is closer to black-box testing; after enumeration the natural next step is finding weaknesses, so this key looks questionable.

whyNot.B: A risk analysis evaluates likelihood and impact of threats and is not the hands-on step that follows network enumeration during a penetration test.
whyNot.C: A vulnerability assessment is what normally follows enumeration, although the supplied key does not select it.
whyNot.D: An external security audit reviews compliance against standards and is not the next technical step after enumeration.
whyNot.E: A red team exercise is a broad adversary simulation, not the specific step that follows enumeration.

cards.keyDoubt: C. A vulnerability assessment is the normal next step after enumeration, and the analyst had no prior information, so this was a black-box test, not gray-box.

cards.front:
A security architect has convened a meeting to discuss an organization's key management policy. The organization has a reliable internal key management system, and some argue that it would be best to manage the cryptographic keys internally as opposed to using a solution from a third party. The company should use:
A. the current internal key management system.
B. a third-party key management system that will reduce operating costs.
C. risk benefits analysis results to make a determination.
D. a software solution including secure key escrow capabilities.
cards.back: C. risk benefits analysis results to make a determination.
cards.why: A risk benefit analysis compares cost, security, and operational risk of internal versus third-party key management, so the decision rests on evidence rather than assumption.

whyNot.A: Keeping the current internal key management system without analysis assumes it is best and ignores possible gaps in cost, resilience, or compliance.
whyNot.B: Choosing a third-party key management system for lower operating costs considers only cost and ignores security and risk tradeoffs.
whyNot.D: Selecting a software solution with key escrow presumes a solution before analysis, and escrow adds its own risks that must be weighed.

cards.front:
After a recent internal breach, a company decided to regenerate and reissue all certificates used in the transmission of confidential information. The company places the greatest importance on confidentiality and non-repudiation, and decided to generate dual key pairs for each client. Which of the following BEST describes how the company will use these certificates?
A. One key pair will be used for encryption and decryption. The other will be used to digitally sign the data.
B. One key pair will be used for encryption. The other key pair will provide extended validation.
C. Data will be encrypted once by each key, doubling the confidentiality and non-repudiation strength.
D. One key pair will be used for internal communication, and the other will be used for external communication.
cards.back: A. One key pair will be used for encryption and decryption. The other will be used to digitally sign the data.
cards.why: Dual key pairs separate duties: one pair encrypts and decrypts for confidentiality, while the other digitally signs data so the sender cannot deny sending it, which provides non-repudiation.

whyNot.B: Extended validation is a certificate vetting level for identity assurance and is not a function a second key pair provides.
whyNot.C: Encrypting data twice does not double non-repudiation, because non-repudiation comes from digital signatures made with a private key only the signer holds.
whyNot.D: Splitting key pairs between internal and external communication does not deliver the required confidentiality and non-repudiation separation.

cards.front:
A security manager is creating an account management policy for a global organization with sales personnel who must access corporate network resources while traveling all over the world. Which of the following practices is the security manager MOST likely to enforce with the policy? (Select TWO)
A. Time-of-day restrictions
B. Password complexity
C. Location-based authentication
D. Group-based access control
E. Standard naming convention
cards.back:
B. Password complexity
D. Group-based access control
cards.why: Password complexity protects accounts exposed to travel and untrusted networks, and group-based access control gives a global sales workforce consistent permissions to corporate resources without managing each account individually.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions would block or complicate access for personnel working across many time zones while traveling worldwide.
whyNot.C: Location-based authentication would conflict with salespeople who must connect from constantly changing locations around the world.
whyNot.E: A standard naming convention helps account administration but is not a security practice that protects travelers' remote access.

cards.front:
A network administrator at a small office wants to simplify the configuration of mobile clients connecting to an encrypted wireless network. Which of the following should be implemented if the administrator does not want to provide the wireless password or certificate to the employees?
A. WPS
B. 802.1x
C. WPA2-PSK
D. TKIP
cards.why: WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) lets clients join an encrypted network using a push button or PIN (Personal Identification Number), so users never need the wireless password or a certificate.

whyNot.B: 802.1X (port-based network access control) authentication normally requires each user to have credentials or a certificate, which the administrator wants to avoid distributing.
whyNot.C: WPA2-PSK (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 Pre-Shared Key) requires every employee to be given the shared wireless password.
whyNot.D: TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol) is a legacy encryption protocol and does not simplify client onboarding or avoid distributing credentials.

cards.front:
A security administrator learns that PII, which was gathered by the organization, has been found in an open forum. As a result, several C-level executives found their identities were compromised, and they were victims of a recent whaling attack. Which of the following would prevent these problems in the future? (Select TWO).
A. Implement a reverse proxy.
B. Implement an email DLP.
C. Implement a spam filter.
D. Implement a host-based firewall.
E. Implement a HIDS.
cards.back:
B. Implement an email DLP.
C. Implement a spam filter.
cards.why: Email DLP (Data Loss Prevention) stops PII (Personally Identifiable Information) leaving by email, and a spam filter reduces whaling and phishing messages aimed at C-level executives, addressing both the leak and the attack.

whyNot.A: A reverse proxy protects and load-balances inbound traffic to servers and does not stop PII (Personally Identifiable Information) leaks or whaling emails.
whyNot.D: A host-based firewall filters network traffic by port and application and does not inspect email content for leaked data or phishing lures.
whyNot.E: A HIDS (Host-based Intrusion Detection System) detects suspicious host activity but does not prevent whaling emails or block PII (Personally Identifiable Information) from leaving.

cards.front:
A security engineer is configuring a wireless network with EAP-TLS. Which of the following activities is a requirement for this configuration?
A. Setting up a server
B. Configuring federation between authentication servers
C. Enabling TOTP
D. Deploying certificates to endpoint devices
cards.back: D. Deploying certificates to endpoint devices
cards.why: EAP-TLS (Extensible Authentication Protocol with Transport Layer Security) uses mutual certificate authentication, so a client certificate must be deployed to every endpoint device in addition to the server certificate.

whyNot.A: Setting up a server is too generic; the specific EAP-TLS (Extensible Authentication Protocol with Transport Layer Security) requirement is certificates on endpoint devices.
whyNot.B: Federation between authentication servers is not required for EAP-TLS (Extensible Authentication Protocol with Transport Layer Security), which works with a single authentication server.
whyNot.C: TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) is a different authentication factor and is not part of EAP-TLS (Extensible Authentication Protocol with Transport Layer Security).

cards.front:
Ann is the IS manager for several new systems in which the classification of the systems' data are being decided. She is trying to determine the sensitivity level of the data being processed. Which of the following people should she consult to determine the data classification?
A. Steward
B. Custodian
C. User
D. Owner
cards.why: The data owner is accountable for the data and decides its classification and sensitivity level, so the manager should consult the owner.

whyNot.A: A data steward manages data quality and governance day to day but does not decide the classification level.
whyNot.B: A data custodian implements and maintains the controls that protect the data, following the classification the owner sets.
whyNot.C: A user only accesses data under assigned permissions and has no authority to determine its classification.

cards.front:
Which of the following BEST describes a network-based attack that can allow an attacker to take full control of a vulnerable host?
A. Remote exploit
B. Amplification
C. Sniffing
D. Man-in-the-middle
cards.why: A remote exploit abuses a vulnerability in a network-reachable service, which can give the attacker code execution and full control of the vulnerable host.

whyNot.B: An amplification attack uses reflected traffic to overwhelm a target, causing denial of service rather than host takeover.
whyNot.C: Sniffing passively captures network traffic and does not by itself give an attacker control of a host.
whyNot.D: A man-in-the-middle attack intercepts or alters communications between parties and does not directly take control of a vulnerable host.

cards.front:
A systems administrator wants to generate a self-signed certificate for an internal website. Which of the following steps should the systems administrator complete prior to installing the certificate on the server?
A. Provide the private key to a public CA.
B. Provide the public key to the internal CA.
C. Provide the public key to a public CA.
D. Provide the private key to the internal CA.
E. Provide the public/private key pair to the internal CA.
F. Provide the public/private key pair to a public CA.
cards.back: D. Provide the private key to the internal CA.
cards.why: The key says to give the private key to the internal CA (Certificate Authority), but a private key should never be shared and a self-signed certificate needs no CA, so this key looks wrong.

whyNot.A: Giving a private key to a public CA (Certificate Authority) exposes it and is unnecessary for an internal website.
whyNot.B: Providing the public key to the internal CA (Certificate Authority) is the safe, standard way to get a certificate issued for an internal website.
whyNot.C: A public CA (Certificate Authority) is not needed for an internal website, and a self-signed certificate does not involve one.
whyNot.E: Handing the full key pair to the internal CA (Certificate Authority) exposes the private key, which must stay secret.
whyNot.F: Handing the full key pair to a public CA (Certificate Authority) exposes the private key and is unnecessary for an internal site.

cards.keyDoubt: B. Only the public key is ever submitted to a CA (Certificate Authority); the private key must never be shared.

cards.front:
A security analyst has received the following alert snippet from the HIDS appliance: PROTOCOL SIG SRC.PORT DST.PORT TCP XMAS SCAN 192.168.1.1:1091 192.168.1.2:8891 TCP XMAS SCAN 192.168.1.1:649 192.168.1.2:9001 TCP XMAS SCAN 192.168.1.1:2264 192.168.1.2:6455 TCP XMAS SCAN 192.168.1.1:3464 192.168.1.2:8744 Given the above logs, which of the following is the cause of the attack?
A. The TCP ports on destination are all open.
B. FIN, URG, and PSH flags are set in the packet header.
C. TCP MSS is configured improperly.
D. There is improper Layer 2 segmentation.
cards.back: B. FIN, URG, and PSH flags are set in the packet header.
cards.why: A TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) XMAS scan sets the FIN (Finish), URG (Urgent), and PSH (Push) flags together, which the HIDS (Host-based Intrusion Detection System) signature detects.

whyNot.A: The scan flags do not show that the destination TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) ports are open; XMAS scans are used to probe port state.
whyNot.C: MSS (Maximum Segment Size) misconfiguration affects packet size and would not trigger an XMAS scan signature based on flag combinations.
whyNot.D: Improper Layer 2 segmentation concerns Open Systems Interconnection model Layer 2 separation and does not cause the unusual TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) flag combination.

cards.front:
Which of the following controls allows a security guard to perform a post-incident review?
A. Detective
B. Preventive
C. Corrective
D. Deterrent
cards.why: A detective control identifies and records events so they can be reviewed. A security guard performing a post-incident review is detecting and analyzing what already happened.

whyNot.B: A preventive control stops an incident before it happens, and a review after the fact does not do that.
whyNot.C: A corrective control restores systems or limits damage after an incident, and reviewing the incident is not a fix.
whyNot.D: A deterrent control discourages attackers from acting, and a post-incident review does not discourage anyone.

cards.front:
Attackers have been using revoked certificates for MITM attacks to steal credentials from employees of Company.com. Which of the following options should Company.com implement to mitigate these attacks?
A. Captive portal
B. Extended validation certificate
C. OCSP stapling
D. Object identifiers
E. Key escrow
cards.why: OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) stapling has the server attach a signed, timestamped revocation status to the TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshake. Clients can then reject revoked certificates presented in MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attacks.

whyNot.A: A captive portal is a web login page for network access and does not check certificate revocation.
whyNot.B: An EV (Extended Validation) certificate proves stronger organizational identity but can still be revoked and then misused.
whyNot.D: OIDs (Object Identifiers) are numeric labels for certificate fields and algorithms, and they do not check revocation.
whyNot.E: Key escrow stores copies of private keys for recovery and does nothing to detect revoked certificates.

cards.front:
After attempting to harden a web server, a security analyst needs to determine if an application remains vulnerable to SQL injection attacks. Which of the following would BEST assist the analyst in making this determination?
A. tracert
B. Fuzzer
C. nslookup
D. Nmap
E. netcat
cards.why: A fuzzer sends malformed and unexpected input to an application, which reveals whether it is still vulnerable to SQL (Structured Query Language) injection after hardening.

whyNot.A: tracert (trace route) maps the network hops to a host and does not test application input handling.
whyNot.C: nslookup (name server lookup) queries DNS (Domain Name System) records and cannot test for SQL (Structured Query Language) injection.
whyNot.D: Nmap (Network Mapper) discovers hosts, ports, and services, but it does not test application input for SQL (Structured Query Language) injection.
whyNot.E: netcat (network cat) opens raw network connections, and it is not an automated tool for testing application input.

cards.front:
A company is allowing a BYOD policy for its staff. Which of the following is a best practice that can decrease the risk of users jailbreaking mobile devices?
A. Install a corporately monitored mobile antivirus on the devices.
B. Prevent the installation of applications from a third-party application store.
C. Build a custom ROM that can prevent jailbreaking.
D. Require applications to be digitally signed.
cards.back: B. Prevent the installation of applications from a third-party application store.
cards.why: Blocking installs from third-party app stores removes the main route for sideloading jailbreak tools and untrusted apps on BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) phones, so it reduces the risk of jailbreaking.

whyNot.A: Antivirus on a BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) phone detects malware, but it does not stop a user from jailbreaking the device.
whyNot.C: Building a custom ROM (Read-Only Memory firmware image) is impractical on personal devices and is not a standard BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) control.
whyNot.D: Requiring digitally signed apps is bypassed by a jailbreak, which disables signature enforcement.

cards.front:
Which of the following describes the key difference between vishing and phishing attacks?
A. Phishing is used by attackers to steal a person's identity.
B. Vishing attacks require some knowledge of the target of attack.
C. Vishing attacks are accomplished using telephony services.
D. Phishing is a category of social engineering attack.
cards.back: C. Vishing attacks are accomplished using telephony services.
cards.why: Vishing is voice phishing, so it is carried out over telephony services such as phone calls or VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol). Phishing typically uses email or messages.

whyNot.A: Both phishing and vishing can steal identities, so this does not distinguish them.
whyNot.B: Both attacks may be targeted or generic, so required target knowledge is not the defining difference.
whyNot.D: Vishing is also a social engineering category, so this statement does not separate the two attacks.

cards.front:
Which of the following should a security analyst perform FIRST to determine the vulnerabilities of a legacy system?
A. Passive scan
B. Aggressive scan
C. Credentialed scan
D. Intrusive scan
cards.why: A passive scan observes traffic without sending probes, so it identifies vulnerabilities on a fragile legacy system with little risk of disrupting it. It is the safest first step.

whyNot.B: An aggressive scan sends many probes and could crash or slow a fragile legacy system.
whyNot.C: A credentialed scan needs valid logins and actively queries the system, so it is not the safest first step.
whyNot.D: An intrusive scan can alter or disrupt the target, which makes it risky for a legacy system.

cards.front:
Which of the following components of printers and MFDs are MOST likely to be used as vectors of compromise if they are improperly configured?
A. Embedded web server
B. Spooler
C. Network interface
D. LCD control panel
cards.why: The embedded web server provides a management interface that is often left with default credentials or unpatched. This makes it the most likely vector of compromise on printers and MFDs (Multifunction Devices).

whyNot.B: The spooler is the print queue software, and it is less commonly the main entry point than the management web interface.
whyNot.C: The network interface is the transport hardware, and compromise usually happens through the services running on it.
whyNot.D: The LCD (Liquid Crystal Display) control panel requires physical access, which makes it a less likely remote attack vector.

cards.front:
A hacker has a packet capture that contains: ....Joe Smith.........E289F21CD33E4F57890DDEA5CF267ED2.. ...Jane.Doe...........AD1FAB10D33E4F57890DDEA5CF267ED2.. ....John.Key..........3374E9E7E33E4F57890DDEA5CF267ED2.. Which of the following tools will the hacker use against this type of capture?
A. Password cracker
B. Vulnerability scanner
C. DLP scanner
D. Fuzzer
cards.why: The capture holds usernames next to password hashes. A password cracker recovers plaintext passwords from captured hashes through brute force, dictionary, or rainbow table attacks.

whyNot.B: A vulnerability scanner finds weaknesses in systems and does not recover passwords from captured hashes.
whyNot.C: A DLP (Data Loss Prevention) scanner detects sensitive data leaving an organization and does not attack captured hashes.
whyNot.D: A fuzzer sends malformed input to applications to find bugs and does not process captured hashes.

cards.front:
A user downloads and installs an MP3 converter, and runs the application. Upon running the application, the antivirus detects a new port in a listening state. Which of the following has the user MOST likely executed?
A. RAT
B. Worm
C. Ransomware
D. Bot
cards.why: A RAT (Remote Access Trojan) is often bundled with a free utility and opens a listening port so an attacker can connect and control the system. The new listening port points to this.

whyNot.B: A worm spreads itself across the network, and a new listening port from a user-run installer does not point to one.
whyNot.C: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, and it does not typically show up as a new listening port.
whyNot.D: A bot usually makes outbound connections to a C2 (Command and Control) server rather than listening for inbound ones.

cards.front: An attacker exploited a vulnerability on a mail server using the code below. " + "URL:" +"document.location) ; /> Which of the following BEST explains what the attacker is doing? A. The attacker is replacing a cookie. B. The attacker is stealing a document. C. The attacker is replacing a document. D. The attacker is deleting a cookie.
cards.back: C. The attacker is replacing a document.
cards.why: The script uses document.location.replace to replace the current HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) document with a page on the attacker's server. Among the choices, replacing a document best describes that action.

whyNot.A: The script reads the cookie and sends it along in the URL (Uniform Resource Locator), but it does not replace the cookie.
whyNot.B: The script redirects the browser and sends cookie data, but it does not steal the document itself.
whyNot.D: Nothing in the script deletes or expires a cookie, because it only reads document.cookie.

cards.front:
A security analyst is securing smartphones and laptops for a highly mobile workforce. Priorities include: Remote wipe capabilities Geolocation services Patch management and reporting Mandatory screen locks Ability to require passcodes and pins Ability to require encryption Which of the following would BEST meet these requirements?
A. Implementing MDM software
B. Deploying relevant group policies to the devices
C. Installing full device encryption
D. Removing administrative rights to the devices
cards.why: MDM (Mobile Device Management) software centrally enforces remote wipe, geolocation, patch reporting, screen locks, passcodes, and encryption on both smartphones and laptops.

whyNot.B: Group policies (Group Policy Objects) mainly manage domain-joined Windows systems and do not cover smartphones or remote wipe.
whyNot.C: Full device encryption covers only the encryption requirement and not wipe, geolocation, patching, or passcode policy.
whyNot.D: Removing administrative rights limits user actions but provides no remote wipe, geolocation, or patch reporting.

cards.front:
A technician receives a device with the following anomalies: Frequent pop-up ads Show response-time switching between active programs Unresponsive peripherals The technician reviews the following log file entries: File Name Source MD5 Target MD5 Status antivirus.exe F794F21CD33E4F57890DDEA5CF267ED2 F794F21CD33E4F57890DDEA5CF267ED2 Automatic iexplore.exe 7FAAF21CD33E4F57890DDEA5CF29CCEA AA87F21CD33E4F57890DDEAEE2197333 Automatic service.exe 77FF390CD33E4F57890DDEA5CF28881F 77FF390CD33E4F57890DDEA5CF28881F Manual USB.exe E289F21CD33E4F57890DDEA5CF28EDC0 E289F21CD33E4F57890DDEA5CF28EDC0 Stopped Based on the above output, which of the following should be reviewed?
A. The web application firewall
B. The file integrity check
C. The data execution prevention
D. The removable media control
cards.why: In the log, the MD5 (Message Digest 5) hashes for iexplore.exe differ between source and target, which shows the file was altered. A file integrity check should be reviewed.

whyNot.A: A WAF (Web Application Firewall) filters web application traffic, and the log shows a modified executable on the host.
whyNot.C: DEP (Data Execution Prevention) blocks code running from memory regions and does not explain the mismatched hashes.
whyNot.D: The USB (Universal Serial Bus) executable has matching hashes and a Stopped status, so removable media is not the issue.

cards.front:
A systems administrator is attempting to recover from a catastrophic failure in the datacenter. To recover the domain controller, the systems administrator needs to provide the domain administrator credentials. Which of the following account types is the systems administrator using?
A. Guest account
B. Service account
C. User account
D. Local Account
