cards.why: A domain administrator is a privileged user account in the directory, so the administrator is using a user account that has elevated rights.

whyNot.A: A guest account has minimal access and cannot hold domain administrator rights for recovery.
whyNot.B: A service account is used by applications and services and not by a person for recovery tasks.
whyNot.D: A local account exists on a single machine and is not the domain-wide administrator identity.

cards.front:
An organization plans to implement multifactor authentication techniques within the enterprise network architecture. Each authentication factor is expected to be a unique control. Which of the following BEST describes the proper employment of multifactor authentication?
A. Proximity card, fingerprint scanner, PIN
B. Fingerprint scanner, voice recognition, proximity card
C. Smart card, user PKI certificate, privileged user certificate
D. Voice recognition, smart card, proximity card
cards.back: A. Proximity card, fingerprint scanner, PIN
cards.why: A proximity card is something you have, a fingerprint scanner is something you are, and a PIN (Personal Identification Number) is something you know. Together these are three distinct authentication factors.

whyNot.B: Fingerprint and voice recognition are both biometric, something you are, so two of the three are the same factor.
whyNot.C: A smart card and PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) certificates are all possession-based, so they are the same factor.
whyNot.D: Smart card and proximity card are both something you have, so two of the three are the same factor.

cards.front:
Multiple organizations operating in the same vertical want to provide seamless wireless access for their employees as they visit the other organizations. Which of the following should be implemented if all the organizations use the native 802.1x client on their mobile devices?
A. Shibboleth
B. RADIUS federation
C. SAML
D. OAuth
E. OpenlD connect
cards.why: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) federation lets organizations trust each other's authentication servers, so visiting employees authenticate with the native 802.1X (IEEE port-based network access control) client.

whyNot.A: Shibboleth is a SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) based web single sign-on system and does not serve native 802.1X wireless clients.
whyNot.C: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) exchanges web authentication assertions and is not used by native 802.1X wireless clients.
whyNot.D: OAuth (Open Authorization) delegates API access and is not an authentication method for 802.1X wireless.
whyNot.E: OpenID Connect adds web identity on top of OAuth (Open Authorization) and does not work with native 802.1X clients.

cards.front:
Upon entering an incorrect password, the logon screen displays a message informing the user that the password does not match the username provided and is not the required length of 12 characters. Which of the following secure coding techniques should a security analyst address with the application developers to follow security best practices?
A. Input validation
B. Error handling
C. Obfuscation
D. Data exposure
cards.why: Error handling means failure messages must be generic and must not reveal why a logon failed. Disclosing the username mismatch and the 12-character password policy gives attackers details to refine guesses.

whyNot.A: Input validation checks data entering the application, but this problem is the content of the message the application returns to the user.
whyNot.C: Obfuscation hides the meaning of code or data, and it does not control what logon failure messages say.
whyNot.D: Data exposure means sensitive stored or transmitted data is left unprotected, while this flaw is a verbose error message.

cards.front:
A security administrator is developing controls for creating audit trails and tracking if a PHI data breach is to occur. The administrator has been given the following requirements: *All access must be correlated to a user account. *All user accounts must be assigned to a single individual. *User access to the PHI data must be recorded. *Anomalies in PHI data access must be reported. *Logs and records cannot be deleted or modified. Which of the following should the administrator implement to meet the above requirements? (Select THREE).
A. Eliminate shared accounts.
B. Create a standard naming convention for accounts.
C. Implement usage auditing and review.
D. Enable account lockout thresholds.
E. Copy logs in real time to a secured WORM drive.
F. Implement time-of-day restrictions.
G. Perform regular permission audits and reviews.
cards.back:
A. Eliminate shared accounts.
C. Implement usage auditing and review.
E. Copy logs in real time to a secured WORM drive.
cards.why: Eliminating shared accounts ties every access to one individual, usage auditing and review records PHI (Protected Health Information) access and reports anomalies, and a WORM (Write Once Read Many) drive prevents log deletion or modification.

whyNot.B: A naming convention keeps accounts consistent, but it does not make accounts single-owner, record access, or protect logs.
whyNot.D: Account lockout thresholds slow password guessing, but they do not create audit trails or protect PHI (Protected Health Information) logs.
whyNot.F: Time-of-day restrictions limit when users can log on, but they do not record access, report anomalies, or protect logs from changes.
whyNot.G: Permission audits and reviews verify privileges periodically, but they do not record each PHI (Protected Health Information) access or make logs tamper-proof.

cards.front:
An administrator is replacing a wireless router. The configuration of the old wireless router was not documented before it stopped functioning. The equipment connecting to the wireless network uses older legacy equipment that was manufactured prior to the release of the 802.11i standard. Which of the following configuration options should the administrator select for the new wireless router?
A. WPA+CCMP
B. WPA2+CCMP
C. WPA+TKIP
D. WPA2+TKIP
cards.why: WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) with TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol) was the interim security designed to run on legacy hardware made before the 802.11i standard, so only it works with these older devices.

whyNot.A: CCMP (Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol) needs newer hardware, which devices made before 802.11i generally do not support.
whyNot.B: WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) implements 802.11i and requires newer hardware, so pre-802.11i devices cannot use it.
whyNot.D: WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) is the 802.11i implementation, and devices made before that standard do not support it.

cards.front:
Which of the following threat actors is MOST likely to steal a company's proprietary information to gain a market edge and reduce time to market?
A. Competitor
B. Hacktivist
C. Insider
D. Organized crime
cards.why: A competitor is motivated to steal proprietary information such as designs or trade secrets to gain a market edge and shorten its own time to market.

whyNot.B: Hacktivists are driven by political or social causes and not by gaining a commercial advantage in the market.
whyNot.C: An insider usually acts from personal gain or grievance and is not typically trying to give a rival company a market edge.
whyNot.D: Organized crime seeks direct financial profit through fraud or extortion and does not usually aim to speed up its own product development.

cards.front:
Which of the following BEST describes an important security advantage yielded by implementing vendor diversity?
A. Sustainability
B. Homogeneity
C. Resiliency
D. Configurability
cards.why: Vendor diversity improves resiliency because a flaw or failure in one vendor's product is unlikely to affect products from other vendors, which avoids a single point of failure.

whyNot.A: Sustainability concerns long-term environmental or operational viability and is not the main security advantage of using multiple vendors.
whyNot.B: Homogeneity means using the same product everywhere, which is the opposite of vendor diversity and creates a single point of failure.
whyNot.D: Configurability describes how adjustable a product's settings are, and it is not a benefit that comes from using multiple vendors.

cards.front:
Which of the following specifically describes the exploitation of an interactive process to access otherwise restricted areas of the OS?
A. Pivoting
B. Process affinity
C. Buffer overflow
D. XSS
cards.why: A buffer overflow exploits a running process by writing past its memory buffer, which can let an attacker run code and reach restricted areas of the OS (operating system).

whyNot.A: Pivoting uses an already compromised host to reach other network systems, and it is not exploitation of a process to reach restricted OS (operating system) areas.
whyNot.B: Process affinity binds a process to specific CPU (central processing unit) cores for scheduling, and it is not an attack technique.
whyNot.D: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) injects scripts into web pages viewed by other users and does not give access to restricted OS (operating system) areas.

cards.front:
Which of the following differentiates a collision attack from a rainbow table attack?
A. A rainbow table attack performs a hash lookup.
B. A rainbow table attack uses the hash as a password.
C. In a collision attack, the hash and the input data are equivalent.
D. In a collision attack, the same input results in different hashes.
cards.back: A. A rainbow table attack performs a hash lookup.
cards.why: A rainbow table attack works by looking up a hash in precomputed tables to find the matching plaintext, while a collision attack finds two different inputs that produce the same hash.

whyNot.B: Using a hash directly as a password is a pass-the-hash attack, and a rainbow table attack looks the hash up to recover the original password.
whyNot.C: In a collision attack two different inputs yield the same hash, so the hash and the input data are not equivalent.
whyNot.D: A hash function is deterministic, so the same input always produces the same hash, and a collision attack involves different inputs.

cards.front:
A security analyst observes the following events in the logs of an employee workstation: 1/23 1:07:16 865 Access to C:\Users\user\temp\oasdfkh.hta has been restricted by your administrator by the default restriction policy level. 1/23 1:07:09 1034 The scan is completed. No detections were found. The security analyst reviews the file system and observes the following: C:\>dir C:\Users\user\temp 1/23 1:07:02 oasdfkh.hta 1/23 1:07:02 update.bat 1/23 1:07:02 msg.txt Given the information provided, which of the following MOST likely occurred on the workstation?
A. Application whitelisting controls blocked an exploit payload from executing.
B. Antivirus software found and quarantined three malware files.
C. Automatic updates were initiated but failed because they had not been approved.
D. The SIEM log aged was not tuned properly and reported a false positive.
cards.back: A. Application whitelisting controls blocked an exploit payload from executing.
cards.why: The log says the file was restricted by a policy level while the scan found nothing, which indicates application whitelisting blocked a suspicious script payload from executing.

whyNot.B: The scan completed with no detections, so antivirus software did not find or quarantine anything, and the files remain on disk.
whyNot.C: The log shows a restriction policy blocking a file from running, which is not a failed update waiting for approval.
whyNot.D: The messages come from the workstation's own policy enforcement and show a real block, not a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) false positive.

cards.front:
A security technician has been receiving alerts from several servers that indicate load balancers have had a significant increase in traffic. The technician initiates a system scan. The scan results illustrate that the disk space on several servers has reached capacity. The scan also indicates that incoming internet traffic to the servers has increased. Which of the following is the MOST likely cause of the decreased disk space?
A. Misconfigured devices
B. Logs and events anomalies
C. Authentication issues
D. Unauthorized software
cards.why: Rising inbound traffic together with full disks suggests unauthorized software, such as malware or a file-sharing or botnet service, was installed and is storing data and serving traffic.

whyNot.A: Misconfigured devices might change traffic patterns, but they would not explain the traffic increase combined with disks filling on several servers.
whyNot.B: Log and event anomalies are symptoms to investigate, and they do not identify an underlying cause of both the traffic surge and the disk exhaustion.
whyNot.C: Authentication issues involve failed or abnormal logons and do not consume disk space on several servers.

cards.front:
A security administrator is diagnosing a server where the CPU utilization is at 100% for 24 hours. The main culprit of CPU utilization is the antivirus program. Which of the following issue could occur if left unresolved? (Select TWO)
A. MITM attack
B. DoS attack
C. DLL injection
D. Buffer overflow
E. Resource exhaustion
cards.back:
B. DoS attack
E. Resource exhaustion
cards.why: A central processing unit held at 100 percent can make the server unresponsive, causing a DoS (Denial of Service), and it signals resource exhaustion because the antivirus program is starving other processes.

whyNot.A: A MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attack intercepts network traffic and is not caused by high central processing unit utilization.
whyNot.C: DLL (Dynamic Link Library) injection is an attack technique used to run code in a process, and it is not a result of high utilization.
whyNot.D: A buffer overflow is a coding flaw that exploits memory handling, and sustained central processing unit load does not cause it.

cards.front:
Which of the following is used to validate the integrity of data?
A. CBC
B. Blowfish
C. MD5
D. RSA
cards.why: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is a hashing algorithm that produces a digest which changes if the data changes, so comparing digests validates data integrity.

whyNot.A: CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) is a block cipher mode that provides confidentiality and does not validate data integrity by itself.
whyNot.B: Blowfish is a symmetric encryption cipher that protects confidentiality and does not produce a digest for checking integrity.
whyNot.D: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) is an asymmetric algorithm for encryption, key exchange, and signatures, and it is not a hash used to validate integrity.

cards.front:
A user typically works remotely over the holidays using a web-based VPN to access corporate resources. The user reports getting untrusted host errors and being unable to connect. Which of the following is MOST likely the case?
A. The certificate has expired
B. The browser does not support SSL
C. The user's account is locked out
D. The VPN software has reached the seat license maximum
cards.why: Web-based VPN (Virtual Private Network) portals rely on digital certificates, and a certificate that expired while the user was away would cause untrusted host errors on return.

whyNot.B: A browser without SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) support would fail every time, but the user has connected this way before.
whyNot.C: A locked account produces an authentication failure after the secure session is set up, not an untrusted host error.
whyNot.D: Reaching the seat license maximum would deny the connection with a license or capacity message, not a certificate trust error.

cards.front:
When it comes to cloud computing, if one of the requirements for a project is to have the most control over the systems in the cloud, which of the following is a service model that would be BEST suited for this goal?
A. Infrastructure
B. Platform
C. Software
D. Virtualization
cards.why: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) gives the customer control of operating systems, storage, and deployed applications, so it provides the most control among the service models.

whyNot.B: PaaS (Platform as a Service) has the provider manage the operating system and infrastructure, which gives the customer less control than IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service).
whyNot.C: SaaS (Software as a Service) delivers a finished application managed by the provider, which gives the customer the least control.
whyNot.D: Virtualization is an underlying technology and not a cloud service model.

cards.front:
A company was recently audited by a third party. The audit revealed the company's network devices were transferring files in the clear. Which of the following protocols should the company use to transfer files?
A. HTTPS
B. LDAPS
C. SCP
D. SNMPv3
cards.why: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) transfers files over SSH (Secure Shell), encrypting data in transit and replacing cleartext file transfer methods.

whyNot.A: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts web traffic, but it is not the standard protocol network devices use to transfer files.
whyNot.B: LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol Secure) secures directory queries and authentication and is not a file transfer protocol.
whyNot.D: SNMPv3 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 3) secures device monitoring and management and is not used to transfer files.

cards.front:
A security analyst is acquiring data from a potential network incident. Which of the following evidence is the analyst MOST likely to obtain to determine the incident?
A. Volatile memory capture
B. Traffic and logs
C. Screenshots
D. System image capture
cards.why: For a network incident, traffic captures and logs show what communicated, when, and how, so they are the most likely evidence to reveal the incident.

whyNot.A: A volatile memory capture is valuable for host investigations, but it shows one machine's state and not the network activity of the incident.
whyNot.C: Screenshots capture only what was displayed at one moment, and they are weak and easily altered evidence for a network incident.
whyNot.D: A system image capture preserves one host's disk, which is useful for host forensics but does not show network communications.

cards.front:
A cybersecurity analyst is looking into the payload of a random packet capture file that was selected for analysis. The analyst notices that an internal host had a socket established with another internal host over a non-standard port. Upon investigation, the origin host that initiated the socket shows this output: usera@host>history mkdir /local/usr/bin/somedirectory nc -1 192.168.5.1 -p 9856 ping -c 30 8.8.8.8 -a 600 rm /etc/dir2/somefile rm -rm /etc/dir2/ traceroute 8.8.8.8 pakill pid 9487 usera@host> Given the above output, which of the following commands would have established the questionable socket?
A. traceroute 8.8.8.8
B. ping -1 30 8.8.8.8 -a 600
C. nc -1 192.168.5.1 -p 9856
D. pskill pid 9487
cards.why: The nc (netcat) command with the listen option, shown as nc -1 192.168.5.1 -p 9856, opens a socket on the non-standard port 9856. That matches the unexplained internal connection between the two hosts.

whyNot.A: The traceroute command only maps network hops toward 8.8.8.8 and does not open a listening or connected socket on an internal host.
whyNot.B: The ping command sends echo requests and does not create a socket on a non-standard port between two internal hosts.
whyNot.D: The pskill command terminates a process and does not establish any network socket.

cards.front:
A security administrator has written a script that will automatically upload binary and text-based configuration files onto a remote server using a scheduled task. The configuration files contain sensitive information. Which of the following should the administrator use? (Select TWO)
A. TOPT
B. SCP
C. FTP over a non-standard pot
D. SRTP
E. Certificate-based authentication
F. SNMPv3
cards.why: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) transfers both binary and text files over an SSH (Secure Shell) encrypted channel. Certificate-based authentication lets a scheduled script authenticate without a stored interactive password.

whyNot.A: TOPT, meaning TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password), needs a changing code that an unattended scheduled script cannot supply.
whyNot.C: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) sends data and credentials in cleartext, and moving it to a non-standard port does not add encryption.
whyNot.D: SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) secures voice and video media streams and is not a file transfer method.
whyNot.F: SNMPv3 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 3) secures device monitoring and management traffic and is not used to upload configuration files.

cards.front:
A security analyst conducts a manual scan on a known hardened host that identifies many non-compliant items. Which of the following BEST describe why this has occurred? (Select TWO)
A. Privileged-user certificated were used to scan the host
B. Non-applicable plug ins were selected in the scan policy
C. The incorrect audit file was used
D. The output of the report contains false positives
E. The target host has been compromised
cards.back:
B. Non-applicable plug ins were selected in the scan policy
D. The output of the report contains false positives
cards.why: A hardened host should pass most checks, so many failures point to scan misconfiguration. Non-applicable plug-ins in the scan policy and false positives in the report both produce misleading non-compliant findings.

whyNot.A: Scanning with privileged-user credentials gives more accurate results and would not make a hardened host look non-compliant.
whyNot.C: An incorrect audit file could also cause mismatches, but the keyed answers describe the more direct scan policy and reporting problems.
whyNot.E: A compromised host is not the most likely explanation, because the known hardened baseline points to scan errors rather than an intrusion.

cards.front:
Which of the following solutions should an administrator use to reduce the risk from an unknown vulnerability in a third-party software application?
A. Sandboxing
B. Encryption
C. Code signing
D. Fuzzing
cards.why: Sandboxing isolates the application so that an exploited unknown vulnerability cannot reach the rest of the system. It limits the damage without needing a patch or knowledge of the flaw.

whyNot.B: Encryption protects data confidentiality and does not contain an application that is being exploited through an unknown flaw.
whyNot.C: Code signing verifies who published the software and that it was not altered, but it does not stop a flaw in legitimate signed code.
whyNot.D: Fuzzing is a testing technique that finds flaws before release, and an administrator generally cannot use it to protect a deployed third-party application.

cards.front:
A network administrator needs to allocate a new network for the R&D group. The network must not be accessible from the Internet regardless of the network firewall or other external misconfigurations. Which of the following settings should the network administrator implement to accomplish this?
A. Configure the OS default TTL to 1
B. Use NAT on the R&D network
C. Implement a router ACL
D. Enable protected ports on the switch
cards.back: A. Configure the OS default TTL to 1
cards.why: Setting the operating system default TTL (Time To Live) to 1 means packets expire after the first router hop. The network therefore cannot be routed to the Internet even if the firewall is misconfigured.

whyNot.B: NAT (Network Address Translation) hides internal addresses but still allows outbound and sometimes inbound connectivity if the firewall is misconfigured.
whyNot.C: A router ACL (Access Control List) is an external control that can itself be misconfigured, which the question rules out.
whyNot.D: Protected ports on a switch isolate hosts from each other at layer 2 and do not block Internet access.

cards.keyDoubt: D. Protected ports are a real switch isolation feature, though TTL of 1 is the keyed trick answer, so treat this key as questionable rather than clearly wrong.

cards.front:
To help prevent one job role from having sufficient access to create, modify, and approve payroll data, which of the following practices should be employed?
A. Least privilege
B. Job rotation
C. Background checks
D. Separation of duties
cards.why: Separation of duties divides a critical process among different people so no single role can create, modify, and approve payroll data alone. This reduces fraud and error.

whyNot.A: Least privilege limits each user to the access needed for their job, but it does not by itself split one process across multiple roles.
whyNot.B: Job rotation moves staff between roles periodically to expose fraud and does not stop one role from holding all three payroll permissions.
whyNot.C: Background checks screen people before hire and do not restrict what access a role has once employed.

cards.front:
When attackers use a compromised host as a platform for launching attacks deeper into a company's network, it is said that they are:
A. escalating privilege
B. becoming persistent
C. fingerprinting
D. pivoting
cards.why: Pivoting means using a compromised host as a foothold to attack other systems deeper in the network. The attacker routes traffic through the first victim to reach otherwise unreachable targets.

whyNot.A: Privilege escalation means gaining higher permissions on a system, not using one host to reach other hosts.
whyNot.B: Persistence means keeping access across reboots or logouts, not launching attacks onward from a compromised host.
whyNot.C: Fingerprinting identifies operating systems and services on a target and is a reconnaissance step, not a launch platform.

cards.front:
The help desk received a call after hours from an employee who was attempting to log into the payroll server remotely. When the help desk returned the call the next morning, the employee was able to log into the server remotely without incident. However, the incident occurred again the next evening. Which of the following BEST describes the cause of the issue?
A. The password expired on the account and needed to be reset
B. The employee does not have the rights needed to access the database remotely
C. Time-of-day restrictions prevented the account from logging in
D. The employee's account was locked out and needed to be unlocked
cards.back: C. Time-of-day restrictions prevented the account from logging in
cards.why: The failure happens only after hours and works in the morning, which matches a time-of-day restriction on the account. Such a restriction blocks logins outside permitted hours.

whyNot.A: An expired password would block the login at all times until reset, but the login worked the next morning without a reset.
whyNot.B: Missing rights would block access at every time of day, not only in the evening.
whyNot.D: A lockout would persist until an administrator or timer unlocked it, and the employee was not unlocked yet the login worked in the morning and failed again the next evening.

cards.front:
An analyst receives an alert from the SIEM showing an IP address that does not belong to the assigned network can be seen sending packets to the wrong gateway. Which of the following network devices is misconfigured and which of the following should be done to remediate the issue?
A. Firewall; implement an ACL on the interface
B. Router; place the correct subnet on the interface
C. Switch; modify the access port to trunk port
D. Proxy; add the correct transparent interface
cards.back: B. Router; place the correct subnet on the interface
cards.why: A host with an address outside the assigned network reaching the wrong gateway indicates the router interface has an incorrect subnet. Placing the correct subnet on the router interface fixes the addressing mismatch.

whyNot.A: A firewall ACL (Access Control List) filters traffic and does not correct a gateway and subnet addressing mismatch.
whyNot.C: Changing an access port to a trunk port carries multiple VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) and does not fix a wrong subnet on the gateway.
whyNot.D: A proxy handles application requests for clients and is not the device that defines the gateway and subnet for hosts.

cards.front:
A home invasion occurred recently in which an intruder compromised a home network and accessed a WiFI- enabled baby monitor while the baby's parents were sleeping. Which of the following BEST describes how the intruder accessed the monitor?
A. Outdated antivirus
B. WiFi signal strength
C. Social engineering
D. Default configuration
cards.why: Many consumer devices ship with default configurations such as factory usernames, passwords, and open settings. An intruder on the home network can use those defaults to access the baby monitor.

whyNot.A: Outdated antivirus is not typically installed on a baby monitor and would not explain access to the device itself.
whyNot.B: WiFi signal strength affects connection quality and does not give an intruder access to the monitor.
whyNot.C: Social engineering manipulates people, but the scenario describes access to a device while the parents were asleep.

cards.front:
A security engineer must install the same x.509 certificate on three different servers. The client application that connects to the server performs a check to ensure the certificate matches the host name. Which of the following should the security engineer use?
A. Wildcard certificate
B. Extended validation certificate
C. Certificate chaining
D. Certificate utilizing the SAN file
cards.back:
D. Certificate utilizing the SAN file

SAN = Subject Alternate Names
cards.why: A certificate using the SAN (Subject Alternative Name) field can list several host names, so one x.509 certificate on three servers passes the client host name check for each of them.

whyNot.A: A wildcard certificate covers one level of subdomains under a single domain and fails if the three servers use differently named hosts.
whyNot.B: An EV (Extended Validation) certificate proves stronger organization identity but does not by itself cover multiple host names.
whyNot.C: Certificate chaining links a certificate to its issuing authorities and does not make one certificate match several host names.

cards.front:
Which of the following refers to the term used to restore a system to its operational state?
A. MTBF
B. MTTR
C. RTO
D. RPO
cards.why: MTTR (Mean Time To Repair) measures the average time needed to restore a failed system to its operational state.

whyNot.A: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) measures how long a system typically runs before failing, not how long restoration takes.
whyNot.C: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the target maximum downtime, which is a goal and not the measured time to restore.
whyNot.D: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines how much data loss is acceptable, measured back from the failure point.

cards.front:
A Chief Information Officer (CIO) recently saw on the news that a significant security flaws exists with a specific version of a technology the company uses to support many critical application. The CIO wants to know if this reported vulnerability exists in the organization and, if so, to what extent the company could be harmed. Which of the following would BEST provide the needed information?
A. Penetration test
B. Vulnerability scan
C. Active reconnaissance
D. Patching assessment report
cards.why: A penetration test exploits the reported vulnerability to confirm it exists and to show how far an attacker could go. That answers the question of how much harm the company could suffer.

whyNot.B: A vulnerability scan detects whether the flaw is present but does not demonstrate the extent of potential harm through exploitation.
whyNot.C: Active reconnaissance gathers information about targets by probing them and does not measure the impact of a specific vulnerability.
whyNot.D: A patching assessment report shows patch status and does not demonstrate exploitability or business impact.

cards.front:
An organization is expanding its network team. Currently, it has local accounts on all network devices, but with growth, it wants to move to centrally managed authentication. Which of the following are the BEST solutions for the organization? (Sect TWO)
A. TACACS+
B. CHAP
C. LDAP
D. RADIUS
E. MSCHAPv2
cards.why: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) and RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) are centralized AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) protocols widely used to authenticate administrators on network devices.

whyNot.B: CHAP (Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol) is a challenge-response method and does not provide centralized management by itself.
whyNot.C: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a directory service and is not the usual centralized login protocol for network device administration.
whyNot.E: MSCHAPv2 (Microsoft Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol version 2) is an authentication method carried inside other protocols and is not itself a centralized management solution.

cards.front:
An active/passive configuration has an impact on:
A. confidentiality
B. integrity
C. availability
D. non-repudiation
cards.why: An active/passive configuration keeps a standby system ready to take over if the active one fails, which improves availability by reducing downtime.

whyNot.A: Confidentiality protects data from unauthorized disclosure, and a standby system does not change who can read data.
whyNot.B: Integrity protects data from unauthorized modification, and a passive standby does not change that.
whyNot.D: Non-repudiation prevents a person from denying an action, and failover configuration does not affect it.

cards.front:
Which of the following attack types BEST describes a client-side attack that is used to manipulate an HTML iframe with JavaScript code via a web browser?
A. Buffer overflow
B. MITM
C. XSS
D. SQLi
cards.why: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) injects attacker JavaScript that runs in the victim's web browser, including by manipulating an HTML (HyperText Markup Language) iframe. That makes it a client-side attack.

whyNot.A: A buffer overflow overwrites memory in a vulnerable program and is not a browser JavaScript and iframe manipulation attack.
whyNot.B: MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) intercepts traffic between two parties and does not inject script into a page.
whyNot.D: SQLi (SQL injection, where SQL means Structured Query Language) targets the server-side database, not the client browser.

cards.front:
Which of the following would provide additional security by adding another factor to a smart card?
A. Token
B. Proximity badge
C. Physical key
D. PIN
cards.why: A PIN (Personal Identification Number) is something you know. Adding it to a smart card, which is something you have, creates two-factor authentication (2FA) with a different factor type.

whyNot.A: A token is another something-you-have item, so it adds a second possession factor rather than a new factor type.
whyNot.B: A proximity badge is a something-you-have item, the same factor type as the smart card.
whyNot.C: A physical key is also a something-you-have item, so it does not add a new factor type.

cards.front:
A security analyst receives an alert from a WAF with the following payload: var data = "<test test test> ++ <../../../../../../etc/passwd>" Which of the following types of attacks is this?
A. Cross-site request forgery
B. Buffer overflow
C. SQL injection
D. JavaScript data insertion
E. Firewall evasion script
cards.why: The payload is script-style data containing a path string that a WAF (Web Application Firewall) flagged as injected data. Of the listed options, JavaScript data insertion fits best.

whyNot.A: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a request, and the payload shows no forged request.
whyNot.B: A buffer overflow needs oversized input to overrun memory, and this payload is not oversized or crafted to overflow.
whyNot.C: SQL (Structured Query Language) injection needs database syntax such as quotes or UNION statements, and none appears here.
whyNot.E: A firewall evasion script is not a standard attack category, and the payload targets the application rather than hiding from the firewall.

cards.front:
Which of the following uses precomputed hashes to guess passwords?
A. Iptables
B. NAT tables
C. Rainbow tables
D. ARP tables
cards.why: Rainbow tables are precomputed tables of password hashes that let an attacker look up a hash and find the matching password quickly, instead of hashing each guess.

whyNot.A: Iptables is the Linux firewall rule tool and has nothing to do with guessing passwords.
whyNot.B: NAT (Network Address Translation) tables map private addresses to public addresses and do not store password hashes.
whyNot.D: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) tables map IP (Internet Protocol) addresses to MAC (Media Access Control) addresses, not hashes to passwords.

cards.front:
A systems administrator wants to provide balance between the security of a wireless network and usability. The administrator is concerned with wireless encryption compatibility of older devices used by some employees. Which of the following would provide strong security backward compatibility when accessing the wireless network?
A. Open wireless network and SSL VPN
B. WPA using a preshared key
C. WAP2 using a RADIUS back-end for 802.1x authentication
D. WEP with a 40-bit key
cards.back: A. Open wireless network and SSL VPN
cards.why: An open network accepts any device, including older ones with no modern encryption support. An SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) VPN (Virtual Private Network) then encrypts the traffic itself, which gives strong security with full compatibility.

whyNot.B: WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) with a PSK (preshared key) is weaker, and one shared key is exposed to every user.
whyNot.C: WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) with RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) and 802.1x is strong, but many older devices cannot support it.
whyNot.D: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) with a 40-bit key is easily broken and gives almost no real protection.

cards.front:
In determining when it may be necessary to perform a credentialed scan against a system instead of a non- credentialed scan, which of the following requirements is MOST likely to influence its decisions?
A. The scanner must be able to enumerate the host OS of devices scanner
B. The scanner must be able to footprint the network
C. The scanner must be able to check for open ports with listening services
D. The scanner must be able to audit file system permissions
cards.back: D. The scanner must be able to audit file system permissions
cards.why: A credentialed scan logs in to the host, so it can audit file system permissions, configuration settings, and patch levels. A non-credentialed scan cannot see those internal details.

whyNot.A: A non-credentialed scan can often identify the host OS (operating system) by fingerprinting network responses.
whyNot.B: Footprinting a network is done from outside and does not require logging in to hosts.
whyNot.C: Checking for open ports with listening services is a standard non-credentialed port scan task.

cards.front:
A security administrator receives an alert from a third-party vendor that indicates a certificate that was installed in the browser has been hijacked at the root of a small public CA. The security administrator knows there are at least four different browsers in use on more than a thousand computers in the domain worldwide. Which of the following solutions would be BEST for the security administrator to implement to most efficiently assist with this issue?
A. SSL
B. CRL
C. PKI
D. ACL
cards.why: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) published by the CA (Certificate Authority) lists revoked certificates. Browsers check it, so the compromised certificate can be blocked across all browsers and computers at once.

whyNot.A: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) is an encryption protocol and cannot revoke a compromised certificate.
whyNot.C: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is the overall certificate framework, not the specific mechanism for revoking one certificate.
whyNot.D: An ACL (Access Control List) filters traffic or permissions and cannot revoke a certificate in browsers.

cards.front:
After a user reports slow computer performance, a systems administrator detects a suspicious file, which was installed as part of a freeware software package. The systems administrator reviews the output below: c:\Windows\system32>netstat -nab Active Connections Pronto Local Address Foreign Address State TCP 0.0.0.0:135 0.0.0.0 RpcSs [svchoat.exe] TCP 0.0.0.0:445 0.0.0.0 [svchost.exe] TCP 192.168.1.10:5000 10.37.213.20 winserver.exe UDP 192.168.1.10:1900 *.* SSDPSVR Based on the above information, which of the following types of malware was installed on the user's computer?
A. RAT
B. Keylogger
C. Spyware
D. Worm
E. Bot
cards.why: A RAT (Remote Access Trojan) bundled with freeware opens a connection to a remote host. The unknown winserver.exe holding a connection to an external address on port 5000 fits remote control.

whyNot.B: A keylogger records keystrokes and the output does not show that, so it is not the best fit for this connection.
whyNot.C: Spyware gathers user information, but the persistent remote connection points to remote control rather than only data collection.
whyNot.D: A worm spreads itself across the network, and the output shows no self-propagation activity.
whyNot.E: A bot joins a botnet and takes commands from a command server, but the output points more directly to a remote access program.

cards.front:
A company has noticed multiple instances of proprietary information on public websites. It has also observed an increase in the number of email messages sent to random employees containing malicious links and PDFs. Which of the following changes should the company make to reduce the risks associated with phishing attacks? (Select TWO)
A. Install an additional firewall
B. Implement a redundant email server
C. Block access to personal email on corporate systems
D. Update the X.509 certificates on the corporate email server
E. Update corporate policy to prohibit access to social media websites
F. Review access violation on the file server
cards.back:
C. Block access to personal email on corporate systems
E. Update corporate policy to prohibit access to social media websites
cards.why: Blocking personal email on corporate systems and prohibiting social media access cut off the main channels for phishing messages and for leaking proprietary information to public sites.

whyNot.A: An additional firewall does not stop phishing messages that users receive and open through allowed email.
whyNot.B: A redundant email server improves availability, not protection against phishing.
whyNot.D: Updating X.509 digital certificates on the email server keeps encryption trusted but does not stop malicious links and PDFs (Portable Document Format files).
whyNot.F: Reviewing access violations on the file server does not address phishing email or information posted to public websites.

cards.front:
A security analyst is investigating a potential reach. Upon gathering, documenting, and securing the evidence, which of the following actions is the NEXT step to minimize the business impact?
A. Launch an investigation to identify the attacking host
B. Initiate the incident response plan
C. Review lessons learned captured in the process
D. Remove malware and restore the system to normal operation
cards.back: D. Remove malware and restore the system to normal operation
cards.why: After evidence is gathered, documented, and secured, the containment and eradication steps remove the malware and restore normal operation. That is the next step to reduce business impact.

whyNot.A: Identifying the attacking host is useful, but it delays restoring the business and is not the next step to limit impact.
whyNot.B: The incident response plan was already started, since the analyst has already collected and secured evidence.
whyNot.C: Lessons learned is the last phase and happens only after recovery is complete.

cards.front:
Joe, a salesman, was assigned to a new project that requires him to travel to a client site. While waiting for a flight, Joe, decides to connect to the airport wireless network without connecting to a VPN,and the sends confidential emails to fellow colleagues. A few days later, the company experiences a data breach. Upon investigation, the company learns Joe's emails were intercepted. Which of the following MOST likely caused the data breach?
A. Policy violation
B. Social engineering
C. Insider threat
D. Zero-day attack
cards.why: Joe broke the company's policy by using a public wireless network without a VPN (Virtual Private Network) to send confidential email. That policy violation exposed the emails to interception.

whyNot.B: Social engineering manipulates a person into giving up information, and nobody manipulated Joe here.
whyNot.C: An insider threat is deliberate or malicious misuse by an employee, and Joe acted carelessly rather than with malicious intent.
whyNot.D: A zero-day attack exploits an unknown software vulnerability, and no such flaw is involved in this case.

cards.front:
An information security specialist is reviewing the following output from a Linux server: user@server:~$ -l 5 * * * * /usr/local/bin.backup.sh user@server:~$ cat /usr/local/bin/backup.sh #!/bin/bash if ! grep --quiet joeuser /etc/passwd the rm -rf / fi Based on the above information, which of the following types of malware was installed on the server?
A. Logic bomb
B. Trojan
C. Backdoor
D. Ransomware
E. Rootkit
cards.why: The script runs on a schedule and deletes the file system if the user joeuser no longer exists in the password file. That is a logic bomb, which fires on a condition.

whyNot.B: A Trojan pretends to be legitimate software to trick users, but this script is a conditional trigger and not a disguise.
whyNot.C: A backdoor gives an attacker hidden access, and this script gives no access.
whyNot.D: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment, but this script deletes data and demands nothing.
whyNot.E: A rootkit hides its presence at a deep level, and this script does not hide itself.

cards.front:
A company wants to ensure confidential data from storage media is sanitized in such a way that the drive cannot be reused. Which of the following method should the technician use?
A. Shredding
B. Wiping
C. Low-level formatting
D. Repartitioning
E. Overwriting
cards.why: Shredding physically destroys the drive, so the data cannot be recovered and the drive cannot be reused. That meets the requirement of sanitizing the media so it is unusable.

whyNot.B: Wiping erases the data but leaves the drive intact and reusable.
whyNot.C: A low-level format erases the drive's data but leaves a working, reusable drive.
whyNot.D: Repartitioning changes the disk layout only and leaves data recoverable, and the drive remains reusable.
whyNot.E: Overwriting replaces the data with new data, but the drive stays usable, so it does not meet the no-reuse requirement.

cards.front:
A forensic expert is given a hard drive from a crime scene and is asked to perform an investigation. Which of the following is the FIRST step the forensic expert needs to take the chain of custody?
A. Make a forensic copy
B. Create a hash of the hard rive
C. Recover the hard drive data
D. Update the evidence log
cards.why: Chain of custody starts by documenting who received the evidence and when. Updating the evidence log first records the drive's handover before anything else is done to it.

whyNot.A: Making a forensic copy comes after the evidence has been logged and its custody recorded.
whyNot.B: Hashing the drive proves integrity, but the receipt of the drive should be documented first.
whyNot.C: Recovering data is analysis work that happens only after the evidence is logged and preserved.

cards.front:
An incident response manager has started to gather all the facts related to a SIEM alert showing multiple systems may have been compromised. The manager has gathered these facts: The breach is currently indicated on six user PCs One service account is potentially compromised Executive management has been notified In which of the following phases of the IRP is the manager currently working?
A. Recovery
B. Eradication
C. Containment
D. Identification
cards.why: The manager is determining the scope of the incident by confirming affected systems and accounts and notifying management. That work belongs to the identification phase of the IRP (Incident Response Plan).

whyNot.A: Recovery restores systems to normal operation, and the manager is still learning what was affected.
whyNot.B: Eradication removes the threat, and the manager has not yet started removing it.
whyNot.C: Containment isolates affected systems, and the facts gathered describe scope rather than isolation actions.

cards.front:
A stock trading company had the budget for enhancing its secondary datacenter approved. Since the main site is a hurricane-affected area and the disaster recovery site is 100 mi (161 km) away, the company wants to ensure its business is always operational with the least amount of man hours needed. Which of the following types of disaster recovery sites should the company implement?
A. Hot site
B. Warm site
C. Cold site
D. Cloud-based site
cards.why: A cloud-based disaster recovery site gives always-on, geographically separate capacity that is provisioned and scaled by the provider, so it needs the fewest staff hours to keep the business operational.

whyNot.A: A hot site is a fully duplicated facility, but the company must staff, maintain and pay for the hardware itself, which costs more man hours.
whyNot.B: A warm site needs hardware brought online and data restored, so it is not always operational and takes more staff effort.
whyNot.C: A cold site is only space and power with no equipment or data, so recovery is slow and labor intensive.

cards.front:
A systems administrator is attempting to recover from a catastrophic failure in the datacenter. To recover the domain controller, the systems administrator needs to provide the domain administrator credentials. Which of the following account types is the system administrator using?
A. Shared accounts
B. Guest account
C. Service account
D. User account
cards.why: The administrator signs in with a domain administrator credential, which is an individual user account that has been granted elevated privileges, not a shared, guest or service account.

whyNot.A: A shared account is used by several people at once, which does not describe one administrator supplying a named domain administrator credential.
whyNot.B: A guest account is a low-privilege, limited-access account and could not recover a domain controller.
whyNot.C: A service account runs applications or services non-interactively and is not what a person uses to recover a domain controller.

cards.front:
User from two organizations, each with its own PKI, need to begin working together on a joint project. Which of the following would allow the users of the separate PKIs to work together without connection errors?
A. Trust model
B. Stapling
C. Intermediate CA
D. Key escrow
cards.why: A trust model, such as cross-certification or a bridge between the two Public Key Infrastructures (PKIs), lets each side accept the other's certificates, so users can work together without certificate errors.

whyNot.B: Stapling attaches Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) revocation responses to a certificate and does not create trust between two separate PKIs.
whyNot.C: An intermediate Certificate Authority (CA) issues certificates within one hierarchy and does not make two independent PKIs trust each other.
whyNot.D: Key escrow stores copies of private keys for recovery and has nothing to do with cross-organization certificate trust.

cards.front:
A security analyst is migrating a pass-the-hash vulnerability on a Windows infrastructure. Given the requirement, which of the following should the security analyst do to MINIMIZE the risk?
A. Enable CHAP
B. Disable NTLM
C. Enable Kerebos
D. Disable PAP
cards.why: Pass-the-hash abuses captured New Technology LAN Manager (NTLM) password hashes, so disabling NTLM removes the hash-based authentication that the attack relies on.

whyNot.A: Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP) is a point-to-point link authentication protocol and does not stop Windows pass-the-hash attacks.
whyNot.C: Enabling Kerberos helps, but NTLM stays available as a fallback unless it is disabled, so the risk is not minimized by this step alone.
whyNot.D: Password Authentication Protocol (PAP) is a legacy link protocol unrelated to Windows NTLM hash reuse.

cards.front:
An organization requires users to provide their fingerprints to access an application. To improve security, the application developers intend to implement multifactor authentication. Which of the following should be implemented?
A. Use a camera for facial recognition
B. Have users sign their name naturally
C. Require a palm geometry scan
D. Implement iris recognition
cards.back: B. Have users sign their name naturally
cards.why: Fingerprints are an inherent factor, so a second factor must be a different type; a natural signature is a behavioral something-you-do factor, which adds a different category.

whyNot.A: Facial recognition is another inherent biometric, so it repeats the same factor type as the fingerprint.
whyNot.C: A palm geometry scan is also an inherent physical biometric, so it adds no new factor category.
whyNot.D: Iris recognition is another inherent physical biometric, so it repeats the same factor type.

cards.front:
A security analyst is reviewing an assessment report that includes software versions, running services, supported encryption algorithms, and permission settings. Which of the following produced the report?
A. Vulnerability scanner
B. Protocol analyzer
C. Network mapper
D. Web inspector
cards.why: A vulnerability scanner reports software versions, running services, supported encryption algorithms and permission settings, then compares them against known weaknesses.

whyNot.B: A protocol analyzer captures and decodes network traffic and does not inventory software versions and permission settings.
whyNot.C: A network mapper discovers hosts and open ports but does not normally report permission settings and encryption details in depth.
whyNot.D: A web inspector examines web page content and requests and does not produce a host-wide assessment report.

cards.front:
A Chief Information Officer (CIO) asks the company's security specialist if the company should spend any funds on malware protection for a specific server. Based on a risk assessment, the ARO value of a malware infection for a server is 5 and the annual cost for the malware protection is $2500. Which of the following SLE values warrants a recommendation against purchasing the malware protection?
A. $500
B. $1000
C. $2000
D. $2500
cards.why: Annualized Loss Expectancy (ALE) equals Single Loss Expectancy (SLE) times Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO). With an ARO of 5, a $500 SLE gives $2,500, which does not exceed the $2,500 protection cost, so spending is not justified.

whyNot.B: A $1,000 Single Loss Expectancy (SLE) times an Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO) of 5 is $5,000, which exceeds the $2,500 cost and supports buying protection.
whyNot.C: A $2,000 Single Loss Expectancy (SLE) times an Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO) of 5 is $10,000, far above the $2,500 cost, so protection is justified.
whyNot.D: A $2,500 Single Loss Expectancy (SLE) times an Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO) of 5 is $12,500, far above the $2,500 cost, so protection is justified.

cards.front:
The computer resource center issue smartphones to all first-level and above managers. The managers have the ability to install mobile tools. Which of the following tools should be implemented with the type of tools the managers installed?
A. Download manager
B. Content manager
C. Segmentation manager
D. Application manager
cards.why: An application manager, as part of mobile device management, controls which apps can be installed and run on company phones, which fits managers who install their own mobile tools.

whyNot.A: A download manager handles file transfers and does not control which applications are installed on company devices.
whyNot.B: A content manager controls documents and data on the device, not which applications users may install.
whyNot.C: A segmentation manager separates networks or data zones and does not govern installed applications.

cards.front:
A systems administrator wants to provide for and enforce wireless access accountability during events where external speakers are invited to make presentations to a mixed audience of employees and non-employees. Which of the following should the administrator implement?
A. Shared accounts
B. Preshared passwords
C. Least privilege
D. Sponsored guest
cards.why: A sponsored guest account ties each non-employee's wireless access to an employee sponsor, which provides individual accountability for visitors during events.

whyNot.A: Shared accounts are used by many people at once, which destroys individual accountability.
whyNot.B: A preshared password is the same for everyone, so activity cannot be traced to a specific person.
whyNot.C: Least privilege limits permissions but does not by itself identify or hold individual guests accountable.

cards.front:
A recent internal audit is forcing a company to review each internal business unit's VMs because the cluster they are installed on is in danger of running out of computer resources. Which of the following vulnerabilities exist?
A. Buffer overflow
B. End-of-life systems
C. System sprawl
D. Weak configuration
cards.why: System sprawl is the uncontrolled growth of virtual machines (VMs) that consume cluster resources, which is what the audit found as the cluster nears exhaustion.

whyNot.A: A buffer overflow is a memory-handling flaw in software and does not explain a cluster running out of compute resources.
whyNot.B: End-of-life systems no longer receive vendor support, which is not the same as running out of cluster resources.
whyNot.D: Weak configuration means insecure settings and does not describe too many virtual machines (VMs) exhausting capacity.

cards.front:
A security administrator has found a hash in the environment known to belong to malware. The administrator then finds this file to be in the preupdate area of the OS, which indicated it was pushed from the central patch system. File: winx86_adobe_upgrade.exe Hash: 99ac28bede43ab869b853ba62c4ea243 Administrator pulls a report from the patch management system with the following output: Install Date Package Name Target Device Hash 10/10/2017 java_11.2_x64.exe HQ PC's 01ab28bbde63aa879b35bba62cdea282 10/10/2017 winx86_adobe_flash_upgrade.exe HQ PC's 99ac28bede43ab86b853ba62c4ea243 Given the above output, which of the following MOST likely happened?
A. The file was corrupted after it left the patch system
B. The file was infected when the patch manager downloaded it
C. The file was not approved in the application whitelist system
D. The file was embedded with a logic bomb to evade detection
cards.back: B. The file was infected when the patch manager downloaded it
cards.why: The patch system's own report lists a package with the malicious hash, so the file was already infected when the patch manager downloaded it from the source.

whyNot.A: Corruption after leaving the patch system would give a different hash in the report than the one the patch system recorded, but the recorded hash already matches the malware.
whyNot.C: Application whitelist approval would not explain why the patch system itself holds a file with the known malware hash.
whyNot.D: A logic bomb is code that triggers on a condition; nothing in the output shows that, and the matching hash points to infection at download.

cards.front:
Two users must encrypt and transmit large amounts of data between them. Which of the following should they use to encrypt and transmit the data?
A. Symmetric algorithm
B. Hash function
C. Digital signature
D. Obfuscation
cards.why: A symmetric algorithm, such as Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), uses one shared key and is fast, which makes it the right choice for encrypting large amounts of data between two users.

whyNot.B: A hash function produces a fixed-length digest and cannot be reversed, so it cannot encrypt data for transmission.
whyNot.C: A digital signature proves origin and integrity but does not encrypt the data itself.
whyNot.D: Obfuscation hides meaning without real cryptographic protection and is not a sound way to encrypt data.

cards.front:
A new Chief Information Officer (CIO) has been reviewing the badging and decides to write a policy that all employees must have their badges rekeyed at least annually. Which of the following controls BEST describes this policy?
A. Physical
B. Corrective
C. Technical
D. Administrative
cards.why: A policy requiring badges to be rekeyed annually is an administrative control, because it is a rule or procedure set by management rather than a physical device or technical mechanism.

whyNot.A: A physical control is the lock, badge reader or barrier itself, while this item is the written policy that governs it.
whyNot.B: A corrective control fixes damage after an incident, but an annual rekeying policy is routine and not a response to an event.
whyNot.C: A technical control is enforced by technology such as software or hardware, whereas this is a management policy.

cards.front:
A software developer is concerned about DLL hijacking in an application being written. Which of the following is the MOST viable mitigation measure of this type of attack?
A. The DLL of each application should be set individually
B. All calls to different DLLs should be hard-coded in the application
C. Access to DLLs from the Windows registry should be disabled
D. The affected DLLs should be renamed to avoid future hijacking
cards.back: B. All calls to different DLLs should be hard-coded in the application
cards.why: Hard-coding the full path of each Dynamic Link Library (DLL) the application calls prevents Windows from searching attacker-controlled directories, which is how DLL hijacking works.

whyNot.A: Setting each application's Dynamic Link Library (DLL) individually does not stop the search-order lookup that attackers abuse.
whyNot.C: Disabling DLL access from the Windows registry would break normal application loading and does not address search-order hijacking.
whyNot.D: Renaming the affected Dynamic Link Libraries (DLLs) does not stop an attacker from planting a file under the new name in a searched location.

cards.front:
A security engineer wants to implement a site-to-site VPN that will require SSL certificates for mutual authentication. Which of the following should the engineer implement if the design requires client MAC addresses to be visible across the tunnel?
A. Tunnel mode IPSec
B. Transport mode VPN IPSec
C. L2TP
D. SSL VPN
cards.why: A Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) Virtual Private Network (VPN) can run in a bridged, layer 2 mode with certificate-based mutual authentication, which lets client Media Access Control (MAC) addresses be visible across the tunnel.

whyNot.A: Tunnel mode Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) encapsulates layer 3 packets, so client Media Access Control (MAC) addresses are not carried across the tunnel.
whyNot.B: Transport mode Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) protects only the payload of layer 3 packets and does not carry client Media Access Control (MAC) addresses.
whyNot.C: Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) alone provides no encryption or certificate-based mutual authentication, and it is normally paired with Internet Protocol Security (IPsec).

cards.front:
An application was recently compromised after some malformed data came in via web form. Which of the following would MOST likely have prevented this?
A. Input validation
B. Proxy server
C. Stress testing
D. Encoding
cards.why: Input validation (checking and sanitizing user-supplied data against expected format, type, and length) rejects malformed web form data before the application processes it, preventing the compromise.

whyNot.B: A proxy server (an intermediary that forwards requests) filters or caches traffic but does not validate data inside the application's own form handling.
whyNot.C: Stress testing (load testing under extreme conditions) checks capacity and stability, not whether malformed input is handled safely.
whyNot.D: Encoding (converting data into a safe representation for output) mainly protects output contexts and does not reject malformed input at entry.

cards.front:
While working on an incident, Joe, a technician, finished restoring the OS and applications on a workstation from the original media. Joe is about to begin copying the user's files back onto the hard drive. Which of the following incident response steps is Joe working on now?
A. Recovery
B. Eradication
C. Containment
D. Identification
cards.why: Recovery is the incident response phase where systems are restored to normal operation, including rebuilding the OS and applications and restoring user data from backup.

whyNot.B: Eradication (removing the threat, such as malware or compromised accounts) comes before recovery; restoring user files back is no longer removing the cause.
whyNot.C: Containment (isolating affected systems to stop the incident from spreading) happens before eradication and restoration.
whyNot.D: Identification (detecting and confirming that an incident has occurred) is an early phase, not the restoration of data.

cards.front:
A systems administrator found a suspicious file in the root of the file system. The file contains URLs, usernames, passwords, and text from other documents being edited on the system. Which of the following types of malware would generate such a file?
A. Keylogger
B. Rootkit
C. Bot
D. RAT
cards.why: A keylogger records keystrokes, which captures typed URLs, usernames, passwords, and text from documents being edited, and often stores them in a local file for later retrieval.

whyNot.B: A rootkit (malware that hides its presence with elevated privileges) conceals itself but does not by nature log typed credentials and document text.
whyNot.C: A bot (a compromised host controlled remotely, usually as part of a botnet) is used for tasks like DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service), not keystroke capture.
whyNot.D: A RAT (Remote Access Trojan) gives an attacker remote control, but the captured typed data in a file points specifically to keylogging.

cards.front:
A computer emergency response team is called at midnight to investigate a case in which a mail server was restarted. After an initial investigation, it was discovered that email is being exfiltrated through an active connection. Which of the following is the NEXT step the team should take?
A. Identify the source of the active connection
B. Perform eradication of active connection and recover
C. Performance containment procedure by disconnecting the server
D. Format the server and restore its initial configuration
cards.back: A. Identify the source of the active connection
cards.why: In incident response, the team must first identify the scope and source of the active exfiltration so that later containment and eradication target the right connection and systems.

whyNot.B: Eradication and recovery come after containment, so performing them first would skip steps and could destroy evidence while exfiltration continues.
whyNot.C: Disconnecting the server is containment, which follows identification of the source and scope, and doing it first may lose volatile evidence.
whyNot.D: Formatting and restoring the server destroys forensic evidence and skips identification and containment, so it is premature.

cards.front:
A remote intruder wants to take inventory of a network so exploits can be researched. The intruder is looking for information about software versions on the network. Which of the following techniques is the intruder using?
A. Banner grabbing
B. Port scanning
C. Packet sniffing
D. Virus scanning
cards.why: Banner grabbing connects to network services and reads their response banners, which reveal software names and versions that an intruder can then match to known exploits.

whyNot.B: Port scanning finds open ports and running services but does not by itself reliably reveal the specific software versions.
whyNot.C: Packet sniffing captures traffic passing on the network, which is passive and not a targeted technique for inventorying software versions.
whyNot.D: Virus scanning looks for malware on a host and does not inventory software versions across a network.

cards.front:
An analyst is reviewing a simple program for potential security vulnerabilities before being deployed to a Windows server. Given the following code: void foo (char *bar) { car random_user_input[12]; stropy (random_user_input, bar); } Which of the following vulnerabilities is present?
A. Bad memory pointer
B. Buffer overflow
C. Integer overflow
D. Backdoor
cards.why: The code copies user-supplied input into a 12-byte buffer using strcpy, which does not check length, so longer input overflows the buffer. This is a buffer overflow vulnerability.

whyNot.A: A bad memory pointer involves an invalid or uninitialized pointer being dereferenced, but the pointer here is valid and the problem is the unchecked copy size.
whyNot.C: An integer overflow occurs when arithmetic exceeds the range of an integer type, and no arithmetic is performed in this code.
whyNot.D: A backdoor is a hidden access mechanism deliberately placed in software, and nothing in this code provides such access.

cards.front:
A company has a data classification system with definitions for "Private" and "Public". the company's security policy outlines how data should be protected based on type. The company recently added data type "Proprietary". Which of the following is the MOST likely reason the company added this data type?
A. Reduced cost
B. More searchable data
C. Better data classification
D. Expanded authority of the privacy officer
cards.why: Adding a Proprietary data type refines the classification scheme so data can be labeled more precisely, letting the security policy apply more appropriate protections. This is better data classification.

whyNot.A: Adding a category does not reduce cost, and finer classification may even add handling expense.
whyNot.B: Classification labels control handling and protection, not how searchable the data is.
whyNot.D: A new data type does not expand the privacy officer's authority; it only changes how data is categorized.

cards.front:
A security technician is configuring an access management system to track and record user actions. Which of the following functions should the technician configure?
A. Accounting
B. Authorization
C. Authentication
D. Identification
cards.why: Accounting (the part of AAA, Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting, that tracks and records user actions) produces logs and audit trails of what users did.

whyNot.B: Authorization determines what an authenticated user is permitted to access, rather than recording what they do.
whyNot.C: Authentication verifies that a user is who they claim to be, and does not log subsequent actions.
whyNot.D: Identification is the user claiming an identity, such as a username, and does not track actions.

cards.front:
A security administrator installed a new network scanner that identifies new host systems on the network. Which of the following did the security administrator install?
A. Vulnerability scanner
B. Network-based IDS
C. Rogue system detection
D. Configuration compliance scanner
cards.why: Rogue system detection finds unauthorized or unknown hosts that appear on the network, which matches a scanner that identifies new host systems.

whyNot.A: A vulnerability scanner looks for weaknesses on known hosts, such as missing patches, not for newly appearing unauthorized hosts.
whyNot.B: A network-based IDS (Intrusion Detection System) monitors traffic for malicious activity and does not inventory new hosts.
whyNot.D: A configuration compliance scanner checks that systems match a defined security baseline, not whether hosts are new or unauthorized.

cards.front:
A Chief Information Officer (CIO) has decided it is not cost effective to implement safeguards against a known vulnerability. Which of the following risk responses does this BEST describe?
A. Transference
B. Avoidance
C. Mitigation
D. Acceptance
cards.why: Risk acceptance means knowingly choosing to take no action against a risk, typically because the cost of safeguards outweighs the potential loss, which is what the CIO decided.

whyNot.A: Transference shifts risk to another party, such as through insurance or outsourcing, and nothing was transferred here.
whyNot.B: Avoidance eliminates the risk by stopping the risky activity, but the CIO is keeping the exposure.
whyNot.C: Mitigation reduces the likelihood or impact of risk through safeguards, which the CIO declined to implement.

cards.front:
An audit takes place after company-wide restructuring, in which several employees changed roles. The following deficiencies are found during the audit regarding access to confidential data. Employee Job Function Audit Finding Ann Sales Manager *Access to confidential payroll shares *Access to payroll processing program *Access to marketing shares Jeff Marketing Director *Access to human resources annual review folder *Access to shared human resources mailbox John Sales Manager *Active account *Access to human resources annual review folder *Access to confidential payroll shares Which of the following would be the BEST method to prevent similar audit finding in the future?
A. Implement separation of duties for the payroll department
B. Implement a DLP solution on the payroll and human resources reviews
C. Implement rule-based access controls on the human resources server
D. Implement regular permission auditing and reviews
cards.back: D. Implement regular permission auditing and reviews
cards.why: The findings show users keeping old permissions after changing roles (privilege creep). Regular permission auditing and reviews, along with access recertification, catch and remove stale access.

whyNot.A: Separation of duties splits critical tasks among people, but it would not remove the leftover permissions from earlier roles.
whyNot.B: A DLP (Data Loss Prevention) solution detects or blocks data leaving the organization, and does not fix excessive role-based permissions.
whyNot.C: Rule-based access control applies fixed rules to access, but it would not by itself clean up permissions retained after role changes.

cards.front:
A technician is investigating a potentially compromised device with the following symptoms: Browser slowness Frequent browser crashes Hourglass stuck New search toolbar Increased memory consumption Which of the following types of malware has infected the system?
A. Man-in-the-browser
B. Spoofer
C. Spyware
D. Adware
cards.why: Adware causes unwanted ads, new toolbars, and browser slowness and crashes, along with high memory use. A new search toolbar is a classic adware sign.

whyNot.A: Man-in-the-browser malware intercepts and alters web transactions, typically for banking fraud, and is not usually marked by new toolbars.
whyNot.B: A spoofer impersonates an identity or address, such as IP (Internet Protocol) or email, and is not malware causing these browser symptoms.
whyNot.C: Spyware secretly gathers user information, but typically without visible toolbars and ads that adware shows.

cards.front:
A penetration tester has written an application that performs a bit-by-bit XOR 0xFF operation on binaries prior to transmission over untrusted media. Which of the following BEST describes the action performed by this type of application?
A. Hashing
B. Key exchange
C. Encryption
D. Obfusication
cards.why: XORing every byte with a fixed value like 0xFF is trivially reversible without a secret key, so it only obscures the data. That is obfuscation, not true encryption.

whyNot.A: Hashing is a one-way function that produces a fixed-size digest, whereas this XOR operation is reversible.
whyNot.B: Key exchange securely establishes shared keys between parties, and this operation exchanges nothing.
whyNot.C: Encryption relies on a secret key and a strong algorithm, and a fixed XOR with 0xFF has no key and offers no real security.

cards.front:
An audit reported has identifies a weakness that could allow unauthorized personnel access to the facility at its main entrance and from there gain access to the network. Which of the following would BEST resolve the vulnerability?
A. Faraday cage
B. Air gap
C. Mantrap
D. Bollards
cards.why: A mantrap is a two-door vestibule that allows only one person through at a time after authentication, preventing tailgating and unauthorized entry at the main entrance.

whyNot.A: A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic signals, such as wireless emissions, and does not control who physically enters.
whyNot.B: An air gap physically isolates a network from other networks, and does not stop people entering through the entrance.
whyNot.D: Bollards stop vehicles from ramming into buildings but do not control pedestrian access through the entrance.

cards.front:
When attempting to secure a mobile workstation, which of the following authentication technologies rely on the user's physical characteristics? (Select TWO)
A. MAC address table
B. Retina scan
C. Fingerprint scan
D. Two-factor authentication
E. CAPTCHA
F. Password string
cards.back:
B. Retina scan
C. Fingerprint scan
cards.why: Retina scans and fingerprint scans are biometric authentication methods (something you are) that rely on the user's physical characteristics.

whyNot.A: A MAC (Media Access Control) address table maps device addresses to switch ports and is not a user authentication factor.
whyNot.D: Two-factor authentication combines two factor types and is not itself a physical characteristic.
whyNot.E: CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) distinguishes humans from bots and does not identify a specific user.
whyNot.F: A password string is something you know, not a physical characteristic.

cards.front:
Systems administrator and key support staff come together to simulate a hypothetical interruption of service. The team updates the disaster recovery processes and documentation after meeting. Which of the following describes the team's efforts?
A. Business impact analysis
B. Continuity of operation
C. Tabletop exercise
D. Order of restoration
cards.why: A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based simulation in which key staff walk through a hypothetical service interruption and then update disaster recovery plans based on what they learned.

whyNot.A: A business impact analysis identifies critical functions and the cost of downtime. It does not simulate an interruption or test recovery procedures.
whyNot.B: Continuity of operation is the planning concept for keeping essential functions running. It is not a simulated walkthrough of a hypothetical event.
whyNot.D: Order of restoration is the sequence in which systems are brought back online. It is a plan component, not a simulation exercise.

cards.front:
A company has two wireless networks utilizing captive portals. Some employees report getting a trust error in their browsers when connecting to one of the networks.
