Both captive portals are using the same server certificate for authentication, but the analyst notices the following differences between the two certificate details: Certificate 1 Certificate Path: Geotrust Global CA *company.com Certificate 2 Certificate Path: *company.com Which of the following would resolve the problem?
A. Use a wildcard certificate.
B. Use certificate chaining.
C. Use a trust model.
D. Use an extended validation certificate.
cards.why: Certificate chaining means the server presents the intermediate certificate authority certificate (Geotrust Global CA) along with its own, so browsers can build a trusted path to the root and stop showing the trust error.

whyNot.A: Both portals already use the same wildcard certificate for *company.com. The wildcard itself is not what differs between them.
whyNot.C: A trust model describes how certificate authorities establish trust in general. It is not a fix for a server missing its intermediate certificate.
whyNot.D: An extended validation certificate changes the vetting level of the identity. It does not supply a missing intermediate certificate in the chain.

cards.front:
Company A has acquired Company B. Company A has different domains spread globally, and typically migrates its acquisitions infrastructure under its own domain infrastructure. Company B, however, cannot be merged into Company A's domain infrastructure. Which of the following methods would allow the two companies to access one another's resources?
A. Attestation
B. Federation
C. Single sign-on
D. Kerberos
cards.why: Federation lets two separate identity domains trust each other's authentication, so users from Company B can access Company A resources without merging domains.

whyNot.A: Attestation is verifying that a system or claim is genuine, such as hardware integrity. It does not enable cross-domain resource access.
whyNot.C: Single sign-on (SSO) lets a user log in once within a trust boundary. By itself it does not connect two independent domains.
whyNot.D: Kerberos is a ticket-based authentication protocol that normally operates within a realm or domain. It does not by itself bridge unmergeable organizations.

cards.front:
A technician is configuring a load balancer for the application team to accelerate the network performance of their applications. The applications are hosted on multiple servers and must be redundant. Given this scenario, which of the following would be the BEST method of configuring the load balancer?
A. Round-robin
B. Weighted
C. Least connection
D. Locality-based
cards.why: Locality-based load balancing sends each request to the server closest to the client, which reduces latency and speeds up application performance while multiple servers keep the service redundant.

whyNot.A: Round-robin rotates requests evenly among servers without considering distance or performance, so it does not specifically accelerate network performance.
whyNot.B: Weighted balancing sends more traffic to higher-capacity servers. It addresses capacity differences, not network proximity or speed.
whyNot.C: Least connection sends traffic to the server with the fewest active sessions. It balances load but does not reduce network distance or latency.

cards.front:
Ann is the IS manager for several new systems in which the classifications of the systems' data are being decided. She is trying to determine the sensitivity level of the data being processed. Which of the following people should she consult to determine the data classification?
A. Steward
B. Custodian
C. User
D. Owner
cards.why: The data owner is the senior person accountable for the data and decides its sensitivity and classification level, so Ann should consult the owner.

whyNot.A: A data steward manages data quality and handling standards day to day. The steward does not make the final classification decision.
whyNot.B: A data custodian implements technical controls such as storage and backups. The custodian applies the classification but does not decide it.
whyNot.C: A user only consumes the data under assigned permissions. Users have no authority to set its classification.

cards.front:
An organization's employees currently use three different sets of credentials to access multiple internal resources. Management wants to make this process less complex. Which of the following would be the BEST option to meet this goal?
A. Transitive trust
B. Single sign-on
C. Federation
D. Secure token
cards.why: Single sign-on (SSO) lets employees authenticate once and access multiple internal resources, replacing three separate credential sets and reducing complexity.

whyNot.A: A transitive trust extends trust between domains automatically. It does not combine separate credentials for different internal resources into one login.
whyNot.C: Federation links identities across separate organizations. The resources here are all internal, so federation adds unnecessary complexity.
whyNot.D: A secure token is a device or software that generates or carries authentication data. It does not by itself consolidate multiple credential sets.

cards.front:
An external attacker can modify the ARP cache of an internal computer. Which of the following types of attacks is described?
A. Replay
B. Spoofing
C. DNS poisoning
D. Client-side attack
cards.why: Modifying the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache with false address mappings is ARP poisoning, a form of spoofing in which the attacker impersonates another device's hardware address.

whyNot.A: A replay attack resends previously captured valid traffic. It does not alter the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache.
whyNot.C: DNS (Domain Name System) poisoning corrupts name-to-IP (Internet Protocol) address records, not the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache that maps IP to hardware addresses.
whyNot.D: A client-side attack exploits software on the user's machine, such as a browser flaw. It is not manipulation of the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache.

cards.front:
A systems administrator has isolated an infected system from the network and terminated the malicious process from executing. Which of the following should the administrator do NEXT according to the incident response process?
A. Restore lost data from a backup.
B. Wipe the system.
C. Document the lessons learned.
D. Determine the scope of impact.
cards.back: A. Restore lost data from a backup.
cards.why: After containment (isolating the system and stopping the malicious process), the incident response process moves to eradication and recovery, which includes restoring lost data from a backup.

whyNot.B: Wiping the system is a drastic eradication choice and is not the logical immediate next step when the process was already terminated and data needs recovery.
whyNot.C: Documenting lessons learned is the final phase of incident response, performed after recovery is complete.
whyNot.D: Determining the scope of impact is part of identification and analysis, which normally occurs before or during containment, not after it.

cards.front:
A new security administrator ran a vulnerability scanner for the first time and caused a system outage. Which of the following types of scans MOST likely caused the outage?
A. Non-intrusive credentialed scan
B. Non-intrusive non-credentialed scan
C. Intrusive credentialed scan
D. Intrusive non-credentialed scan
cards.why: An intrusive non-credentialed scan actively sends exploit-like probes without logon access, which can crash fragile services or systems and cause an outage.

whyNot.A: A non-intrusive credentialed scan only reads configuration and patch data using a valid account, so it rarely disrupts systems.
whyNot.B: A non-intrusive non-credentialed scan passively observes and identifies services without sending harmful probes, so it is unlikely to cause an outage.
whyNot.C: An intrusive credentialed scan can disrupt systems, but the non-credentialed intrusive scan is the more likely cause because it relies on blind exploit-style probing.

cards.front:
A security analyst is hardening a WiFi infrastructure. The primary requirements are the following: The infrastructure must allow staff to authenticate using the most secure method. The infrastructure must allow guests to use an "open" WiFi network that logs valid email addresses before granting access to the Internet. Given these requirements, which of the following statements BEST represents what the analyst should recommend and configure?
A. Configure a captive portal for guests and WPS for staff.
B. Configure a captive portal for staff and WPA for guests.
C. Configure a captive portal for staff and WEP for guests.
D. Configure a captive portal for guest and WPA2 Enterprise for staff.
cards.back: D. Configure a captive portal for guest and WPA2 Enterprise for staff.
cards.why: A captive portal on the open guest network can log valid email addresses before granting Internet access, and WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) Enterprise uses 802.1X authentication, the most secure method for staff.

whyNot.A: WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) is a weak PIN-based feature vulnerable to brute force, so it is not the most secure staff authentication.
whyNot.B: A captive portal is not the most secure way to authenticate staff, and guests are supposed to use an open network, not WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access).
whyNot.C: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) is broken and obsolete, and a captive portal does not give staff the most secure authentication.

cards.front:
A security administrator is trying to eradicate a worm, which is spreading throughout the organization, using an old remote vulnerability in the SMB protocol. The worm uses Nmap to identify target hosts within the company. The administrator wants to implement a solution that will eradicate the current worm and any future attacks that may be using zero-day vulnerabilities. Which of the following would BEST meet the requirements when implemented?
A. Host-based firewall
B. Enterprise patch management system
C. Network-based intrusion prevention system
D. Application blacklisting
E. File integrity checking
cards.why: A network-based intrusion prevention system (NIPS) can block worm traffic and scanning behavior at the network level and, with behavioral or anomaly detection, can stop zero-day attacks as well.

whyNot.A: A host-based firewall must be configured on each host and does not stop all worm traffic or detect unknown zero-day exploit patterns.
whyNot.B: An enterprise patch management system fixes known vulnerabilities such as the old SMB (Server Message Block) flaw but cannot protect against zero-day vulnerabilities.
whyNot.D: Application blacklisting blocks known bad programs, so it will not catch unknown zero-day attacks or stop network spread of the worm.
whyNot.E: File integrity checking detects changes to files after the fact. It neither eradicates the worm nor prevents future zero-day attacks.

cards.front:
Which of the following is a deployment concept that can be used to ensure only the required OS access is exposed to software applications?
A. Staging environment
B. Sandboxing
C. Secure baseline
D. Trusted OS
cards.why: Sandboxing runs an application in an isolated environment that exposes only the operating system resources it needs, limiting the damage if the application is compromised.

whyNot.A: A staging environment is a pre-production copy used for testing before release. It does not restrict an application's operating system access.
whyNot.C: A secure baseline is a standard hardened configuration. It does not isolate individual applications from operating system resources.
whyNot.D: A trusted operating system enforces mandatory access controls at the system level. It is not a deployment concept for limiting what one application can reach.

cards.front:
A procedure differs from a policy in that it:
A. is a high-level statement regarding the company's position on a topic.
B. sets a minimum expected baseline of behavior.
C. provides step-by-step instructions for performing a task.
D. describes adverse actions when violations occur.
cards.back: C. provides step-by-step instructions for performing a task.
cards.why: A procedure is a detailed, step-by-step set of instructions for carrying out a specific task, unlike a policy, which states high-level intent.

whyNot.A: A high-level statement of company position on a topic describes a policy, not a procedure.
whyNot.B: Setting a minimum expected baseline of behavior describes a standard or baseline, not a procedure.
whyNot.D: Describing adverse actions for violations describes the enforcement or sanctions portion of a policy, not a procedure.

cards.front:
Ann, a user, reports she is unable to access an application from her desktop. A security analyst verifies Ann's access and checks the SIEM for any errors. The security analyst reviews the log file from Ann's system and notices the following output: 2017--08-21 10:48:12 DROP TCP 172.20.89.232 239.255.255.255 443 1900 250 -------- RECEIVE 2017--08-21 10:48:12 DROP UDP 192.168.72.205 239.255.255.255 443 1900 250 -------- RECEIVE Which of the following is MOST likely preventing Ann from accessing the application from the desktop?
A. Web application firewall
B. DLP
C. Host-based firewall
D. UTM
E. Network-based firewall
cards.back:
C. Host-based firewall

Webmail is being blocked. The 250 response code is for SMTP.
cards.why: The log shows traffic to multicast address 239.255.255.255 on UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 1900 being dropped on Ann's own system, which points to the host-based firewall on her desktop blocking it.

whyNot.A: A web application firewall (WAF) protects web servers from attacks like injection. It would not log dropped multicast traffic from Ann's desktop.
whyNot.B: DLP (Data Loss Prevention) monitors and blocks sensitive data leaving the organization. It does not produce this kind of dropped-packet log.
whyNot.D: A UTM (Unified Threat Management) appliance sits on the network, not on Ann's system, and the log comes from her machine.
whyNot.E: A network-based firewall would log on the network device, but this log was taken from Ann's own system.

cards.front:
Which of the following types of penetration test will allow the tester to have access only to password hashes prior to the penetration test?
A. Black box
B. Gray box
C. Credentialed
D. White box
cards.why: A gray box test gives the tester partial knowledge, such as password hashes, before the test begins, falling between black box (none) and white box (full).

whyNot.A: A black box test gives the tester no prior information about the target, not even password hashes.
whyNot.C: A credentialed test uses valid logon accounts, usually for scanning, rather than only password hashes.
whyNot.D: A white box test gives the tester full knowledge, such as source code, diagrams, and credentials, which is more than just password hashes.

cards.front:
Which of the following threats has sufficient knowledge to cause the MOST danger to an organization?
A. Competitors
B. Insiders
C. Hacktivists
D. Script kiddies
cards.why: Insiders already have legitimate access, system knowledge, and trust, so they can cause the most damage to an organization. This is the insider threat concept.

whyNot.A: Competitors may be well funded but usually lack internal knowledge and legitimate access to the organization's systems.
whyNot.C: Hacktivists (activist hackers) are motivated by ideology and typically use public attacks like defacement, with limited inside knowledge.
whyNot.D: Script kiddies (unskilled attackers) run prewritten tools and lack the knowledge to cause the most serious harm.

cards.front:
While troubleshooting a client application connecting to the network, the security administrator notices the following error: Certificate is not valid. Which of the following is the BEST way to check if the digital certificate is valid?
A. PKI
B. CRL
C. CSR
D. IPSec
cards.why: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) is published by the certificate authority and lists revoked certificates, so checking it shows whether a certificate is still valid.

whyNot.A: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is the overall framework for managing certificates, not the specific tool for checking one certificate's validity.
whyNot.C: A CSR (Certificate Signing Request) is submitted to a certificate authority to request a certificate, not to validate an existing one.
whyNot.D: IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) encrypts and authenticates IP traffic and does not check certificate validity.

cards.front:
To determine the ALE of a particular risk, which of the following must be calculated? (Select TWO).
A. ARO
B. ROI
C. RPO
D. SLE
E. RTO
cards.why: ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) equals SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) multiplied by ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence), so both values must be calculated.

whyNot.B: ROI (Return on Investment) measures the financial benefit of a purchase or control and is not part of the ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) formula.
whyNot.C: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines acceptable data loss in time and is a business continuity measure, not an ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) input.
whyNot.E: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) defines how quickly a system must be restored and is not used to calculate ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy).

cards.front:
A business sector is highly competitive, and safeguarding trade secrets and critical information is paramount. On a seasonal basis, an organization employs temporary hires and contractor personnel to accomplish its mission objectives. The temporary and contract personnel require access to network resources only when on the clock. Which of the following account management practices are the BEST ways to manage these accounts?
A. Employ time-of-day restrictions.
B. Employ password complexity.
C. Employ a random key generator strategy.
D. Employ an account expiration strategy.
E. Employ a password lockout policy.
cards.back: D. Employ an account expiration strategy.
cards.why: An account expiration strategy automatically disables temporary and contractor accounts at the end of their engagement, preventing lingering access to trade secrets. This is account lifecycle management.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions limit login hours but would not disable accounts when the temporary workers leave, so access could linger.
whyNot.B: Password complexity strengthens passwords but does not limit how long a temporary account remains active.
whyNot.C: A random key generator strategy creates unpredictable keys or passwords but does not control account lifetime.
whyNot.E: A password lockout policy blocks guessing attacks after failed attempts but does not end access for departed workers.

cards.keyDoubt: A. Because staff need access only when on the clock, time-of-day restrictions match the stated requirement most directly, though expiration also helps.

cards.front:
Which of the following locations contain the MOST volatile data?
A. SSD
B. Paging file
C. RAM
D. Cache memory
cards.why: Cache memory sits closest to the CPU (Central Processing Unit) and loses its contents fastest, so it is the most volatile location in the order of volatility.

whyNot.A: An SSD (Solid State Drive) is nonvolatile storage and keeps data without power, so it is far less volatile.
whyNot.B: The paging file lives on disk and persists across reboots, making it less volatile than CPU (Central Processing Unit) cache.
whyNot.C: RAM (Random Access Memory) is volatile, but it ranks below CPU (Central Processing Unit) cache in the order of volatility.

cards.front:
Ann, a customer, is reporting that several important files are missing from her workstation. She recently received communication from an unknown party who is requesting funds to restore the files. Which of the following attacks has occurred?
A. Ransomware
B. Keylogger
C. Buffer overflow
D. Rootkit
cards.why: Ransomware makes files unavailable, often by encrypting or removing them, and demands payment to restore them. The unknown party requesting funds matches this attack.

whyNot.B: A keylogger records keystrokes to steal information and does not remove files or demand payment.
whyNot.C: A buffer overflow exploits memory handling flaws to run code or crash software and does not involve a ransom demand.
whyNot.D: A rootkit hides malicious activity with deep system access but does not itself demand payment for restored files.

cards.front:
Every morning, a systems administrator monitors failed login attempts on the company's log management server. The administrator notices the DBAdmin account has five failed username and/or password alerts during a ten-minute window. The systems administrator determines the user account is a dummy account used to attract attackers. Which of the following techniques should the systems administrator implement?
A. Role-based access control
B. Honeypot
C. Rule-based access control
D. Password cracker
cards.why: A honeypot is a decoy system or account designed to attract attackers so their activity can be observed. A dummy account drawing failed logins fits this concept.

whyNot.A: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) assigns permissions by job role and is not a decoy used to attract attackers.
whyNot.C: Rule-based access control applies rules such as time or location restrictions and is not a decoy used to attract attackers.
whyNot.D: A password cracker is an attacker tool for recovering passwords, not a defensive decoy technique.

cards.front:
Joe, a user, has been trying to send Ann, a different user, an encrypted document via email. Ann has not received the attachment but is able to receive the header information. Which of the following is MOST likely preventing Ann from receiving the encrypted file?
A. Unencrypted credentials
B. Authentication issues
C. Weak cipher suite
D. Permission issues
cards.why: Encrypted email attachments depend on proper authentication and key or certificate exchange. If Ann cannot authenticate or lacks the correct key, the encrypted attachment will not be delivered while headers still arrive.

whyNot.A: Unencrypted credentials would expose login information but would not selectively block delivery of an encrypted attachment.
whyNot.C: A weak cipher suite reduces encryption strength but would not stop the attachment from arriving.
whyNot.D: Permission issues affect file or resource access rights and do not explain why only the attachment is missing from the email.

cards.front:
A systems administrator is configuring a system that uses data classification labels. Which of the following will the administrator need to implement to enforce access control?
A. Discretionary access control
B. Mandatory access control
C. Role-based access control
D. Rule-based access control
cards.why: MAC (Mandatory Access Control) enforces access using data classification labels and user clearances set by the system, which matches the labeled data described.

whyNot.A: DAC (Discretionary Access Control) lets data owners decide who gets access and does not enforce access through classification labels.
whyNot.C: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) grants access by job role, not by data classification label.
whyNot.D: Rule-based access control applies predefined rules such as time or network conditions, not classification labels.

cards.front:
An analyst is using a vulnerability scanner to look for common security misconfigurations on devices. Which of the following might be identified by the scanner? (Select TWO).
A. The firewall is disabled on workstations.
B. SSH is enabled on servers.
C. Browser homepages have not been customized.
D. Default administrator credentials exist on networking hardware.
E. The OS is only set to check for updates once a day.
cards.back:
A. The firewall is disabled on workstations.
D. Default administrator credentials exist on networking hardware.
cards.why: Vulnerability scanners detect misconfigurations such as a disabled host firewall and default administrator credentials on network hardware. Both are common security configuration weaknesses.

whyNot.B: SSH (Secure Shell) enabled on servers is normal, secure remote administration and is not a misconfiguration by itself.
whyNot.C: A browser homepage that has not been customized is not a security weakness a scanner would flag.
whyNot.E: Checking for operating system updates once a day is an acceptable configuration and not a typical scanner finding.

cards.front:
A security analyst is reviewing patches on servers. One of the servers is reporting the following error message in the WSUS management console: The computer has not reported status in 30 days. Given this scenario, which of the following statements BEST represents the issue with the output above?
A. The computer in question has not pulled the latest ACL policies for the firewall.
B. The computer in question has not pulled the latest GPO policies from the management server.
C. The computer in question has not pulled the latest antivirus definitions from the antivirus program.
D. The computer in question has not pulled the latest application software updates.
cards.back: D. The computer in question has not pulled the latest application software updates.
cards.why: WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) distributes Microsoft patches and operating system updates. A computer that has not reported status in 30 days has not pulled the latest updates, which may include application software updates.

whyNot.A: ACL (Access Control List) firewall policies are not delivered or reported through WSUS (Windows Server Update Services).
whyNot.B: GPO (Group Policy Object) settings come from Active Directory, not WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) status reporting.
whyNot.C: Antivirus definitions come from the antivirus vendor's management console, not WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) in this scenario.

cards.front:
Two users must encrypt and transmit large amount of data between them. Which of the following should they use to encrypt and transmit the data?
A. Symmetric algorithm
B. Hash function
C. Digital signature
D. Obfuscation
cards.why: A symmetric algorithm uses one shared key and is fast, making it best for encrypting large amounts of data between two parties.

whyNot.B: A hash function creates a fixed-length digest for integrity and is one-way, so it cannot encrypt data for later decryption.
whyNot.C: A digital signature provides authentication and non-repudiation, not bulk data encryption.
whyNot.D: Obfuscation hides meaning by making data harder to read but is not true encryption and provides weak protection.

cards.front:
A security administrator is reviewing the following PowerShell script referenced in the Task Scheduler on a database server: $members = GetADGroupMemeber -Identity "Domain Admins" -Recursive | Select - ExpandProperty name if ($members -notcontains "JohnDoe"){ Remove-Item -path C:\Database -recurse -force } Which of the following did the security administrator discover?
A. Ransomeware
B. Backdoor
C. Logic bomb
D. Trojan
cards.why: A logic bomb runs malicious code when a condition is met. Here the script deletes the database folder if JohnDoe is no longer in the Domain Admins group.

whyNot.A: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment, but this script only deletes files and makes no ransom demand.
whyNot.B: A backdoor provides covert remote access, but this script destroys data rather than granting access.
whyNot.D: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users, but this is a conditional destructive script.

cards.front:
A bank is experiencing a DoS attack against an application designed to handle 500IP-based sessions. in addition, the perimeter router can only handle 1Gbps of traffic. Which of the following should be implemented to prevent a DoS attacks in the future?
A. Deploy multiple web servers and implement a load balancer
B. Increase the capacity of the perimeter router to 10 Gbps
C. Install a firewall at the network to prevent all attacks
D. Use redundancy across all network devices and services
cards.back: D. Use redundancy across all network devices and services
cards.why: Redundancy across network devices and services removes single points of failure and provides capacity and resilience against DoS (Denial of Service) attacks, covering both the application session limit and the router bandwidth limit.

whyNot.A: Multiple web servers and a load balancer address only the application limit, leaving the 1 Gbps (Gigabits per second) router as a bottleneck.
whyNot.B: Upgrading the router to 10 Gbps (Gigabits per second) addresses only bandwidth, leaving the application session limit and other single points of failure.
whyNot.C: A firewall cannot prevent all attacks and can itself be overwhelmed by a DoS (Denial of Service) flood.

cards.front:
A malicious system continuously sends an extremely large number of SYN packets to a server. Which of the following BEST describes the resulting effect?
A. The server will be unable to server clients due to lack of bandwidth
B. the server's firewall will be unable to effectively filter traffic due to the amount of data transmitted
C. The server will crash when trying to reassemble all the fragmented packets
D. The server will exhaust its memory maintaining half-open connections
cards.back: D. The server will exhaust its memory maintaining half-open connections
cards.why: A SYN (Synchronize) flood leaves many half-open TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections waiting for the final handshake step, which exhausts the server's memory and connection table.

whyNot.A: A SYN (Synchronize) flood mainly exhausts connection resources rather than bandwidth, since SYN packets are small.
whyNot.B: The firewall is not the main target of a SYN (Synchronize) flood, and the described effect concerns the server's connection state.
whyNot.C: SYN (Synchronize) packets are not fragmented, so there is no reassembly of fragments that would crash the server.

cards.front:
A systems administrator is deploying a new mission essential server into a virtual environment. Which of the following is BEST mitigated by the environment's rapid elasticity characteristic?
A. Data confidentiality breaches
B. VM escape attacks
C. Lack of redundancy
D. Denial of service
cards.why: Rapid elasticity lets a virtual environment automatically scale resources up under heavy load, so a flood of traffic is absorbed and a Denial of Service (DoS) attack is less likely to exhaust the server.

whyNot.A: Elasticity adds capacity, not confidentiality controls, so it does not stop data confidentiality breaches.
whyNot.B: A virtual machine (VM) escape exploits hypervisor flaws, and scaling resources does nothing to prevent that.
whyNot.C: Redundancy comes from failover and duplicate systems; elasticity adjusts capacity but does not by itself provide redundant copies.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the proper order for logging a user into a system from the first step to the last step?
A. Identification, authentication, authorization
B. Identification, authorization, authentication
C. Authentication, identification, authorization
D. Authentication, identification, authorization
E. Authorization, identification, authentication
cards.why: A user first claims an identity (identification), then proves it, such as with a password (authentication), and only then is granted permissions (authorization).

whyNot.B: Authorization cannot come before authentication, because permissions are only granted after the identity is verified.
whyNot.C: Authentication cannot come before identification, because there must be a claimed identity to verify.
whyNot.D: Authentication cannot come before identification, because there must be a claimed identity to verify.
whyNot.E: Authorization comes last, since access rights depend on a verified identity.

cards.front:
A company stores highly sensitive data files used by the accounting system on a server file share. The accounting system uses a service account named accounting-svc to access the file share. The data is protected will a full disk encryption, and the permissions are set as follows: File system permissions: Users = Read Only Share permission: accounting-svc = Read Only Given the listed protections are in place and unchanged, to which of the following risks is the data still subject?
A. Exploitation of local console access and removal of data
B. Theft of physical hard drives and a breach of confidentiality
C. Remote exfiltration of data using domain credentials
D. Disclosure of sensitive data to third parties due to excessive share permissions
cards.back: A. Exploitation of local console access and removal of data
cards.why: Full disk encryption only protects data at rest while the system is powered off, so someone with local console access to the running server can read and copy the data.

whyNot.B: Full disk encryption protects against theft of physical hard drives, so confidentiality would not be breached that way.
whyNot.C: Only the accounting-svc service account has share permission, and it is read only, which limits remote access with ordinary domain credentials.
whyNot.D: The share permission is limited to the single service account, so it is not excessive and does not expose data to third parties.

cards.front:
A bank uses a wireless network to transmit credit card purchases to a billing system. Which of the following would be MOST appropriate to protect credit card information from being accessed by unauthorized individuals outside of the premises?
A. Air gap
B. Infrared detection
C. Faraday cage
D. Protected distributions
cards.why: A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic signals from leaving or entering the premises, so wireless transmissions cannot be intercepted by unauthorized people outside the building.

whyNot.A: An air gap isolates a network from others, but it does not work for a wireless network that must transmit purchases to a billing system.
whyNot.B: Infrared detection senses heat or motion and does not stop radio signals from leaking outside the premises.
whyNot.D: Protected distribution systems secure physical cabling, not wireless radio transmissions.

cards.front:
Joe, a salesman, was assigned to a new project that requires him to travel to a client site. While waiting for a flight, Joe decides to connect to the airport wireless network without connecting to a VPN, and then sends confidential emails to fellow colleagues. A few days later, the company experiences a data breach. Upon investigation, the company learns Joe's emails were intercepted. Which of the following MOST likely caused the data breach?
A. Policy violation
B. Social engineering
C. Insider threat
D. Zero--day attack
cards.why: Joe broke company policy by using an untrusted public wireless network without a Virtual Private Network (VPN) to send confidential email, which exposed the messages to interception.

whyNot.B: Nobody tricked Joe into acting; he chose to use the airport network himself, so this is not social engineering.
whyNot.C: Joe did not intend harm, and the interception was by an outside party, so this is not an insider threat.
whyNot.D: A zero-day attack exploits an unknown software flaw, and nothing here suggests one was used.

cards.front:
A help desk technician receives a phone call from an individual claiming to be an employee of the organization and requesting assistance to access a locked account. The help desk technician asks the individual to provide proof of identity before access can be granted. Which of the following types of attack is the caller performing?
A. Phishing
B. Shoulder surfing
C. Impersonation
D. Dumpster diving
cards.why: The caller is pretending to be an employee in order to gain access to an account, which is impersonation, a form of social engineering.

whyNot.A: Phishing is a deceptive electronic message such as email, while this attack happened by phone call, which would be vishing.
whyNot.B: Shoulder surfing means watching someone enter sensitive information, and the caller is not observing anyone.
whyNot.D: Dumpster diving means searching discarded materials for information, which did not happen here.

cards.front:
Confidential emails from an organization were posted to a website without the organization's knowledge. Upon investigation, it was determined that the emails were obtained from an internal actor who sniffed the emails in plain text. Which of the following protocols, if properly implemented, would have MOST likely prevented the emails from being sniffed? (Select TWO)
A. Secure IMAP
B. DNSSEC
C. S/MIME
D. SMTPS
E. HTTPS
cards.back:
C. S/MIME
D. SMTPS

SMTPS (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Secure) is a deprecated method for securing SMTP with transport layer security. It is intended to provide authentication of the communication partners, as well as data integrity and confidentiality.
cards.why: S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) encrypts the message content itself, and SMTPS (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts mail in transit, so an insider sniffing the network would not read plain text.

whyNot.A: Secure IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) protects only client mailbox retrieval traffic, not message-level confidentiality or server-to-server mail relay.
whyNot.B: DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) validates DNS records and does not encrypt email content.
whyNot.E: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) protects web traffic and does not secure email transported by mail protocols.

cards.front:
A company wants to implement an access management solution that allows employees to use the same usernames and passwords for multiple applications without having to keep multiple credentials synchronized. Which of the following solutions would BEST meet these requirements?
A. Multifactor authentication
B. SSO
C. Biometrics
D. PKI
E. Federation
cards.why: SSO (single sign-on) lets a user authenticate once with one set of credentials for multiple applications, and federation extends that shared login across separate systems or organizations without synchronizing credentials.

whyNot.A: Multifactor authentication adds more verification factors but does not let one credential set work across multiple applications.
whyNot.C: Biometrics is an authentication factor based on physical traits and does not unify credentials across applications.
whyNot.D: PKI (public key infrastructure) manages certificates and keys and does not provide a shared username and password login.

cards.front:
An external auditor visits the human resources department and performs a physical security assessment. The auditor observed documents on printers that are unclaimed. A closer look at these documents reveals employee names, addresses, ages, and types of medical and dental coverage options each employee has selected. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate actions to take?
A. Flip the documents face down so no one knows these documents are PII sensitive
B. Shred the documents and let the owner print the new set
C. Retrieve the documents, label them with a PII cover sheet, and return them to the printer
D. Report to the human resources manager that their personnel are violating a privacy policy
cards.back: D. Report to the human resources manager that their personnel are violating a privacy policy
cards.why: The auditor should report the exposed Personally Identifiable Information (PII) to the human resources manager, who owns the process and can correct the privacy policy violation.

whyNot.A: Flipping documents face down only hides them temporarily and leaves the underlying policy violation unaddressed.
whyNot.B: Shredding another department's documents is outside an auditor's authority and destroys records the owner may still need.
whyNot.C: A cover sheet does not protect Personally Identifiable Information (PII), and returning documents to an open printer leaves them exposed.

cards.front:
Which of the following authentication concepts is a gait analysis MOST closely associated?
A. Somewhere you are
B. Something you are
C. Something you do
D. Something you know
cards.why: Gait analysis identifies a person by how they walk, which is a behavior, so it falls under something you do.

whyNot.A: Somewhere you are refers to location, such as geolocation or an Internet Protocol (IP) address, and not to walking behavior.
whyNot.B: Something you are covers physical traits such as fingerprints, while gait is a learned behavior and not a fixed physical trait.
whyNot.D: Something you know refers to secrets like passwords or PINs (personal identification numbers), and gait is not knowledge.

cards.front:
Which of the following metrics are used to calculate the SLE? (Select TWO)
A. ROI
B. ARO
C. ALE
D. MTBF
E. MTTF
F. TCO
cards.why: The keyed answer reflects that ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) and ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) are tied to SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) by the formula ALE equals SLE times ARO.

whyNot.A: ROI (Return on Investment) measures financial benefit of a control and is not an input to Single Loss Expectancy.
whyNot.D: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) measures reliability of repairable systems and is not used to calculate Single Loss Expectancy.
whyNot.E: MTTF (Mean Time To Failure) measures the expected life of non-repairable items and is not used to calculate Single Loss Expectancy.
whyNot.F: TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) measures lifetime cost of an asset and is not used to calculate Single Loss Expectancy.

cards.keyDoubt: None of the listed letters fits: SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) is calculated from asset value times exposure factor, and ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) is the result of SLE times ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence), so the question likely meant ALE.

cards.front:
Due to regulatory requirements, server in a global organization must use time synchronization. Which of the following represents the MOST secure method of time synchronization?
A. The server should connect to external Stratum 0 NTP servers for synchronization
B. The server should connect to internal Stratum 0 NTP servers for synchronization
C. The server should connect to external Stratum 1 NTP servers for synchronization
D. The server should connect to external Stratum 1 NTP servers for synchronization
cards.back:
B. The server should connect to internal Stratum 0 NTP servers for synchronization

Configure your own Internal NTP hierarchical service for your network. It is possible to purchase Stratum 1 or Stratum 0 NTP appliances to use internally for less than the cost of a typical server.
cards.why: Stratum 0 devices are the authoritative time sources such as atomic clocks or Global Positioning System (GPS) receivers, and keeping them internal avoids relying on external Network Time Protocol (NTP) sources that could be spoofed or manipulated.

whyNot.A: External Stratum 0 sources are reached over untrusted networks, which exposes the Network Time Protocol (NTP) traffic to tampering and spoofing.
whyNot.C: External Stratum 1 servers are outside the organization's control, so they are less secure than an internal time source.
whyNot.D: External Stratum 1 servers are outside the organization's control, so they are less secure than an internal time source.

cards.front:
When sending messages using symmetric encryption, which of the following must happen FIRST?
A. Exchange encryption key
B. Establish digital signatures
C. Agree on an encryption method
D. Install digital certificates
cards.back: C. Agree on an encryption method
cards.why: Both parties must first agree on the encryption method, meaning the algorithm to use, before they can exchange the shared secret key for symmetric encryption.

whyNot.A: The key exchange happens after the algorithm is chosen, since the key must suit the agreed method.
whyNot.B: Digital signatures provide integrity and non-repudiation, and they are not required before symmetric encryption starts.
whyNot.D: Digital certificates are used with asymmetric cryptography and are not a prerequisite for choosing a symmetric method.

cards.front:
Which of the following scenarios BEST describes an implementation of non-repudiation?
A. A user logs into a domain workstation and access network file shares for another department
B. A user remotely logs into the mail server with another user's credentials
C. A user sends a digitally signed email to the entire finance department about an upcoming meeting
D. A user access the workstation registry to make unauthorized changes to enable functionality within an application
cards.back: C. A user sends a digitally signed email to the entire finance department about an upcoming meeting
cards.why: A digitally signed email proves who sent it and cannot later be denied by the sender, which is non-repudiation.

whyNot.A: Accessing another department's file shares is an access control issue and does not prove who performed an action.
whyNot.B: Using another user's credentials defeats accountability, which is the opposite of non-repudiation.
whyNot.D: Making unauthorized registry changes is a malicious or policy-violating act and does not provide proof of origin.

cards.front:
An office manager found a folder that included documents with various types of data relating to corporate clients. The office manager notified the data included dates of birth, addresses, and phone numbers for the clients. The office manager then reported this finding to the security compliance officer. Which of the following portions of the policy would the security officer need to consult to determine if a breach has occurred?
A. Public
B. Private
C. PHI
D. PII
cards.why: Dates of birth, addresses, and phone numbers are Personally Identifiable Information (PII), so the officer would consult the PII portion of the policy to decide whether a breach occurred.

whyNot.A: Public data is meant for open release, and client personal details are not public information.
whyNot.B: Private is a general data classification label and is not the policy section covering personally identifying client details.
whyNot.C: PHI (Protected Health Information) concerns health records, and none were mentioned in the folder.

cards.front:
Which of the following is an asymmetric function that generates a new and separate key every time it runs?
A. RSA
B. DSA
C. DHE
D. HMAC
E. PBKDF2
cards.back:
C. DHE

Although Diffie-Hellman key agreement itself is a non-authenticated key-agreement protocol, it provides the basis for a variety of authenticated protocols, and is used to provide forward secrecy in Transport Layer Security's ephemeral modes (referred to as EDH...
cards.why: DHE (Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral) is an asymmetric key exchange that generates a new, separate key pair for every session, which provides forward secrecy.

whyNot.A: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) normally uses a long-term key pair, so it does not generate a new key every time it runs.
whyNot.B: DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) creates digital signatures with a long-term key pair and does not generate a new key per run.
whyNot.D: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) is a symmetric integrity function that uses a shared secret key, not an asymmetric function.
whyNot.E: PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) stretches a password into a key and is not an asymmetric function.

cards.front:
Which of the following would be considered multifactor authentication?
A. Hardware token and smart card
B. Voice recognition and retina scan
C. Strong password and fingerprint
D. PIN and security questions
cards.why: MFA (Multifactor Authentication) requires two different factor categories. A strong password is something you know and a fingerprint is something you are.

whyNot.A: A hardware token and a smart card are both something you have, so this is only one factor category.
whyNot.B: Voice recognition and a retina scan are both biometrics (something you are), so this is only one factor category.
whyNot.D: A PIN (Personal Identification Number) and security questions are both something you know, so this is only one factor category.

cards.front:
Users report the following message appear when browsing to the company's secure site: This website cannot be trusted. Which of the following actions should a security analyst take to resolve these messages? (Select TWO)
A. Verify the certificate has not expired on the server
B. Ensure the certificate has a .pfx extension on the server
C. Update the root certificate into the client computer certificate store
D. Install the updated private key on the web server
E. Have users clear their browsing history and relaunch the session
cards.back:
A. Verify the certificate has not expired on the server
C. Update the root certificate into the client computer certificate store
cards.why: An expired server certificate fails validation, and a client that lacks the issuing root CA (Certificate Authority) certificate cannot build a trust chain. Both cause a 'cannot be trusted' warning.

whyNot.B: A .pfx (Personal Information Exchange) extension only describes the file format and does not affect whether clients trust the certificate.
whyNot.D: The private key stays on the server and is not what clients use to validate trust, so replacing it does not fix the warning.
whyNot.E: Clearing browsing history does not change certificate validity or the client's trusted root certificate store.

cards.front:
Despite having implemented password policies, users continue to set the same weak passwords and reuse old passwords. Which of the following technical controls would help prevent these policy violations?
A. Password expiration
B. Password length
C. Password complexity
D. Password history
E. Password lockout
cards.back:
A. Password expiration
D. Password history
cards.why: Password history blocks users from reusing old passwords, which directly addresses reuse. Password expiration forces periodic changes, which the key treats as the second control.

whyNot.B: Password length sets a minimum size, but users can still choose a long, weak, or previously used password.
whyNot.C: Password complexity enforces a mix of character types, but users can still pick predictable passwords that meet the rule and can still reuse old ones.
whyNot.E: Password lockout limits failed login attempts and does not control which passwords users choose or reuse.

cards.keyDoubt: C and D: password complexity blocks weak passwords and password history blocks reuse, whereas password expiration prevents neither problem.

cards.front:
A security auditor is testing perimeter security in a building that is protected by badge readers. Which of the following types of attacks would MOST likely gain access?
A. Phishing
B. Man-in-the-middle
C. Tailgating
D. Watering hole
E. Shoulder surfing
cards.why: Tailgating (following an authorized person through a door) bypasses badge readers because the attacker never needs a valid badge.

whyNot.A: Phishing is a deceptive message attack delivered electronically and does not defeat a physical badge reader.
whyNot.B: A Man-in-the-Middle attack intercepts network traffic and does not gain physical entry through a badge-protected door.
whyNot.D: A watering hole attack compromises a website that targets visit and is not a physical entry technique.
whyNot.E: Shoulder surfing observes someone entering secrets, and badge readers do not rely on a secret an observer could read.

cards.front:
Which of the following encryption methods does PKI typically use to securely protect keys?
A. Elliptic curve
B. Digital signatures
C. Asymmetric
D. Obfuscation
cards.why: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) relies on asymmetric encryption, where a public and private key pair protects keys and establishes trust.

whyNot.A: Elliptic curve is one specific asymmetric algorithm family, not the general encryption method PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) uses.
whyNot.B: Digital signatures provide authenticity and integrity and are not an encryption method that protects keys.
whyNot.D: Obfuscation hides or scrambles data without strong cryptography and does not securely protect keys.

cards.front:
A department head at a university resigned on the first day of spring semester. It was subsequently determined that the department head deleted numerous files and directories from the server-based home directory while the campus was closed. Which of the following policies or procedures could have prevented this form occurring?
A. Time-of-day restrictions
B. Permissions auditing and review
C. Offboarding
D. Account expiration
cards.why: Offboarding procedures disable or remove a departing employee's accounts and access at separation, so the former department head could not have deleted files after resigning.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions limit login hours, but the campus closure would not stop a user whose account was still active remotely.
whyNot.B: Permissions auditing and review finds excessive rights periodically and does not remove access at the moment of resignation.
whyNot.D: Account expiration only works if an end date was preset, and a sudden resignation date is not known in advance.

cards.front:
An organization wants to upgrade its enterprise-wide desktop computer solution. The organization currently has 500 PCs active on the network. the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) suggests that the organization employ desktop imaging technology for such a large scale upgrade. Which of the following is a security benefit of implementing an imaging solution?
A. it allows for faster deployment
B. it provides a consistent baseline
C. It reduces the number of vulnerabilities
D. It decreases the boot time
cards.back: B. it provides a consistent baseline
cards.why: Imaging deploys every PC (personal computer) from the same hardened master image, which gives a consistent security baseline across all 500 systems.

whyNot.A: Faster deployment is an operational convenience and not in itself a security benefit.
whyNot.C: Imaging does not reduce vulnerabilities by itself, because the image can contain flaws or become outdated.
whyNot.D: Decreased boot time is a performance matter and is not a security benefit.

cards.front:
A senior incident response manager receives a call about some external IPs communicating with internal computers during off hours. Which of the following types of malware is MOST likely causing this issue?
A. Botnet
B. Ransomware
C. Polymorphic malware
D. Armored virus
cards.why: A botnet is a group of compromised computers that communicate with external command and control servers, often at off hours, which matches external IPs (Internet Protocol addresses) contacting internal machines.

whyNot.B: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, and its main symptom is locked data rather than off-hours outside communication.
whyNot.C: Polymorphic malware changes its code to evade antivirus detection, which describes evasion and not external communication.
whyNot.D: An armored virus uses techniques to resist analysis and reverse engineering, which does not explain external communication.

cards.front:
An organization has implemented an IPSec VPN access for remote users. Which of the following IPSec modes would be the MOST secure for this organization to implement?
A. Tunnel mode
B. Transport mode
C. AH-only mode
D. ESP-only mode
cards.back:
A. Tunnel mode

In both ESP and AH cases with IPSec Transport mode, the IP header is exposed. The IP header is not exposed in IPSec Tunnel mode.
cards.why: IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) tunnel mode encapsulates and protects the entire original packet, including its headers, which makes it the most secure choice for remote user VPN (Virtual Private Network) access.

whyNot.B: Transport mode protects only the payload and leaves the original IP (Internet Protocol) header exposed, so it is less secure.
whyNot.C: AH (Authentication Header) provides integrity and authentication but no encryption, so data remains readable.
whyNot.D: ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) alone does not specify tunnel mode, so original headers may remain exposed.

cards.front:
A security engineer is configuring a wireless network with EAP-TLS. Which of the following activities is a requirement for this configuration?
A. Setting up a TACACS+ server
B. Configuring federation between authentication servers
C. Enabling TOTP
D. Deploying certificates to endpoint devices
cards.back: D. Deploying certificates to endpoint devices
cards.why: EAP-TLS (Extensible Authentication Protocol-Transport Layer Security) uses mutual certificate authentication, so each endpoint device needs its own client certificate.

whyNot.A: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) is used for device administration and is not required for EAP-TLS.
whyNot.B: Federation between authentication servers is not required, because EAP-TLS works with certificates and a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server.
whyNot.C: TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) is a different authentication method and EAP-TLS does not use it.

cards.front:
Several workstations on a network are found to be on OS versions that are vulnerable to a specific attack. Which of the following is considered to be a corrective action to combat this vulnerability?
A. Install an antivirus definition patch
B. Educate the workstation users
C. Leverage server isolation
D. Install a vendor-supplied patch
E. Install an intrusion detection system
cards.why: Installing a vendor-supplied patch fixes the vulnerable operating system code, which is a corrective control because it removes the weakness itself.

whyNot.A: An antivirus definition update detects known malware and does not fix a vulnerability in the operating system.
whyNot.B: Educating users is an administrative, preventive measure and does not fix the vulnerable operating system.
whyNot.C: Server isolation limits exposure but leaves the vulnerable operating system unpatched, so it is a compensating control.
whyNot.E: An IDS (intrusion detection system) only detects attacks and does not correct the vulnerability.

cards.front:
A user suspects someone has been accessing a home network without permission by spoofing the MAC address of an authorized system. While attempting to determine if an unauthorized user is logging into the home network, the user reviews the wireless router, which shows the following table for systems that are currently on the home network: Hostname IP Address MAC MAC Filter DadPC 192.168.1.15 00:1D:1A:44:17:B5 On MomPC 192.168.1.15 21:13:D6:C5:42:A2 Off JuniorPC 192.168.2.16 42:A7:D1:25:11:52 On Unknown 192.168.1.18 10:B3:22:1A:FF:21 Off Which of the following should be the NEXT step to determine if there is an unauthorized user on the network?
A. Apply MAC filtering and see if the router drops any of the systems
B. Physically check each of the authorized systems to determine if they are logged onto the network
C. Deny the "unknown" host because the hostname is not known and MAC filtering is not applied to this host
D. Conduct a ping sweep of each of the authorized systems and see if an echo response is received
cards.back:
B. Physically check each of the authorized systems to determine if they are logged onto the network

Dad's PC and Mom's PC have the same IP address. One of them is doing ARP spoofing.
cards.why: Physically checking each authorized system shows which ones are actually connected, so any extra entry on the router table can be identified as an unauthorized device.

whyNot.A: Applying MAC (Media Access Control) filtering can be defeated by spoofing and does not show who is currently connected.
whyNot.C: Blocking a host only because its name is unknown is a guess and does not establish whether anyone is unauthorized.
whyNot.D: A ping sweep (ICMP, Internet Control Message Protocol, echo requests) only shows which addresses respond and cannot distinguish a spoofed device from the real one.

cards.front:
The POODLE attack is an MITM exploit that affects:
A. TLS1.0 with CBC mode cipher
B. SSLv2.0 with CBC mode cipher
C. SSLv3.0 with CBC mode cipher
D. SSLv3.0 with ECB mode cipher
cards.back:
C. SSLv3.0 with CBC mode cipher

A flaw was found in the way SSL 3.0 handled padding bytes when decrypting messages encrypted using block ciphers in cipher block chaining (CBC) mode.
cards.why: POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption) exploits the padding handling of CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode ciphers in SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) version 3.0, using a forced protocol downgrade.

whyNot.A: TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.0 was not the original POODLE target, which was SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) version 3.0.
whyNot.B: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) version 2.0 is a different, older protocol with other flaws and is not the POODLE target.
whyNot.D: ECB (Electronic Codebook) mode is not the cipher mode POODLE abuses, because the attack depends on CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) padding.

cards.front:
Security administrators attempted corrective action after a phishing attack. Users are still experiencing trouble logging in, as well as an increase in account lockouts. Users' email contacts are complaining of an increase in spam and social networking requests. Due to the large number of affected accounts, remediation must be accomplished quickly. Which of the following actions should be taken FIRST? (Select TWO)
A. Disable the compromised accounts
B. Update WAF rules to block social networks
C. Remove the compromised accounts with all AD groups
D. Change the compromised accounts' passwords
E. Disable the open relay on the email server
F. Enable sender policy framework
cards.back:
E. Disable the open relay on the email server
F. Enable sender policy framework

Sender Policy Framework (SPF) is a simple email-validation system designed to detect email spoofing by providing a mechanism to allow receiving mail exchangers to check that incoming mail from a domain comes from a host authorized by that domain's administrato...
cards.why: An open mail relay lets attackers send spam through the server, and SPF (Sender Policy Framework) blocks forged senders. Both are quick, server-wide fixes for many affected accounts.

whyNot.A: Disabling the compromised accounts helps but is slow across many accounts and does not stop the open relay.
whyNot.B: Updating WAF (Web Application Firewall) rules to block social networks does not stop email spam or the lockouts.
whyNot.C: Removing the accounts from every AD (Active Directory) group is slow and disruptive and does not stop spam relaying.
whyNot.D: Changing passwords for many accounts is slow and does not stop an open relay or sender forgery.

cards.keyDoubt: A and D: disabling the compromised accounts and resetting their passwords stops attacker access first, while an open relay and SPF (Sender Policy Framework) do not explain the login trouble.

cards.front:
Ann, a security administrator, wants to ensure credentials are encrypted in transit when implementing a RADIUS server for SSO. Which of the following are needed given these requirements? (Select TWO)
A. Public key
B. Shared key
C. Elliptic curve
D. MD5
E. Private key
F. DES
cards.back:
A. Public key
E. Private key
cards.why: Encrypting credentials in transit for a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) SSO (Single Sign-On) deployment relies on PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) asymmetric cryptography, where the public key encrypts the session and the private key decrypts it.

whyNot.B: A shared key is symmetric and only protects the RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server-to-client link, not the credentials end to end, so it is not the pair this question wants.
whyNot.C: Elliptic curve is a type of algorithm, not a key that must be provisioned to protect credentials in transit.
whyNot.D: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is a hashing algorithm that provides integrity, not encryption, and it is considered weak.
whyNot.F: DES (Data Encryption Standard) is an obsolete symmetric cipher with a short key and should not protect credentials.

cards.front:
Which of the following allows an auditor to test proprietary-software compiled code for security flaws?
A. Fuzzing
B. Static review
C. Code signing
D. Regression testing
cards.why: Fuzzing sends malformed or random input to a running program, so an auditor can find crashes and security flaws in compiled code without needing the source.

whyNot.B: Static review examines source code or disassembly without running it, and it generally needs source access for proprietary software.
whyNot.C: Code signing proves who published the code and that it was not altered, but it does not test for flaws.
whyNot.D: Regression testing confirms that earlier functionality still works after changes, and it is not a security flaw discovery method.

cards.front:
Which of the following s the BEST reason to run an untested application is a sandbox?
A. To allow the application to take full advantage of the host system's resources and storage
B. To utilize the host systems antivirus and firewall applications instead of running it own protection
C. To prevent the application from acquiring escalated privileges and accessing its host system
D. To increase application processing speed so the host system can perform real-time logging
cards.back: C. To prevent the application from acquiring escalated privileges and accessing its host system
cards.why: A sandbox isolates an untested application from the host, which prevents it from escalating privileges or reaching the host system's files and processes if it is malicious or buggy.

whyNot.A: Sandboxing deliberately restricts resource and storage access rather than granting full access to the host.
whyNot.B: A sandbox provides isolation by design, and relying on the host's antivirus and firewall is not its purpose.
whyNot.D: Sandboxing adds overhead and does not speed up processing or support real-time logging.

cards.front:
A manager wants to distribute a report to several other managers within the company. Some of them reside in remote locations that are not connected to the domain but have a local server. Because there is sensitive data within the report and the size is beyond the limit of the email attachment size, emailing the report is not an option. Which of the following protocols should be implemented to distribute the report securely? (Select THREE)
A. S/MIME
B. SSH
C. SNMPv3
D. FTPS
E. SRTP
F. HTTPS
G. LDAPS
cards.back:
B. SSH
D. FTPS
F. HTTPS
cards.why: SSH (Secure Shell) enables encrypted file transfer through SCP (Secure Copy) or SFTP (Secure File Transfer Protocol), FTPS (File Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts file transfers with TLS (Transport Layer Security), and HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts web downloads. All can send large sensitive files to remote servers.

whyNot.A: S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) secures email content, but email is ruled out because of the attachment size limit.
whyNot.C: SNMPv3 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 3) secures network device management and monitoring, not file distribution.
whyNot.E: SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) protects voice and video streams, not file transfers.
whyNot.G: LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol Secure) secures directory queries, not report distribution.

cards.front:
A company is performing an analysis of the corporate enterprise network with the intent of identifying what will cause losses in revenue, referrals, and/or reputation when out of commission. Which of the following is an element of a BIA that is being addressed?
A. Mission-essential function
B. Single point of failure
C. backup and restoration plans
D. Identification of critical systems
cards.back:
D. Identification of critical systems

The BIA is composed of the following three steps: Determine mission/business processes and recovery criticality.
cards.why: Identifying which systems cause revenue, referral, and reputation losses when unavailable is the identification of critical systems, a core element of a BIA (Business Impact Analysis).

whyNot.A: A mission-essential function is a business activity that must continue, whereas this scenario analyzes the systems whose outage causes losses.
whyNot.B: A single point of failure is a component whose failure stops a service, which is a different analysis from assessing business impact.
whyNot.C: Backup and restoration plans are recovery measures that come after the BIA (Business Impact Analysis) identifies what matters.

cards.front:
Ann, a user, states that her machine has been behaving erratically over the past week. She has experienced slowness and input lag and found text files that appear to contain pieces of her emails or online conversations with coworkers. The technician runs a standard virus scan but detects nothing. Which of the following types of malware has infected the machine?
A. Ransomware
B. Rootkit
C. Backdoor
D. Keylogger
cards.why: A keylogger secretly records keystrokes and saves them to files, which explains the text files containing pieces of emails and conversations, along with the slowness and input lag.

whyNot.A: Ransomware (malware that encrypts files for payment) announces itself and locks files, and it does not capture typed text.
whyNot.B: A rootkit hides malware presence and could conceal a keylogger, but it does not itself record typed text into files.
whyNot.C: A backdoor gives an attacker remote access, but it does not by itself record typed conversations into text files.

cards.front:
A security analyst is attempting to identify vulnerabilities in a customer's web application without impacting the system or its data. Which of the following BEST describes the vulnerability scanning concept performed?
A. Aggressive scan
B. Passive scan
C. Non-credentialed scan
D. Compliance scan
cards.back:
B. Passive scan

Passive scanning is a method of vulnerability detection that relies on information gleaned from network data that is captured from a target computer without direct interaction.
cards.why: A passive scan observes traffic and system information without sending probes or exploit attempts, so it finds vulnerabilities without impacting the web application or its data.

whyNot.A: An aggressive scan sends many probes and tests, which can disrupt the system or alter its data.
whyNot.C: A non-credentialed scan describes access level (no login), not whether the scan is non-impacting, and it still sends active probes.
whyNot.D: A compliance scan checks configuration against a policy or standard, and it does not define impact on the system.

cards.front:
A systems administrator wants to implement a wireless protocol that will allow the organization to authenticate mobile devices prior to providing the user with a captive portal login. Which of the following should the systems administrator configure?
A. L2TP with MAC filtering
B. EAP-TTLS
C. WPA2-CCMP with PSK
D. RADIUS federation
cards.back:
D. RADIUS federation

RADIUS generally includes 802.1X that pre-authenticates devices.
cards.why: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) federation lets the organization authenticate devices or users through a trusted authentication server before the captive portal login is presented.

whyNot.A: L2TP (Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol) is a VPN (Virtual Private Network) tunneling protocol, and MAC (Media Access Control) filtering is easily spoofed and is not a wireless authentication protocol.
whyNot.B: EAP-TTLS (Extensible Authentication Protocol Tunneled Transport Layer Security) authenticates users in a TLS tunnel, but it is not the federated pre-portal device authentication being asked about.
whyNot.C: WPA2-CCMP (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 with Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol) with a PSK (Pre-Shared Key) uses one shared password and does not authenticate individual devices.

cards.front:
A user receives an email from ISP indicating malicious traffic coming from the user's home network is detected. The traffic appears to be Linux-based, and it is targeting a website that was recently featured on the news as being taken offline by an Internet attack. The only Linux device on the network is a home surveillance camera system. Which of the following BEST describes what is happening?
A. The camera system is infected with a bot.
B. The camera system is infected with a RAT.
C. The camera system is infected with a Trojan.
D. The camera system is infected with a backdoor.
cards.back: A. The camera system is infected with a bot.
cards.why: A compromised Internet-connected camera that sends attack traffic to a target is a bot, a device under remote control as part of a botnet used for DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attacks.

whyNot.B: A RAT (Remote Access Trojan) gives an attacker interactive control of a victim, but it does not describe the device being used to flood another site.
whyNot.C: A Trojan is malware disguised as legitimate software, which describes how it got in rather than the attack behavior shown.
whyNot.D: A backdoor is a hidden access method, and it does not explain the device sending attack traffic at a third party.

cards.front:
While on a business trip, a user's mobile device goes missing. The user immediately contacts the organization's service desk to report the incident. Which of the following actions is the best response to protect the data stored on the user's mobile device.
A. Encrypt all of the data on the device
B. Remotely wipe the mobile device via the mobile device manager to ensure the data is not compromised.
C. Report the device as lost or stolen to the authorities
D. Call the help desk to change your password
cards.back: B. Remotely wipe the mobile device via the mobile device manager to ensure the data is not compromised.
cards.why: Remotely wiping the device through the MDM (Mobile Device Management) system destroys the stored data right away, which is the best protection when the device is missing and out of the owner's control.

whyNot.A: Encrypting the data on a device you no longer physically hold cannot be done reliably and does not remove the data.
whyNot.C: Reporting to the authorities may help recover the device but does nothing to protect the data on it.
whyNot.D: Changing the password protects the account but does not protect data stored locally on the device.

cards.front:
A security analyst launches the Task Manager on a server with poor performance, and notices private bytes are being exhausted and the application pool is constantly recycling. Which of the following Best describes the cause of the negative impact to application availability?
A. Integer Overflow
B. Buffer Overflow
C. Race Condition
D. Memory Leaks
cards.back:
D. Memory Leaks

Private Bytes refer to the amount of memory that the process executable has asked for - not necessarily the amount it is actually using. They are "private" because they (usually) exclude memory-mapped files (i.e. shared DLLs).
cards.why: Private bytes being exhausted and the application pool constantly recycling indicates a memory leak, where the application allocates memory and never releases it until resources run out.

whyNot.A: An integer overflow occurs when arithmetic exceeds a variable's range and causes wrong values, not steady exhaustion of memory.
whyNot.B: A buffer overflow writes past allocated memory and typically causes crashes or code execution, not gradual private byte growth.
whyNot.C: A race condition arises from timing conflicts between processes or threads, and it does not cause continuous memory growth.

cards.front:
While trying to manage a firewall's ACL, a security administrator (User3) receives an "Access Denied" error. The manager reviews the following information. Security_admins: User1, User2 Firewall Access ACL Read: Security_admins ACL Write: Security_admins Reboot: Managers Audit: User3 Which of the following is preventing the administrator from
A. Rule based access control
B. Mandatory access control
C. Discretionary access's control
D. RBAC
cards.why: Access is decided by the rules in the ACL (Access Control List), which grants User3 only the Audit permission, so management requests are denied by rule.

whyNot.B: MAC (Mandatory Access Control) uses security labels and clearances set by the system, and no labels appear in the listing.
whyNot.C: DAC (Discretionary Access Control) lets the resource owner grant access at their discretion, which is not what the fixed rules show.
whyNot.D: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) assigns permissions by job role, but the listing shows rules per resource operation rather than role definitions.

cards.front:
Which of the following are the differences between incremental and differential backups?
A. Both backup types or almost identical except for the time that the backup is run
B. Differential backup take less time to complete
C. Incremental backups take less time than differential
D. Incremental backup back up all of the data since the last differential
E. Differential backups take more time to restore than incremental backups
F. Differential backups only backup files since the last full backup
cards.back:
C. Incremental backups take less time than differential
F. Differential backups only backup files since the last full backup
cards.why: Incremental backups copy only data changed since the last backup of any type, so they run faster. Differential backups copy everything changed since the last full backup.

whyNot.A: The two types differ in what they copy, not just in when they run.
whyNot.B: Differential backups grow larger each day because they repeat earlier changes, so they take longer, not less time.
whyNot.D: Incremental backups copy data since the last backup of any type, not since the last differential.
whyNot.E: Differential restores are faster, needing only the full backup plus the latest differential, while incremental restores need every increment.

cards.front:
A security analyst has been dealing with a large number of malware infections on workstations with legacy operating systems. The infections are not being detected by the current AV suite. Further analysis shows that the signatures are up to date and the AV engines are functioning correctly. The company is unable to afford next-generation AV that prevents these attacks. Which of the following methods should the security analyst employ to prevent future outbreaks?
A. Application Blacklisting
B. Application Whitelisting
C. Blockchain analysis
D. Strong ACL's
cards.why: Application whitelisting allows only approved programs to run, so unknown malware that signature-based antivirus misses cannot execute on legacy workstations, and it needs no costly next-generation antivirus.

whyNot.A: Application blacklisting blocks only known bad programs, so new or unknown malware that antivirus missed would still run.
whyNot.C: Blockchain analysis tracks cryptocurrency transactions and does not stop malware from executing.
whyNot.D: Strong ACLs (Access Control Lists) restrict access to resources but do not stop a program the user runs from executing.

cards.front:
A network administrator is reviewing the following IDS logs: Based on the above information, which of the following types of malware is triggering the IDS?
A. Trojan
B. Bot
C. Logic Bomb
D. Worm
cards.why: As keyed, the IDS (Intrusion Detection System) log pattern matches a worm, which is malware that replicates and spreads across the network on its own without user action.

whyNot.A: A Trojan is disguised malware that depends on the user running it and does not spread by itself across the network.
whyNot.B: A bot connects to a command and control server and awaits orders, which is different from self-propagating scanning behavior.
whyNot.C: A logic bomb activates on a specific time or condition and does not generate spreading network traffic.

cards.front:
