A security analyst is checking the bash command history on a Linux host that was involved in a data breach. The data breach stemmed from the Linux host running a series of commands against a web server on the internal network, which exploited a vulnerability in an unpatched Apache module. Given this scenario, which of the following commands might the analyst find in the bash command history for banner grabbing? (Select Three)
A. Arp
B. Tracert
C. NMAP
D. Net Cat (NC)
E. Telnet
F. Grep
G. Nslookup
H. Netstat
cards.back:
C. NMAP
D. Net Cat (NC)
E. Telnet
cards.why: Banner grabbing connects to a service and reads the identifying greeting it returns. NMAP (Network Mapper) with version detection, Netcat (NC), and Telnet can each open a connection to a port and show the Apache banner.

whyNot.A: Arp (Address Resolution Protocol) shows or edits the table mapping IP (Internet Protocol) addresses to MAC (Media Access Control) addresses, so it cannot read a service banner.
whyNot.B: Tracert (Trace Route) maps the router hops to a destination and does not connect to a service port to read its banner.
whyNot.F: Grep (Global Regular Expression Print) only searches text for patterns and makes no network connection to the web server.
whyNot.G: Nslookup (Name Server Lookup) queries DNS (Domain Name System) for name and address records and does not return a service banner.
whyNot.H: Netstat (Network Statistics) lists the local host's connections and listening ports and does not probe a remote server for banners.

cards.front:
Which of the following would a security specialist be able to determine upon examination of a server's certificate?
A. CA public key
B. Server private key
C. CSR
D. OID
cards.why: A server certificate lists OIDs (Object Identifiers) that identify the signature algorithm, key usages, and policies, so they are visible on examination. The other items are not found in the server's certificate.

whyNot.A: The Certificate Authority's public key sits in the Certificate Authority's own certificate; the server certificate only carries the server's public key and the Certificate Authority's signature.
whyNot.B: A server's private key is never placed in a certificate and must always be kept secret.
whyNot.C: A CSR (Certificate Signing Request) is a separate file sent to the Certificate Authority before issuance, not part of the issued certificate.

cards.front:
A security analyst is diagnosing an incident in which a system was compromised from an external IP address. The socket identified on the firewall was traced to 207.46.130.0:6666. Which of the following should the security analyst do to determine if the compromised system still has an active connection?
A. tracert
B. netstat
C. ping
D. nslookup
cards.why: The netstat command lists current network sockets and connection states, so the analyst can check whether the compromised system still has an established connection to 207.46.130.0 on port 6666.

whyNot.A: The tracert command only maps router hops toward a destination and does not show active connections on the local system.
whyNot.C: The ping command tests reachability with ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo and does not show connection state or sockets.
whyNot.D: The nslookup command queries DNS (Domain Name System) records and does not display active connections.

cards.front:
Multiple organizations operating in the same vertical want to provide seamless wireless access for their employees as they visit the other organizations. Which of the following should be implemented if all the organizations use the native 802.1x client on their mobile devices?
A. Shibboleth
B. RADIUS federation
C. SAML
D. OAuth
E. OpenID connect
cards.why: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) federation lets organizations trust each other's authentication servers, so visiting employees authenticate through their home organization using the native 802.1X port-based network access control client.

whyNot.A: Shibboleth is a web single sign-on system built on SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) and is not used by native 802.1X wireless clients.
whyNot.C: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) is a browser-based federation standard and is not spoken by native 802.1X wireless supplicants.
whyNot.D: OAuth (Open Authorization) delegates access to web resources and APIs (Application Programming Interfaces), not network access authentication.
whyNot.E: OpenID Connect is an authentication layer on top of OAuth (Open Authorization) for web applications, not for 802.1X wireless access.

cards.front:
Which of the following BEST describes an important security advantage yielded by implementing vendor diversity?
A. Sustainability
B. Homogeneity
C. Resiliency
D. Configurability
cards.why: Vendor diversity means using products from multiple vendors, so a single vendor's flaw, outage, or exploit does not take down every system. This improves resiliency.

whyNot.A: Sustainability concerns long-term environmental or operational viability and is not the security advantage of using multiple vendors.
whyNot.B: Homogeneity is the opposite of vendor diversity; relying on one vendor creates common vulnerabilities across all systems.
whyNot.D: Configurability describes how flexible a product's settings are and is not a result of vendor diversity.

cards.front:
In a corporation where compute utilization spikes several times a year, the Chief Information Officer (CIO) has requested a cost-effective architecture to handle the variable capacity demand. Which of the following characteristics BEST describes what the CIO has requested?
A. Elasticity
B. Scalability
C. High availability
D. Redundancy
cards.back:
A. Elasticity

Elasticity is defined as "the degree to which a system is able to adapt to workload changes by provisioning and de-provisioning resources in an autonomic manner, such that at each point in time the available resources match the current demand as closely as pos...
cards.why: Elasticity is the ability to automatically add and remove compute capacity as demand changes, so the company pays for extra capacity only during the few yearly spikes.

whyNot.B: Scalability is the ability to grow capacity for sustained growth and does not imply releasing resources after short spikes to save cost.
whyNot.C: High availability keeps services running with minimal downtime and does not address matching capacity to variable demand.
whyNot.D: Redundancy duplicates components for failover and would be costly if built permanently for rare peak loads.

cards.front:
A security engineer is configuring a system that requires the X.509 certificate information to be pasted into a form field in Base64 encoded format to import it into the system. Which of the following certificate formats should the engineer use to obtain the information in the required format?
A. PFX
B. PEM
C. DER
D. CER
cards.why: PEM (Privacy-Enhanced Mail) is the certificate format that stores the X.509 certificate as Base64 encoded ASCII text between BEGIN and END lines, so it can be pasted into a form field.

whyNot.A: PFX (Personal Information Exchange) is a binary container that can bundle the certificate and private key, so it is not pasteable Base64 text.
whyNot.C: DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules) is a binary encoding and cannot be pasted as readable Base64 text.
whyNot.D: CER (certificate file extension) may hold either DER binary or Base64 data, so it does not guarantee the required Base64 format.

cards.front:
Which of the following attacks specifically impacts data availability?
A. DDoS
B. Trojan
C. MITM
D. Rootkit
cards.why: A DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack floods a target with traffic from many sources so legitimate users cannot reach it, directly attacking availability.

whyNot.B: A Trojan is malware disguised as legitimate software that mainly provides unauthorized access, which threatens confidentiality rather than availability.
whyNot.C: A MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attack intercepts or alters traffic, targeting confidentiality and integrity rather than availability.
whyNot.D: A rootkit hides malicious activity and maintains privileged access, so it does not specifically target availability.

cards.front:
A security analyst is hardening a server with the directory services role installed. The analyst must ensure LDAP traffic cannot be monitored or sniffed and maintains compatibility with LDAP clients. Which of the following should the analyst implement to meet these requirements? (Select two.)
A. Generate an X.509-compliant certificate that is signed by a trusted CA.
B. Install and configure an SSH tunnel on the LDAP server.
C. Ensure port 389 is open between the clients and the servers using the communication.
D. Ensure port 636 is open between the clients and the servers using the communication.
E. Remote the LDAP directory service role from the server.
cards.back:
A. Generate an X.509-compliant certificate that is signed by a trusted CA.
D. Ensure port 636 is open between the clients and the servers using the communication.
cards.why: A certificate signed by a trusted CA (Certificate Authority) enables LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol over Secure Sockets Layer or Transport Layer Security), and port 636 carries LDAPS, so traffic is encrypted and clients stay compatible.

whyNot.B: An SSH (Secure Shell) tunnel is not native to LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) clients, so it hurts compatibility and adds configuration burden.
whyNot.C: Port 389 carries plaintext LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), which can be monitored or sniffed unless StartTLS (Transport Layer Security upgrade) is used.
whyNot.E: Removing the directory services role disables the service entirely and does not secure LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) traffic.

cards.front:
Which of the following threat actors is MOST likely to steal a company's proprietary information to gain a market edge and reduce time to market?
A. Competitor
B. Hacktivist
C. Insider
D. Organized crime.
cards.why: A competitor is motivated to steal proprietary information to gain a market edge and shorten its own time to market, which is classic industrial espionage.

whyNot.B: Hacktivists are driven by political or social causes, not by gaining a competitive advantage in the market.
whyNot.C: An insider threat is usually driven by revenge, financial gain, or negligence, and is not specifically aimed at speeding up a rival's product release.
whyNot.D: Organized crime seeks direct financial profit, such as through ransom or selling stolen data, rather than market advantage.

cards.front:
A penetration tester is crawling a target website that is available to the public. Which of the following represents the actions the penetration tester is performing?
A. URL hijacking
B. Reconnaissance
C. White box testing
D. Escalation of privilege
cards.why: Crawling a public website to gather information about its structure and content is reconnaissance, the information-gathering phase of a penetration test.

whyNot.A: URL hijacking, also called typosquatting, means registering look-alike domain names to trick users, which is not what a crawler does.
whyNot.C: White box testing means the tester has full internal knowledge such as source code, and crawling a public site does not imply that.
whyNot.D: Escalation of privilege means gaining higher access rights than granted, and merely crawling public pages does not do that.

cards.front:
Which of the following characteristics differentiate a rainbow table attack from a brute force attack? (Select two.)
A. Rainbow table attacks greatly reduce compute cycles at attack time.
B. Rainbow tables must include precomputed hashes.
C. Rainbow table attacks do not require access to hashed passwords.
D. Rainbow table attacks must be performed on the network.
E. Rainbow table attacks bypass maximum failed login restrictions.
cards.back:
B. Rainbow tables must include precomputed hashes.
E. Rainbow table attacks bypass maximum failed login restrictions.
cards.why: Rainbow tables must contain precomputed hashes, and because they are used offline against stolen hashes they avoid maximum failed login restrictions such as account lockouts.

whyNot.A: This is also a true advantage, since lookup replaces hashing at attack time, though the answer key does not count it.
whyNot.C: Rainbow table attacks absolutely require the hashed passwords, because the table is matched against captured hash values.
whyNot.D: Rainbow table attacks are performed offline against captured hashes and do not need to run over the network.

cards.keyDoubt: A rather than E: reduced compute at attack time is the defining difference from brute force, while bypassing lockouts applies equally to any offline cracking, including offline brute force.

cards.front:
Which of the following best describes routine in which semicolons, dashes, quotes, and commas are removed from a string?
A. Error handling to protect against program exploitation
B. Exception handling to protect against XSRF attacks.
C. Input validation to protect against SQL injection.
D. Padding to protect against string buffer overflows.
cards.back: C. Input validation to protect against SQL injection.
cards.why: Stripping semicolons, dashes, quotes, and commas is input validation or sanitization, which prevents attackers from injecting SQL (Structured Query Language) syntax into queries.

whyNot.A: Error handling deals with how an application reports and recovers from failures and does not remove special characters from input.
whyNot.B: Exception handling manages runtime errors and does not sanitize strings; XSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) is mitigated with anti-forgery tokens.
whyNot.D: Padding adds filler data and does not remove characters; buffer overflows are prevented by bounds checking.

cards.front:
A security analyst wishes to increase the security of an FTP server. Currently, all traffic to the FTP server is unencrypted. Users connecting to the FTP server use a variety of modern FTP client software. The security analyst wants to keep the same port and protocol, while also still allowing unencrypted connections. Which of the following would BEST accomplish these goals?
A. Require the SFTP protocol to connect to the file server.
B. Use implicit TLS on the FTP server.
C. Use explicit FTPS for connections.
D. Use SSH tunneling to encrypt the FTP traffic.
cards.back: C. Use explicit FTPS for connections.
cards.why: Explicit FTPS (File Transfer Protocol Secure) starts on the standard FTP port 21 and upgrades to TLS (Transport Layer Security) on request, so encrypted and unencrypted clients can both connect.

whyNot.A: SFTP (Secure Shell File Transfer Protocol) uses a different protocol and port 22 and does not allow unencrypted connections.
whyNot.B: Implicit TLS (Transport Layer Security) uses a separate port, commonly 990, and rejects unencrypted connections, so it fails the requirements.
whyNot.D: SSH (Secure Shell) tunneling requires extra client configuration, changes the connection port, and does not preserve the existing FTP (File Transfer Protocol) port and protocol behavior.

cards.front:
Which of the following explains why vendors publish MD5 values when they provide software patches for their customers to download over the Internet?
A. The recipient can verify integrity of the software patch.
B. The recipient can verify the authenticity of the site used to download the patch.
C. The recipient can request future updates to the software using the published MD5 value.
D. The recipient can successfully activate the new software patch.
cards.back: A. The recipient can verify integrity of the software patch.
cards.why: Publishing an MD5 (Message Digest 5) hash lets the recipient hash the downloaded patch and compare values, verifying that the file was not corrupted or altered, which is integrity.

whyNot.B: A hash does not authenticate the download site, because an attacker hosting a modified file could publish a matching hash alongside it.
whyNot.C: A hash value is not used to request updates; it only describes the contents of a specific file.
whyNot.D: Activating software requires a license key or similar mechanism, not an MD5 (Message Digest 5) hash value.

cards.front:
Refer to the following code: Which of the following vulnerabilities would occur if this is executed?
A. Page exception
B. Pointer deference
C. NullPointerException
D. Missing null check
cards.why: A missing null check means code uses a reference or pointer without verifying it is not null, which can cause a crash or undefined behavior. The code was not shown, so this assumes the key is correct.

whyNot.A: Page exception is not a standard vulnerability category; it would at most be a symptom of a memory fault.
whyNot.B: Pointer dereference is the operation being performed; the vulnerability is the lack of a check before it happens.
whyNot.C: NullPointerException is the runtime error that results when the check is missing, not the underlying vulnerability.

cards.front:
Multiple employees receive an email with a malicious attachment that begins to encrypt their hard drives and mapped shares on their devices when it is opened. The network and security teams perform the following actions: Shut down all network shares. Run an email search identifying all employees who received the malicious message. Reimage all devices belonging to users who opened the attachment. Next, the teams want to re-enable the network shares. Which of the following BEST describes this phase of the incident response process?
A. Eradication
B. Containment
C. Recovery
D. Lessons learned
cards.why: Re-enabling the network shares after reimaging the infected devices is the Recovery phase of incident response, which restores normal operations once the threat has been removed.

whyNot.A: Eradication is removing the malware, which the reimaging already accomplished before this step.
whyNot.B: Containment is limiting the spread, which shutting down the shares and searching email already did.
whyNot.D: Lessons learned is the post-incident review phase and happens after services are restored.

cards.front:
An organization has determined it can tolerate a maximum of three hours of downtime. Which of the following has been specified?
A. RTO
B. RPO
C. MTBF
D. MTTR
cards.why: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum tolerable downtime before a system must be restored, which matches the three-hour limit.

whyNot.B: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time, not downtime.
whyNot.C: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) measures average operating time between failures, not tolerable downtime.
whyNot.D: MTTR (Mean Time To Repair) measures the average time to fix a failure, not the maximum downtime the business accepts.

cards.front:
Which of the following types of keys is found in a key escrow?
A. Public
B. Private
C. Shared
D. Session
cards.why: Key escrow stores copies of private keys with a trusted third party so encrypted data can be recovered if the owner loses access.

whyNot.A: Public keys are meant to be shared openly and do not need to be escrowed.
whyNot.C: Shared keys, also called symmetric keys, are typically exchanged between parties and are not the standard item held in key escrow.
whyNot.D: Session keys are temporary and discarded after one communication session, so escrowing them is not useful.

cards.front:
A security analyst is reviewing the following output from an IPS: Given this output, which of the following can be concluded? (Select two.)
A. The source IP of the attack is coming from 250.19.18.22.
B. The source IP of the attack is coming from 250.19.18.71.
C. The attacker sent a malformed IGAP packet, triggering the alert.
D. The attacker sent a malformed TCP packet, triggering the alert.
E. The TTL value is outside of the expected range, triggering the alert.
cards.back:
B. The source IP of the attack is coming from 250.19.18.71.
C. The attacker sent a malformed IGAP packet, triggering the alert.
cards.why: Based on the IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) output as keyed, the attack originates from 250.19.18.71 and the alert was triggered by a malformed packet of the type named in option C.

whyNot.A: The IP (Internet Protocol) address 250.19.18.22 is not the source of the attack according to the output.
whyNot.D: The output does not show a malformed TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) packet as the trigger for the alert.
whyNot.E: The TTL (Time To Live) value is not what triggered the alert in the IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) output.

cards.front:
Despite having implemented password policies, users continue to set the same weak passwords and reuse old passwords. Which of the following technical controls would help prevent these policy violations? (Select two.)
A. Password expiration
B. Password length
C. Password complexity
D. Password history
E. Password lockout
cards.back:
C. Password complexity
D. Password history
cards.why: Password complexity forces stronger passwords that mix character types, and password history blocks users from reusing old passwords, directly addressing both violations.

whyNot.A: Password expiration forces periodic changes but does not stop weak passwords or reuse of old ones.
whyNot.B: Password length requires a minimum number of characters but does not prevent reuse of old passwords.
whyNot.E: Password lockout limits failed login attempts and does not control password strength or reuse.

cards.front:
Which of the following types of cloud infrastructures would allow several organizations with similar structures and interests to realize the benefits of shared storage and resources?
A. Private
B. Hybrid
C. Public
D. Community
cards.why: A community cloud is shared by several organizations with similar structures, interests, or compliance needs, so they share storage and resources.

whyNot.A: A private cloud serves a single organization and is not shared among several.
whyNot.B: A hybrid cloud combines private and public clouds and is not designed for organizations with shared interests.
whyNot.C: A public cloud is open to the general public and is not limited to organizations with similar interests.

cards.front:
A company is currently using the following configuration: IAS server with certificate-based EAP-PEAP and MSCHAP Unencrypted authentication via PAP A security administrator needs to configure a new wireless setup with the following configurations: PAP authentication method PEAP and EAP provide two-factor authentication Which of the following forms of authentication are being used? (Select two.)
A. PAP
B. PEAP
C. MSCHAP
D. PEAP- MSCHAP
E. EAP
F. EAP-PEAP
cards.why: PAP (Password Authentication Protocol) and MSCHAP (Microsoft Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol) are the authentication methods named in the configurations; the others are tunneling or framework protocols.

whyNot.B: PEAP (Protected Extensible Authentication Protocol) is a tunneling method that protects another authentication protocol, not a basic authentication method itself.
whyNot.D: PEAP-MSCHAP (Protected Extensible Authentication Protocol with Microsoft Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol) is a combination, not one of the individual methods being asked for.
whyNot.E: EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) is a framework that carries authentication methods, not an authentication method itself.
whyNot.F: EAP-PEAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol with Protected Extensible Authentication Protocol) describes the wrapper rather than the underlying authentication methods.

cards.front:
An auditor wants to test the security posture of an organization by running a tool that will display the following: Which of the following commands should be used?
A. nbtstat
B. nc
C. arp
D. ipconfig
cards.why: nbtstat (NetBIOS over TCP/IP statistics) displays NetBIOS name tables and sessions, which an auditor uses to see what a host exposes on the network.

whyNot.B: nc (netcat) opens network connections and transfers data, and does not display NetBIOS statistics.
whyNot.C: arp (Address Resolution Protocol) shows the mapping of IP (Internet Protocol) addresses to MAC (Media Access Control) addresses only.
whyNot.D: ipconfig (Internet Protocol configuration) shows local interface settings and does not show NetBIOS statistics.

cards.front:
A company determines that it is prohibitively expensive to become compliant with new credit card regulations. Instead, the company decides to purchase insurance to cover the cost of any potential loss. Which of the following is the company doing?
A. Transferring the risk
B. Accepting the risk
C. Avoiding the risk
D. Migrating the risk
cards.why: Buying insurance shifts the financial impact of a potential loss to the insurer, which is risk transference.

whyNot.B: Risk acceptance means bearing the loss without outside help, but the company is buying insurance.
whyNot.C: Risk avoidance means stopping the risky activity altogether, which the company is not doing.
whyNot.D: Migrating the risk is not a standard risk response, and moving the loss to an insurer is called transference.

cards.front:
A company is using a mobile device deployment model in which employees use their personal devices for work at their own discretion. Some of the problems the company is encountering include the following: There is no standardization. Employees ask for reimbursement for their devices. Employees do not replace their devices often enough to keep them running efficiently. The company does not have enough control over the devices. Which of the following is a deployment model that would help the company overcome these problems?
A. BYOD
B. VDI
C. COPE
D. CYOD
cards.why: CYOD (Choose Your Own Device) lets employees pick from an approved list of company-purchased devices, giving standardization, company control, and managed replacement cycles.

whyNot.A: BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) is the model the company already uses and is the source of these problems.
whyNot.B: VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure) delivers virtual desktops and does not address who buys or chooses mobile devices.
whyNot.C: COPE (Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled) gives employees company-picked devices with no choice, so it does not match the standardization-with-selection need as well as CYOD (Choose Your Own Device).

cards.front:
A botnet has hit a popular website with a massive number of GRE-encapsulated packets to perform a DDoS attack. News outlets discover a certain type of refrigerator was exploited and used to send outbound packets to the website that crashed. To which of the following categories does the refrigerator belong?
A. SoC
B. ICS
C. IoT
D. MFD
cards.why: A smart refrigerator is a network-connected consumer appliance, which is an IoT (Internet of Things) device, and these are commonly hijacked into botnets.

whyNot.A: SoC (System on a Chip) is an integrated chip design, not a category of device like a refrigerator.
whyNot.B: ICS (Industrial Control System) refers to industrial and manufacturing process control, not household appliances.
whyNot.D: MFD (Multifunction Device) refers to printers that also scan, copy, and fax, not refrigerators.

cards.front:
Users report the following message appears when browsing to the company's secure site: This website cannot be trusted. Which of the following actions should a security analyst take to resolve these messages? (Select two.)
A. Verify the certificate has not expired on the server.
B. Ensure the certificate has a .pfx extension on the server.
C. Update the root certificate into the client computer certificate store.
D. Install the updated private key on the web server.
E. Have users clear their browsing history and relaunch the session.
cards.back:
A. Verify the certificate has not expired on the server.
C. Update the root certificate into the client computer certificate store.
cards.why: The trust warning is commonly caused by an expired server certificate or a client missing the issuing root certificate, so verify expiration and update the root certificate in the client store.

whyNot.B: The .pfx (Personal Information Exchange) file extension is only a file format and does not affect whether a browser trusts the certificate.
whyNot.D: Installing an updated private key on the web server does not fix trust, which depends on the certificate chain and validity.
whyNot.E: Clearing browsing history does not change certificate validity or the client's trusted root store.

cards.front:
When trying to log onto a company's new ticketing system, some employees receive the following message: Access denied: too many concurrent sessions. The ticketing system was recently installed on a small VM with only the recommended hardware specifications. Which of the following is the MOST likely cause for this error message?
A. Network resources have been exceeded.
B. The software is out of licenses.
C. The VM does not have enough processing power.
D. The firewall is misconfigured.
cards.back: C. The VM does not have enough processing power.
cards.why: The key says an under-resourced VM (Virtual Machine) lacks processing power. Hardware limits are the keyed cause of the concurrent session denial.

whyNot.A: Exceeded network resources would cause slowness or timeouts, not a concurrent session denial message.
whyNot.B: A licensing limit is the most direct cause of an access denied message about concurrent sessions.
whyNot.D: A misconfigured firewall would block connections entirely rather than return a concurrent session error.

cards.keyDoubt: B. A message saying too many concurrent sessions most directly indicates the software has run out of licensed sessions, not that the VM (Virtual Machine) lacks processing power.

cards.front:
Joe, an employee, wants to show his colleagues how much he knows about smartphones. Joe demonstrates a free movie application that he installed from a third party on his corporate smartphone. Joe's colleagues were unable to find the application in the app stores. Which of the following allowed Joe to install the application? (Select two.)
A. Near-field communication.
B. Rooting/jailbreaking
C. Ad-hoc connections
D. Tethering
E. Sideloading
cards.why: Rooting or jailbreaking removes vendor restrictions on the operating system, and sideloading installs apps from outside the official app stores, which together allow installing the third-party app.

whyNot.A: NFC (near-field communication) is a short-range wireless technology for data exchange and does not install apps from third parties.
whyNot.C: Ad-hoc connections are direct device-to-device wireless links and do not bypass app store restrictions.
whyNot.D: Tethering shares a device's internet connection and does not install unauthorized applications.

cards.front:
Which of the following can be provided to an AAA system for the identification phase?
A. Username
B. Permissions
C. One-time token
D. Private certificate
cards.why: In an AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) system, a username is the claimed identity supplied during the identification phase.

whyNot.B: Permissions are assigned during authorization, after the user has been identified and authenticated.
whyNot.C: A one-time token is a credential used to prove identity during authentication, not identification.
whyNot.D: A private certificate is used as proof of identity during authentication, not to claim identity during identification.

cards.front:
Which of the following implements two-factor authentication?
A. A phone system requiring a PIN to make a call
B. At ATM requiring a credit card and PIN
C. A computer requiring username and password
D. A datacenter mantrap requiring fingerprint and iris scan
cards.back: B. At ATM requiring a credit card and PIN
cards.why: An ATM (Automated Teller Machine) card is something you have and a PIN (Personal Identification Number) is something you know. Two different factor categories make this two-factor authentication.

whyNot.A: A PIN (Personal Identification Number) alone is a single knowledge factor, so this is only one-factor authentication.
whyNot.C: A username and password are both knowledge factors, so this is single-factor authentication, not two-factor.
whyNot.D: A fingerprint and an iris scan are both something-you-are biometrics, so this is the same factor type used twice.

cards.front:
Malicious traffic from an internal network has been detected on an unauthorized port on an application server. Which of the following network-based security controls should the engineer consider implementing?
A. ACLs
B. HIPS
C. NAT
D. MAC filtering
cards.why: ACLs (Access Control Lists) on routers, switches, or firewalls can block traffic on unauthorized ports. This is a network-based control that stops the malicious internal traffic.

whyNot.B: HIPS (Host-based Intrusion Prevention System) runs on the host itself, so it is not a network-based security control.
whyNot.C: NAT (Network Address Translation) maps IP (Internet Protocol) addresses and does not filter traffic by port to block malicious traffic.
whyNot.D: MAC (Media Access Control) filtering restricts devices by hardware address and does not control which ports traffic uses.

cards.front:
A network administrator wants to implement a method of securing internal routing. Which of the following should the administrator implement?
A. DMZ
B. NAT
C. VPN
D. PAT
cards.why: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) can authenticate and encrypt traffic between routers, protecting routing updates in transit. This secures the exchange of internal routing information.

whyNot.A: A DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) isolates public-facing servers and does not secure internal routing exchanges.
whyNot.B: NAT (Network Address Translation) rewrites addresses and provides no authentication or encryption for routing traffic.
whyNot.D: PAT (Port Address Translation) maps many internal addresses to one address using ports and does not secure routing.

cards.front:
A security administrator is developing controls for creating audit trails and tracking if a PHI data breach is to occur. The administrator has been given the following requirements: All access must be correlated to a user account. All user accounts must be assigned to a single individual. User access to the PHI data must be recorded. Anomalies in PHI data access must be reported. Logs and records cannot be deleted or modified. Which of the following should the administrator implement to meet the above requirements? (Select three.)
A. Eliminate shared accounts.
B. Create a standard naming convention for accounts.
C. Implement usage auditing and review.
D. Enable account lockout thresholds.
E. Copy logs in real time to a secured WORM drive.
F. Implement time-of-day restrictions.
G. Perform regular permission audits and reviews.
cards.back:
A. Eliminate shared accounts.
C. Implement usage auditing and review.
G. Perform regular permission audits and reviews.
cards.why: Eliminating shared accounts ties every action to one individual. Usage auditing and review records PHI (Protected Health Information) access and reports anomalies. Regular permission audits and reviews confirm only authorized users keep access.

whyNot.B: A naming convention makes accounts consistent but does not assign them to one person or record or report access.
whyNot.D: Account lockout thresholds limit password guessing and do not create audit trails or protect log integrity.
whyNot.E: Copying logs in real time to a WORM (Write Once Read Many) drive directly meets the requirement that logs cannot be deleted or modified.
whyNot.F: Time-of-day restrictions limit when accounts can log in and do not meet any of the listed audit trail requirements.

cards.keyDoubt: E, because a WORM (Write Once Read Many) drive is the only option that satisfies the requirement that logs and records cannot be deleted or modified, which permission reviews do not address.

cards.front:
Which of the following encryption methods does PKI typically use to securely protect keys?
A. Elliptic curve
B. Digital signatures
C. Asymmetric
D. Obfuscation
cards.why: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) relies on asymmetric encryption, using public and private key pairs, to protect keys and securely exchange symmetric session keys.

whyNot.A: Elliptic curve is one specific asymmetric algorithm family, not the general encryption method PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) typically uses.
whyNot.B: Digital signatures provide authentication and integrity, not encryption that protects keys.
whyNot.D: Obfuscation hides data by making it hard to read and is not a cryptographic method for protecting keys.

cards.front:
An organization is using a tool to perform a source code review. Which of the following describes the case in which the tool incorrectly identifies the vulnerability?
A. False negative
B. True negative
C. False positive
D. True positive
cards.why: A false positive occurs when a tool reports a vulnerability that does not actually exist. That is the tool incorrectly identifying a vulnerability.

whyNot.A: A false negative is a real vulnerability that the tool fails to detect, which is the opposite error.
whyNot.B: A true negative means the tool correctly finds no vulnerability where none exists.
whyNot.D: A true positive means the tool correctly identifies a vulnerability that really exists.

cards.front:
An organization's internal auditor discovers that large sums of money have recently been paid to a vendor that management does not recognize. The IT security department is asked to investigate the organization's ERP system to determine how the accounts payable module has been used to make these vendor payments. The IT security department finds the following security configuration for the accounts payable module: New Vendor Entry - Required Role: Accounts Payable Clerk New Vendor Approval - Required Role: Accounts Payable Clerk Vendor Payment Entry - Required Role: Accounts Payable Clerk Vendor Payment Approval - Required Role: Accounts Payable Manager Which of the following changes to the security configuration of the accounts payable module would BEST mitigate the risk?
A. 
B. 
C. 
D.

A department head at a university resigned on the first day of the spring semester. It was subsequently determined that the department head deleted numerous files and directories from the server-based home directory while the campus was closed. Which of the following policies or procedures could have prevented this from occurring?
A. Time-of-day restrictions
B. Permission auditing and review
C. Offboarding
D. Account expiration
cards.why: Offboarding procedures disable accounts and revoke access when an employee resigns. Doing this promptly would have prevented the former department head from deleting files from the server.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions limit login hours, but the campus being closed would not stop an account that is still valid.
whyNot.B: Permission auditing and review finds excess access periodically and does not remove access at the moment someone resigns.
whyNot.D: Account expiration only works if an end date was set in advance, which is unlikely for a resignation on an unknown date.

cards.front:
A database backup schedule consists of weekly full backups performed on Saturday at 12:00 a.m. and daily differential backups also performed at 12:00 a.m. If the database is restored on Tuesday afternoon, which of the following is the number of individual backups that would need to be applied to complete the database recovery?
A. 1
B. 2
C. 3
D. 4
cards.why: Restoring on Tuesday afternoon needs the last full backup from Saturday plus the most recent differential, made Tuesday at 12:00 a.m. A differential contains all changes since the full backup.

whyNot.A: One backup is not enough because a differential backup cannot be restored without the full backup it is based on.
whyNot.C: Three is wrong because differentials are cumulative, so earlier differentials from Sunday and Monday are not needed.
whyNot.D: Four would apply only if every daily backup had to be applied, as with incremental backups, not differential backups.

cards.front:
Which of the following security controls does an iris scanner provide?
A. Logical
B. Administrative
C. Corrective
D. Physical
E. Detective
F. Deterrent
cards.why: An iris scanner is a physical security control because it restricts physical access to a space using a biometric characteristic of the person.

whyNot.A: Logical controls are technical controls in software or systems, such as access control lists, and an iris scanner is a physical device.
whyNot.B: Administrative controls are policies and procedures, and an iris scanner is hardware rather than a policy.
whyNot.C: Corrective controls fix problems after an incident, and an iris scanner does not repair or restore anything.
whyNot.E: Detective controls identify events after or while they occur, whereas an iris scanner mainly prevents entry.
whyNot.F: Deterrent controls discourage attempts through warnings or visibility, and an iris scanner actually blocks access.

cards.front:
As part of a new industry regulation, companies are required to utilize secure, standardized OS settings. A technical must ensure the OS settings are hardened. Which of the following is the BEST way to do this?
A. Use a vulnerability scanner.
B. Use a configuration compliance scanner.
C. Use a passive, in-line scanner.
D. Use a protocol analyzer.
cards.back: B. Use a configuration compliance scanner.
cards.why: A configuration compliance scanner compares OS (Operating System) settings against a standardized secure baseline, showing whether the system is hardened as the regulation requires.

whyNot.A: A vulnerability scanner looks for missing patches and known flaws and does not verify settings against a hardening baseline.
whyNot.C: A passive, in-line scanner watches network traffic and does not inspect OS (Operating System) configuration settings.
whyNot.D: A protocol analyzer captures and decodes network packets and cannot assess whether OS (Operating System) settings are hardened.

cards.front:
A user has attempted to access data at a higher classification level than the user's account is currently authorized to access. Which of the following access control models has been applied to this user's account?
A. MAC
B. DAC
C. RBAC
D. ABAC
cards.why: MAC (Mandatory Access Control) uses classification labels and clearances set by the system. A user cannot access data labeled above their clearance level.

whyNot.B: DAC (Discretionary Access Control) lets data owners grant access and does not enforce classification levels.
whyNot.C: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) grants access by job role, not by comparing data classification to clearance.
whyNot.D: ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control) evaluates attributes and policies, not a fixed classification and clearance hierarchy.

cards.front:
A security consultant discovers that an organization is using the PCL protocol to print documents, utilizing the default driver and print settings. Which of the following is the MOST likely risk in this situation?
A. An attacker can access and change the printer configuration.
B. SNMP data leaving the printer will not be properly encrypted.
C. An MITM attack can reveal sensitive information.
D. An attacker can easily inject malicious code into the printer firmware.
E. Attackers can use the PCL protocol to bypass the firewall of client computers.
cards.back: B. SNMP data leaving the printer will not be properly encrypted.
cards.why: The default PCL (Printer Command Language) setup sends management data such as SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) without strong encryption, so that data leaving the printer is exposed.

whyNot.A: Changing printer configuration requires access or credentials and is not a direct consequence of using PCL (Printer Command Language) with defaults.
whyNot.C: An MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attack is possible but is a general network risk and not the most specific risk of this scenario.
whyNot.D: Injecting malicious firmware is a separate attack that PCL (Printer Command Language) print settings do not make easy.
whyNot.E: PCL (Printer Command Language) is a print job format and cannot be used to bypass client computer firewalls.

cards.keyDoubt: C, because PCL (Printer Command Language) print jobs travel unencrypted by default, so an MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attacker can capture and read the sensitive documents being printed.

cards.front:
An organization finds that most help desk calls are regarding account lockout due to a variety of applications running on different systems. Management is looking for a solution to reduce the number of account lockouts while improving security. Which of the following is the BEST solution for this organization?
A. Create multiple application accounts for each user.
B. Provide secure tokens.
C. Implement SSO.
D. Utilize role-based access control.
cards.why: SSO (Single Sign-On) lets users authenticate once for many applications, which reduces repeated password entry and lockouts and allows stronger, centralized authentication.

whyNot.A: Multiple application accounts per user would mean more passwords to remember, increasing lockouts and weakening security.
whyNot.B: Secure tokens add an authentication factor but do not remove the need to log in separately to each application.
whyNot.D: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) assigns permissions by role and does not reduce authentication failures that cause lockouts.

cards.front:
A user suspects someone has been accessing a home network without permission by spoofing the MAC address of an authorized system. While attempting to determine if an authorized user is logged into the home network, the user reviews the wireless router, which shows the following table for systems that are currently on the home network. Which of the following should be the NEXT step to determine if there is an unauthorized user on the network?
A. Apply MAC filtering and see if the router drops any of the systems.
B. Physically check each of the authorized systems to determine if they are logged onto the network.
C. Deny the "unknown" host because the hostname is not known and MAC filtering is not applied to this host.
D. Conduct a ping sweep of each of the authorized systems and see if an echo response is received.
cards.back: C. Deny the "unknown" host because the hostname is not known and MAC filtering is not applied to this host.
cards.why: The unknown host has no known hostname and is not covered by MAC (Media Access Control) filtering, so denying it removes the unrecognized device from the network.

whyNot.A: MAC (Media Access Control) filtering cannot detect a spoofed address, since the attacker copies an authorized MAC address.
whyNot.B: Physically checking each authorized system confirms whether it is truly connected, which would expose a spoofed duplicate.
whyNot.D: A ping sweep with ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo requests cannot tell a real device from one using a spoofed address.

cards.keyDoubt: B, because physically checking each authorized system shows whether any listed device is not actually connected, which reveals a spoofed MAC (Media Access Control) address before any blocking.

cards.front:
When performing data acquisition on a workstation, which of the following should be captured based on memory volatility? (Select two.)
A. USB-attached hard disk
B. Swap/pagefile
C. Mounted network storage
D. ROM
E. RAM
cards.why: Order of volatility means capturing the most volatile data first. RAM (Random Access Memory) and the swap or pagefile are volatile or semi-volatile, and are lost or changed quickly.

whyNot.A: A USB (Universal Serial Bus) attached hard disk is persistent storage and much less volatile than memory.
whyNot.C: Mounted network storage is persistent remote storage that survives a workstation shutdown, so it is low priority.
whyNot.D: ROM (Read-Only Memory) is non-volatile and keeps its contents without power, so it is not urgent to capture.

cards.front:
Ann, a security administrator, has been instructed to perform fuzz-based testing on the company's applications. Which of the following best describes what she will do?
A. Enter random or invalid data into the application in an attempt to cause it to fault
B. Work with the developers to eliminate horizontal privilege escalation opportunities
C. Test the applications for the existence of built-in- back doors left by the developers
D. Hash the application to verify it won't cause a false positive on the HIPS.
cards.back: A. Enter random or invalid data into the application in an attempt to cause it to fault
cards.why: Fuzz testing, also called fuzzing, feeds random, malformed, or unexpected input into an application to trigger crashes or faults that reveal unhandled errors and vulnerabilities.

whyNot.B: Eliminating horizontal privilege escalation is done through access control design and code review, not by fuzzing input.
whyNot.C: Finding developer-left back doors is done through code review or static analysis, not by sending random input.
whyNot.D: Hashing an application to avoid false positives on a HIPS (Host-based Intrusion Prevention System) is allowlisting, which has nothing to do with fuzzing.

cards.front:
An attacker compromises a public CA and issues unauthorized X.509 certificates for Company.com. In the future, Company.com wants to mitigate the impact of similar incidents. Which of the following would assist Company.com with its goal?
A. Certificate pinning
B. Certificate stapling
C. Certificate chaining
D. Certificate with extended validation
cards.why: Certificate pinning binds a service to a specific certificate or public key, so a fraudulent certificate issued by a compromised CA (Certificate Authority) is rejected even if it chains to a trusted root.

whyNot.B: Certificate stapling delivers OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) revocation status with the handshake, but it does not stop a validly signed fraudulent certificate from being accepted.
whyNot.C: Certificate chaining is the trust path from a certificate to a root CA (Certificate Authority); a fraudulent certificate from a trusted CA would still chain correctly.
whyNot.D: An EV (Extended Validation) certificate only means stricter identity vetting by the issuer, and it does not stop clients trusting a certificate wrongly issued by a compromised CA (Certificate Authority).

cards.front:
A systems administrator is attempting to recover from a catastrophic failure in the datacenter. To recover the domain controller, the systems administrator needs to provide the domain administrator credentials. Which of the following account types is the systems administrator using?
A. Shared account
B. Guest account
C. Service account
D. User account
cards.why: A service account is a non-interactive, privileged account used by systems and processes, such as recovery tooling, to perform operations like restoring a domain controller with elevated rights.

whyNot.A: A shared account is used by multiple people with common credentials, which does not describe a recovery task performed by one administrator.
whyNot.B: A guest account has minimal, restricted access and could never hold domain administrator rights to restore a domain controller.
whyNot.D: A standard user account has ordinary, limited privileges and would not be able to supply domain administrator credentials for recovery.

cards.front:
A security administrator has found a hash in the environment known to belong to malware. The administrator then finds this file to be in in the preupdate area of the OS, which indicates it was pushed from the central patch system. File: winx86_adobe_flash_upgrade.exe Hash: 99ac28bede43ab869b853ba62c4ea243 The administrator pulls a report from the patch management system with the following output: Given the above outputs, which of the following MOST likely happened?
A. The file was corrupted after it left the patch system.
B. The file was infected when the patch manager downloaded it.
C. The file was not approved in the application whitelist system.
D. The file was embedded with a logic bomb to evade detection.
cards.back: B. The file was infected when the patch manager downloaded it.
cards.why: The malware hash matches a file that came from the central patch system, so the file was most likely already infected when the patch manager downloaded it from the source, a supply chain compromise.

whyNot.A: Corruption after leaving the patch system would change the hash from the vendor's value, but the patch system's own record already reflects the malicious hash.
whyNot.C: Application allowlist approval status does not explain why the malicious file originated inside the patch management system.
whyNot.D: A logic bomb is code that triggers on a condition; it does not explain how the malicious file entered the patch repository.

cards.front:
A network administrator at a small office wants to simplify the configuration of mobile clients connecting to an encrypted wireless network. Which of the following should be implemented if the administrator does not want to provide the wireless password or the certificate to the employees?
A. WPS
B. 802.1x
C. WPA2-PSK
D. TKIP
cards.why: WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) lets clients join an encrypted wireless network by pushing a button or entering a short PIN (Personal Identification Number), so users never receive the passphrase or a certificate.

whyNot.B: IEEE 802.1X port-based authentication normally requires each client to have credentials or a certificate, which the administrator wants to avoid distributing.
whyNot.C: WPA2-PSK (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 Pre-Shared Key) requires giving every employee the wireless password, which the administrator does not want to do.
whyNot.D: TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol) is a legacy encryption protocol and does not simplify client configuration or hide the password.

cards.front:
When connected to a secure WAP, which of the following encryption technologies is MOST likely to be configured when connecting to WPA2-PSK?
A. DES
B. AES
C. MD5
D. WEP
cards.why: WPA2-PSK (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 Pre-Shared Key) uses CCMP (Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol), which is built on AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) for encrypting wireless traffic.

whyNot.A: DES (Data Encryption Standard) is an outdated 56-bit cipher and is not used by WPA2-PSK (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 Pre-Shared Key).
whyNot.C: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is a hashing algorithm, not an encryption technology used to protect wireless traffic.
whyNot.D: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) is an older, broken wireless protocol that predates and is replaced by WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2).

cards.front:
A company has a data classification system with definitions for "Private" and "Public". The company's security policy outlines how data should be protected based on type. The company recently added the data type "Proprietary". Which of the following is the MOST likely reason the company added this data type?
A. Reduced cost
B. More searchable data
C. Better data classification
D. Expanded authority of the privacy officer
cards.why: Adding a more granular data type like Proprietary refines the classification scheme, letting the company apply protections that better match the sensitivity of each kind of data.

whyNot.A: Adding another classification level typically adds management overhead, and it does not primarily reduce cost.
whyNot.B: Classification labels exist to drive handling and protection requirements, not to make data more searchable.
whyNot.D: A new data type does not expand the authority of the privacy officer; it only changes how data is categorized.

cards.front:
When configuring settings in a mandatory access control environment, which of the following specifies the subjects that can access specific data objects?
A. Owner
B. System
C. Administrator
D. User
cards.why: In MAC (Mandatory Access Control), the administrator sets the security labels and policy that define which subjects may access which objects, and owners and users cannot change them.

whyNot.A: Owners decide access under DAC (Discretionary Access Control), not under MAC (Mandatory Access Control), where policy is centrally enforced.
whyNot.B: The system enforces the policy, but it is the administrator who defines and configures which subjects can access specific objects.
whyNot.D: Users are the subjects being controlled and have no authority to define access in a MAC (Mandatory Access Control) environment.

cards.front:
A high-security defense installation recently begun utilizing large guard dogs that bark very loudly and excitedly at the slightest provocation. Which of the following types of controls does this BEST describe?
A. Deterrent
B. Preventive
C. Detective
D. Compensating
cards.why: Loudly barking guard dogs discourage intruders from attempting entry, which makes them a deterrent control that influences behavior before an attack is attempted.

whyNot.B: A preventive control physically blocks access, such as a locked gate or wall, and barking alone does not stop entry.
whyNot.C: A detective control identifies an event after or as it occurs, whereas the dogs' main purpose here is to discourage intruders.
whyNot.D: A compensating control substitutes for a missing primary control, and nothing in the scenario indicates the dogs replace another required control.

cards.front:
A company's user lockout policy is enabled after five unsuccessful login attempts. The help desk notices a user is repeatedly locked out over the course of a workweek. Upon contacting the user, the help desk discovers the user is on vacation and does not have network access. Which of the following types of attacks are MOST likely occurring? (Choose two.)
A. Replay
B. Rainbow tables
C. Brute force
D. Pass the hash
E. Dictionary
cards.why: Repeated lockouts while the user is away indicate automated guessing of the password: brute force tries many character combinations, and a dictionary attack tries likely words from a wordlist.

whyNot.A: A replay attack resends captured authentication data and would not repeatedly fail and trigger lockouts through wrong password guesses.
whyNot.B: Rainbow table attacks use precomputed hashes offline and do not generate failed online logins that lock out the account.
whyNot.D: A pass the hash attack reuses a captured hash without guessing the password, so it would not cause repeated failed attempts.

cards.front:
Ann, an employee in the payroll department, has contacted the help desk citing multiple issues with her device, including: Slow performance Word documents, PDFs, and images no longer opening A pop-up Ann states the issues began after she opened an invoice that a vendor emailed to her. Upon opening the invoice, she had to click several security warnings to view it in her word processor. With which of the following is the device MOST likely infected?
A. Spyware
B. Crypto-malware
C. Rootkit
D. Backdoor
cards.why: The Word documents, PDF (Portable Document Format) files, and images no longer opening, plus a pop-up after enabling a malicious invoice macro, point to crypto-malware, which encrypts user files and demands a ransom.

whyNot.A: Spyware secretly collects information and does not normally make documents, PDFs, and images unopenable.
whyNot.C: A rootkit hides malicious activity at a deep level and does not typically render user files inaccessible with a pop-up.
whyNot.D: A backdoor gives attackers covert remote access and does not by itself explain multiple file types becoming unreadable.

cards.front:
A company is terminating an employee for misbehavior. Which of the following steps is MOST important in the process of disengagement from this employee?
A. Obtain a list of passwords used by the employee.
B. Generate a report on outstanding projects the employee handled.
C. Have the employee surrender company identification.
D. Have the employee sign an NDA before departing.
cards.back: C. Have the employee surrender company identification.
cards.why: Collecting company identification, such as badges and keys, immediately removes the terminated employee's physical access, which is the most urgent step when disengaging someone who left for misbehavior.

whyNot.A: Employees should not know or hold a list of passwords; the company instead disables the accounts and resets credentials.
whyNot.B: A report on outstanding projects helps with continuity and handover, but it is less urgent than removing access.
whyNot.D: Signing an NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement) at departure is of limited value and does not remove the employee's physical access.

cards.front:
A company is developing a new secure technology and requires computers being used for development to be isolated. Which of the following should be implemented to provide the MOST secure environment?
A. A perimeter firewall and IDS
B. An air gapped computer network
C. A honeypot residing in a DMZ
D. An ad hoc network with NAT
E. A bastion host
cards.back: B. An air gapped computer network
cards.why: An air gapped network is physically isolated from other networks and the internet, which gives the strongest isolation for sensitive development work.

whyNot.A: A perimeter firewall and IDS (Intrusion Detection System) still leave a network connection that could be misconfigured or bypassed.
whyNot.C: A honeypot in a DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) is a decoy exposed to attackers and does not isolate development computers.
whyNot.D: An ad hoc network with NAT (Network Address Translation) is still connected and offers no true isolation.
whyNot.E: A bastion host is a hardened, exposed gateway system, which means it is connected rather than isolated.

cards.front:
Which of the following is an important step to take BEFORE moving any installation packages from a test environment to production?
A. Roll back changes in the test environment
B. Verify the hashes of files
C. Archive and compress the files
D. Update the secure baseline
cards.back: B. Verify the hashes of files
cards.why: Verifying file hashes confirms that the installation packages tested are identical to what will be deployed, ensuring integrity and that nothing was altered or corrupted in transit.

whyNot.A: Rolling back changes in the test environment undoes the testing and does not validate the packages before production.
whyNot.C: Archiving and compressing files is for storage or transfer efficiency and does not verify integrity.
whyNot.D: Updating the secure baseline should happen after a change is approved and deployed, not before moving packages to production.

cards.front:
A user clicked an email link that led to a website than infected the workstation with a virus. The virus encrypted all the network shares to which the user had access. The virus was not deleted or blocked by the company's email filter, website filter, or antivirus. Which of the following describes what occurred?
A. The user's account was over-privileged.
B. Improper error handling triggered a false negative in all three controls.
C. The email originated from a private email server with no malware protection.
D. The virus was a zero-day attack.
cards.back: D. The virus was a zero-day attack.
cards.why: A zero-day attack exploits a previously unknown vulnerability or malware, so the email filter, website filter, and antivirus had no signature and failed to detect or block it.

whyNot.A: Over-privileged accounts widened the damage by exposing many network shares, but they do not explain why all three controls missed the virus.
whyNot.B: Improper error handling is a software flaw and does not explain three independent security controls all failing to detect the virus.
whyNot.C: The scenario says the user clicked a link that led to a website, so the email's origin server is not what caused the infection.

cards.front:
An organization wishes to provide better security for its name resolution services. Which of the following technologies BEST supports the deployment of DNSSEC at the organization?
A. LDAP
B. TPM
C. TLS
D. SSL
E. PKI
cards.why: TLS (Transport Layer Security) provides encrypted, certificate-authenticated transport, which the key treats as the best supporting technology for protecting name resolution with DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions).

whyNot.A: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a directory service and does not secure DNS (Domain Name System) records.
whyNot.B: TPM (Trusted Platform Module) is hardware for local key storage and does not support DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) deployment.
whyNot.D: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) is a deprecated predecessor of TLS (Transport Layer Security) and is not the best choice.
whyNot.E: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is the more usual answer, but it is not the keyed option here.

cards.keyDoubt: E. DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) signs DNS (Domain Name System) records with a chain of trust built on public and private keys, which is PKI (Public Key Infrastructure), not TLS (Transport Layer Security).

cards.front:
A company hires a consulting firm to crawl its Active Directory network with a non-domain account looking for unpatched systems. Actively taking control of systems is out of scope, as is the creation of new administrator accounts. For which of the following is the company hiring the consulting firm?
A. Vulnerability scanning
B. Penetration testing
C. Application fuzzing
D. User permission auditing
cards.why: Vulnerability scanning crawls systems to find weaknesses such as missing patches without exploiting them, which matches a non-domain account search for unpatched systems with taking control out of scope.

whyNot.B: Penetration testing actively exploits weaknesses and takes control of systems, which the scope explicitly forbids.
whyNot.C: Application fuzzing sends malformed input to a program to trigger crashes and does not look for unpatched systems.
whyNot.D: User permission auditing reviews account rights and group memberships, not missing patches on systems.

cards.front:
An administrator is replacing a wireless router. The configuration of the old wireless router was not documented before it stopped functioning. The equipment connecting to the wireless network uses older legacy equipment that was manufactured prior to the release of the 802.11i standard. Which of the following configuration options should the administrator select for the new wireless router?
A. WPA+CCMP
B. WPA2+CCMP
C. WPA+TKIP
D. WPA2+TKIP
cards.why: Equipment made before the 802.11i standard cannot support WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) or AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) based CCMP (Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol). WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) with TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol) is the compatible choice.

whyNot.A: CCMP (Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol) requires AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) hardware support that pre-802.11i legacy devices lack.
whyNot.B: WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) is defined by 802.11i, so devices built before that standard cannot use it.
whyNot.D: WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) is defined by 802.11i, which legacy devices built before the standard do not support.

cards.front:
An application team is performing a load-balancing test for a critical application during off-hours and has requested access to the load balancer to review which servers are up without having the administrator on call. The security analyst is hesitant to give the application team full access due to other critical applications running on the load balancer. Which of the following is the BEST solution for security analyst to process the request?
A. Give the application team administrator access during off-hours.
B. Disable other critical applications before granting the team access.
C. Give the application team read-only access.
D. Share the account with the application team.
cards.back: C. Give the application team read-only access.
cards.why: Read-only access follows the principle of least privilege, letting the application team see which servers are up without being able to change the other critical applications on the load balancer.

whyNot.A: Administrator access, even during off-hours, would let the team modify or break other critical applications.
whyNot.B: Disabling other critical applications causes an outage and is an unacceptable business impact.
whyNot.D: Sharing an account destroys accountability and auditing, and it violates basic security policy.

cards.front:
Which of the following cryptographic attacks would salting of passwords render ineffective?
A. Brute force
B. Dictionary
C. Rainbow tables
D. Birthday
cards.why: Salting adds unique random data to each password before hashing, so precomputed rainbow tables of hashes no longer match and become ineffective.

whyNot.A: Brute force tries every possible input live, and salting only slows it by forcing work per password.
whyNot.B: A dictionary attack hashes guessed words with each salt, so salting does not make it ineffective, only slower.
whyNot.D: A birthday attack finds hash collisions and is not defeated by salting passwords.

cards.front:
A security analyst is hardening an authentication server. One of the primary requirements is to ensure there is mutual authentication and delegation. Given these requirements, which of the following technologies should the analyst recommend and configure?
A. LDAP services
B. Kerberos services
C. NTLM services
D. CHAP services
cards.back:
B. Kerberos services

Only Kerberos that can do Mutual Auth and Delegation.
cards.why: Kerberos provides mutual authentication between client and server through tickets issued by a Key Distribution Center, and it supports delegation through ticket forwarding.

whyNot.A: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a directory access protocol and does not provide mutual authentication with delegation.
whyNot.C: NTLM (New Technology LAN Manager) uses challenge-response authentication of the client only and lacks mutual authentication and delegation.
whyNot.D: CHAP (Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol) authenticates only the client to the server and does not support delegation.

cards.front:
Two users need to send each other emails over unsecured channels. The system should support the principle of non-repudiation. Which of the following should be used to sign the user's certificates?
A. RA
B. CA
C. CRL
D. CSR
cards.why: A CA (Certificate Authority) signs user certificates, which binds each identity to a public key and allows digital signatures that support non-repudiation of email.

whyNot.A: An RA (Registration Authority) verifies identities for requests but does not sign certificates itself.
whyNot.C: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) lists revoked certificates and does not sign new ones.
whyNot.D: A CSR (Certificate Signing Request) is the request a user submits to be signed and is not the signer.

cards.front:
Which of the following attack types BEST describes a client-side attack that is used to manipulate an HTML iframe with JavaScript code via a web browser?
A. Buffer overflow
B. MITM
C. XSS
D. SQLi
cards.why: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) injects malicious JavaScript that runs in the victim's web browser, including manipulation of an HTML (HyperText Markup Language) inline frame.

whyNot.A: A buffer overflow overwrites memory in a vulnerable program and is not browser-side script manipulation of an inline frame.
whyNot.B: A MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attack intercepts traffic between parties and does not itself inject script into an inline frame.
whyNot.D: SQLi (Structured Query Language injection) targets back-end databases on the server, not client-side browser scripts.

cards.front:
An incident responder receives a call from a user who reports a computer is exhibiting symptoms consistent with a malware infection. Which of the following steps should the responder perform NEXT?
A. Capture and document necessary information to assist in the response.
B. Request the user capture and provide a screenshot or recording of the symptoms.
C. Use a remote desktop client to collect and analyze the malware in real time.
D. Ask the user to back up files for later recovery.
cards.back: A. Capture and document necessary information to assist in the response.
cards.why: After receiving a report, the responder should first capture and document the necessary information, such as symptoms, user, time, and system details, to guide the rest of the incident response.

whyNot.B: Asking the user for a screenshot or recording comes after basic information is documented and relies on an untrained user.
whyNot.C: Using remote desktop to analyze malware live risks spreading the infection and skips initial documentation.
whyNot.D: Backing up files from a possibly infected computer can copy malware and alter evidence before containment.

cards.front:
A senior incident response manager receives a call about some external IPs communicating with internal computers during off hours. Which of the following types of malware is MOST likely causing this issue?
A. Botnet
B. Ransomware
C. Polymorphic malware
D. Armored virus
cards.why: A botnet is a group of compromised computers that receive commands from external command-and-control servers, which explains external Internet Protocol addresses communicating with internal computers during off hours.

whyNot.B: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, and it does not primarily show as off-hours external communication.
whyNot.C: Polymorphic malware changes its code to evade antivirus detection and does not describe this communication pattern.
whyNot.D: An armored virus uses techniques to resist analysis and reverse engineering and does not describe external command traffic.

cards.front:
Which of the following technologies employ the use of SAML? (Select two.)
A. Single sign-on
B. Federation
C. LDAP
D. Secure token
E. RADIUS
cards.why: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) exchanges authentication assertions between identity providers and service providers, which enables single sign-on and federation across organizations.

whyNot.C: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a directory protocol and does not use SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) assertions.
whyNot.D: A secure token is a generic authentication device or credential and is not a technology that employs SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language).
whyNot.E: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is a separate authentication protocol that does not use SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language).

cards.front:
Which of the following specifically describes the exploitation of an interactive process to access otherwise restricted areas of the OS?
A. Privilege escalation
B. Pivoting
C. Process affinity
D. Buffer overflow
cards.why: Privilege escalation exploits a flaw in a running interactive process to gain higher rights and reach restricted areas of the operating system.

whyNot.B: Pivoting uses a compromised host to attack other systems on a network rather than gaining higher rights on the same operating system.
whyNot.C: Process affinity binds a process to specific processors and is a performance setting, not an attack.
whyNot.D: A buffer overflow is a specific flaw that can be used for escalation, but it does not describe the access goal itself.

cards.front:
After a user reports slow computer performance, a system administrator detects a suspicious file, which was installed as part of a freeware software package. The systems administrator reviews the output below: Based on the above information, which of the following types of malware was installed on the user's computer?
A. RAT
B. Keylogger
C. Spyware
D. Worm
E. Bot
cards.why: A RAT (Remote Access Trojan) bundled with freeware gives an attacker remote control of the computer, which fits the suspicious file and the slow performance the user reported.

whyNot.B: A keylogger only records keystrokes and does not provide remote control of the computer.
whyNot.C: Spyware gathers user activity information covertly but does not give an attacker remote control.
whyNot.D: A worm spreads on its own across networks, and this case shows a single file installed from freeware.
whyNot.E: A bot joins the computer to a botnet for coordinated attacks and is a narrower case than remote control.

cards.front:
Which of the following network vulnerability scan indicators BEST validates a successful, active scan?
A. The scan job is scheduled to run during off-peak hours.
B. The scan output lists SQL injection attack vectors.
C. The scan data identifies the use of privileged-user credentials.
D. The scan results identify the hostname and IP address.
cards.back: B. The scan output lists SQL injection attack vectors.
cards.why: Listing SQL (Structured Query Language) injection attack vectors shows the scanner actively probed the target and found exploitable weaknesses, which validates a successful active scan.

whyNot.A: Scheduling a scan for off-peak hours is a planning choice and does not show that the scan succeeded.
whyNot.C: Use of privileged-user credentials indicates a credentialed scan, not whether an active scan was successful.
whyNot.D: Hostname and Internet Protocol address results can come from passive discovery and do not prove active probing succeeded.

cards.front:
An analyst wants to implement a more secure wireless authentication for office access points. Which of the following technologies allows for encrypted authentication of wireless clients over TLS?
A. PEAP
B. EAP
C. WPA2
D. RADIUS
cards.back:
A. PEAP

EAP by itself is only an authentication framework. PEAP (Protected Extensible Authentication Protocol) fully encapsulates EAP and is designed to work within a TLS (Transport Layer Security) tunnel that may be encrypted but is authenticated.
cards.why: PEAP (Protected Extensible Authentication Protocol) wraps EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) inside an encrypted TLS (Transport Layer Security) tunnel, which protects wireless client authentication.

whyNot.B: EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) is a framework that does not itself provide a TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypted tunnel.
whyNot.C: WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) is a wireless security standard that is not the protocol tunneling authentication over TLS (Transport Layer Security).
whyNot.D: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is the authentication server protocol and does not by itself tunnel client authentication over TLS (Transport Layer Security).

cards.front:
When systems, hardware, or software are not supported by the original vendor, it is a vulnerability known as:
A. system sprawl
B. end-of-life systems
C. resource exhaustion
D. a default configuration
cards.why: End-of-life systems no longer receive vendor patches or security updates, so newly discovered flaws stay open indefinitely. That makes unsupported hardware or software a known vulnerability category.

whyNot.A: System sprawl is uncontrolled growth of unmanaged systems, not the loss of vendor support.
whyNot.C: Resource exhaustion is a denial-of-service condition where memory, CPU (Central Processing Unit) or connections run out, unrelated to vendor support status.
whyNot.D: A default configuration is a vulnerability from unchanged factory settings, not from lack of vendor support.

cards.front:
A company has three divisions, each with its own networks and services. The company decides to make its secure web portal accessible to all employees utilizing their existing usernames and passwords.
