The security administrator has elected to use SAML to support authentication. In this scenario, which of the following will occur when users try to authenticate to the portal? (Select two.)
A. The portal will function as a service provider and request an authentication assertion.
B. The portal will function as an identity provider and issue an authentication assertion.
C. The portal will request an authentication ticket from each network that is transitively trusted.
D. The back-end networks will function as an identity provider and issue an authentication assertion.
E. The back-end networks will request authentication tickets from the portal, which will act as the third-party service provider authentication store.
F. The back-end networks will verify the assertion token issued by the portal functioning as the identity provider.
cards.back:
C. The portal will request an authentication ticket from each network that is transitively trusted.
D. The back-end networks will function as an identity provider and issue an authentication assertion.
cards.why: In SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language), the back-end networks that hold the existing usernames and passwords act as identity providers and issue authentication assertions to the portal.

whyNot.A: This is actually a true SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) statement, since the portal is the service provider requesting an assertion, which is why the key looks wrong.
whyNot.B: The portal consumes assertions as a service provider and does not issue them, so it is not the identity provider.
whyNot.E: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) uses assertions, not tickets, and the portal is not an authentication store for the back-end networks.
whyNot.F: The portal does not issue the assertion; the back-end identity providers do, and the portal is the party that verifies it.

cards.keyDoubt: A instead of C: with SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language), the portal acts as service provider requesting an assertion, whereas requesting tickets from transitively trusted networks describes Kerberos-style trust, not SAML.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the BEST explanation of why control diversity is important in a defense- in-depth architecture?
A. Social engineering is used to bypass technical controls, so having diversity in controls minimizes the risk of demographic exploitation
B. Hackers often impact the effectiveness of more than one control, so having multiple copies of individual controls provides redundancy
C. Technical exploits to defeat controls are released almost every day; control diversity provides overlapping protection.
D. Defense-in-depth relies on control diversity to provide multiple levels of network hierarchy that allow user domain segmentation
cards.back: D. Defense-in-depth relies on control diversity to provide multiple levels of network hierarchy that allow user domain segmentation
cards.why: The key says defense in depth uses control diversity to create multiple levels of network hierarchy and user domain segmentation, which is a weak match for what diversity means.

whyNot.A: Diversity does not minimize risk of demographic exploitation; that phrase is not a real security concept.
whyNot.B: Multiple copies of the same control is redundancy, not diversity, and a single exploit could defeat every copy.
whyNot.C: This is actually the best description, since using different control types gives overlapping protection when one control is defeated.

cards.keyDoubt: C because control diversity means layering different technical, managerial and operational control types so one exploit cannot defeat every layer, giving overlapping protection.

cards.front:
A system administrator wants to provide balance between the security of a wireless network and usability. The administrator is concerned with wireless encryption compatibility of older devices used by some employees. Which of the following would provide strong security and backward compatibility when accessing the wireless network?
A. Open wireless network and SSL VPN
B. WPA using a preshared key
C. WPA2 using a RADIUS back-end for 802.1x authentication
D. WEP with a 40-bit key
cards.back: B. WPA using a preshared key
cards.why: WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) with a preshared key is supported by most older devices while still being much stronger than WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy), balancing security and backward compatibility.

whyNot.A: An open wireless network sends traffic unencrypted at the wireless layer, so it does not give strong security.
whyNot.C: WPA2 with RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) and 802.1x is strong but many older devices cannot support it, hurting compatibility.
whyNot.D: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) with a 40-bit key is easily cracked and provides weak security.

cards.front:
An information security specialist is reviewing the following output from a Linux server. Based on the above information, which of the following types of malware was installed on the server?
A. Logic bomb
B. Trojan
C. Backdoor
D. Ransomware
E. Rootkit
cards.why: The keyed answer is a logic bomb, malicious code that lies dormant until a condition such as a date, time or event triggers it. The output exhibit is not shown, so this relies on the key.

whyNot.B: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software and does not wait for a trigger condition.
whyNot.C: A backdoor provides hidden remote access and is not defined by a time or event trigger.
whyNot.D: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment, which is a different behavior from a dormant triggered payload.
whyNot.E: A rootkit hides its presence and privileged access at the operating system level, not a conditional trigger.

cards.front:
In terms of encrypting data, which of the following is BEST described as a way to safeguard password data by adding random data to it in storage?
A. Using salt
B. Using hash algorithms
C. Implementing elliptical curve
D. Implementing PKI
cards.why: Salting adds random data to each password before hashing, so identical passwords produce different stored hashes and precomputed rainbow table attacks fail.

whyNot.B: Hash algorithms transform data into fixed-length digests but do not by themselves add random data, so identical passwords still match.
whyNot.C: Elliptic curve cryptography is an asymmetric key technique and does not add random data to stored passwords.
whyNot.D: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) manages certificates and keys and does not protect stored password data with random additions.

cards.front:
A system administrator wants to provide for and enforce wireless access accountability during events where external speakers are invited to make presentations to a mixed audience of employees and non-employees. Which of the following should the administrator implement?
A. Shared accounts
B. Preshared passwords
C. Least privilege
D. Sponsored guest
cards.why: A sponsored guest account is tied to an employee who vouches for the visitor, so wireless access is individually identifiable and accountable while remaining separate from employee access.

whyNot.A: Shared accounts hide who did what, which defeats accountability.
whyNot.B: Preshared passwords are known by everyone who has them, so individual activity cannot be attributed.
whyNot.C: Least privilege limits permissions but does not identify or hold individual guests accountable.

cards.front:
Which of the following would MOST likely appear in an uncredentialed vulnerability scan?
A. Self-signed certificates
B. Missing patches
C. Auditing parameters
D. Inactive local accounts
cards.why: The key says inactive local accounts, but that detail normally requires logging in, so it is a weak match for an uncredentialed scan.

whyNot.A: This is actually visible to an uncredentialed scan, because a self-signed certificate is presented to any network client during the TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshake.
whyNot.B: Missing patches generally need a credentialed scan to inspect installed software versions on the host.
whyNot.C: Auditing parameters are internal operating system settings that require authenticated access to read.

cards.keyDoubt: A because an uncredentialed scan sees only what a network client sees, such as a self-signed certificate, while inactive local accounts require authenticated access to enumerate.

cards.front:
A security analyst observes the following events in the logs of an employee workstation: Given the information provided, which of the following MOST likely occurred on the workstation?
A. Application whitelisting controls blocked an exploit payload from executing.
B. Antivirus software found and quarantined three malware files.
C. Automatic updates were initiated but failed because they had not been approved.
D. The SIEM log agent was not tuned properly and reported a false positive.
cards.back: A. Application whitelisting controls blocked an exploit payload from executing.
cards.why: The keyed answer is that application whitelisting blocked an exploit payload, since whitelisting allows only approved programs to run and logs denied execution attempts. The log exhibit is not shown, so this relies on the key.

whyNot.B: Antivirus quarantine events would show detection and quarantine messages, not execution blocks from an allow list.
whyNot.C: Failed automatic updates would show update service errors, not blocked execution of unapproved payloads.
whyNot.D: A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) false positive would show an agent tuning problem, not control enforcement events on the workstation.

cards.front:
When identifying a company's most valuable assets as part of a BIA, which of the following should be the FIRST priority?
A. Life
B. Intellectual property
C. Sensitive data
D. Public reputation
cards.why: In a BIA (Business Impact Analysis), human life and safety is always the first priority, ahead of data, property or reputation.

whyNot.B: Intellectual property is valuable but ranks below human safety in a BIA (Business Impact Analysis).
whyNot.C: Sensitive data matters for confidentiality, but it does not outrank protecting people.
whyNot.D: Public reputation is an important business concern but is lower priority than human life.

cards.front:
An organization needs to implement a large PKI. Network engineers are concerned that repeated transmission of the OCSP will impact network performance. Which of the following should the security analyst recommend is lieu of an OCSP?
A. CSR
B. CRL
C. CA
D. OID
cards.why: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) is a periodically published list of revoked certificates that clients download and cache, avoiding the repeated per-certificate queries of OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol).

whyNot.A: A CSR (Certificate Signing Request) is how an applicant asks a certificate authority for a certificate, not a revocation checking method.
whyNot.C: A CA (Certificate Authority) issues and signs certificates and is not a revocation status mechanism.
whyNot.D: An OID (Object Identifier) is a numeric label for certificate fields or policies, not a revocation method.

cards.front:
When considering a third-party cloud service provider, which of the following criteria would be the BEST to include in the security assessment process? (Select two.)
A. Use of performance analytics
B. Adherence to regulatory compliance
C. Data retention policies
D. Size of the corporation
E. Breadth of applications support
cards.back:
B. Adherence to regulatory compliance
C. Data retention policies
cards.why: Regulatory compliance and data retention policies directly affect how the provider protects, stores and disposes of your data, so both belong in a cloud security assessment.

whyNot.A: Performance analytics describe speed and usage, which is an operational concern rather than a security criterion.
whyNot.D: The size of the corporation does not indicate how well it secures customer data.
whyNot.E: Breadth of application support is a feature consideration, not a security measure.

cards.front:
Which of the following occurs when the security of a web application relies on JavaScript for input validation?
A. The integrity of the data is at risk.
B. The security of the application relies on antivirus.
C. A host-based firewall is required.
D. The application is vulnerable to race conditions.
cards.back: A. The integrity of the data is at risk.
cards.why: JavaScript validation runs in the client browser, where an attacker can bypass or modify it, so unvalidated malicious input reaches the server and the integrity of the data is at risk.

whyNot.B: Client-side validation weakness has nothing to do with relying on antivirus software.
whyNot.C: A host-based firewall does not fix missing server-side input validation.
whyNot.D: Race conditions come from timing between concurrent operations, not from client-side input validation.

cards.front:
An analyst is reviewing a simple program for potential security vulnerabilities before being deployed to a Windows server. Given the following code: Which of the following vulnerabilities is present?
A. Bad memory pointer
B. Buffer overflow
C. Integer overflow
D. Backdoor
cards.why: The keyed answer is a buffer overflow, where code copies input into a fixed-size buffer without checking length and overwrites adjacent memory. The code exhibit is not shown, so this relies on the key.

whyNot.A: A bad memory pointer involves dereferencing invalid or null addresses, which is a different flaw from overrunning a buffer.
whyNot.C: An integer overflow occurs when arithmetic exceeds a numeric type's range, not when data exceeds a buffer.
whyNot.D: A backdoor is intentionally hidden access, and a coding mistake in bounds checking is not a backdoor.

cards.front:
An organization's file server has been virtualized to reduce costs. Which of the following types of backups would be MOST appropriate for the particular file server?
A. Snapshot
B. Full
C. Incremental
D. Differential
cards.why: The key says incremental, which backs up only changes since the last backup, but for a virtualized server the usual fit is a snapshot.

whyNot.A: A snapshot captures the virtual machine state quickly and is the typical backup method for virtualized servers, which is why the key looks wrong.
whyNot.B: A full backup copies everything each time, which is slow and storage-heavy for a routine file server.
whyNot.D: A differential backup copies all changes since the last full backup, growing larger each day.

cards.keyDoubt: A because a snapshot captures the virtual machine disk and state at a point in time, which is the most appropriate and fastest backup method for a virtualized file server.

cards.front:
A wireless network uses a RADIUS server that is connected to an authenticator, which in turn connects to a supplicant. Which of the following represents the authentication architecture in use?
A. Open systems authentication
B. Captive portal
C. RADIUS federation
D. 802.1x
cards.why: IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1X is port-based network access control. A supplicant authenticates through an authenticator, which relays the request to a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) authentication server.

whyNot.A: Open systems authentication accepts any client without verifying credentials and does not use a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server.
whyNot.B: A captive portal redirects users to a web login page and has no supplicant and authenticator roles.
whyNot.C: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) federation links authentication servers across organizations and does not describe the supplicant, authenticator and server roles.

cards.front:
An employer requires that employees use a key-generating app on their smartphones to log into corporate applications. In terms of authentication of an individual, this type of access policy is BEST defined as:
A. Something you have.
B. Something you know.
C. Something you do.
D. Something you are.
cards.why: A key-generating app on a smartphone proves possession of a specific device, so it is the something you have factor. It typically produces TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) codes.

whyNot.B: Something you know is a secret the user remembers, such as a password or PIN (Personal Identification Number).
whyNot.C: Something you do is a behavior, such as a gesture or typing pattern, and generating a code is not one.
whyNot.D: Something you are is a biometric trait such as a fingerprint, and the app does not measure one.

cards.front:
Adhering to a layered security approach, a controlled access facility employs security guards who verify the authorization of all personnel entering the facility. Which of the following terms BEST describes the security control being employed?
A. Administrative
B. Corrective
C. Deterrent
D. Compensating
cards.why: Security guards checking authorization apply a policy and procedure carried out by people, which fits an administrative control. Of the listed options it is the closest match.

whyNot.B: Corrective controls restore systems or operations after an incident, and checking people at entry happens before any incident.
whyNot.C: Deterrent controls discourage attempts through visible warnings, whereas verifying authorization is an enforced access procedure.
whyNot.D: Compensating controls substitute for a primary control that cannot be implemented, and nothing here suggests that.

cards.front:
A security analyst is hardening a web server, which should allow a secure certificate-based session using the organization's PKI infrastructure. The web server should also utilize the latest security techniques and standards. Given this set of requirements, which of the following techniques should the analyst implement to BEST meet these requirements? (Select two.)
A. Install an X- 509-compliant certificate.
B. Implement a CRL using an authorized CA.
C. Enable and configure TLS on the server.
D. Install a certificate signed by a public CA.
E. Configure the web server to use a host header.
cards.back:
A. Install an X- 509-compliant certificate.
C. Enable and configure TLS on the server.
cards.why: An X.509 certificate from the organization's PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) provides certificate-based identity, and TLS (Transport Layer Security) provides the encrypted session using current standards. Together they meet both requirements.

whyNot.B: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) only reports revoked certificates and does not establish the secure session itself.
whyNot.D: A certificate from a public CA (Certificate Authority) does not use the organization's own PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) as required.
whyNot.E: A host header lets one web server host multiple sites and adds no certificate-based security.

cards.front:
A manager wants to distribute a report to several other managers within the company. Some of them reside in remote locations that are not connected to the domain but have a local server. Because there is sensitive data within the report and the size of the report is beyond the limit of the email attachment size, emailing the report is not an option. Which of the following protocols should be implemented to distribute the report securely? (Select three.)
A. S/MIME
B. SSH
C. SNMPv3
D. FTPS
E. SRTP
F. HTTPS
G. LDAPS
cards.back:
B. SSH
D. FTPS
F. HTTPS
cards.why: SSH (Secure Shell) file transfer, FTPS (File Transfer Protocol Secure) and HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) all send large files over encrypted channels to remote servers without using email.

whyNot.A: S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) protects email, and email is ruled out by the attachment size limit.
whyNot.C: SNMPv3 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 3) manages and monitors network devices and is not used to distribute reports.
whyNot.E: SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) secures voice and video streams and does not transfer files.
whyNot.G: LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol Secure) secures directory queries and does not distribute documents.

cards.front:
An auditor is reviewing the following output from a password-cracking tool: Which of the following methods did the auditor MOST likely use?
A. Hybrid
B. Dictionary
C. Brute force
D. Rainbow table
cards.why: A hybrid attack combines dictionary words with modifications such as appended numbers or substituted characters. It sits between a pure dictionary attack and brute force. The tool output is not shown, so this relies on the key.

whyNot.B: A pure dictionary attack tries only unmodified wordlist entries and does not mutate them.
whyNot.C: Brute force tries every possible character combination and does not start from words.
whyNot.D: A rainbow table looks up precomputed hash values and does not generate guesses during the attack.

cards.front:
Which of the following must be intact for evidence to be admissible in court?
A. Chain of custody
B. Order of volatility
C. Legal hold
D. Preservation
cards.why: Chain of custody documents who handled the evidence, when, and how, proving it was not altered. Courts require it to be intact before admitting evidence.

whyNot.B: Order of volatility dictates which evidence is collected first, such as memory before disk, and does not prove integrity.
whyNot.C: A legal hold stops the deletion of relevant data but does not document handling of evidence.
whyNot.D: Preservation protects data from change, but admissibility depends on documented custody records proving that protection.

cards.front:
A vulnerability scanner that uses its running service's access level to better assess vulnerabilities across multiple assets within an organization is performing a:
A. Credentialed scan.
B. Non-intrusive scan.
C. Privilege escalation test.
D. Passive scan.
cards.why: A credentialed scan logs in with an account and its access level, letting the scanner see patches, configurations and local weaknesses. It finds more than an unauthenticated scan.

whyNot.B: A non-intrusive scan avoids disruptive checks, but that describes its impact and not the use of an access level.
whyNot.C: A privilege escalation test tries to gain higher rights than granted and does not use existing service access to assess.
whyNot.D: A passive scan only observes network traffic and does not authenticate to the assets.

cards.front:
Which of the following cryptography algorithms will produce a fixed-length, irreversible output?
A. AES
B. 3DES
C. RSA
D. MD5
cards.why: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is a hashing algorithm that turns any input into a fixed 128-bit digest that cannot be reversed. Hashing is one-way by design.

whyNot.A: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is reversible symmetric encryption, and its output size follows the input.
whyNot.B: 3DES (Triple Data Encryption Standard) is reversible symmetric encryption that can be decrypted with the key.
whyNot.C: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) is reversible asymmetric encryption, decryptable with the private key.

cards.front:
A technician suspects that a system has been compromised. The technician reviews the following log entry: WARNING- hash mismatch: C:\Window\SysWOW64\user32.dll WARNING- hash mismatch: C:\Window\SysWOW64\kernel32.dll Based solely ono the above information, which of the following types of malware is MOST likely installed on the system?
A. Rootkit
B. Ransomware
C. Trojan
D. Backdoor
cards.why: Hash mismatches on core system DLLs (Dynamic Link Libraries) show operating system files were modified. Rootkits typically replace or patch system files to hide themselves and keep privileged access.

whyNot.B: Ransomware encrypts user files and demands payment, and modified system library hashes alone do not indicate that.
whyNot.C: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software, and the log shows no such disguised program, only altered system files.
whyNot.D: A backdoor gives remote access, but the log shows only changed system files, not remote access.

cards.front:
A new firewall has been places into service at an organization. However, a configuration has not been entered on the firewall. Employees on the network segment covered by the new firewall report they are unable to access the network. Which of the following steps should be completed to BEST resolve the issue?
A. The firewall should be configured to prevent user traffic form matching the implicit deny rule.
B. The firewall should be configured with access lists to allow inbound and outbound traffic.
C. The firewall should be configured with port security to allow traffic.
D. The firewall should be configured to include an explicit deny rule.
cards.back: A. The firewall should be configured to prevent user traffic form matching the implicit deny rule.
cards.why: A firewall with no configuration falls back to the implicit deny rule, blocking everything. Users need rules so their traffic no longer matches the implicit deny.

whyNot.B: Allow rules in ACLs (Access Control Lists) are actually the practical fix and say nearly the same thing as the key.
whyNot.C: Port security is a switch feature limiting MAC (Media Access Control) addresses per port and is not a firewall configuration.
whyNot.D: An explicit deny rule would block traffic and make the problem no better.

cards.keyDoubt: B. The keyed wording is awkward, and creating ACL (Access Control List) allow rules for inbound and outbound traffic is what actually fixes the problem.

cards.front:
A security analyst is testing both Windows and Linux systems for unauthorized DNS zone transfers within a LAN on comptia.org from example.org. Which of the following commands should the security analyst use? (Select two.)
A. 
B. 
C. dig -axfr comptia.org @example.org
D. ipconfig /flushDNS
E. 
F. dig @example.org comptia.org
cards.why: The dig command with the AXFR (full zone transfer) query type, directed at the example.org server for comptia.org, tests whether DNS (Domain Name System) zone transfers are allowed. Exact dig syntax is usually written as axfr or -t axfr.

whyNot.A: This option text is blank in the question, so it cannot be judged.
whyNot.B: This option text is blank in the question, so it cannot be judged.
whyNot.D: ipconfig /flushDNS clears the local DNS (Domain Name System) resolver cache and does not test zone transfers.
whyNot.E: This option text is blank in the question, so it cannot be judged.
whyNot.F: This dig command performs an ordinary DNS (Domain Name System) lookup without requesting a zone transfer.

cards.front:
Which of the following are the MAIN reasons why a systems administrator would install security patches in a staging environment before the patches are applied to the production server? (Select two.)
A. To prevent server availability issues
B. To verify the appropriate patch is being installed
C. To generate a new baseline hash after patching
D. To allow users to test functionality
E. To ensure users are trained on new functionality
cards.back:
A. To prevent server availability issues
D. To allow users to test functionality
cards.why: Testing patches in staging prevents outages from a bad patch reaching production, which protects availability. It also lets users confirm that functionality still works before deployment.

whyNot.B: Confirming the correct patch is installed is a routine check that does not require a separate staging environment.
whyNot.C: A new baseline hash is generated after patching the production system, not as a reason to use staging.
whyNot.E: Staging is for compatibility and functionality testing, and training users on new features is a separate matter.

cards.front:
A Chief Information Officer (CIO) drafts an agreement between the organization and its employees. The agreement outlines ramifications for releasing information without consent and/or approvals. Which of the following BEST describes this type of agreement?
A. ISA
B. NDA
C. MOU
D. SLA
cards.why: An NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement) is a binding agreement that protects confidential information and spells out consequences for releasing it without consent or approval.

whyNot.A: An ISA (Interconnection Security Agreement) defines security requirements for connecting two organizations' systems, not employee disclosure.
whyNot.C: An MOU (Memorandum of Understanding) states shared intentions between parties and usually lacks disclosure penalties.
whyNot.D: An SLA (Service Level Agreement) defines expected service performance, not confidentiality obligations.

cards.front:
Which of the following would meet the requirements for multifactor authentication?
A. Username, PIN, and employee ID number
B. Fingerprint and password
C. Smart card and hardware token
D. Voice recognition and retina scan
cards.why: A fingerprint (something you are) combined with a password (something you know) uses two different factor categories. That is what multifactor authentication requires.

whyNot.A: A username, PIN (Personal Identification Number) and employee identification number are all something you know, so there is only one factor type.
whyNot.C: A smart card and a hardware token are both something you have, so there is only one factor type.
whyNot.D: Voice recognition and a retina scan are both biometrics, something you are, so there is only one factor type.

cards.front:
A manager suspects that an IT employee with elevated database access may be knowingly modifying financial transactions for the benefit of a competitor. Which of the following practices should the manager implement to validate the concern?
A. Separation of duties
B. Mandatory vacations
C. Background checks
D. Security awareness training
cards.why: Separation of duties prevents one person from controlling a whole transaction process, which limits fraud and gives the manager a way to check for tampering. It is the keyed answer.

whyNot.B: Mandatory vacations force another person to take over duties, which exposes fraud, but this is not the keyed practice.
whyNot.C: Background checks screen candidates before hiring and do not validate a suspicion about a current employee.
whyNot.D: Security awareness training teaches policy and threats and does not detect deliberate insider fraud.

cards.keyDoubt: B. Mandatory vacations are the control that reveals ongoing fraud, because a replacement employee can spot altered transactions while the suspect is away, whereas separation of duties only prevents it.

cards.front:
A penetration tester finds that a company's login credentials for the email client were being sent in clear text. Which of the following should be done to provide encrypted logins to the email server?
A. Enable IPSec and configure SMTP.
B. Enable SSH and LDAP credentials.
C. Enable MIME services and POP3.
D. Enable an SSL certificate for IMAP services.
cards.back: D. Enable an SSL certificate for IMAP services.
cards.why: Enabling an SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) certificate for IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) wraps the mail login in encryption, so credentials are no longer sent in clear text.

whyNot.A: IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) with SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is not the standard way to encrypt mailbox logins, and SMTP only sends mail.
whyNot.B: SSH (Secure Shell) and LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) credentials are not mail retrieval services and do not secure the email client login.
whyNot.C: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) formats message content and POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3) without TLS still sends credentials in clear text.

cards.front:
Before an infection was detected, several of the infected devices attempted to access a URL that was similar to the company name but with two letters transposed. Which of the following BEST describes the attack vector used to infect the devices?
A. Cross-site scripting
B. DNS poisoning
C. Typo squatting
D. URL hijacking
cards.why: Typo squatting registers a domain that is a misspelling or transposition of a legitimate name, so users who mistype the address land on a malicious site that infects them.

whyNot.A: Cross-site scripting injects script into a legitimate web page and does not rely on lookalike domain names.
whyNot.B: DNS (Domain Name System) poisoning corrupts resolver records so correct names resolve to bad addresses, and the users here typed a wrong name.
whyNot.D: URL (Uniform Resource Locator) hijacking is largely a synonym for typo squatting, but C is the more precise and keyed term.

cards.front:
A system administrator is reviewing the following information from a compromised server. Given the above information, which of the following processes was MOST likely exploited via remote buffer overflow attack?
A. Apache
B. LSASS
C. MySQL
D. TFTP
cards.why: Apache is a network-facing web server that runs on open ports and has a history of remote buffer overflow vulnerabilities, so it is the process most likely exploited remotely here.

whyNot.B: LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service) is a Windows credential process, usually attacked locally for credential theft rather than by remote buffer overflow.
whyNot.C: MySQL is a database service that is normally not exposed to remote untrusted users, so it is a less likely remote overflow target.
whyNot.D: TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) is a simple file transfer service, and nothing here points to it as the exploited process.

cards.front:
Joe, a security administrator, needs to extend the organization's remote access functionality to be used by staff while travelling. Joe needs to maintain separate access control functionalities for internal, external, and VOIP services. Which of the following represents the BEST access technology for Joe to use?
A. RADIUS
B. TACACS+
C. Diameter
D. Kerberos
cards.why: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) separates authentication, authorization, and accounting, so Joe can apply distinct access controls to internal, external, and VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) services.

whyNot.A: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) combines authentication and authorization, so it does not give the same separate per-service control.
whyNot.C: Diameter is a successor to RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) aimed at carrier and mobile networks, and it does not offer the keyed separate control.
whyNot.D: Kerberos provides ticket-based single sign-on authentication and is not a remote access technology with separate per-service access control.

cards.front:
The availability of a system has been labeled as the highest priority. Which of the following should be focused on the MOST to ensure the objective?
A. Authentication
B. HVAC
C. Full-disk encryption
D. File integrity checking
cards.why: HVAC (Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning) keeps equipment within safe temperature and humidity, so environmental controls directly protect system availability from overheating and hardware failure.

whyNot.A: Authentication verifies identity and supports confidentiality, and it does not keep systems running.
whyNot.C: Full-disk encryption protects confidentiality of stored data and does not improve uptime.
whyNot.D: File integrity checking detects unauthorized changes, which supports integrity rather than availability.

cards.front:
As part of the SDLC, a third party is hired to perform a penetration test. The third party will have access to the source code, integration tests, and network diagrams. Which of the following BEST describes the assessment being performed?
A. Black box
B. Regression
C. White box
D. Fuzzing
cards.why: White box testing gives the tester full knowledge of the system, including source code, integration tests, and network diagrams, which matches the access described.

whyNot.A: Black box testing gives the tester no internal knowledge, which contradicts the access provided here.
whyNot.B: Regression testing re-checks that existing functionality still works after changes and is not a penetration test type.
whyNot.D: Fuzzing sends malformed or random input to find flaws and does not describe testing with full internal documentation.

cards.front:
A dumpster diver recovers several hard drives from a company and is able to obtain confidential data from one of the hard drives. The company then discovers its information is posted online. Which of the following methods would have MOST likely prevented the data from being exposed?
A. Removing the hard drive from its enclosure
B. Using software to repeatedly rewrite over the disk space
C. Using Blowfish encryption on the hard drives
D. Using magnetic fields to erase the data
cards.back: D. Using magnetic fields to erase the data
cards.why: Degaussing with strong magnetic fields destroys the magnetic data on a hard drive so it cannot be recovered, which would have stopped the dumpster diver from reading it.

whyNot.A: Removing the drive from its enclosure does nothing to the stored data, which remains fully readable.
whyNot.B: Repeated overwriting can sanitize a drive, but it is less reliable than degaussing for fully destroying data, so it is not the keyed answer.
whyNot.C: Blowfish encryption protects data, but the question asks about sanitization before disposal, and encryption alone does not remove data.

cards.front:
Which of the following are methods to implement HA in a web application server environment? (Select two.)
A. Load balancers
B. Application layer firewalls
C. Reverse proxies
D. VPN concentrators
E. Routers
cards.back:
A. Load balancers
B. Application layer firewalls
cards.why: Load balancers distribute requests across multiple web servers and remove failed ones from rotation, which provides HA (High Availability). The keyed answer also lists application layer firewalls.

whyNot.B: Application layer firewalls filter traffic for security and do not add redundancy or failover.
whyNot.C: Reverse proxies can distribute traffic and fail over between servers, but the key does not include them.
whyNot.D: VPN (Virtual Private Network) concentrators terminate remote access tunnels and do not provide web server redundancy.
whyNot.E: Routers forward packets between networks and do not by themselves provide web server redundancy.

cards.keyDoubt: C instead of B. A reverse proxy can balance load and fail over between web servers, which supports HA (High Availability), whereas an application layer firewall only filters traffic.

cards.front:
An application developer is designing an application involving secure transports from one service to another that will pass over port 80 for a request. Which of the following secure protocols is the developer MOST likely to use?
A. FTPS
B. SFTP
C. SSL
D. LDAPS
E. SSH
cards.why: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) encrypts a transport session between services and can wrap an HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) request, so it fits a secure transport over port 80 for a service request.

whyNot.A: FTPS (File Transfer Protocol Secure) secures file transfers and uses ports such as 990 or 21, not port 80.
whyNot.B: SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) transfers files over SSH (Secure Shell) on port 22, not port 80.
whyNot.D: LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol over SSL) secures directory queries on port 636, not port 80.
whyNot.E: SSH (Secure Shell) provides encrypted remote administration on port 22 and is not a transport for a service request on port 80.

cards.front:
Which of the following precautions MINIMIZES the risk from network attacks directed at multifunction printers, as well as the impact on functionality at the same time?
A. Isolating the systems using VLANs
B. Installing a software-based IPS on all devices
C. Enabling full disk encryption
D. Implementing a unique user PIN access functions
cards.back: A. Isolating the systems using VLANs
cards.why: Isolating multifunction printers in their own VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) limits what attackers can reach from or through them while the printers keep working normally.

whyNot.B: Installing a software-based IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) on printers is usually not possible and could hurt functionality.
whyNot.C: Full disk encryption protects stored data at rest and does not reduce network attacks against the printer.
whyNot.D: A unique user PIN (Personal Identification Number) controls who can use the printer and does not stop network attacks.

cards.front:
After an identified security breach, an analyst is tasked to initiate the IR process. Which of the following is the NEXT step the analyst should take?
A. Recovery
B. Identification
C. Preparation
D. Documentation
E. Escalation
cards.why: After a breach is reported, the IR (Incident Response) process moves into identification, where the analyst confirms the incident, determines its scope, and classifies it.

whyNot.A: Recovery comes late in IR (Incident Response), after containment and eradication.
whyNot.C: Preparation happens before any incident, so it is not the step after a breach.
whyNot.D: Documentation continues throughout IR (Incident Response) and is not the next distinct phase.
whyNot.E: Escalation to management follows once the incident has been identified and assessed.

cards.front:
A company was recently audited by a third party. The audit revealed the company's network devices were transferring files in the clear. Which of the following protocols should the company use to transfer files?
A. HTTPS
B. LDAPS
C. SCP
D. SNMPv3
cards.why: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) transfers files over SSH (Secure Shell), so the file contents and credentials are encrypted instead of being sent in clear text.

whyNot.A: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts web traffic and is not the typical file transfer method for network devices.
whyNot.B: LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol over SSL) secures directory queries and does not transfer files.
whyNot.D: SNMPv3 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 3) secures device management and monitoring and is not a file transfer protocol.

cards.front:
During a monthly vulnerability scan, a server was flagged for being vulnerable to an Apache Struts exploit. Upon further investigation, the developer responsible for the server informs the security team that Apache Struts is not installed on the server. Which of the following BEST describes how the security team should reach to this incident?
A. The finding is a false positive and can be disregarded
B. The Struts module needs to be hardened on the server
C. The Apache software on the server needs to be patched and updated
D. The server has been compromised by malware and needs to be quarantined.
cards.back: A. The finding is a false positive and can be disregarded
cards.why: A false positive occurs when a scanner reports a vulnerability that does not exist. Apache Struts is not installed, so the finding can be disregarded after verification.

whyNot.B: Hardening a Struts module is pointless when Struts is not installed.
whyNot.C: Patching Apache does not apply because the flagged component, Struts, is not present on the server.
whyNot.D: Nothing indicates compromise, and a mistaken scanner finding alone does not justify quarantining the server for malware.

cards.front:
A systems administrator wants to protect data stored on mobile devices that are used to scan and record assets in a warehouse. The control must automatically destroy the secure container of mobile devices if they leave the warehouse. Which of the following should the administrator implement? (Select two.)
A. Geofencing
B. Remote wipe
C. Near-field communication
D. Push notification services
E. Containerization
cards.why: Geofencing detects when a device leaves a defined location and triggers an action, and containerization keeps the data in a separate secure container that can be destroyed automatically.

whyNot.B: Remote wipe erases the whole device on a manual command and does not automatically destroy only the secure container on leaving the warehouse.
whyNot.C: NFC (Near-Field Communication) is a short-range wireless technology and does not track location or destroy data.
whyNot.D: Push notification services send alerts to devices and do not enforce location-based data destruction.

cards.front:
A security analyst is performing a quantitative risk analysis. The risk analysis should show the potential monetary loss each time a threat or event occurs. Given this requirement, which of the following concepts would assist the analyst in determining this value? (Select two.)
A. ALE
B. AV
C. ARO
D. EF
E. ROI
cards.why: ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) and ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) are quantitative risk terms, but they express yearly loss and event frequency, not the loss from a single event.

whyNot.B: AV (Asset Value) is an input to SLE (Single Loss Expectancy), so it arguably belongs in the answer, though the key leaves it out.
whyNot.D: EF (Exposure Factor) multiplied by AV (Asset Value) gives SLE (Single Loss Expectancy), the per-event loss, so it arguably belongs in the answer.
whyNot.E: ROI (Return on Investment) measures the financial return of a control or investment, not the loss from one threat event.

cards.keyDoubt: B and D, because AV (Asset Value) times EF (Exposure Factor) gives SLE (Single Loss Expectancy), the monetary loss per occurrence, while ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) and ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) are annual figures.

cards.front:
Which of the following AES modes of operation provide authentication? (Select two.)
A. CCM
B. CBC
C. GCM
D. DSA
E. CFB
cards.why: CCM (Counter with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code) and GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) are AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) modes that provide authenticated encryption, giving both confidentiality and integrity.

whyNot.B: CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) provides confidentiality only and has no built-in authentication of the data.
whyNot.D: DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) is a signature algorithm, not an AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) mode of operation.
whyNot.E: CFB (Cipher Feedback) provides confidentiality only and has no built-in authentication of the data.

cards.front:
An audit takes place after company-wide restricting, in which several employees changed roles. The following deficiencies are found during the audit regarding access to confidential data: Which of the following would be the BEST method to prevent similar audit findings in the future?
A. Implement separation of duties for the payroll department.
B. Implement a DLP solution on the payroll and human resources servers.
C. Implement rule-based access controls on the human resources server.
D. Implement regular permission auditing and reviews.
cards.back: D. Implement regular permission auditing and reviews.
cards.why: Regular permission auditing and reviews, also called user access reviews, catch stale permissions left over when employees change roles, which prevents privilege creep after a reorganization.

whyNot.A: Separation of duties splits critical tasks among people but does not remove outdated permissions after role changes.
whyNot.B: DLP (Data Loss Prevention) detects or blocks data leaving the organization but does not correct excess access rights.
whyNot.C: Rule-based access control applies fixed rules to access but does not clean up permissions that employees keep after changing roles.

cards.front:
A security engineer is configuring a wireless network that must support mutual authentication of the wireless client and the authentication server before users provide credentials. The wireless network must also support authentication with usernames and passwords. Which of the following authentication protocols MUST the security engineer select?
A. EAP-FAST
B. EAP-TLS
C. PEAP
D. EAP
cards.why: PEAP (Protected Extensible Authentication Protocol) first builds a TLS (Transport Layer Security) tunnel in which the server proves its identity, then the user authenticates inside it with a username and password.

whyNot.A: EAP-FAST (Extensible Authentication Protocol Flexible Authentication via Secure Tunneling) relies on a PAC (Protected Access Credential) for tunnel setup rather than server certificate authentication, so it is not the best fit.
whyNot.B: EAP-TLS (Extensible Authentication Protocol Transport Layer Security) requires client certificates and does not use usernames and passwords.
whyNot.D: EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) is only a framework and does not itself provide a protected tunnel or mutual authentication.

cards.front:
A system's administrator has finished configuring firewall ACL to allow access to a new web server: The security administrator confirms form the following packet capture that there is network traffic from the internet to the web server: The company's internal auditor issues a security finding and requests that immediate action be taken. With which of the following is the auditor MOST concerned?
A. Misconfigured firewall
B. Clear text credentials
C. Implicit deny
D. Default configuration
cards.why: The packet capture shows credentials sent in clear text, such as over FTP (File Transfer Protocol) or Telnet, so anyone on the path could read them, which is the auditor's main concern.

whyNot.A: The ACL (Access Control List) is allowing the intended traffic, so the firewall is not the issue the auditor raised.
whyNot.C: Implicit deny is a normal firewall behavior that blocks unlisted traffic and is a good practice, not a finding.
whyNot.D: A default configuration is not shown in the capture; the problem is unencrypted credentials in transit.

cards.front:
Which of the following vulnerability types would the type of hacker known as a script kiddie be MOST dangerous against?
A. Passwords written on the bottom of a keyboard
B. Unpatched exploitable Internet-facing services
C. Unencrypted backup tapes
D. Misplaced hardware token
cards.why: Script kiddies run prebuilt tools and exploits, so unpatched, exploitable Internet-facing services are the easiest and most reachable targets for them.

whyNot.A: Passwords on a keyboard require physical access, which a remote script kiddie typically does not have.
whyNot.C: Unencrypted backup tapes also require physical access to obtain, which is not how script kiddies usually operate.
whyNot.D: A misplaced hardware token requires finding the physical device, which does not suit automated remote tools.

cards.front:
An in-house penetration tester is using a packet capture device to listen in on network communications. This is an example of:
A. Passive reconnaissance
B. Persistence
C. Escalation of privileges
D. Exploiting the switch
cards.why: Listening to network traffic with a packet capture device gathers information without interacting with or altering targets, which is passive reconnaissance.

whyNot.B: Persistence means keeping long-term access to a compromised system, which capturing packets does not do.
whyNot.C: Escalation of privileges means gaining higher access rights, which passive listening does not do.
whyNot.D: Exploiting the switch would mean attacking the device, such as through MAC (Media Access Control) flooding, not just capturing traffic.

cards.front:
A black hat hacker is enumerating a network and wants to remain covert during the process. The hacker initiates a vulnerability scan. Given the task at hand the requirement of being covert, which of the following statements BEST indicates that the vulnerability scan meets these requirements?
A. The vulnerability scanner is performing an authenticated scan.
B. The vulnerability scanner is performing local file integrity checks.
C. The vulnerability scanner is performing in network sniffer mode.
D. The vulnerability scanner is performing banner grabbing.
cards.back: C. The vulnerability scanner is performing in network sniffer mode.
cards.why: A scanner in network sniffer mode only listens to existing traffic and sends no probes, so it is passive and very hard to detect.

whyNot.A: An authenticated scan logs in to hosts, which creates logs and noticeable activity.
whyNot.B: Local file integrity checks need access to the host and generate detectable activity.
whyNot.D: Banner grabbing connects to services and sends requests, which can be logged and detected.

cards.front:
A development team has adopted a new approach to projects in which feedback is iterative and multiple iterations of deployments are provided within an application's full life cycle. Which of the following software development methodologies is the development team using?
A. Waterfall
B. Agile
C. Rapid
D. Extreme
cards.why: Agile uses iterative development with frequent feedback and multiple deployments across the application's life cycle.

whyNot.A: Waterfall is sequential, with each phase finishing before the next begins, and offers little iterative feedback.
whyNot.C: Rapid development is not the standard name for the iterative feedback methodology described here.
whyNot.D: Extreme programming is one specific Agile practice set, not the general iterative approach the question describes.

cards.front:
A Chief Executive Officer (CEO) suspects someone in the lab testing environment is stealing confidential information after working hours when no one else is around. Which of the following actions can help to prevent this specific threat?
A. Implement time-of-day restrictions.
B. Audit file access times.
C. Secretly install a hidden surveillance camera.
D. Require swipe-card access to enter the lab.
cards.back: D. Require swipe-card access to enter the lab.
cards.why: Swipe-card access controls who can physically enter the lab and records entries, which restricts and tracks after-hours presence.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions limit account logons by hour, which would arguably block after-hours access better than the key suggests.
whyNot.B: Auditing file access times is detective, so it shows theft after it happens and does not prevent it.
whyNot.C: A hidden camera only records events and does not prevent theft.

cards.keyDoubt: A, because time-of-day restrictions directly prevent after-hours use of accounts, while swipe-card access mainly controls and logs entry without stopping an authorized person.

cards.front:
A company hires a third-party firm to conduct an assessment of vulnerabilities exposed to the Internet. The firm informs the company that an exploit exists for an FTP server that had a version installed from eight years ago. The company has decided to keep the system online anyway, as no upgrade exists form the vendor. Which of the following BEST describes the reason why the vulnerability exists?
A. Default configuration
B. End-of-life system
C. Weak cipher suite
D. Zero-day threats
cards.why: A version installed eight years ago with no vendor upgrade available is an end-of-life system, which no longer receives patches for known vulnerabilities.

whyNot.A: A default configuration issue involves insecure factory settings, which the scenario does not describe.
whyNot.C: A weak cipher suite concerns outdated encryption algorithms, not an unsupported software version.
whyNot.D: A zero-day threat has no known exploit or patch, but here an exploit is already known.

cards.front:
An organization uses SSO authentication for employee access to network resources. When an employee resigns, as per the organization's security policy, the employee's access to all network resources is terminated immediately. Two weeks later, the former employee sends an email to the help desk for a password reset to access payroll information from the human resources server. Which of the following represents the BEST course of action?
A. Approve the former employee's request, as a password reset would give the former employee access to only the human resources server.
B. Deny the former employee's request, since the password reset request came from an external email address.
C. Deny the former employee's request, as a password reset would give the employee access to all network resources.
D. Approve the former employee's request, as there would not be a security issue with the former employee gaining access to network resources.
cards.back: C. Deny the former employee's request, as a password reset would give the employee access to all network resources.
cards.why: With SSO (Single Sign-On), one password reset restores access to every connected resource, and a former employee should have no access, so the request must be denied.

whyNot.A: Under SSO (Single Sign-On) a reset would not limit access to only the human resources server.
whyNot.B: The external email address is a sign of concern, but the main reason to deny is that SSO (Single Sign-On) would restore all access.
whyNot.D: There is a clear security issue because a former employee should not regain access to any network resources.

cards.front:
Joe, a user, wants to send Ann, another user, a confidential document electronically. Which of the following should Joe do to ensure the document is protected from eavesdropping?
A. Encrypt it with Joe's private key
B. Encrypt it with Joe's public key
C. Encrypt it with Ann's private key
D. Encrypt it with Ann's public key
cards.back: D. Encrypt it with Ann's public key
cards.why: Encrypting with the recipient's public key means only Ann's private key can decrypt the document, which protects it from eavesdropping.

whyNot.A: Encrypting with Joe's private key creates a signature anyone with Joe's public key can read, so it gives no confidentiality.
whyNot.B: Encrypting with Joe's public key means only Joe could decrypt it, so Ann could not read it.
whyNot.C: Ann's private key is secret and Joe should not have it, so he cannot use it to encrypt.

cards.front:
A director of IR is reviewing a report regarding several recent breaches. The director compiles the following statistic's -Initial IR engagement time frame -Length of time before an executive management notice went out -Average IR phase completion The director wants to use the data to shorten the response time. Which of the following would accomplish this?
A. CSIRT
B. Containment phase
C. Escalation notifications
D. Tabletop exercise
cards.why: A tabletop exercise lets the team rehearse the response process, exposing delays in engagement, escalation, and phase completion so they can be shortened.

whyNot.A: A CSIRT (Computer Security Incident Response Team) is the responding team itself, and having one does not improve response times by itself.
whyNot.B: The containment phase is only one phase of the process and does not address the measured delays.
whyNot.C: Escalation notifications address only the executive notice delay, not all measured timeframes.

cards.front:
To reduce disk consumption, an organization's legal department has recently approved a new policy setting the data retention period for sent email at six months. Which of the following is the BEST way to ensure this goal is met?
A. Create a daily encrypted backup of the relevant emails.
B. Configure the email server to delete the relevant emails.
C. Migrate the relevant emails into an "Archived" folder.
D. Implement automatic disk compression on email servers.
cards.back: A. Create a daily encrypted backup of the relevant emails.
cards.why: The key chooses a daily encrypted backup, but a backup keeps copies of the emails and does not enforce a six-month retention limit or reduce disk use.

whyNot.B: Configuring the email server to delete old emails, as the retention policy requires, would enforce the goal and arguably belongs in the answer.
whyNot.C: Moving emails to an Archived folder keeps them on disk and does not enforce deletion.
whyNot.D: Disk compression reduces size but does not enforce the six-month retention period.

cards.keyDoubt: B, because configuring the email server to delete emails older than six months is the only option that enforces the retention period and reduces disk use.

cards.front:
A security administrator is configuring a new network segment, which contains devices that will be accessed by external users, such as web and FTP server. Which of the following represents the MOST secure way to configure the new network segment?
A. The segment should be placed on a separate VLAN, and the firewall rules should be configured to allow external traffic.
B. The segment should be placed in the existing internal VLAN to allow internal traffic only.
C. The segment should be placed on an intranet, and the firewall rules should be configured to allow external traffic.
D. The segment should be placed on an extranet, and the firewall rules should be configured to allow both internal and external traffic.
cards.back: D. The segment should be placed on an extranet, and the firewall rules should be configured to allow both internal and external traffic.
cards.why: An extranet is a controlled, semi-trusted zone for externally reachable servers such as web and FTP (File Transfer Protocol) servers. Firewall rules govern both internal and external access, keeping these hosts apart from the internal network.

whyNot.A: A separate VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) with rules only for external traffic ignores how internal users and administrators must also reach these servers.
whyNot.B: Placing externally accessed servers in the internal VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) exposes the internal network and blocks the external users who need access.
whyNot.C: An intranet is a private internal network, so it is the wrong place for servers that external users must reach.

cards.keyDoubt: A. A separate VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) behind firewall rules is the classic isolated DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) design, while an extranet is meant for trusted partner access.

cards.front:
Which of the following types of attacks precedes the installation of a rootkit on a server?
A. Pharming
B. DDoS
C. Privilege escalation
D. DoS
cards.why: Privilege escalation gives an attacker the administrative or root rights needed to install a rootkit, which modifies the operating system at a deep level. Without elevated privileges, the installation would fail.

whyNot.A: Pharming redirects users to fake websites through DNS (Domain Name System) manipulation and does not give an attacker rights on a server.
whyNot.B: A DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack floods a target with traffic from many sources and does not lead to rootkit installation.
whyNot.D: A DoS (Denial of Service) attack makes a service unavailable and does not give the attacker the access needed to install software.

cards.front:
Which of the following cryptographic algorithms is irreversible?
A. RC4
B. SHA-256
C. DES
D. AES
cards.why: SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit) is a one-way hash function. It produces a fixed-length digest from which the original input cannot be recovered, so it is irreversible.

whyNot.A: RC4 (Rivest Cipher 4) is a symmetric stream cipher, so anyone holding the key can decrypt the data.
whyNot.C: DES (Data Encryption Standard) is a symmetric block cipher, so the correct key reverses the encryption.
whyNot.D: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is a symmetric block cipher, so the correct key reverses the encryption.

cards.front:
A security analyst receives an alert from a WAF with the following payload: var data= "<test test test>" ++ <../../../../../../etc/passwd>" Which of the following types of attacks is this?
A. Cross-site request forgery
B. Buffer overflow
C. SQL injection
D. JavaScript data insertion
E. Firewall evasion script
cards.why: The payload embeds a script-like data string and a path reference to /etc/passwd, which is an attempt to insert crafted data into the application's input handling. Of the listed choices, this fits JavaScript data insertion best.

whyNot.A: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks an authenticated user's browser into sending unwanted requests and does not use a payload like this.
whyNot.B: A buffer overflow sends oversized input to overwrite memory, and this payload is not about exceeding a buffer's length.
whyNot.C: SQL (Structured Query Language) injection uses query syntax such as quotes, UNION or OR clauses, none of which appear here.
whyNot.E: A firewall evasion script obfuscates or fragments traffic to slip past filters, and the payload here is not doing that.

cards.front:
A workstation puts out a network request to locate another system. Joe, a hacker on the network, responds before the real system does, and he tricks the workstation into communicating with him. Which of the following BEST describes what occurred?
A. The hacker used a race condition.
B. The hacker used a pass-the-hash attack.
C. The hacker-exploited improper key management.
D. The hacker exploited weak switch configuration.
cards.back: D. The hacker exploited weak switch configuration.
cards.why: The workstation's broadcast request, such as an ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) lookup, was answered by the attacker first. A switch without protections like port security or dynamic ARP inspection lets a rogue host poison this exchange.

whyNot.A: A race condition exploits timing between operations inside software, not a spoofed reply on the network.
whyNot.B: Pass-the-hash reuses captured password hashes to authenticate and does not involve answering a lookup request.
whyNot.C: Improper key management concerns weak handling of cryptographic keys, and no keys are involved in this scenario.

cards.front:
Audit logs from a small company's vulnerability scanning software show the following findings: Destinations scanned: -Server001- Internal human resources payroll server -Server101-Internet-facing web server -Server201- SQL server for Server101 -Server301-Jumpbox used by systems administrators accessible from the internal network Validated vulnerabilities found: -Server001- Vulnerable to buffer overflow exploit that may allow attackers to install software -Server101- Vulnerable to buffer overflow exploit that may allow attackers to install software -Server201-OS updates not fully current -Server301- Accessible from internal network without the use of jumpbox -Server301-Vulnerable to highly publicized exploit that can elevate user privileges Assuming external attackers who are gaining unauthorized information are of the highest concern, which of the following servers should be addressed FIRST?
A. Server001
B. Server101
C. Server201
D. Server301
cards.why: Server101 is internet-facing and has a buffer overflow that could allow software installation. External attackers can reach it directly, so it carries the highest risk when outside attackers are the main concern.

whyNot.A: Server001 has the same flaw but is an internal payroll server, so external attackers cannot reach it directly.
whyNot.C: Server201 only has operating system updates that are not fully current, which is a lower-severity finding than an exploitable overflow.
whyNot.D: Server301 is reachable only from the internal network, so external attackers cannot exploit its privilege escalation flaw directly.

cards.front:
A security analyst wants to harden the company's VoIP PBX. The analyst is worried that credentials may be intercepted and compromised when IP phones authenticate with the BPX. Which of the following would best prevent this from occurring?
A. Implement SRTP between the phones and the PBX.
B. Place the phones and PBX in their own VLAN.
C. Restrict the phone connections to the PBX.
D. Require SIPS on connections to the PBX.
cards.back: A. Implement SRTP between the phones and the PBX.
cards.why: SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) encrypts the voice media stream between the phones and the PBX (Private Branch Exchange), protecting the call traffic from interception.

whyNot.B: Placing phones and the PBX (Private Branch Exchange) in their own VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) limits exposure but does not encrypt credentials in transit.
whyNot.C: Restricting phone connections to the PBX (Private Branch Exchange) limits who can connect but does not protect credentials from being intercepted.
whyNot.D: SIPS (Session Initiation Protocol Secure) protects signaling, which is where authentication occurs, but the key prefers SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol).

cards.keyDoubt: D. SIPS (Session Initiation Protocol Secure) encrypts the signaling channel where phones send credentials, whereas SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) only protects the voice media stream.

cards.front:
An organization is comparing and contrasting migration from its standard desktop configuration to the newest version of the platform. Before this can happen, the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) voices the need to evaluate the functionality of the newer desktop platform to ensure interoperability with existing software in use by the organization. In which of the following principles of architecture and design is the CISO engaging?
A. Dynamic analysis
B. Change management
C. Baselining
D. Waterfalling
cards.why: Change management evaluates a planned change, such as migrating to a new desktop platform, for impact and interoperability with existing software before it is approved and deployed.

whyNot.A: Dynamic analysis tests running code for flaws and does not assess whether a new platform works with existing software.
whyNot.C: Baselining records a standard configuration or performance reference and does not evaluate a proposed migration.
whyNot.D: Waterfalling refers to the sequential waterfall development model, which is not a way to evaluate platform compatibility.

cards.front:
A security administrator suspects a MITM attack aimed at impersonating the default gateway is underway. Which of the following tools should the administrator use to detect this attack? (Select two.)
A. Ping
B. Ipconfig
C. Tracert
D. Netstat
E. Dig
F. Nslookup
cards.why: Ipconfig shows the default gateway address configured on the host, and tracert reveals the hops along the path. An unexpected extra hop or changed gateway address indicates an attacker is impersonating the gateway.

whyNot.A: Ping only tests reachability and response time, so it cannot show whether the gateway has been impersonated.
whyNot.D: Netstat lists local connections and listening ports and does not show the gateway or the path traffic takes.
whyNot.E: Dig queries DNS (Domain Name System) records and does not reveal gateway impersonation.
whyNot.F: Nslookup queries DNS (Domain Name System) records and does not reveal gateway impersonation.

cards.front:
A user is presented with the following items during the new-hire onboarding process: -Laptop -Secure USB drive -Hardware OTP token -External high-capacity HDD -Password complexity policy -Acceptable use policy -HASP key -Cable lock Which of the following is one component of multifactor authentication?
A. Secure USB drive
B. Cable lock
C. Hardware OTP token
D. HASP key
cards.why: A hardware OTP (One-Time Password) token is a possession factor, something the user has. Combined with a password it forms multifactor authentication.

whyNot.A: A secure USB (Universal Serial Bus) drive stores data and is not an authentication factor in this list.
whyNot.B: A cable lock is a physical security device that deters laptop theft and does not authenticate a user.
whyNot.D: A HASP (Hardware Against Software Piracy) key is a software licensing dongle, not a user authentication factor.

cards.front:
An organization requires users to provide their fingerprints to access an application. To improve security, the application developers intend to implement multifactor authentication. Which of the following should be implemented?
A. Use a camera for facial recognition
B. Have users sign their name naturally
C. Require a palm geometry scan
D. Implement iris recognition
cards.back: B. Have users sign their name naturally
cards.why: A fingerprint is a biometric factor, something you are. A natural signature is a behavioral characteristic, something you do, and adds a different factor type to the fingerprint.

whyNot.A: Facial recognition is another physical biometric, the same something-you-are factor as the fingerprint, so it adds no new factor type.
whyNot.C: A palm geometry scan is another physical biometric, the same something-you-are factor as the fingerprint, so it adds no new factor type.
whyNot.D: Iris recognition is another physical biometric, the same something-you-are factor as the fingerprint, so it adds no new factor type.

cards.front:
A network technician is setting up a segmented network that will utilize a separate ISP to provide wireless access to the public area for a company. Which of the following wireless security methods should the technician implement to provide basic accountability for access to the public network?
A. Pre-shared key
B. Enterprise
C. Wi-Fi Protected setup
D. Captive portal
cards.why: A captive portal forces users to accept terms or register before getting access, which provides basic accountability for a public wireless network without requiring complex credential infrastructure.

whyNot.A: A PSK (Pre-Shared Key) is shared by everyone, so individual users cannot be identified or held accountable.
whyNot.B: Enterprise authentication with 802.1X (port-based network access control) is stronger than needed and requires a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server, which is not basic public access.
whyNot.C: WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) simplifies device pairing with a PIN (Personal Identification Number), is known to be insecure, and gives no user accountability.

cards.front:
After a routine audit, a company discovers that engineering documents have been leaving the network on a particular port. The company must allow outbound traffic on this port, as it has a legitimate business use. Blocking the port would cause an outage. Which of the following technology controls should the company implement?
A. NAC
B. Web proxy
C. DLP
D. ACL
cards.why: DLP (Data Loss Prevention) inspects content leaving the network and can block or alert on engineering documents while still permitting the legitimate traffic on that port.

whyNot.A: NAC (Network Access Control) checks the posture of devices connecting to the network and does not inspect outbound document content.
whyNot.B: A web proxy filters web traffic by destination or category and would not reliably identify engineering documents on an arbitrary port.
whyNot.D: An ACL (Access Control List) permits or denies by address or port, so blocking the port would cause the outage the company must avoid.

cards.front:
A security analyst has received the following alert snippet from the HIDS appliance: Given the above logs, which of the following is the cause of the attack?
A. The TCP ports on destination are all open
B. FIN, URG, and PSH flags are set in the packet header
C. TCP MSS is configured improperly
D. There is improper Layer 2 segmentation
cards.back: B. FIN, URG, and PSH flags are set in the packet header
cards.why: A packet with FIN (Finish), URG (Urgent) and PSH (Push) flags all set is the signature of an Xmas scan, a reconnaissance technique, and the HIDS (Host-based Intrusion Detection System) flagged these abnormal flags.

whyNot.A: Open TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) ports on the destination are not what triggers the alert, and the attack stems from the crafted packets.
whyNot.C: An improperly configured TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) MSS (Maximum Segment Size) affects packet sizing, not the flag combination that triggered the alert.
whyNot.D: Improper Layer 2 segmentation would affect traffic separation between network segments and is not indicated by the flag pattern.

cards.front:
A security analyst reviews the following output: The analyst loads the hash into the SIEM to discover if this hash is seen in other parts of the network. After inspecting a large number of files, the security analyst reports the following: Which of the following is the MOST likely cause of the hash being found in other areas?
A. Jan Smith is an insider threat
B. There are MD5 hash collisions
C. The file is encrypted
D. Shadow copies are present
cards.back: B. There are MD5 hash collisions
cards.why: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is a weak hash with known collisions, so different files can produce the same hash. This explains the same hash appearing on unrelated files across the network.

whyNot.A: Nothing in the findings ties the hash matches to deliberate insider activity, since a collision explains the matches without any malicious user.
whyNot.C: Encryption would change file contents and produce different hashes, not identical hashes across many files.
whyNot.D: Shadow copies are duplicates of the same files, which would not account for matches across unrelated areas of the network.

cards.front:
A company's AUP requires: Passwords must meet complexity requirements. Passwords are changed at least once every six months. Passwords must be at least eight characters long. An auditor is reviewing the following report: Which of the following controls should the auditor recommend to enforce the AUP?
A. Account lockout thresholds
B. Account recovery
C. Password expiration
D. Prohibit password reuse
cards.why: Password expiration enforces the AUP (Acceptable Use Policy) requirement that passwords be changed at least every six months. Complexity and length are already covered, so the missing control is a maximum password age.

whyNot.A: Account lockout thresholds limit failed guesses, but the AUP (Acceptable Use Policy) says nothing about locking accounts after failed attempts.
whyNot.B: Account recovery handles regaining access after a forgotten password and does not force periodic password changes.
whyNot.D: Prohibiting password reuse stops old passwords from returning, but the AUP (Acceptable Use Policy) requires a change interval, not reuse limits.

cards.front:
An organization's primary datacenter is experiencing a two-day outage due to an HVAC malfunction. The node located in the datacenter has lost power and is no longer operational, impacting the ability of all users to connect to the alternate datacenter. Which of the following BIA concepts BEST represents the risk described in this scenario?
A. SPoF
B. RTO
C. MTBF
D. MTTR
cards.why: SPoF (Single Point of Failure) describes one component whose loss stops the whole service. Here, one datacenter node losing power cut every user off from the alternate datacenter.

whyNot.B: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the target time to restore service, not the risk of a single component taking everything down.
whyNot.C: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) measures average operating time between failures, not dependence on one critical node.
whyNot.D: MTTR (Mean Time To Repair) measures average repair duration and does not describe a single node causing a total outage.

cards.front:
A security analyst notices anomalous activity coming from several workstations in the organizations. Upon identifying and containing the issue, which of the following should the security analyst do NEXT?
A. Document and lock the workstations in a secure area to establish chain of custody
B. Notify the IT department that the workstations are to be reimaged and the data restored for reuse
C. Notify the IT department that the workstations may be reconnected to the network for the users to continue working
D. Document findings and processes in the after-action and lessons learned report
cards.back: D. Document findings and processes in the after-action and lessons learned report
cards.why: After containment, the analyst should preserve evidence by documenting and securing the workstations to establish chain of custody. That keeps the evidence usable before any reimaging or recovery.

whyNot.B: Reimaging the workstations before evidence is preserved would destroy forensic data and skips proper eradication analysis.
whyNot.C: Reconnecting the workstations to the network before eradication and verification risks reinfection and further spread.
