whyNot.D: The after-action lessons learned report is the final incident response phase, written after eradication and recovery are complete.

cards.keyDoubt: A is the better next step, because lessons learned comes last and evidence must be preserved first after containment.

cards.front:
An employee receives an email, which appears to be from the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), asking for a report of security credentials for all users. Which of the following types of attack is MOST likely occurring?
A. Policy violation
B. Social engineering
C. Whaling
D. Spear phishing
cards.why: Spear phishing is a targeted email attack that impersonates a trusted person, here the CEO (Chief Executive Officer), to trick a specific employee into giving up credentials.

whyNot.A: A policy violation is a breach of company rules, not a type of external attack using a spoofed email.
whyNot.B: Social engineering is the broad category that includes this attack, but spear phishing is the more specific and accurate answer.
whyNot.C: Whaling targets senior executives as victims, but here the CEO (Chief Executive Officer) is only impersonated and the victim is an ordinary employee.

cards.front:
An information security analyst needs to work with an employee who can answer questions about how data for a specific system is used in the business. The analyst should seek out an employee who has the role of:
A. steward
B. owner
C. privacy officer
D. systems administrator
cards.why: The data owner is the business role accountable for a system's data and can explain how that data is used and who should have access to it.

whyNot.A: A data steward handles day-to-day data quality and labeling, and is less authoritative on business use than the owner.
whyNot.C: A privacy officer oversees regulatory privacy compliance and is not the person who knows how a specific system's data is used.
whyNot.D: A systems administrator manages the technical operation of the system and does not decide or define business use of the data.

cards.front:
A group of non-profit agencies wants to implement a cloud service to share resources with each other and minimize costs. Which of the following cloud deployment models BEST describes this type of effort?
A. Public
B. Hybrid
C. Community
D. Private
cards.why: A community cloud is shared by organizations with common interests or needs, such as a group of non-profit agencies, which lets them split the costs.

whyNot.A: A public cloud is open to the general public and does not limit sharing to a specific group of related organizations.
whyNot.B: A hybrid cloud combines two or more different deployment models and does not describe a shared resource among similar agencies.
whyNot.D: A private cloud is built for a single organization, so it does not fit multiple agencies sharing resources.

cards.front:
An administrator is configuring access to information located on a network file server named "Bowman". The files are located in a folder named "BalkFiles". The files are only for use by the "Matthews" division and should be read-only. The security policy requires permissions for shares to be managed at the file system layer and also requires those permissions to be set according to a least privilege model. Security policy for this data type also dictates that administrator-level accounts on the system have full access to the files. The administrator configures the file share according to the following table: Which of the following rows has been misconfigured?
A. Row 1
B. Row 2
C. Row 3
D. Row 4
E. Row 5
cards.why: Row 4 is keyed as the misconfiguration, meaning its permissions violate the least privilege model or the administrator full-access rule. The table is not shown, so this relies on the answer key.

whyNot.A: Row 1 is keyed as correctly configured under the read-only, least privilege policy, though the table is not shown.
whyNot.B: Row 2 is keyed as correctly configured under the policy, though the table is not shown.
whyNot.C: Row 3 is keyed as correctly configured under the policy, though the table is not shown.
whyNot.E: Row 5 is keyed as correctly configured under the policy, though the table is not shown.

cards.front:
A copy of a highly confidential salary report was recently found on a printer in the IT department. The human resources department does not have this specific printer mapped to its devices, and it is suspected that an employee in the IT department browsed to the share where the report was located and printed it without authorization. Which of the following technical controls would be the BEST choice to immediately prevent this from happening again?
A. Implement a DLP solution and classify the report as confidential, restricting access only to human resources staff
B. Restrict access to the share where the report resides to only human resources employees and enable auditing
C. Have all members of the IT department review and sign the AUP and disciplinary policies
D. Place the human resources computers on a restricted VLAN and configure the ACL to prevent access from the IT department
cards.back: B. Restrict access to the share where the report resides to only human resources employees and enable auditing
cards.why: Restricting the share to HR (Human Resources) employees and enabling auditing immediately enforces least privilege on the file's source and records any further access attempts.

whyNot.A: Deploying DLP (Data Loss Prevention) and classifying data takes time to roll out, so it is not the best immediate fix.
whyNot.C: Signing the AUP (Acceptable Use Policy) is an administrative control, not a technical control, and does not block access.
whyNot.D: Placing HR (Human Resources) computers on a restricted VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) with an ACL (Access Control List) is complex and does not directly secure the share itself.

cards.front:
A company is developing a new system that will unlock a computer automatically when an authorized user sits in front of it, and then lock the computer when the user leaves. The user does not have to perform any action for this process to occur. Which of the following technologies provides this capability?
A. Facial recognition
B. Fingerprint scanner
C. Motion detector
D. Smart cards
cards.why: Facial recognition is a biometric that identifies an authorized user passively from their face, so it can unlock on arrival and lock on departure with no user action.

whyNot.B: A fingerprint scanner requires the user to deliberately place a finger on it, which is a required action.
whyNot.C: A motion detector senses movement but cannot tell whether the person is authorized, so it cannot authenticate anyone.
whyNot.D: A smart card must be inserted or tapped by the user, which is a required action, and it does not detect the user leaving.

cards.front:
A security analyst accesses corporate web pages and inputs random data in the forms. The response received includes the type of database used and SQL commands that the database accepts. Which of the following should the security analyst use to prevent this vulnerability?
A. Application fuzzing
B. Error handling
C. Input validation
D. Pointer dereference
cards.why: The forms leaked the database type and accepted SQL (Structured Query Language) commands in verbose error messages. Input validation is the keyed fix, though error handling addresses the leak directly.

whyNot.A: Application fuzzing is a testing technique that finds flaws like this, but it does not prevent them.
whyNot.B: Error handling suppresses verbose database errors, which is the actual information leak shown, although it does not stop injection itself.
whyNot.D: Pointer dereference is a memory-handling flaw in native code and is unrelated to web form errors revealing database details.

cards.keyDoubt: B because the described problem is verbose error output exposing the database type and accepted commands, which proper error handling prevents.

cards.front:
Which of the following differentiates a collision attack from a rainbow table attack?
A. A rainbow table attack performs a hash lookup
B. A rainbow table attack uses the hash as a password
C. In a collision attack, the hash and the input data are equivalent
D. In a collision attack, the same input results in different hashes
cards.back: A. A rainbow table attack performs a hash lookup
cards.why: A rainbow table attack looks up a captured hash in a precomputed table to find a matching plaintext, while a collision attack finds two different inputs producing the same hash.

whyNot.B: A rainbow table attack does not use the hash as a password, which is a pass-the-hash idea, but instead looks up the matching plaintext.
whyNot.C: In a collision attack the hash values match, but the input data are different, not equivalent.
whyNot.D: This reverses the idea, because a hash function gives the same hash for the same input, and collisions are different inputs giving the same hash.

cards.front:
A help desk is troubleshooting user reports that the corporate website is presenting untrusted certificate errors to employees and customers when they visit the website. Which of the following is the MOST likely cause of this error, provided the certificate has not expired?
A. The certificate was self signed, and the CA was not imported by employees or customers
B. The root CA has revoked the certificate of the intermediate CA
C. The valid period for the certificate has passed, and a new certificate has not been issued
D. The key escrow server has blocked the certificate from being validated
cards.back: B. The root CA has revoked the certificate of the intermediate CA
cards.why: A revoked intermediate CA (Certificate Authority) certificate breaks the chain of trust, so every certificate it issued shows as untrusted even when not expired.

whyNot.A: A self-signed certificate with an unimported CA (Certificate Authority) would cause this error, and it is the more common real-world cause.
whyNot.C: The question states the certificate has not expired, so an elapsed validity period is ruled out.
whyNot.D: A key escrow server stores recovery keys and plays no role in validating certificates presented to browsers.

cards.keyDoubt: A because a self-signed certificate not trusted by users is the most likely cause of widespread untrusted certificate errors.

cards.front:
A security analyst is investigating a suspected security breach and discovers the following in the logs of the potentially compromised server: Which of the following would be the BEST method for preventing this type of suspected attack in the future?
A. Implement password expirations
B. Implement restrictions on shared credentials
C. Implement account lockout settings
D. Implement time-of-day restrictions on this server
cards.why: Account lockout settings stop brute-force or password-guessing attacks by locking an account after a set number of failed logins, which is what repeated failures in the logs indicate.

whyNot.A: Password expiration forces periodic changes but does not stop rapid repeated guessing against an account.
whyNot.B: Restricting shared credentials limits account sharing and does not stop automated password guessing.
whyNot.D: Time-of-day restrictions limit when logins are allowed, but attackers can still guess passwords during permitted hours.

cards.front:
A security administrator is trying to encrypt communication. For which of the following reasons should administrator take advantage of the Subject Alternative Name (SAM) attribute of a certificate?
A. It can protect multiple domains
B. It provides extended site validation
C. It does not require a trusted certificate authority
D. It protects unlimited subdomains
cards.back: B. It provides extended site validation
cards.why: The keyed answer says extended validation, but a SAN (Subject Alternative Name) actually lists additional hostnames, letting one certificate protect multiple domains. The key appears to be wrong.

whyNot.A: Protecting multiple domains is the real purpose of a SAN (Subject Alternative Name), so this option is actually correct.
whyNot.C: Every publicly trusted certificate with a SAN (Subject Alternative Name) still needs a trusted CA (Certificate Authority).
whyNot.D: Unlimited subdomains are covered by a wildcard certificate, not by a SAN (Subject Alternative Name) list of named entries.

cards.keyDoubt: A because a SAN (Subject Alternative Name) lets one certificate cover multiple domains, while extended validation is a separate certificate type.

cards.front:
After a merger between two companies a security analyst has been asked to ensure that the organization's systems are secured against infiltration by any former employees that were terminated during the transition. Which of the following actions are MOST appropriate to harden applications against infiltration by former employees? (Select TWO)
A. Monitor VPN client access
B. Reduce failed login out settings
C. Develop and implement updated access control policies
D. Review and address invalid login attempts
E. Increase password complexity requirements
F. Assess and eliminate inactive accounts
cards.back:
C. Develop and implement updated access control policies
F. Assess and eliminate inactive accounts
cards.why: Updated access control policies define who keeps access after the merger, and eliminating inactive accounts removes dormant credentials that former employees could exploit.

whyNot.A: Monitoring VPN (Virtual Private Network) client access only detects use and does not remove the former employees' access.
whyNot.B: Reducing failed login settings targets guessing attacks, not former employees who may still hold valid credentials.
whyNot.D: Reviewing invalid login attempts is detective and reactive, and does not harden accounts against valid credentials of former staff.
whyNot.E: Increasing password complexity does not help when former employees already know their existing credentials.

cards.front:
A new mobile application is being developed in-house. Security reviews did not pick up any major flaws, however vulnerability scanning results show fundamental issues at the very end of the project cycle. Which of the following security activities should also have been performed to discover vulnerabilities earlier in the lifecycle?
A. Architecture review
B. Risk assessment
C. Protocol analysis
D. Code review
cards.why: Code review (manual or static analysis of source code during development) finds fundamental coding flaws early in the lifecycle, instead of waiting for vulnerability scanning of the finished application.

whyNot.A: Architecture review checks the overall design, but it would not find implementation flaws in the source code that a vulnerability scan later exposes.
whyNot.B: Risk assessment ranks threats and impact at a high level and does not inspect the application's code for flaws.
whyNot.C: Protocol analysis examines network traffic and communication protocols, not the in-house application's source code.

cards.front:
A security administrator is creating a subnet on one of the corporate firewall interfaces to use as a DMZ which is expected to accommodate at most 14 physical hosts. Which of the following subnets would BEST meet the requirements?
A. 192.168.0.16 255.25.255.248
B. 192.168.0.16/28
C. 192.168.1.50 255.255.25.240
D. 192.168.2.32/27
cards.why: A /28 CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) prefix gives 16 addresses, 14 of them usable for hosts, and 192.168.0.16 is a valid /28 network boundary. This fits 14 hosts with no waste.

whyNot.A: The mask 255.25.255.248 is malformed, and a 29-bit prefix would give only 6 usable host addresses anyway.
whyNot.C: The mask 255.255.25.240 is not a valid subnet mask, and 192.168.1.50 is not on a /28 network boundary.
whyNot.D: A /27 prefix gives 30 usable host addresses, which is more than needed, so it is not the best fit.

cards.front:
A company has a security policy that specifies all endpoint computing devices should be assigned a unique identifier that can be tracked via an inventory management system. Recent changes to airline security regulations have cause many executives in the company to travel with mini tablet devices instead of laptops. These tablet devices are difficult to tag and track. An RDP application is used from the tablet to connect into the company network. Which of the following should be implemented in order to meet the security policy requirements?
A. Virtual desktop infrastructure (IDI)
B. WS-security and geo-fencing
C. A hardware security module (HSM)
D. RFID tagging system
E. MDM software
F. Security Requirements Traceability Matrix (SRTM)
cards.why: MDM (Mobile Device Management) software enrolls tablets, assigns each a unique identifier, and tracks it in inventory without a physical tag, satisfying the policy even though the tablets only use RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol).

whyNot.A: VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure) hosts desktops centrally, but it does not assign or track unique identifiers for the physical tablet endpoints.
whyNot.B: WS-Security (Web Services Security) protects web service messages, and geo-fencing limits location, so neither inventories devices.
whyNot.C: An HSM (Hardware Security Module) stores and protects cryptographic keys and does not track endpoint devices.
whyNot.D: An RFID (Radio-Frequency Identification) tagging system needs a physical tag, and the question says these small tablets are difficult to tag.
whyNot.F: An SRTM (Security Requirements Traceability Matrix) maps requirements to tests during development and does not track devices.

cards.front:
The security administrator receives an email on a non-company account from a coworker stating that some reports are not exporting correctly. Attached to the email was an example report file with several customers' names and credit card numbers with the PIN. Which of the following is the BEST technical controls that will help mitigate this risk of disclosing sensitive data?
A. Configure the mail server to require TLS connections for every email to ensure all transport data is encrypted
B. Create a user training program to identify the correct use of email and perform regular audits to ensure compliance
C. Implement a DLP solution on the email gateway to scan email and remove sensitive data or files
D. Classify all data according to its sensitivity and inform the users of data that is prohibited to share
cards.back: C. Implement a DLP solution on the email gateway to scan email and remove sensitive data or files
cards.why: DLP (Data Loss Prevention) on the email gateway is a technical control that scans outbound messages and attachments, then blocks or strips sensitive data such as card numbers and PINs (Personal Identification Numbers).

whyNot.A: Requiring TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts email in transit but does not stop a user from sending sensitive data to an outside account.
whyNot.B: User training and audits are administrative controls, not technical controls, and they cannot automatically block a sensitive file.
whyNot.D: Data classification and user notices are administrative measures that rely on people following rules and do not technically prevent disclosure.

cards.front:
A technician is configuring a wireless guest network. After applying the most recent changes the technician finds the new devices can no longer find the wireless network by name but existing devices are still able to use the wireless network. Which of the following security measures did the technician MOST likely implement to cause this Scenario?
A. Deactivation of SSID broadcast
B. Reduction of WAP signal output power
C. Activation of 802.1X with RADIUS
D. Implementation of MAC filtering
E. Beacon interval was decreased
cards.why: Deactivating SSID (Service Set Identifier) broadcast hides the network name, so new devices cannot find it by name, while existing devices with the saved profile keep connecting.

whyNot.B: Reducing WAP (Wireless Access Point) power shrinks coverage for all devices, and existing devices would also be affected.
whyNot.C: Activating 802.1X (IEEE port-based network access control) with RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) requires authentication, but the network name would still be visible.
whyNot.D: MAC (Media Access Control) address filtering blocks unapproved devices from connecting, but it does not hide the network name from discovery.
whyNot.E: A shorter beacon interval makes the access point advertise more often, which makes the network easier to discover, not harder.

cards.front:
A security administrator has been assigned to review the security posture of the standard corporate system image for virtual machines. The security administrator conducts a thorough review of the system logs, installation procedures, and network configuration of the VM image. Upon reviewing the access logs and user accounts, the security administrator determines that several accounts will not be used in production. Which of the following would correct the deficiencies?
A. Mandatory access controls
B. Disable remote login
C. Host hardening
D. Disabling services
cards.why: Host hardening removes or disables unnecessary accounts, services, and settings from a system image, so unused accounts that will not be needed in production should be removed as part of it.

whyNot.A: Mandatory access controls enforce label-based permissions, but they do not remove unneeded accounts from the image.
whyNot.B: Disabling remote login limits one access path, but it does not address the unused accounts that remain in the image.
whyNot.D: Disabling services covers running services only, not unused user accounts, and is just one part of host hardening.

cards.front:
Although a web enabled application appears to only allow letters in the comment field of a web form, malicious user was able to carry a SQL injection attack by sending special characters through the web comment field. Which of the following has the application programmer failed to implement?
A. Revision control system
B. Client side exception handling
C. Server side validation
D. Server hardening
cards.why: Server-side validation checks and sanitizes all input on the server, so special characters used in SQL (Structured Query Language) injection are rejected even when client-side checks are bypassed.

whyNot.A: A revision control system tracks code changes and does nothing to filter malicious input at runtime.
whyNot.B: Client-side exception handling runs in the user's browser, which an attacker can bypass, and it handles errors rather than validating input.
whyNot.D: Server hardening reduces the attack surface of the host, but it does not validate the data the application accepts.

cards.front:
An attacker discovers a new vulnerability in an enterprise application. The attacker takes advantage of the vulnerability by developing new malware. After installing the malware, the attacker is provided with access to the infected machine. Which of the following is being described?
A. Zero-day exploit
B. Remote code execution
C. Session hijacking
D. Command injection
cards.why: A zero-day exploit uses a previously unknown vulnerability that has no patch. The attacker found a new flaw and wrote malware to exploit it, which matches this scenario.

whyNot.B: Remote code execution describes an outcome of running code remotely, not the use of a newly discovered, unpatched vulnerability.
whyNot.C: Session hijacking takes over a legitimate user's active session and does not involve developing malware for a new flaw.
whyNot.D: Command injection inserts operating system commands through an input field and is not defined by a brand-new vulnerability.

cards.front:
A security administrator returning from a short vacation receives an account lock-out message when attempting to log into the computer. After getting the account unlocked the security administrator immediately notices a large amount of emails alerts pertaining to several different user accounts being locked out during the past three days. The security administrator uses system logs to determine that the lock-outs were due to a brute force attack on all accounts that has been previously logged into that machine. Which of the following can be implemented to reduce the likelihood of this attack going undetected?
A. Password complexity rules
B. Continuous monitoring
C. User access reviews
D. Account lockout policies
cards.why: Continuous monitoring watches logs and events in near real time and alerts on activity such as repeated failed logins, so a brute force attack is noticed quickly instead of days later.

whyNot.A: Password complexity rules make passwords harder to guess, but they do not help detect an attack in progress.
whyNot.C: User access reviews periodically check who holds which permissions and would not reveal a brute force attack as it happens.
whyNot.D: Account lockout policies were already working, since accounts locked, but they did not make anyone notice the attack for three days.

cards.front:
A bank requires tellers to get manager approval when a customer wants to open a new account. A recent audit shows that there have been four cases in the previous year where tellers opened accounts without management approval. The bank president thought separation of duties would prevent this from happening. In order to implement a true separation of duties approach the bank could:
A. Require the use of two different passwords held by two different individuals to open an account
B. Administer account creation on a role based access control approach
C. Require all new accounts to be handled by someone else other than a teller since they have different duties
D. Administer account creation on a rule based access control approach
cards.back: C. Require all new accounts to be handled by someone else other than a teller since they have different duties
cards.why: True separation of duties splits a task between different roles, so a teller cannot complete the sensitive step alone. Giving account creation to someone other than a teller enforces that split.

whyNot.A: Two passwords held by two people is dual control or split knowledge, and a teller could still start and finish the process.
whyNot.B: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) assigns permissions by job role but does not by itself split one task across separate people.
whyNot.D: Rule-based access control applies fixed rules such as time or location and does not divide a task between different people.

cards.front:
A security administrator has been tasked with improving the overall security posture related to desktop machines on the network. An auditor has recently that several machines with confidential customer information displayed in the screens are left unattended during the course of the day. Which of the following could the security administrator implement to reduce the risk associated with the finding?
A. Implement a clean desk policy
B. Security training to prevent shoulder surfing
C. Enable group policy based screensaver timeouts
D. Install privacy screens on monitors
cards.back: C. Enable group policy based screensaver timeouts
cards.why: Group Policy screensaver timeouts automatically lock unattended machines after a set idle time, which directly reduces the risk of confidential information staying visible on unattended screens.

whyNot.A: A clean desk policy covers papers and items on desks, not the information displayed on unattended computer screens.
whyNot.B: Shoulder surfing training addresses people watching over a shoulder, not machines left unattended and unlocked.
whyNot.D: Privacy screens limit viewing angles for nearby observers but do not lock an unattended machine or hide its content from someone standing in front of it.

cards.front:
Company policy requires the use if passphrases instead if passwords. Which of the following technical controls MUST be in place in order to promote the use of passphrases?
A. Reuse
B. Length
C. History
D. Complexity
cards.why: Passphrases are long strings of words, so a minimum length requirement is the control that must be in place to encourage them over short passwords.

whyNot.A: Reuse is not a control that promotes passphrases, and restricting password reuse does nothing to make passwords longer.
whyNot.C: Password history stops users from cycling back to old passwords but does not make them create longer passphrases.
whyNot.D: Complexity rules force mixed character types, which pushes users toward short, hard-to-remember passwords instead of long passphrases.

cards.front:
During a routine audit, it is discovered that someone has been using a stale administrator account to log into a seldom used server. The person has been using the server to view inappropriate websites that are prohibited to end users. Which of the following could best prevent this from occurring again?
A. Credential management
B. Group policy management
C. Acceptable use policy
D. Account expiration policy
cards.why: An account expiration policy automatically disables accounts that are stale or no longer needed, so an unused administrator account could not be used to log into the server.

whyNot.A: Credential management stores and handles credentials but does not automatically disable stale accounts when they are no longer in use.
whyNot.B: Group Policy management pushes settings to systems, but it does not by itself retire dormant accounts.
whyNot.C: An AUP (Acceptable Use Policy) states what users may do, but it does not technically stop a stale account from logging in.

cards.front:
Which of the following should identify critical systems and components?
A. MOU
B. BPA
C. ITCP
D. BCP
cards.why: A BCP (Business Continuity Plan) identifies the critical systems and components the business needs to keep running and describes how to keep them operating during a disruption.

whyNot.A: An MOU (Memorandum of Understanding) is a non-binding agreement between parties and does not identify critical systems.
whyNot.B: A BPA (Business Partnership Agreement) defines the relationship between business partners, not the company's critical systems.
whyNot.C: An ITCP (Information Technology Contingency Plan) covers recovery of IT services, and it relies on the business continuity plan to say which systems are critical.

cards.front:
Which of the following works by implanting software on systems but delays execution until a specific set of conditions is met?
A. Logic bomb
B. Trojan
C. Scareware
D. Ransomware
cards.why: A logic bomb is malicious code planted on a system that stays dormant until specific conditions, such as a date or an event, are met, and then it executes.

whyNot.B: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software and runs when the user installs or opens it, not on a set condition.
whyNot.C: Scareware uses fake warnings to frighten users into buying or installing something, and it does not wait for a trigger.
whyNot.D: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, and it normally runs immediately instead of waiting for a specific condition.

cards.front:
A web application is configured to target browsers and allow access to bank accounts to siphon money to a foreign account. This is an example of which of the following attacks?
A. SQL injection
B. Header manipulation
C. Cross-site scripting
D. Flash cookie exploitation
cards.why: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) injects malicious script into a web application so it runs in victims' browsers, letting attackers act within authenticated banking sessions and move money.

whyNot.A: SQL (Structured Query Language) injection targets the back-end database through unsanitized input, not the users' browsers.
whyNot.B: Header manipulation alters HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) headers and does not by itself run attacker code in a victim's browser session.
whyNot.D: Flash cookie exploitation abuses locally shared objects for tracking or data theft and is not the browser-targeting script attack described.

cards.front:
Technicians working with servers hosted at the company's datacenter are increasingly complaining of electric shocks when touching metal items which have been linked to hard drive failures. Which of the following should be implemented to correct this issue?
A. Decrease the room temperature
B. Increase humidity in the room
C. Utilize better hot/cold aisle configurations
D. Implement EMI shielding
cards.back: B. Increase humidity in the room
cards.why: Low humidity allows static electricity to build up, causing shocks and ESD (Electrostatic Discharge) that damages hard drives. Raising humidity to a proper range reduces static.

whyNot.A: Lowering the temperature does not reduce static buildup and can lower humidity further, making ESD (Electrostatic Discharge) worse.
whyNot.C: Hot and cold aisle layouts improve cooling airflow efficiency but do not control static electricity.
whyNot.D: EMI (Electromagnetic Interference) shielding blocks radiated interference on signals and does not prevent static discharge shocks to technicians.

cards.front:
A portable data storage device has been determined to have malicious firmware. Which of the following is the BEST course of action to ensure data confidentiality?
A. Format the device
B. Re-image the device
C. Perform virus scan in the device
D. Physically destroy the device
cards.back: C. Perform virus scan in the device
cards.why: Malicious firmware lives below the file system, so formatting, re-imaging, or scanning cannot be trusted to remove it. Physical destruction is the only sure way to protect confidentiality.

whyNot.A: Formatting rewrites the file system but does not remove or reliably overwrite compromised firmware on the device controller.
whyNot.B: Re-imaging restores the storage contents but leaves the malicious firmware in place, so it can still steal data.
whyNot.C: A virus scan runs on the host operating system and generally cannot inspect or clean device firmware.

cards.keyDoubt: D: Malicious firmware survives scanning, formatting, and re-imaging, so physically destroying the device is the best way to guarantee data confidentiality.

cards.front:
A security administrator must implement a system to ensure that invalid certificates are not used by a custom developed application. The system must be able to check the validity of certificates even when internet access is unavailable. Which of the following MUST be implemented to support this requirement?
A. CSR
B. OCSP
C. CRL
D. SSH
cards.why: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) can be downloaded and cached locally, so the application can check certificate validity without live internet access.

whyNot.A: A CSR (Certificate Signing Request) is submitted to a certificate authority to obtain a certificate and does not check validity.
whyNot.B: OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) queries a responder in real time, so it fails when internet access is unavailable.
whyNot.D: SSH (Secure Shell) provides encrypted remote administration and has no role in checking certificate revocation status.

cards.front:
A technician has installed new vulnerability scanner software on a server that is joined to the company domain. The vulnerability scanner is able to provide visibility over the patch posture of all company's clients. Which of the following is being used?
A. Gray box vulnerability testing
B. Passive scan
C. Credentialed scan
D. Bypassing security controls
cards.why: A credentialed scan logs in to hosts with valid domain credentials, giving deep visibility into installed patches and configuration that an unauthenticated scan cannot see.

whyNot.A: Gray box testing describes partial knowledge of the target and does not describe authenticated access to read patch posture.
whyNot.B: A passive scan only observes network traffic and cannot reliably enumerate the patch levels of every client.
whyNot.D: Bypassing security controls means evading protections, whereas the scanner here is using legitimate access to gather patch information.

cards.front:
The Chief Security Officer (CISO) at a multinational banking corporation is reviewing a plan to upgrade the entire corporate IT infrastructure. The architecture consists of a centralized cloud environment hosting the majority of data, small server clusters at each corporate location to handle the majority of customer transaction processing, ATMs, and a new mobile banking application accessible from smartphones, tablets, and the Internet via HTTP. The corporation does business having varying data retention and privacy laws. Which of the following technical modifications to the architecture and corresponding security controls should be implemented to provide the MOST complete protection of data?
A. Revoke exiting root certificates, re-issue new customer certificates, and ensure all transactions are digitally signed to minimize fraud, implement encryption for data in-transit between data centers
B. Ensure all data is encryption according to the most stringent regulatory guidance applicable, implement encryption for data in-transit between data centers, increase data availability by replicating all data, transaction data, logs between each corporate location
C. Store customer data based on national borders, ensure end-to end encryption between ATMs, end users, and servers, test redundancy and COOP plans to ensure data is not inadvertently shifted from one legal jurisdiction to another with more stringent regulations
D. Install redundant servers to handle corporate customer processing, encrypt all customer data to ease the transfer from one country to another, implement end-to-end encryption between mobile applications and the cloud.
cards.back: C. Store customer data based on national borders, ensure end-to end encryption between ATMs, end users, and servers, test redundancy and COOP plans to ensure data is not inadvertently shifted from one legal jurisdiction to another with more stringent regulations
cards.why: Storing data by national border, using end-to-end encryption, and testing COOP (Continuity of Operations Plan) so data never crosses into a different legal jurisdiction addresses the varying retention and privacy laws.

whyNot.A: Reissuing certificates and signing transactions reduces fraud but ignores data residency laws and encrypts only data in transit between data centers.
whyNot.B: Replicating all data between every location can move data across jurisdictions and violate local privacy and retention laws.
whyNot.D: Encrypting data to ease cross-country transfer ignores legal restrictions on moving data, and it omits ATM (Automated Teller Machine) protection.

cards.front:
While reviewing the monthly internet usage it is noted that there is a large spike in traffic classified as "unknown" and does not appear to be within the bounds of the organizations Acceptable Use Policy. Which of the following tool or technology would work BEST for obtaining more information on this traffic?
A. Firewall logs
B. IDS logs
C. Increased spam filtering
D. Protocol analyzer
cards.why: A protocol analyzer captures and decodes actual packets, so it can identify what protocols and content make up the unclassified traffic. This gives the most detail about the unknown spike.

whyNot.A: Firewall logs record connection metadata such as addresses and ports, which is likely how the traffic was already classified as unknown.
whyNot.B: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) logs only show alerts matching known signatures, so they add little for traffic that is unclassified.
whyNot.C: Spam filtering targets unwanted email and has no bearing on identifying unknown network traffic.

cards.keyDoubt: D: A protocol analyzer decodes the packets themselves, which is the best way to learn what unclassified traffic actually is, whereas IDS (Intrusion Detection System) logs only show signature matches.

cards.front:
A network administrator wants to ensure that users do not connect any unauthorized devices to the company network. Each desk needs to connect a VoIP phone and computer. Which of the following is the BEST way to accomplish this?
A. Enforce authentication for network devices
B. Configure the phones on one VLAN, and computers on another
C. Enable and configure port channels
D. Make users sign an Acceptable use Agreement
cards.back: A. Enforce authentication for network devices
cards.why: Enforcing authentication for network devices, such as 802.1X (port-based network access control), prevents unauthorized devices from joining the network even when plugged into a desk port.

whyNot.B: Separating phones and computers into different VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) organizes traffic but does not stop an unauthorized device from connecting.
whyNot.C: Port channels bundle links for bandwidth and redundancy and do nothing to control which devices connect.
whyNot.D: An Acceptable Use Agreement is an administrative policy and cannot technically block unauthorized devices from connecting.

cards.front:
An administrator has concerns regarding the traveling sales team who works primarily from smart phones. Given the sensitive nature of their work, which of the following would BEST prevent access to the data in case of loss or theft?
A. Enable screensaver locks when the phones are not in use to prevent unauthorized access
B. Configure the smart phones so that the stored data can be destroyed from a centralized location
C. Configure the smart phones so that all data is saved to removable media and kept separate from the device
D. Enable GPS tracking on all smart phones so that they can be quickly located and recovered
cards.back: B. Configure the smart phones so that the stored data can be destroyed from a centralized location
cards.why: Remote wipe lets administrators destroy data from a central location after a phone is lost or stolen, which best prevents data access regardless of the device's state.

whyNot.A: Screensaver locks can be bypassed or brute forced and do not remove data from a device that is lost.
whyNot.C: Saving data to removable media leaves it easy to steal or lose alongside the phone and is impractical for mobile work.
whyNot.D: GPS (Global Positioning System) tracking helps locate a device but does nothing to prevent someone accessing its data.

cards.front:
A user of the wireless network is unable to gain access to the network. The symptoms are: 1.) Unable to connect to both internal and Internet resources 2.) The wireless icon shows connectivity but has no network access The wireless network is WPA2 Enterprise and users must be a member of the wireless security group to authenticate. Which of the following is the MOST likely cause of the connectivity issues?
A. The wireless signal is not strong enough
B. A remote DDoS attack against the RADIUS server is taking place
C. The user's laptop only supports WPA and WEP
D. The DHCP scope is full
E. The dynamic encryption key did not update while the user was offline
cards.back: C. The user's laptop only supports WPA and WEP
cards.why: WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) Enterprise needs a supported cipher. A laptop supporting only WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) and WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) cannot complete authentication with the network.

whyNot.A: A weak signal would show poor or no connectivity, not an icon indicating connection.
whyNot.B: A DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack on the RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server would affect many users, not a single user.
whyNot.D: The DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) scope being full would affect multiple new clients and is not suggested by a single user's problem.
whyNot.E: Dynamic keys are renegotiated automatically at reconnect, so an offline user missing an update would not cause this failure.

cards.keyDoubt: D: A connected wireless icon with no network access, for both internal and Internet resources, points to no IP (Internet Protocol) address being assigned because the DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) scope is full.

cards.front:
A chief Financial Officer (CFO) has asked the Chief Information Officer (CISO) to provide responses to a recent audit report detailing deficiencies in the organization security controls. The CFO would like to know ways in which the organization can improve its authorization controls. Given the request by the CFO, which of the following controls should the CISO focus on in the report? (Select Three)
A. Password complexity policies
B. Hardware tokens
C. Biometric systems
D. Role-based permissions
E. One time passwords
F. Separation of duties
G. Multifactor authentication
H. Single sign-on
I. Lease privilege
cards.back:
D. Role-based permissions
F. Separation of duties
I. Lease privilege
cards.why: Role-based permissions and separation of duties are authorization controls that limit what authenticated users can do. Least privilege is the third control, which the key omits.

whyNot.A: Password complexity policies strengthen authentication, not authorization.
whyNot.B: Hardware tokens are an authentication factor, not an authorization control.
whyNot.C: Biometric systems verify identity, which is authentication rather than authorization.
whyNot.E: OTPs (One-Time Passwords) are an authentication method and do not define user permissions.
whyNot.G: MFA (Multifactor Authentication) strengthens identity verification, which is authentication rather than authorization.
whyNot.H: SSO (Single Sign-On) simplifies authentication across systems and does not control access rights.
whyNot.I: Least privilege is also a valid authorization control and is the missing third answer, since the question says select three.

cards.keyDoubt: I: The question asks for three, and least privilege is an authorization control just like role-based permissions and separation of duties, so the key is missing it.

cards.front:
A mobile device user is concerned about geographic positioning information being included in messages sent between users on a popular social network platform. The user turns off the functionality in the application, but wants to ensure the application cannot re-enable the setting without the knowledge of the user. Which of the following mobile device capabilities should the user disable to achieve the stated goal?
A. Device access control
B. Location based services
C. Application control
D. GEO-Tagging
cards.why: Disabling location based services at the device level removes the location data source, so the application cannot re-enable geotagging without the user's knowledge.

whyNot.A: Device access control governs who can unlock or use the device and does not stop apps from using location data.
whyNot.C: Application control restricts which apps can be installed or run and does not block location access by an approved app.
whyNot.D: Geo-tagging is the app-level setting the user already turned off, and the app could re-enable it, so disabling it again does not meet the goal.

cards.keyDoubt: B: Turning off location based services at the operating system level prevents any app from obtaining position data, which meets the goal that the app cannot re-enable it.

cards.front:
A member of a digital forensics team, Joe arrives at a crime scene and is preparing to collect system data. Before powering the system off, Joe knows that he must collect the most volatile date first. Which of the following is the correct order in which Joe should collect the data?
A. CPU cache, paging/swap files, RAM, remote logging data
B. RAM, CPU cache. Remote logging data, paging/swap files
C. Paging/swap files, CPU cache, RAM, remote logging data
D. CPU cache, RAM, paging/swap files, remote logging data
cards.back: D. CPU cache, RAM, paging/swap files, remote logging data
cards.why: The order of volatility says to collect the CPU cache first, then RAM (Random Access Memory), then paging/swap files on disk, then remote logging data, which is the least volatile.

whyNot.A: This places paging/swap files before RAM (Random Access Memory), but RAM is more volatile and must be collected first.
whyNot.B: This collects RAM (Random Access Memory) before the CPU (Central Processing Unit) cache and puts remote logs before swap files, both out of order.
whyNot.C: This starts with paging/swap files, which are far less volatile than the CPU (Central Processing Unit) cache and RAM (Random Access Memory).

cards.front:
An organization has hired a penetration tester to test the security of its ten web servers. The penetration tester is able to gain root/administrative access in several servers by exploiting vulnerabilities associated with the implementation of SMTP, POP, DNS, FTP, Telnet, and IMAP. Which of the following recommendations should the penetration tester provide to the organization to better protect their web servers in the future?
A. Use a honeypot
B. Disable unnecessary services
C. Implement transport layer security
D. Increase application event logging
cards.why: The compromises came through services such as SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), POP (Post Office Protocol), DNS (Domain Name System), FTP (File Transfer Protocol), Telnet, and IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol). Disabling unnecessary services shrinks the attack surface.

whyNot.A: A honeypot is a decoy for detecting and studying attackers and does not fix vulnerable services on production servers.
whyNot.C: TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts traffic but does not remove vulnerabilities in the service implementations themselves.
whyNot.D: More event logging helps detection and investigation but does not prevent exploitation of unneeded vulnerable services.

cards.front:
A security engineer is faced with competing requirements from the networking group and database administrators. The database administrators would like ten application servers on the same subnet for ease of administration, whereas the networking group would like to segment all applications from one another. Which of the following should the security administrator do to rectify this issue?
A. Recommend performing a security assessment on each application, and only segment the applications with the most vulnerability
B. Recommend classifying each application into like security groups and segmenting the groups from one another
C. Recommend segmenting each application, as it is the most secure approach
D. Recommend that only applications with minimal security features should be segmented to protect them
cards.back: B. Recommend classifying each application into like security groups and segmenting the groups from one another
cards.why: Classifying applications into groups with similar security requirements and segmenting the groups balances administrative ease with security isolation, satisfying both teams.

whyNot.A: Assessing each application and segmenting only the most vulnerable ones leaves other applications exposed and is costly and inconsistent.
whyNot.C: Segmenting every application ignores the administrators' need for manageability and is not required for all applications.
whyNot.D: Segmenting only low-security applications neglects the high-value applications that most need isolation.

cards.front:
A security analyst has been asked to perform a review of an organization's software development lifecycle. The analyst reports that the lifecycle does not contain a phase in which team members evaluate and provide critical feedback of another developer's code. Which of the following assessment techniques is BEST described in the analyst's report?
A. Architecture evaluation
B. Baseline reporting
C. Whitebox testing
D. Peer review
cards.why: Peer review is the technique where developers evaluate and give critical feedback on each other's code. The report says the SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle) has no such phase.

whyNot.A: Architecture evaluation examines the overall system design and structure, not another developer's source code line by line.
whyNot.B: Baseline reporting compares current system configuration or performance to an established standard, not code quality.
whyNot.C: Whitebox testing tests software with knowledge of its internals, but it is not a developer-to-developer feedback phase.

cards.front:
An attacker wearing a building maintenance uniform approached a company's receptionist asking for access to a secure area. The receptionist asks for identification, a building access badge and checks the company's list approved maintenance personnel prior to granting physical access to the secure are. The controls used by the receptionist are in place to prevent which of the following types of attacks?
A. Tailgating
B. Shoulder surfing
C. Impersonation
D. Hoax
cards.why: Impersonation is pretending to be a trusted person, such as maintenance staff. Checking identification, a badge, and an approved personnel list verifies that the claimed identity is real.

whyNot.A: Tailgating is following an authorized person through a door without credentials, which does not involve the receptionist verifying identity.
whyNot.B: Shoulder surfing is observing someone entering secrets like passwords, and identity checks at a desk do not prevent it.
whyNot.D: A hoax is a false warning or claim meant to cause unwarranted action, not a person seeking physical entry.

cards.front:
A security administrator is tasked with conducting an assessment made to establish the baseline security posture of the corporate IT infrastructure. The assessment must report actual flaws and weaknesses in the infrastructure. Due to the expense of hiring outside consultants, the testing must be performed using in-house or cheaply available resource. There cannot be a possibility of any requirement being damaged in the test. Which of the following has the administrator been tasked to perform?
A. Risk transference
B. Penetration test
C. Threat assessment
D. Vulnerability assessment
cards.why: A vulnerability assessment finds and reports actual weaknesses using in-house or inexpensive tools such as scanners, and it does not exploit them, so nothing can be damaged.

whyNot.A: Risk transference shifts risk to a third party, such as through insurance, and does not assess the infrastructure.
whyNot.B: A penetration test actively exploits weaknesses, which could damage systems and often needs costly specialists.
whyNot.C: A threat assessment identifies potential threat actors and events, not the actual flaws present in the infrastructure.

cards.front:
A network administrator is attempting to troubleshoot an issue regarding certificates on a secure website. During the troubleshooting process, the network administrator notices that the web gateway proxy on the local network has signed all of the certificates on the local machine. Which of the following describes the type of attack the proxy has been legitimately programmed to perform?
A. Transitive access
B. Spoofing
C. Man-in-the-middle
D. Replay
cards.why: A web gateway proxy that signs certificates with its own certificate authority sits between client and server and decrypts traffic. That is a man-in-the-middle position, here used legitimately for inspection.

whyNot.A: Transitive access is gaining access through a trusted relationship between systems, not re-signing certificates in transit.
whyNot.B: Spoofing is falsifying identity or address to appear as someone else, and the proxy is openly configured as a trusted inspector.
whyNot.D: A replay attack resends previously captured valid data to trick a system, which does not involve re-signing certificates.

cards.front:
Which of the following use the SSH protocol?
A. Stelnet
B. SCP
C. SNMP
D. FTPS
E. SSL
F. SFTP
cards.why: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) and SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) both run over SSH (Secure Shell) to transfer files with encryption.

whyNot.A: Stelnet is not a standard SSH-based protocol; Telnet itself is unencrypted and does not use SSH (Secure Shell).
whyNot.C: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is a network management protocol and does not use SSH (Secure Shell).
whyNot.D: FTPS (File Transfer Protocol Secure) secures FTP with SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) or TLS (Transport Layer Security), not SSH (Secure Shell).
whyNot.E: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) is a separate encryption protocol and is not built on SSH (Secure Shell).

cards.front:
Which of the following is the GREATEST risk to a company by allowing employees to physically bring their personal smartphones to work?
A. Taking pictures of proprietary information and equipment in restricted areas.
B. Installing soft token software to connect to the company's wireless network.
C. Company cannot automate patch management on personally-owned devices.
D. Increases the attack surface by having more target devices on the company's campus
cards.back: A. Taking pictures of proprietary information and equipment in restricted areas.
cards.why: Smartphone cameras let employees capture proprietary information or equipment in restricted areas, causing direct data leakage. This is the most serious risk of allowing personal phones on site.

whyNot.B: Installing a soft token to join the wireless network is a legitimate authentication method, not a significant risk.
whyNot.C: Lack of automated patch management is a real concern but is less severe than direct, easy capture of restricted information.
whyNot.D: A larger attack surface is a general concern, but it is less immediate than deliberate photography of restricted material.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the summary of loss for a given year?
A. MTBF
B. ALE
C. SLA
D. ARO
cards.why: ALE (Annual Loss Expectancy) is the expected monetary loss for a year, calculated as SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) multiplied by ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence).

whyNot.A: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) measures average operating time between failures, not yearly financial loss.
whyNot.C: An SLA (Service Level Agreement) is a contract defining expected service levels, not a loss summary.
whyNot.D: ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) is how many times a threat is expected per year, not the total loss.

cards.front:
A Security Officer on a military base needs to encrypt several smart phones that will be going into the field. Which of the following encryption solutions should be deployed in this situation?
A. Elliptic curve
B. One-time pad
C. 3DES
D. AES-256
cards.why: AES-256 (Advanced Encryption Standard with a 256-bit key) is a strong, widely approved symmetric cipher that is efficient on mobile devices and suitable for military use.

whyNot.A: Elliptic curve cryptography is mainly for key exchange and signatures, not bulk encryption of whole devices.
whyNot.B: A one-time pad needs a random key as long as the data, used once, which is impractical for smartphones.
whyNot.C: 3DES (Triple Data Encryption Standard) is older, slower, and deprecated compared with AES (Advanced Encryption Standard).

cards.front:
An organization relies heavily on an application that has a high frequency of security updates. At present, the security team only updates the application on the first Monday of each month, even though the security updates are released as often as twice a week. Which of the following would be the BEST method of updating this application?
A. Configure testing and automate patch management for the application.
B. Configure security control testing for the application.
C. Manually apply updates for the application when they are released.
D. Configure a sandbox for testing patches before the scheduled monthly update.
cards.back: A. Configure testing and automate patch management for the application.
cards.why: Automating patch management with testing lets frequent updates be validated and deployed quickly. This shortens the exposure window without relying on a slow monthly manual process.

whyNot.B: Security control testing checks that controls work but does not change how often or how fast patches are applied.
whyNot.C: Manually applying updates twice a week is labor intensive, error prone, and skips structured testing.
whyNot.D: A sandbox for testing helps with validation, but keeping the monthly schedule still leaves systems unpatched for weeks.

cards.front:
A technician must configure a firewall to block external DNS traffic from entering a network. Which of the following ports should they block on the firewall?
A. 53
B. 110
C. 143
D. 443
cards.why: DNS (Domain Name System) uses port 53, so blocking port 53 on the firewall stops external DNS traffic from entering the network.

whyNot.B: Port 110 is used by POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3) for email retrieval, not DNS (Domain Name System).
whyNot.C: Port 143 is used by IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) for email access, not DNS (Domain Name System).
whyNot.D: Port 443 is used by HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) for secure web traffic, not DNS (Domain Name System).

cards.front:
A software development company needs to share information between two remote servers, using encryption to protect it. A programmer suggests developing a new encryption protocol, arguing that using an unknown protocol with secure, existing cryptographic algorithm libraries will provide strong encryption without being susceptible to attacks on other known protocols. Which of the following summarizes the BEST response to the programmer's proposal?
A. The newly developed protocol will only be as secure as the underlying cryptographic algorithms used.
B. New protocols often introduce unexpected vulnerabilities, even when developed with otherwise secure and tested algorithm libraries.
C. A programmer should have specialized training in protocol development before attempting to design a new encryption protocol.
D. The obscurity value of unproven protocols against attacks often outweighs the potential for introducing new vulnerabilities.
cards.back: B. New protocols often introduce unexpected vulnerabilities, even when developed with otherwise secure and tested algorithm libraries.
cards.why: Custom protocols often contain design flaws that expose vulnerabilities even when built from sound cryptographic libraries. Established, peer-reviewed protocols are safer than untested ones.

whyNot.A: Security depends on how algorithms are combined in the protocol, so a flawed design can be weaker than its algorithms.
whyNot.C: Training helps, but the best response addresses the technical risk of unvetted protocols rather than the programmer's qualifications.
whyNot.D: Security through obscurity is unreliable, and obscurity does not outweigh the risk of new vulnerabilities.

cards.front:
A security technician would like to obscure sensitive data within a file so that it can be transferred without causing suspicion. Which of the following technologies would BEST be suited to accomplish this?
A. Transport Encryption
B. Stream Encryption
C. Digital Signature
D. Steganography
cards.back:
D. Steganography

Steganography is the process of hiding a message in another message so as to obfuscate its importance. It is also the process of hiding a message in a medium such as a digital image, audio file, or other file.
cards.why: Steganography hides data inside another file, such as an image, so the transfer does not look suspicious. It conceals the existence of the message, not just its content.

whyNot.A: Transport encryption protects data in transit but makes the traffic obviously encrypted, which can draw suspicion.
whyNot.B: Stream encryption scrambles data bit by bit, but the output is still visibly encrypted and does not hide its existence.
whyNot.C: A digital signature proves authenticity and integrity but does not conceal data.

cards.front:
A supervisor in your organization was demoted on Friday afternoon. The supervisor had the ability to modify the contents of a confidential database, as well as other managerial permissions. On Monday morning, the database administrator reported that log files indicated that several records were missing from the database. Which of the following risk mitigation strategies should have been implemented when the supervisor was demoted?
A. Incident management
B. Routine auditing
C. IT governance
D. Monthly user rights reviews
cards.why: Routine auditing reviews logs and changes regularly, which can catch improper modification of records. Here it would have flagged the demoted supervisor's activity soon after.

whyNot.A: Incident management is a response process after an event is detected, not a mitigation applied when someone is demoted.
whyNot.C: IT governance sets overall oversight and policy direction but is not the specific control for changed user permissions.
whyNot.D: Monthly user rights reviews are periodic and would not have removed the supervisor's access by Monday.

cards.keyDoubt: D. A user rights and permissions review at the time of the demotion would have removed the supervisor's database access, directly preventing the record deletion.

cards.front:
Which of the following attack types is being carried out where a target is being sent unsolicited messages via Bluetooth?
A. War chalking
B. Bluejacking
C. Bluesnarfing
D. Rogue tethering
cards.back:
B. Bluejacking

Bluejacking is the sending of unsolicited messages over Bluetooth to Bluetooth-enabled devices such as mobile phones, PDAs or laptop computers, sending a vCard which typically contains a message in the name field (i.e., for bluedating or bluechat) to another B...
cards.why: Bluejacking is sending unsolicited messages to a nearby device over Bluetooth. It is mostly a nuisance and does not take data from the target.

whyNot.A: War chalking is marking public places with symbols to show available wireless networks, not sending Bluetooth messages.
whyNot.C: Bluesnarfing is stealing data such as contacts or email from a device over Bluetooth, not sending messages to it.
whyNot.D: Rogue tethering is an unauthorized mobile hotspot connection to a network, not unsolicited Bluetooth messaging.

cards.front:
Joe is exchanging encrypted email with another party. Joe encrypts the initial email with a key. When Joe receives a response, he is unable to decrypt the response with the same key he used initially. Which of the following would explain the situation?
A. An ephemeral key was used for one of the messages
B. A stream cipher was used for the initial email; a block cipher was used for the reply
C. Out-of-band key exchange has taken place
D. Asymmetric encryption is being used
cards.back:
D. Asymmetric encryption is being used

Asymmetric algorithms use two keys to encrypt and decrypt data. These asymmetric keys are referred to as the public key and the private key.
cards.why: Asymmetric encryption uses a key pair. Joe encrypts with the other party's public key, and the reply is encrypted with Joe's public key, so he must decrypt it with his own private key.

whyNot.A: An ephemeral key is a temporary session key, and using one does not by itself explain why the original key fails.
whyNot.B: Mixing a stream cipher and a block cipher is unusual, and a symmetric reply would normally still use a shared key.
whyNot.C: Out-of-band key exchange only delivers keys through another channel and does not make a different key necessary for decryption.

cards.front:
Recently several employees were victims of a phishing email that appeared to originate from the company president. The email claimed the employees would be disciplined if they did not click on a malicious link in the message. Which of the following principles of social engineering made this attack successful?
A. Authority
B. Spamming
C. Social proof
D. Scarcity
cards.why: Authority is the social engineering principle in which people comply because a request seems to come from a superior. The spoofed email from the company president, with a threat of discipline, exploited that deference.

whyNot.B: Spamming is a delivery method for unsolicited bulk messages, not a social engineering principle that persuades victims.
whyNot.C: Social proof relies on people copying what others are doing, and this email gave no sign that other employees had complied.
whyNot.D: Scarcity pressures victims with limited availability of an item or offer, but this email threatened discipline instead.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the LEAST secure hashing algorithm?
A. SHA1
B. RIPEMD
C. MD5
D. DES
cards.why: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is the weakest of the listed hashing algorithms because it has a 128-bit output and practical collision attacks. It is considered broken for security use.

whyNot.A: SHA1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) is also deprecated for collisions, but it is somewhat stronger than MD5 (Message Digest 5).
whyNot.B: RIPEMD (RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest) has no practical collision attacks in its stronger variants, so it is less weak than MD5 (Message Digest 5).
whyNot.D: DES (Data Encryption Standard) is a symmetric encryption cipher, not a hashing algorithm, so it does not fit the question.

cards.front:
An employee uses RDP to connect back to the office network. If RDP is misconfigured, which of the following security exposures would this lead to?
A. A virus on the administrator's desktop would be able to sniff the administrator's username and password.
B. Result in an attacker being able to phish the employee's username and password.
C. A social engineering attack could occur, resulting in the employee's password being extracted.
D. A man in the middle attack could occur, resulting the employee's username and password being captured.
cards.back: D. A man in the middle attack could occur, resulting the employee's username and password being captured.
cards.why: A misconfigured RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) session may lack proper encryption or server authentication, which lets an attacker perform a man-in-the-middle attack and capture the user's credentials.

whyNot.A: Malware on the administrator's desktop is a separate compromise and does not result from RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) misconfiguration.
whyNot.B: Phishing is a deception attack carried out over email or the web, and it does not depend on how RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) is configured.
whyNot.C: Social engineering manipulates people directly and is unrelated to RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) settings.

cards.front:
Joe, the security administrator, sees this in a vulnerability scan report: "The server 10.1.2.232 is running Apache 2.2.20 which may be vulnerable to a mod_cgi exploit." Joe verifies that the mod_cgi module is not enabled on 10.1.2.232. This message is an example of:
A. a threat.
B. a risk.
C. a false negative.
D. a false positive.
cards.why: A false positive is a scanner reporting a vulnerability that does not actually exist. Joe confirmed the mod_cgi (Common Gateway Interface module) was not enabled, so the finding is false.

whyNot.A: A threat is a potential source of harm, and this scan finding is a mistaken report, not a threat.
whyNot.B: A risk is the likelihood and impact of a real vulnerability being exploited, and here the vulnerability is not present.
whyNot.C: A false negative means a real vulnerability goes undetected, which is the opposite of this situation.

cards.front:
An auditor has identified an access control system that can incorrectly accept an access attempt from an unauthorized user. Which of the following authentication systems has the auditor reviewed?
A. Password-based
B. Biometric-based
C. Location-based
D. Certificate-based
cards.why: Biometric systems can produce a false acceptance, where an unauthorized person's trait is wrongly matched to an enrolled user. This is measured as the FAR (False Acceptance Rate).

whyNot.A: Password-based systems compare exact secrets, so they do not have a statistical false acceptance rate.
whyNot.C: Location-based authentication checks where a request comes from, and it does not match a user's traits probabilistically.
whyNot.D: Certificate-based authentication uses cryptographic validation of a certificate, which is deterministic and does not produce false acceptances.

cards.front:
The Chief Technology Officer (CTO) of a company, Ann, is putting together a hardware budget for the next 10 years. She is asking for the average lifespan of each hardware device so that she is able to calculate when she will have to replace each device. Which of the following categories BEST describes what she is looking for?
A. ALE
B. MTTR
C. MTBF
D. MTTF
cards.why: MTTF (Mean Time To Failure) is the average lifespan of a non-repairable device before it fails. It is what a budget for replacing hardware would use.

whyNot.A: ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) is the expected yearly monetary loss from a risk, not a measure of hardware lifespan.
whyNot.B: MTTR (Mean Time To Repair) measures how long a repair takes, not how long a device lasts.
whyNot.C: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) applies to repairable systems and measures time between failures, not the lifespan of a device that gets replaced.

cards.front:
A software developer wants to ensure that the application is verifying that a key is valid before establishing SSL connections with random remote hosts on the Internet. Which of the following should be used in the code? (Select TWO.)
A. Escrowed keys
B. SSL symmetric encryption key
C. Software code private key
D. Remote server public key
E. OCSP
cards.back:
C. Software code private key
E. OCSP
cards.why: OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) checks whether a certificate is revoked or still valid. The key given is C and E, but the public key from the remote server's certificate is what gets validated.

whyNot.A: Escrowed keys are copies held by a third party for recovery, and they do not validate a remote host.
whyNot.B: An SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) symmetric session key is created after validation, so it cannot be used to verify the remote host.
whyNot.D: The remote server's public key is arguably correct and is what the code validates, but the answer key lists the software code private key instead.

cards.keyDoubt: D, because the code verifies the remote server's public key in its certificate, while a software code private key is for signing and is never used to check a remote host.

cards.front:
A security guard has informed the Chief Information Security Officer that a person with a tablet has been walking around the building. The guard also noticed strange white markings in different areas of the parking lot. The person is attempting which of the following types of attacks?
A. Jamming
B. War chalking
C. Packet sniffing
D. Near field communication
cards.why: War chalking is marking buildings or pavement with symbols to show the location and details of open wireless networks. A person walking around with a tablet to find networks, plus chalk marks, fits this attack.

whyNot.A: Jamming disrupts wireless signals with interference and does not involve chalk markings.
whyNot.C: Packet sniffing captures network traffic and leaves no physical chalk marks in a parking lot.
whyNot.D: NFC (Near Field Communication) works only within a few centimeters and does not involve marking locations.

cards.front:
A system administrator is configuring a site-to-site VPN tunnel. Which of the following should be configured on the VPN concentrator during the IKE phase?
A. RIPEMD
B. ECDHE
C. Diffie-Hellman
D. HTTPS
cards.why: During the IKE (Internet Key Exchange) phase of a site-to-site VPN (Virtual Private Network), Diffie-Hellman is used to securely establish a shared secret key between the two endpoints.

whyNot.A: RIPEMD (RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest) is a hashing algorithm and does not perform key exchange.
whyNot.B: ECDHE (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral) is mainly used in TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshakes, while IKE (Internet Key Exchange) classically uses Diffie-Hellman groups.
whyNot.D: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) secures web traffic and is not part of the IKE (Internet Key Exchange) negotiation.

cards.front:
A network operations manager has added a second row of server racks in the datacenter. These racks face the opposite direction of the first row of racks. Which of the following is the reason the manager installed the racks this way?
A. To lower energy consumption by sharing power outlets
B. To create environmental hot and cold isles
C. To eliminate the potential for electromagnetic interference
D. To maximize fire suppression capabilities
cards.back: B. To create environmental hot and cold isles
cards.why: Facing server racks in opposite directions creates alternating hot aisles and cold aisles, so cool air intake and hot exhaust stay separated and cooling is more efficient.

whyNot.A: Rack orientation does not let racks share power outlets or lower energy use that way.
whyNot.C: Electromagnetic interference is handled with shielding and cable separation, not by rack direction.
whyNot.D: Fire suppression depends on detection and suppression systems, not on which way racks face.

cards.front:
Phishing emails frequently take advantage of high-profile catastrophes reported in the news. Which of the following principles BEST describes the weakness being exploited?
A. Intimidation
B. Scarcity
C. Authority
D. Social proof
cards.why: Social proof exploits people's tendency to follow what others are doing or what seems widely accepted. High-profile news events make people feel that responding to related messages is normal.

whyNot.A: Intimidation uses threats or fear of consequences, and news-based phishing emails usually do not threaten the victim.
whyNot.B: Scarcity pressures victims with limited quantities or time, which is not the main weakness in catastrophe-themed emails.
whyNot.C: Authority relies on impersonating a superior or official body, which is not required for a message built on a news event.

cards.front:
New magnetic locks were ordered for an entire building. In accordance with company policy, employee safety is the top priority. In case of a fire where electricity is cut, which of the following should be taken into consideration when installing the new locks?
A. Fail safe
B. Fault tolerance
C. Fail secure
D. Redundancy
cards.why: Fail safe means locks unlock when power is lost, which lets people leave during a fire. This puts employee safety ahead of keeping the building secure.

whyNot.B: Fault tolerance keeps systems running despite component failures and does not define how a lock behaves without power.
whyNot.C: Fail secure keeps doors locked when power is lost, which could trap employees during a fire.
whyNot.D: Redundancy duplicates components for availability and does not decide whether a lock opens or stays locked.

cards.front:
Anne, the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), has reported that she is getting multiple telephone calls from someone claiming to be from the helpdesk. The caller is asking to verify her network authentication credentials because her computer is broadcasting across the network. This is MOST likely which of the following types of attacks?
A. Vishing
B. Impersonation
C. Spim
D. Scareware
cards.why: Vishing (voice phishing) is a social engineering attack carried out by phone, where the caller pretends to be from the helpdesk to trick the victim into revealing credentials.

whyNot.B: Impersonation describes pretending to be someone else in general, but the phone-call delivery makes vishing the more specific answer.
whyNot.C: Spim is spam delivered through instant messaging, not telephone calls.
whyNot.D: Scareware uses fake warnings on a computer to frighten users into installing malware, and it does not involve phone calls.

cards.front:
An administrator discovers the following log entry on a server: Nov 12 2013 00:23:45 httpd[2342]: GET /app2/prod/proc/process.php?input=change;cd%20../../../etc;cat%20shadow Which of the following attacks is being attempted?
A. Command injection
B. Password attack
C. Buffer overflow
D. Cross-site scripting
