cards.why: The log shows a semicolon followed by cd and cat shadow commands in the input parameter, which is command injection. The attacker is trying to run operating system commands to read the shadow password file.

whyNot.B: A password attack such as brute force or guessing would show repeated login attempts, not shell commands in a web request.
whyNot.C: A buffer overflow sends oversized input to overwrite memory and does not use shell commands like cd and cat.
whyNot.D: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) injects script into pages that run in a victim's browser, not commands that run on the server.

cards.front:
A security team wants to establish an Incident Response plan. The team has never experienced an incident. Which of the following would BEST help them establish plans and procedures?
A. Table top exercises
B. Lessons learned
C. Escalation procedures
D. Recovery procedures
cards.why: Tabletop exercises walk the team through simulated incident scenarios in discussion form. They help a team with no real incident experience build and test their response plans and procedures.

whyNot.B: Lessons learned review a past incident, and this team has never experienced one.
whyNot.C: Escalation procedures are one part of an incident response plan and need to be developed first, not used as the way to develop the plan.
whyNot.D: Recovery procedures are one phase of incident response and do not help the team build the overall plan.

cards.front:
Which of the following would verify that a threat does exist and security controls can easily be bypassed without actively testing an application?
A. Protocol analyzer
B. Vulnerability scan
C. Penetration test
D. Port scanner
cards.back:
B. Vulnerability scan

A vulnerability scan is the automated process of proactively identifying security vulnerabilities of computing systems in a network in order to determine if and where a system can be exploited and/or threatened.
cards.why: A vulnerability scan (an automated, non-intrusive check) identifies that weaknesses exist and that security controls could be bypassed, without actively exploiting the application.

whyNot.A: A protocol analyzer only captures and inspects network traffic and does not assess whether weaknesses or control bypasses exist.
whyNot.C: A penetration test actively exploits weaknesses, which the question rules out by saying the application is not actively tested.
whyNot.D: A port scanner only finds open ports and services and does not verify weaknesses or whether security controls can be bypassed.

cards.front:
Which of the following technologies would be MOST appropriate to utilize when testing a new software patch before a company-wide deployment?
A. Cloud computing
B. Virtualization
C. Redundancy
D. Application control
cards.back:
B. Virtualization

Virtualization is used to host one or more operating systems in the memory of a single host computer and allows multiple operating systems to run simultaneously on the same hardware, reducing costs.
cards.why: Virtualization lets the company test the patch in an isolated VM (Virtual Machine) that can be snapshotted and reverted, so production systems are never put at risk.

whyNot.A: Cloud computing is a hosting model and does not by itself give an isolated, disposable test environment for patches.
whyNot.C: Redundancy provides availability through duplicate components and does not help test whether a patch is safe.
whyNot.D: Application control restricts which programs may run and does not provide a place to test patches.

cards.front:
A system administrator needs to implement 802.1x whereby when a user logs into the network, the authentication server communicates to the network switch and assigns the user to the proper VLAN. Which of the following protocols should be used?
A. RADIUS
B. Kerberos
C. LDAP
D. MSCHAP
cards.why: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is the authentication server protocol used with 802.1x and can return a VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) assignment to the switch after login.

whyNot.B: Kerberos issues tickets for authentication and does not instruct a network switch to place a user into a VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network).
whyNot.C: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) queries directory information and does not communicate with switches to assign VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks).
whyNot.D: MSCHAP (Microsoft Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol) is only a credential exchange method and does not deliver VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) assignments to a switch.

cards.front:
A security administrator receives notice that a third-party certificate authority has been compromised, and new certificates will need to be issued. Which of the following should the administrator submit to receive a new certificate?
A. CRL
B. OSCP
C. PFX
D. CSR
E. CA
cards.why: A CSR (Certificate Signing Request) contains the public key and identity details and is submitted to a CA (Certificate Authority) to obtain a new certificate.

whyNot.A: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) lists revoked certificates and is not submitted to request a new one.
whyNot.B: OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol, written OSCP here) checks whether a certificate is revoked and is not used to request a certificate.
whyNot.C: A PFX (Personal Information Exchange) file is a container format for a certificate and private key, not a request for a new certificate.
whyNot.E: The CA (Certificate Authority) is the entity that issues certificates, so it is what receives the request rather than what is submitted.

cards.front:
A company wants to host a publicly available server that performs the following functions: Evaluates MX record lookup Can perform authenticated requests for A and AAA records Uses RRSIG Which of the following should the company use to fulfill the above requirements?
A. DNSSEC
B. SFTP
C. nslookup
D. dig
E. LDAPS
cards.back:
A. DNSSEC

DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) provides, among other things, cryptographic authenticity of responses using Resource Record Signatures (RRSIG) and authenticated denial of existence using Next-Secure (NSEC) and Hashed-NSEC records (NSEC3).
cards.why: DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) adds RRSIG (Resource Record Signature) records so DNS (Domain Name System) answers, including MX (Mail Exchanger) and address lookups, can be authenticated.

whyNot.B: SFTP (Secure File Transfer Protocol) transfers files securely and does not answer or authenticate DNS (Domain Name System) lookups.
whyNot.C: nslookup is a client tool for querying DNS (Domain Name System) and is not a server that performs authenticated responses.
whyNot.D: dig (Domain Information Groper) is a client query tool and not a publicly hosted service that signs or authenticates records.
whyNot.E: LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol over Secure Sockets Layer) secures directory queries and has nothing to do with DNS (Domain Name System) record lookups.

cards.front:
A security administrator is developing training for corporate users on basic security principles for personal email accounts. Which of the following should be mentioned as the MOST secure way for password recovery?
A. Utilizing a single Qfor password recovery
B. Sending a PIN to a smartphone through text message
C. Utilizing CAPTCHA to avoid brute force attacks
D. Use a different e-mail address to recover password
cards.back: B. Sending a PIN to a smartphone through text message
cards.why: Sending a PIN (Personal Identification Number) to a phone is out-of-band verification, which proves the person holds a second, separate channel that an attacker is unlikely to control.

whyNot.A: A single security question is often guessable or findable from public information, so it is weak for password recovery.
whyNot.C: CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) slows automated attacks but is not a password recovery method.
whyNot.D: A different e-mail address can itself be compromised or protected by a weak password, so it is less trustworthy than a separate device.

cards.front:
A company researched the root cause of a recent vulnerability in its software. It was determined that the vulnerability was the result of two updates made in the last release. Each update alone would not have resulted in the vulnerability. In order to prevent similar situations in the future, the company should improve which of the following?
A. Change management procedures
B. Job rotation policies
C. Incident response management
D. Least privilege access controls
cards.why: Change management procedures require review, testing, and approval of how multiple changes interact before release, which would catch a flaw that only appears when two updates are combined.

whyNot.B: Job rotation moves staff between duties to detect fraud and reduce collusion, and does not test how code changes interact.
whyNot.C: Incident response management handles events after they occur and does not prevent a flawed release from shipping.
whyNot.D: Least privilege access controls limit user permissions and do not address the combined effect of two software updates.

cards.front:
A computer on a company network was infected with a zero-day exploit after an employee accidently opened an email that contained malicious content. The employee recognized the email as malicious and was attempting to delete it, but accidently opened it. Which of the following should be done to prevent this scenario from occurring again in the future?
A. Install host-based firewalls on all computers that have an email client installed
B. Set the email program default to open messages in plain text
C. Install end-point protection on all computers that access web email
D. Create new email spam filters to delete all messages from that sender
cards.back: B. Set the email program default to open messages in plain text
cards.why: Opening messages in plain text prevents HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) and script content from rendering, so accidentally opening a malicious email does not run its embedded exploit.

whyNot.A: Host-based firewalls filter network traffic and do not stop malicious content from being rendered by the email client.
whyNot.C: End-point protection relies largely on known signatures and behavior, and may not stop a zero-day exploit that has never been seen.
whyNot.D: Spam filters for one sender only block that sender and do not stop the same attack from arriving from a different address.

cards.front:
A company wants to ensure that the validity of publicly trusted certificates used by its web server can be determined even during an extended internet outage. Which of the following should be implemented?
A. Recovery agent
B. Ocsp
C. Crl
D. Key escrow
cards.why: The key credits OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) for checking certificate validity, but it requires a live connection to a responder, so it would not work during an extended internet outage.

whyNot.A: A recovery agent restores encrypted data when keys are lost and does not check whether certificates are valid.
whyNot.C: The key rejects CRL (Certificate Revocation List), but a locally cached CRL can be checked offline, which is why keyDoubt prefers it.
whyNot.D: Key escrow stores copies of private keys for recovery and does not verify certificate validity.

cards.keyDoubt: C. A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) can be downloaded and cached locally, so validity can still be checked during an internet outage, while OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) needs a live responder.

cards.front:
An administrator intends to configure an IPSec solution that provides ESP with integrity protection, but not confidentiality protection. Which of the following AES modes of operation would meet this integrity-only requirement?
A. HMAC
B. PCBC
C. CBC
D. GCM
E. CFB
cards.why: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) provides integrity and authentication without encrypting data, which fits ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) used with integrity protection only.

whyNot.B: PCBC (Propagating Cipher Block Chaining) is an encryption mode, so it provides confidentiality, which the requirement excludes.
whyNot.C: CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) encrypts data and provides confidentiality, not integrity-only protection.
whyNot.D: GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) provides both encryption and authentication, so it includes confidentiality, which is not wanted here.
whyNot.E: CFB (Cipher Feedback) is an encryption mode that provides confidentiality and no integrity protection on its own.

cards.front:
The chief security officer (CS0) has issued a new policy that requires that all internal websites be configured for HTTPS traffic only. The network administrator has been tasked to update all internal sites without incurring additional costs. Which of the following is the best solution for the network administrator to secure each internal website?
A. Use certificates signed by the company CA
B. Use a signing certificate as a wild card certificate
C. Use certificates signed by a public ca
D. Use a self-signed certificate on each internal server
cards.back:
A. Use certificates signed by the company CA

This is a way to update all internal sites without incurring additional costs? To be a CA (Certificate Authority), you need an infrastructure that consists of considerable operational elements, hardware, software, policy frameworks and practice statements, aud...
cards.why: Certificates signed by the company's internal CA (Certificate Authority) are trusted by managed internal clients and cost nothing extra, satisfying the HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) policy.

whyNot.B: Using a CA (Certificate Authority) signing certificate as a wildcard certificate is improper and exposes the signing key on every server.
whyNot.C: Certificates from a public CA (Certificate Authority) require fees, which violates the no-additional-cost requirement.
whyNot.D: Self-signed certificates are not trusted by clients, cause browser warnings, and are hard to manage across many servers.

cards.front:
A security program manager wants to actively test the security posture of a system. The system is not yet in production and has no uptime requirement or active user base. Which of the following methods will produce a report which shows vulnerabilities that were actually exploited?
A. Peer review
B. Component testing
C. Penetration testing
D. Vulnerability testing
cards.back:
C. Penetration testing

A penetration test, or pen test, is an attempt to evaluate the security of an IT infrastructure by safely trying to exploit vulnerabilities.
cards.why: Penetration testing actively exploits vulnerabilities and reports which ones were actually exploited, which suits a system with no uptime requirement or users.

whyNot.A: Peer review is a colleague examination of code or design and does not exploit anything.
whyNot.B: Component testing checks that individual parts function correctly and does not attempt to exploit vulnerabilities.
whyNot.D: Vulnerability testing identifies potential weaknesses without exploiting them, so its report does not show what was actually exploited.

cards.front:
A new intern in the purchasing department requires read access to shared documents. Permissions are normally controlled through a group called "Purchasing", however, the purchasing group permissions allow write access. Which of the following would be the BEST course of action?
A. Modify all the shared files with read only permissions for the intern.
B. Create a new group that has only read permissions for the files.
C. Remove all permissions for the shared files.
D. Add the intern to the "Purchasing" group.
cards.back: B. Create a new group that has only read permissions for the files.
cards.why: Creating a new read-only group applies least privilege and role-based access control, giving the intern only the needed access without changing anyone else's permissions.

whyNot.A: Modifying every shared file to read-only would remove write access for the Purchasing staff who need it and is error-prone.
whyNot.C: Removing all permissions would block the intern and all legitimate users from the shared files.
whyNot.D: Adding the intern to the Purchasing group would grant write access, violating the principle of least privilege.

cards.front:
A business has recently deployed laptops to all sales employees. The laptops will be used primarily from home offices and while traveling, and a high amount of wireless mobile use is expected. To protect the laptops while connected to untrusted wireless networks, which of the following would be the BEST method for reducing the risk of having the laptops compromised?
A. MAC filtering
B. Virtualization
C. OS hardening
D. Application white-listing
cards.why: OS (Operating System) hardening removes unneeded services, applies patches, and tightens settings, which reduces the attack surface of laptops exposed on untrusted wireless networks.

whyNot.A: MAC (Media Access Control) filtering is a network-side control that does not protect laptops on networks the company does not manage, and addresses are easily spoofed.
whyNot.B: Virtualization isolates workloads but does not by itself reduce the exposure of the host laptop to network attacks.
whyNot.D: Application white-listing limits which programs run but does not harden the laptop against network-based attacks.

cards.front:
During a data breach cleanup, it is discovered that not all of the sites involved have the necessary data wiping tools. The necessary tools are quickly distributed to the required technicians, but when should this problem BEST be revisited?
A. Reporting
B. Preparation
C. Mitigation
D. Lessons Learned
cards.why: The Lessons Learned phase of incident response reviews what went wrong, such as missing tools, and drives process improvements for future incidents.

whyNot.A: Reporting documents and communicates the incident and does not focus on fixing process gaps.
whyNot.B: Preparation is where the gap originated, but reviewing and improving it happens afterward in Lessons Learned.
whyNot.C: Mitigation is the active containment of the incident in progress and not the time for review of process failures.

cards.front:
Joe, a technician, is working remotely with his company provided laptop at the coffee shop near his home. Joe is concerned that another patron of the coffee shop may be trying to access his laptop. Which of the following is an appropriate control to use to prevent the other patron from accessing Joe's laptop directly?
A. full-disk encryption
B. Host-based firewall
C. Current antivirus definitions
D. Latest OS updates
cards.why: A host-based firewall (software firewall on the laptop) blocks unsolicited inbound connections, so another patron on the same coffee shop network cannot directly reach services on Joe's laptop.

whyNot.A: Full-disk encryption protects data at rest if the device is stolen, but does not stop network connections to a running laptop.
whyNot.C: Current antivirus definitions detect known malware but do not block a nearby person from directly connecting to the laptop.
whyNot.D: The latest operating system updates fix vulnerabilities but do not filter or block direct inbound network connections.

cards.front:
An attacker uses a network sniffer to capture the packets of a transaction that adds $20 to a gift card. The attacker then user a function of the sniffer to push those packets back onto the network again, adding another $20 to the gift card. This can be done many times. Which of the following describes this type of attack?
A. Integer overflow attack
B. Smurf attack
C. Replay attack
D. Buffer overflow attack
E. Cross-site scripting attack
cards.why: A replay attack captures valid network traffic, such as a transaction, and retransmits it later to repeat the effect. Resending the captured gift card packets repeatedly adds value each time.

whyNot.A: An integer overflow attack makes a numeric value exceed its storage limit, not retransmit captured packets.
whyNot.B: A Smurf attack floods a victim with ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo replies via spoofed broadcast requests, which is a denial of service, not a transaction replay.
whyNot.D: A buffer overflow attack writes more data than a memory buffer can hold, not resending captured packets.
whyNot.E: A cross-site scripting attack injects malicious scripts into web pages viewed by users, which does not involve resending sniffed packets.

cards.front:
An organization is moving its human resources system to a cloud services provider. The company plans to continue using internal usernames and passwords with the service provider, but the security manager does not want the service provider to have a company of the passwords. Which of the following options meets all of these requirements?
A. Two-factor authentication
B. Account and password synchronization
C. Smartcards with PINS
D. Federated authentication
cards.why: Federated authentication lets the cloud provider trust the company's identity provider through assertions such as SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language), so users keep internal credentials and the provider never stores their passwords.

whyNot.A: Two-factor authentication adds a second proof of identity but does not prevent the provider from holding copies of passwords.
whyNot.B: Account and password synchronization copies passwords to the provider, which is exactly what the security manager wants to avoid.
whyNot.C: Smartcards with PINs (Personal Identification Numbers) strengthen authentication but do not by themselves keep the provider from receiving or storing credentials.

cards.front:
The data backup window has expanded into the morning hours and has begun to affect production users. The main bottleneck in the process is the time it takes to replicate the backups to separate severs at the offsite data center. Which of the following uses of deduplication could be implemented to reduce the backup window?
A. Implement deduplication at the network level between the two locations
B. Implement deduplication on the storage array to reduce the amount of drive space needed
C. Implement deduplication on the server storage to reduce the data backed up
D. Implement deduplication on both the local and remote servers
cards.back: B. Implement deduplication on the storage array to reduce the amount of drive space needed
cards.why: The bottleneck is the volume of data replicated to the offsite data center, so reducing data on the storage array before replication reduces what must be transferred and shortens the backup window.

whyNot.A: Network-level deduplication between the sites could cut transfer volume, but it is not the keyed choice here and adds appliance complexity.
whyNot.C: Deduplicating on server storage reduces data stored on the source server, but does not necessarily reduce the replicated backup set.
whyNot.D: Deduplicating on both local and remote servers saves storage at both ends but does not specifically address the replication bottleneck.

cards.keyDoubt: A. The bottleneck is replication across the network to the offsite data center, so deduplication at the network level between the two locations directly reduces transferred data.

cards.front:
A penetration testing is preparing for a client engagement in which the tester must provide data that proves and validates the scanning tools' results. Which of the following is the best method for collecting this information?
A. Set up the scanning system's firewall to permit and log all outbound connections
B. Use a protocol analyzer to log all pertinent network traffic
C. Configure network flow data logging on all scanning system
D. Enable debug level logging on the scanning system and all scanning tools used.
cards.back: B. Use a protocol analyzer to log all pertinent network traffic
cards.why: A protocol analyzer (packet capture tool) records the actual network traffic, which provides raw evidence proving and validating what the scanning tools reported.

whyNot.A: Logging outbound connections at the firewall shows only connection metadata, not the packet contents needed to validate scan results.
whyNot.C: Network flow data (such as NetFlow) summarizes traffic statistics but lacks the packet detail needed to prove scan findings.
whyNot.D: Debug logging shows what the tools report internally, which is the data to be validated, not independent proof of it.

cards.front:
Which of the following best describes the initial processing phase used in mobile device forensics?
A. The phone should be powered down and the battery removed to preserve the state of data on any internal or removable storage utilized by the mobile device
B. The removable data storage cards should be processed first to prevent data alteration when examining the mobile device
C. The mobile device should be examined first, then removable storage and lastly the phone without removable storage should be examined again
D. The phone and storage cards should be examined as a complete unit after examining the removable storage cards separately.
cards.back: D. The phone and storage cards should be examined as a complete unit after examining the removable storage cards separately.
cards.why: Per the keyed answer, the phone and storage cards are examined together as a unit after the removable storage cards have been examined separately, so each source is preserved and evaluated.

whyNot.A: Powering down and removing the battery can alter volatile data and may trigger device lock features, so it is not the proper initial processing step.
whyNot.B: Processing only removable storage first does not describe a complete initial processing approach for the whole mobile device.
whyNot.C: Examining the device first, then storage, then the phone again repeats work and risks altering evidence on the device.

cards.keyDoubt: C. This sequence of examining the device, then removable storage, then the phone without storage is closer to recognized mobile forensics guidance, though the key's wording is loosely supported.

cards.front:
Ann a security analyst is monitoring the IDS console and noticed multiple connections from an internal host to a suspicious call back domain. Which of the following tools would aid her to decipher the network traffic?
A. Vulnerability Scanner
B. NMAP
C. NETSTAT
D. Packet Analyzer
cards.why: A packet analyzer (protocol analyzer or sniffer) captures and decodes network traffic so an analyst can inspect the contents of the suspicious connections to the call back domain.

whyNot.A: A vulnerability scanner finds weaknesses in systems but does not decode live network traffic.
whyNot.B: NMAP (Network Mapper) discovers hosts and open ports but does not decipher captured traffic contents.
whyNot.C: NETSTAT (network statistics) lists local connections and listening ports but does not show or decode packet contents.

cards.keyDoubt: D. A packet analyzer is the tool that actually deciphers network traffic, whereas NETSTAT (network statistics) only lists connections.

cards.front:
An administrator is testing the collision resistance of different hashing algorithms. Which of the following is the strongest collision resistance test?
A. Find two identical messages with different hashes
B. Find two identical messages with the same hash
C. Find a common has between two specific messages
D. Find a common hash between a specific message and a random message
cards.back: A. Find two identical messages with different hashes
cards.why: Collision resistance means it should be infeasible to find two different inputs producing the same hash. The keyed wording is garbled, but it points to the strongest test, which is finding any colliding pair.

whyNot.B: Two identical messages always produce the same hash, so finding this proves nothing about collision resistance.
whyNot.C: Finding a common hash for two specific chosen messages is a harder, more constrained target, so it is a weaker practical test than finding any collision.
whyNot.D: Matching a specific message to a random one is a second preimage style search, which is a different property than collision resistance.

cards.keyDoubt: C. Finding a common hash between two specific messages is the closest option to a true collision test, since option A as worded describes an impossible case.

cards.front:
The SSID broadcast for a wireless router has been disabled but a network administrator notices that unauthorized users are accessing the wireless network. The administer has determined that attackers are still able to detect the presence of the wireless network despite the fact the SSID has been disabled. Which of the following would further obscure the presence of the wireless network?
A. Upgrade the encryption to WPA or WPA2
B. Create a non-zero length SSID for the wireless router
C. Reroute wireless users to a honeypot
D. Disable responses to a broadcast probe request
cards.back: D. Disable responses to a broadcast probe request
cards.why: Wireless access points answer broadcast probe requests with their network information even when SSID (Service Set Identifier) broadcast is off. Disabling those responses further hides the network from scanners.

whyNot.A: Upgrading to WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) or WPA2 strengthens encryption but does not hide the presence of the network.
whyNot.B: Creating a non-zero length SSID would make the network name visible, not further obscure it.
whyNot.C: Rerouting users to a honeypot (decoy system) is a deception technique and does not hide the wireless network.

cards.front:
Which of the following should be used to implement voice encryption?
A. SSLv3
B. VDSL
C. SRTP
D. VoIP
cards.why: SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) adds encryption, authentication, and integrity protection to RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) media streams, which is how voice traffic is encrypted.

whyNot.A: SSLv3 (Secure Sockets Layer version 3) is a deprecated, insecure protocol and is not designed for encrypting voice media streams.
whyNot.B: VDSL (Very-high-bit-rate Digital Subscriber Line) is a broadband access technology, not an encryption method.
whyNot.D: VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) is the voice transport technology itself, not an encryption mechanism.

cards.front:
During an application design, the development team specifics a LDAP module for single sign-on communication with the company's access control database. This is an example of which of the following?
A. Application control
B. Data in-transit
C. Identification
D. Authentication
cards.why: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) used for single sign-on verifies a user's credentials against the directory, which is authentication, proving the claimed identity is genuine.

whyNot.A: Application control restricts which programs may run, which is unrelated to verifying users against a directory.
whyNot.B: Data in-transit describes protecting data moving across a network, not the process of verifying user identity.
whyNot.C: Identification is claiming an identity, such as giving a username, while the directory lookup verifying it is authentication.

cards.front:
After a merger, it was determined that several individuals could perform the tasks of a network administrator in the merged organization. Which of the following should have been performed to ensure that employees have proper access?
A. Time-of-day restrictions
B. Change management
C. Periodic auditing of user credentials
D. User rights and permission review
cards.back: D. User rights and permission review
cards.why: A user rights and permission review compares each person's access with their job role, finding excess privileges such as accumulated administrator rights after a merger.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions limit when accounts can log in but do not correct excessive permissions.
whyNot.B: Change management controls how system changes are approved and documented, not whether user access is appropriate.
whyNot.C: Periodic auditing of user credentials checks credential use and strength, whereas the problem here is excess rights, which the rights review addresses.

cards.front:
A company exchanges information with a business partner. An annual audit of the business partner is conducted against the SLA in order to verify:
A. Performance and service delivery metrics
B. Backups are being performed and tested
C. Data ownership is being maintained and audited
D. Risk awareness is being adhered to and enforced
cards.back: A. Performance and service delivery metrics
cards.why: An SLA (Service Level Agreement) defines expected performance and service delivery, so an audit of the partner against it verifies those performance and service delivery metrics are being met.

whyNot.B: Backup performance and testing is a specific operational control that an SLA audit does not primarily verify.
whyNot.C: Data ownership is usually set in contracts or data governance agreements, not verified through SLA (Service Level Agreement) metrics.
whyNot.D: Risk awareness enforcement is a policy and training matter, not what an SLA (Service Level Agreement) audit measures.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the proper way to quantify the total monetary damage resulting from an exploited vulnerability?
A. Calculate the ALE
B. Calculate the ARO
C. Calculate the MTBF
D. Calculate the TCO
cards.why: ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) is SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) multiplied by ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence), giving the expected yearly monetary damage from an exploited vulnerability.

whyNot.B: ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) is only how often an event is expected per year, not a monetary value.
whyNot.C: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) measures how long a system typically operates between failures, not monetary damage.
whyNot.D: TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) measures the full lifetime cost of owning an asset, not the damage from an exploit.

cards.front:
A security administrator needs to implement a system that detects possible intrusions based upon a vendor provided list. Which of the following BEST describes this type of IDS?
A. Signature based
B. Heuristic
C. Anomaly-based
D. Behavior-based
cards.why: A signature based IDS (Intrusion Detection System) compares activity to a database of known attack patterns, such as a vendor provided list, and alerts on matches.

whyNot.B: Heuristic detection uses rules and algorithms to spot suspicious behavior, not a fixed vendor list of known patterns.
whyNot.C: Anomaly-based detection flags deviations from a learned normal baseline rather than matching a provided list.
whyNot.D: Behavior-based detection watches for abnormal actions over time, not matches against a vendor supplied list.

cards.front:
The chief Security Officer (CSO) has reported a rise in data loss but no break ins have occurred. By doing which of the following is the CSO most likely to reduce the number of incidents?
A. Implement protected distribution
B. Empty additional firewalls
C. Conduct security awareness training
D. Install perimeter barricades
cards.why: Data loss with no break-ins points to insider or user error, so security awareness training teaches employees to handle data properly and reduces accidental or careless disclosure.

whyNot.A: Protected distribution (a physically secured cabling system) guards against wire tapping, not data loss caused by user behavior.
whyNot.B: Adding firewalls blocks external network attacks, but no break-ins occurred, so perimeter filtering will not address the data loss.
whyNot.D: Perimeter barricades stop physical vehicle or intruder access, which is irrelevant since no break-ins have occurred.

cards.front:
Having adequate lighting on the outside of a building is an example of which of the following security controls?
A. Deterrent
B. Compensating
C. Detective
D. Preventative
cards.why: Exterior lighting discourages would-be intruders from approaching because they fear being seen, which makes it a deterrent control rather than one that blocks or detects.

whyNot.B: A compensating control substitutes for another control that cannot be implemented, and lighting here is not replacing anything.
whyNot.C: A detective control identifies an event after or as it occurs, such as logs or alarms, and lighting alone does not detect anything.
whyNot.D: A preventative control physically stops an action, such as a lock or fence, while lighting only discourages the attempt.

cards.front:
During a recent audit, it was discovered that several user accounts belonging to former employees were still active and had valid VPN permissions. Which of the following would help reduce the amount of risk the organization incurs in this situation in the future?
A. Time-of-day restrictions
B. User access reviews
C. Group-based privileges
D. Change management policies
cards.why: User access reviews periodically compare active accounts and permissions against current employees, so accounts of former staff with VPN (Virtual Private Network) access are found and disabled.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions limit when accounts can log in, but they do not remove or identify accounts belonging to departed employees.
whyNot.C: Group-based privileges simplify permission assignment, but they do not detect stale accounts that remain active after employees leave.
whyNot.D: Change management policies control how system changes are approved and documented, not the review of user account status.

cards.front:
An organization is working with a cloud services provider to transition critical business applications to a hybrid cloud environment. The organization retains sensitive customer data and wants to ensure the provider has sufficient administrative and logical controls in place to protect its data. In which of the following documents would this concern MOST likely be addressed?
A. Service level agreement
B. Interconnection security agreement
C. Non-disclosure agreement
D. Business process analysis
cards.why: An SLA (Service Level Agreement) defines the services, security responsibilities, and performance a cloud provider must deliver, so it is where required administrative and logical controls would be specified.

whyNot.B: An ISA (Interconnection Security Agreement) governs the technical security of connecting two systems, not the provider's overall administrative and logical controls.
whyNot.C: An NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement) protects confidentiality of shared information but does not specify the provider's required security controls.
whyNot.D: A BPA (Business Process Analysis) examines internal business workflows and does not bind a provider to protect data.

cards.front:
A security administrator wants to implement a company-wide policy to empower data owners to manage and enforce access control rules on various resources. Which of the following should be implemented?
A. Mandatory access control
B. Discretionary access control
C. Role based access control
D. Rule-based access control
cards.why: DAC (Discretionary Access Control) lets the data owner decide who can access a resource and set the access rules, which matches empowering data owners.

whyNot.A: MAC (Mandatory Access Control) uses central labels and clearances set by administrators, so data owners cannot manage the rules.
whyNot.C: RBAC (Role Based Access Control) assigns access by job role defined centrally, not by individual data owners.
whyNot.D: Rule-based access control applies centrally defined rules such as time or location conditions, not owner-managed permissions.

cards.front:
Which of the following BEST describes an attack where communications between two parties are intercepted and forwarded to each party with neither party being aware of the interception and potential modification to the communications?
A. Spear phishing
B. Main-in-the-middle
C. URL hijacking
D. Transitive access
cards.why: A man-in-the-middle attack places the attacker between two parties, relaying and possibly altering their communications while each side believes it is talking directly to the other.

whyNot.A: Spear phishing is a targeted deceptive message to trick a victim, not interception and forwarding of live communications.
whyNot.C: URL hijacking (typosquatting) relies on look-alike domain names to catch mistyped addresses, not on intercepting an ongoing exchange.
whyNot.D: Transitive access is a trust relationship where access passes through an intermediate party, and it is not an interception attack.

cards.front:
A security administrator wishes to implement a secure a method of file transfer when communicating with outside organizations. Which of the following protocols would BEST facilitate secure file transfers? (Select TWO)
A. SCP
B. TFTP
C. SNMP
D. FTP
E. SMTP
F. FTPS
cards.why: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) runs over SSH (Secure Shell) and FTPS (File Transfer Protocol Secure) adds TLS (Transport Layer Security) to FTP, so both encrypt file transfers.

whyNot.B: TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) has no authentication or encryption, so it is not secure for external file transfers.
whyNot.C: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is used for device monitoring and management, not file transfer.
whyNot.D: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) sends credentials and data in clear text, so it is not secure.
whyNot.E: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) transports email and is not a file transfer protocol, and it is unencrypted by default.

cards.front:
A technician needs to implement a system which will properly authenticate users by their username and password only when the users are logging in from a computer in the office building. Any attempt to authenticate from a location other than the office building should be rejected. Which of the following MUST the technician implement?
A. Dual factor authentication
B. Transitive authentication
C. Single factor authentication
D. Biometric authentication
cards.why: Transitive authentication relies on trust established through another element, here the office location or computer, so authentication succeeds only when the login originates from the trusted office system.

whyNot.A: Dual factor authentication requires two different factor types, but the scenario requires only username and password plus a location restriction.
whyNot.C: Single factor authentication checks only one factor and has no way to reject logins based on where they originate.
whyNot.D: Biometric authentication uses physical traits such as fingerprints, which the scenario does not call for.

cards.keyDoubt: A transitive trust is not really a location control; a location-based restriction fits better, and among these options none is clearly correct, so B is the loose best fit.

cards.front:
After correctly configuring a new wireless enabled thermostat to control the temperature of the company's meeting room, Joe, a network administrator determines that the thermostat is not connecting to the internet-based control system. Joe verifies that the thermostat received the expected network parameters and it is associated with the AP. Additionally, the other wireless mobile devices connected to the same wireless network are functioning properly. The network administrator verified that the thermostat works when tested at his residence. Which of the following is the MOST likely reason the thermostat is not connecting to the internet?
A. The company implements a captive portal
B. The thermostat is using the incorrect encryption algorithm
C. the WPA2 shared likely is incorrect
D. The company's DHCP server scope is full
cards.back: A. The company implements a captive portal
cards.why: A captive portal requires a user to interact with a web page before getting internet access, which an embedded thermostat cannot do, so it associates and gets an address but cannot reach the internet.

whyNot.B: An incorrect encryption algorithm would prevent association with the AP (Access Point), but the thermostat is already associated.
whyNot.C: An incorrect WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) shared key would block association, yet the thermostat associated and received network parameters.
whyNot.D: A full DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) scope would prevent an address lease, but the thermostat received the expected network parameters.

cards.front:
A Chief Security Officer (CSO) has been unsuccessful in attempts to access the website for a potential partner (www.example.net). Which of the following rules is preventing the CSO from accessing the site? Blocked sites: *.nonews.com, *.rumorhasit.net, *.mars?
A. Rule 1: deny from inside to outside source any destination any service smtp
B. Rule 2: deny from inside to outside source any destination any service ping
C. Rule 3: deny from inside to outside source any destination {blocked sites} service http-https
D. Rule 4: deny from any to any source any destination any service any
cards.back: C. Rule 3: deny from inside to outside source any destination {blocked sites} service http-https
cards.why: Rule 3 denies HTTP and HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol and its Secure variant) web traffic to the blocked sites list, and the wildcard entries can match the partner's website, preventing access.

whyNot.A: Rule 1 blocks SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) email traffic, which does not affect browsing a website.
whyNot.B: Rule 2 blocks ping (ICMP, Internet Control Message Protocol), which does not stop web page access.
whyNot.D: Rule 4 would block everything, but it would also stop all other web access, which is not described as happening.

cards.front:
Malware that changes its binary pattern on specific dates at specific times to avoid detection is known as a (n):
A. armored virus
B. logic bomb
C. polymorphic virus
D. Trojan
cards.why: A polymorphic virus changes its code or binary pattern to evade signature-based detection, which matches malware that alters its pattern to avoid being identified.

whyNot.A: An armored virus uses techniques to hinder analysis and reverse engineering rather than changing its binary pattern on a schedule.
whyNot.B: A logic bomb triggers a malicious action on a specific condition or date, but it does not change its binary pattern to evade detection.
whyNot.D: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software to get installed, and does not inherently alter its binary pattern.

cards.front:
A company is planning to encrypt the files in several sensitive directories of a file server with a symmetric key. Which of the following could be used?
A. RSA
B. TwoFish
C. Diffie-Helman
D. NTLMv2
E. RIPEMD
cards.why: Twofish is a symmetric block cipher that uses one shared key for both encryption and decryption, which is what file encryption with a symmetric key requires.

whyNot.A: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) is an asymmetric algorithm using a public and private key pair.
whyNot.C: Diffie-Hellman is a key exchange protocol for agreeing on a shared secret, not an algorithm for encrypting files.
whyNot.D: NTLMv2 (NT LAN Manager version 2) is an authentication protocol, not a file encryption cipher.
whyNot.E: RIPEMD (RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest) is a hashing algorithm, which cannot be reversed to decrypt files.

cards.front:
Which of the following is a document that contains detailed information about actions that include how something will be done, when the actions will be performed, and penalties for failure?
A. MOU
B. ISA
C. BPA
D. SLA
cards.why: An SLA (Service Level Agreement) documents what services will be delivered, how and when, and the penalties if the provider fails to meet the agreed levels.

whyNot.A: An MOU (Memorandum of Understanding) states general intent between parties and typically lacks detailed performance terms and penalties.
whyNot.B: An ISA (Interconnection Security Agreement) specifies technical security requirements for connecting systems rather than service penalties.
whyNot.C: A BPA (Business Partnership Agreement) defines the relationship and responsibilities of business partners, not detailed service delivery and penalties.

cards.front:
Which of the following are MOST susceptible to birthday attacks?
A. Hashed passwords
B. Digital certificates
C. Encryption passwords
D. One time passwords
cards.why: Birthday attacks exploit hash collisions, where two different inputs produce the same hash value, so hashed passwords are the most susceptible.

whyNot.B: Digital certificates are signed using hashes, but certificate use is not the most direct target of collision-finding compared with hashed passwords.
whyNot.C: Encryption passwords protect keys or data and are attacked through brute force or dictionary methods, not hash collisions.
whyNot.D: OTP (One Time Passwords) are valid for a single use or short time, so a collision found later gives little advantage.

cards.front:
Joe a computer forensic technician responds to an active compromise of a database server. Joe first collects information in memory, then collects network traffic and finally conducts an image of the hard drive. Which of the following procedures did Joe follow?
A. Order of volatility
B. Chain of custody
C. Recovery procedure
D. Incident isolation
cards.why: The order of volatility collects the most volatile evidence first, such as memory, then network traffic, then disk, because volatile data is lost quickly.

whyNot.B: Chain of custody documents who handled evidence and when, not the sequence in which evidence is collected.
whyNot.C: Recovery procedure restores systems to normal operation after an incident, rather than collecting evidence.
whyNot.D: Incident isolation separates affected systems to contain damage, and it does not define the order of evidence collection.

cards.front:
A system administrator wants to implement an internal communication system that will allow employees to send encrypted messages to each other. The system must also support non- repudiation. Which of the following implements all these requirements?
A. Bcrypt
B. Blowfish
C. PGP
D. SHA
cards.why: PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) encrypts messages for confidentiality and uses digital signatures, which provide non-repudiation because only the sender's private key could have produced the signature.

whyNot.A: Bcrypt is a password hashing function; it cannot encrypt messages for recipients or provide non-repudiation.
whyNot.B: Blowfish is a symmetric cipher that encrypts data but offers no digital signature, so it cannot provide non-repudiation.
whyNot.D: SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm) produces a hash for integrity and does not encrypt messages or prove who sent them.

cards.front:
Given the log output: Max 15 00:15:23.431 CRT: #SEC_LOGIN-5-LOGIN_SUCCESS: Login Success [user: msmith] [Source: 10.0.12.45] [localport: 23] at 00:15:23:431 CET Sun Mar 15 2015 Which of the following should the network administrator do to protect data security?
A. Configure port security for logons
B. Disable telnet and enable SSH
C. Configure an AAA server
D. Disable password and enable RSA authentication
cards.back: B. Disable telnet and enable SSH
cards.why: The log shows a successful login on local port 23, which is Telnet, a protocol that sends credentials and data in cleartext. Disabling Telnet and enabling SSH (Secure Shell) encrypts the session.

whyNot.A: Port security limits which MAC (Media Access Control) addresses use a switch port and does not encrypt Telnet traffic.
whyNot.C: An AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) server centralizes access control but the Telnet session would still travel in cleartext.
whyNot.D: Replacing passwords with RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) authentication does not fix the cleartext transport that Telnet uses.

cards.front:
The firewall administrator is adding a new certificate for the company's remote access solution. The solution requires that the uploaded file contain the entire certificate chain for the certificate to load properly. The administrator loads the company certificate and the root CA certificate into the file. The file upload is rejected. Which of the following is required to complete the certificate chain?
A. Certificate revocation list
B. Intermediate authority
C. Recovery agent
D. Root of trust
cards.why: A certificate chain runs from the end-entity certificate through any intermediate CA (Certificate Authority) up to the root CA. The missing link here is the intermediate authority that issued the company certificate.

whyNot.A: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) reports revoked certificates and is not part of the chain of trust.
whyNot.C: A recovery agent can recover encrypted data keys and is not a certificate chain element.
whyNot.D: The root of trust is the root CA certificate, which the administrator already loaded into the file.

cards.front:
The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of a major defense contracting company a traveling overseas for a conference. The CEO will be taking a laptop. Which of the following should the security administrator implement to ensure confidentiality of the data if the laptop were to be stolen or lost during the trip?
A. Remote wipe
B. Full device encryption
C. BIOS password
D. GPS tracking
cards.why: Full device encryption makes the laptop's drive unreadable without the key or credentials, so data confidentiality is kept even if the device is lost or stolen.

whyNot.A: Remote wipe needs network connectivity to the device, so a thief can keep it offline and still reach the data.
whyNot.C: A BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) password can be bypassed by removing the drive and reading it elsewhere.
whyNot.D: GPS (Global Positioning System) tracking helps locate the laptop but does not protect the data stored on it.

cards.front:
In an effort to reduce data storage requirements, some company devices to hash every file and eliminate duplicates. The data processing routines are time sensitive so the hashing algorithm is fast and supported on a wide range of systems. Which of the following algorithms is BEST suited for this purpose?
A. MD5
B. SHA
C. RIPEMD
D. AES
cards.why: Deduplication needs a fast hash that is widely supported. SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm) is fast, available on nearly every platform, and has far fewer collision weaknesses than MD5 (Message Digest 5).

whyNot.A: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is fast but has known collision weaknesses, which could make different files appear identical.
whyNot.C: RIPEMD (RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest) is a hash that has much less support across systems than SHA.
whyNot.D: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is a symmetric encryption cipher and not a hashing algorithm.

cards.front:
A new security policy in an organization requires that all file transfers within the organization be completed using applications that provide secure transfer. Currently, the organization uses FTP and HTTP to transfer files. Which of the following should the organization implement in order to be compliant with the new policy?
A. Replace FTP with SFTP and replace HTTP with TLS
B. Replace FTP with FTPS and replaces HTTP with TFTP
C. Replace FTP with SFTP and replace HTTP with Telnet
D. Replace FTP with FTPS and replaces HTTP with IPSec
cards.back: A. Replace FTP with SFTP and replace HTTP with TLS
cards.why: SFTP (Secure File Transfer Protocol) runs over SSH (Secure Shell) to replace FTP (File Transfer Protocol), and TLS (Transport Layer Security) secures web traffic by replacing plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) with HTTPS.

whyNot.B: TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) has no encryption or authentication, so it does not replace HTTP securely.
whyNot.C: Telnet transmits everything in cleartext and is not a secure replacement for HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol).
whyNot.D: IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) is a network-layer tunneling suite and not a direct application replacement for HTTP file transfers.

cards.front:
A product manager is concerned about continuing operations at a facility located in a region undergoing significant political unrest. After consulting with senior management, a decision is made to suspend operations at the facility until the situation stabilizes. Which of the following risk management strategies BEST describes management's response?
A. Deterrence
B. Mitigation
C. Avoidance
D. Acceptance
cards.why: Avoidance eliminates the risk by ceasing the risky activity. Suspending operations at the unstable facility removes exposure to the political unrest.

whyNot.A: Deterrence discourages threat actors with warnings or controls and does not stop the activity itself.
whyNot.B: Mitigation reduces the likelihood or impact of a risk while operations continue, but here operations are stopped.
whyNot.D: Acceptance means knowingly continuing operations and living with the risk, which is the opposite of suspending them.

cards.front:
Joe notices there are several user accounts on the local network generating spam with embedded malicious code. Which of the following technical control should Joe put in place to BEST reduce these incidents?
A. Account lockout
B. Group Based Privileges
C. Least privilege
D. Password complexity
cards.why: Account lockout disables an account after repeated failed logins, which limits attackers who brute-force credentials to hijack accounts for spam. It is the best listed technical control here.

whyNot.B: Group based privileges assign permissions by group and do not stop compromised accounts from sending spam.
whyNot.C: Least privilege limits access rights, but a compromised account can still send email with normal user permissions.
whyNot.D: Password complexity makes guessing harder but does not stop repeated attempts the way lockout does.

cards.front:
Two users need to securely share encrypted files via email. Company policy prohibits users from sharing credentials or exchanging encryption keys. Which of the following can be implemented to enable users to share encrypted data while abiding by company policies?
A. Key escrow
B. Digital signatures
C. PKI
D. Hashing
cards.why: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) lets each user encrypt files with the recipient's public key and decrypt with their own private key, so no credentials or keys need to be exchanged.

whyNot.A: Key escrow stores copies of keys with a third party for recovery and does not let users share encrypted files.
whyNot.B: Digital signatures prove origin and integrity but do not encrypt the file contents.
whyNot.D: Hashing creates a one-way digest for integrity and cannot encrypt data for sharing.

cards.front:
An information system owner has supplied a new requirement to the development team that calls for increased non-repudiation within the application. After undergoing several audits, the owner determined that current levels of non-repudiation were insufficient. Which of the following capabilities would be MOST appropriate to consider implementing is response to the new requirement?
A. Transitive trust
B. Symmetric encryption
C. Two-factor authentication
D. Digital signatures
E. One-time passwords
cards.why: Digital signatures use the signer's private key, so only that person could have created them. This provides non-repudiation, since the signer cannot credibly deny the action.

whyNot.A: Transitive trust extends trust between domains and does not prove who performed an action.
whyNot.B: Symmetric encryption uses a shared key, so either party could have created the message and nobody can be proven the author.
whyNot.C: Two-factor authentication strengthens login identity but does not create a verifiable record that binds a person to an action.
whyNot.E: One-time passwords improve authentication but do not give proof of origin that prevents denial.

cards.front:
Joe a website administrator believes he owns the intellectual property for a company invention and has been replacing image files on the company's public facing website in the DMZ. Joe is using steganography to hide stolen data. Which of the following controls can be implemented to mitigate this type of inside threat?
A. Digital signatures
B. File integrity monitoring
C. Access controls
D. Change management
E. Stateful inspection firewall
cards.why: FIM (File Integrity Monitoring) compares file hashes to a baseline and alerts when files such as website images change unexpectedly, which would reveal Joe's steganography-modified images.

whyNot.A: Digital signatures verify authenticity of signed content but do not detect unauthorized replacement of ordinary website files.
whyNot.C: Access controls matter, but Joe is a website administrator who legitimately has write access to those files.
whyNot.D: Change management is a process that Joe could bypass, and it does not detect unauthorized file changes by itself.
whyNot.E: A stateful inspection firewall filters network connections and does not detect altered files on the server.

cards.front:
The process of applying a salt and cryptographic hash to a password then repeating the process many times is known as which of the following?
A. Collision resistance
B. Rainbow table
C. Key stretching
D. Brute force attack
cards.why: Key stretching repeatedly applies a salted hash to a password to slow brute-force attempts. Algorithms such as PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) and bcrypt do this.

whyNot.A: Collision resistance describes a hash's difficulty of producing two inputs with the same output and is not a repeated-hashing process.
whyNot.B: A rainbow table is a precomputed hash lookup table used to attack passwords, and salting defeats it.
whyNot.D: A brute force attack is an attacker guessing passwords, not a defensive hashing technique.

cards.front:
Which of the following is commonly used for federated identity management across multiple organizations?
A. SAML
B. Active Directory
C. Kerberos
D. LDAP
cards.why: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) exchanges authentication and authorization assertions between identity providers and service providers across organizations, enabling federated single sign-on.

whyNot.B: Active Directory is a directory service that manages identities inside one organization's domain and is not a federation standard.
whyNot.C: Kerberos is a ticket-based authentication protocol used mainly within a single realm or domain.
whyNot.D: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) queries directory information and does not provide federation across organizations.

cards.front:
While performing surveillance activities, an attacker determines that an organization is using 802.1X to secure LAN access. Which of the following attack mechanisms can the attacker utilize to bypass the identified network security?
A. MAC spoofing
B. Pharming
C. Xmas attack
D. ARP poisoning
cards.why: MAC (Media Access Control) spoofing lets an attacker copy the address of an authorized device, which can bypass weak MAC-based exceptions such as those used for devices that cannot do 802.1X.

whyNot.B: Pharming redirects users to fake websites through DNS (Domain Name System) manipulation and does not bypass LAN access control.
whyNot.C: An Xmas attack is a port scan using unusual TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) flags and does not bypass 802.1X.
whyNot.D: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) poisoning redirects traffic on a LAN after access is already obtained, so it does not get past 802.1X.

cards.front:
A security administrator has been asked to implement a VPN that will support remote access over IPSEC. Which of the following is an encryption algorithm that would meet this requirement?
A. MD5
B. AES
C. UDP
D. PKI
cards.why: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is a symmetric encryption algorithm commonly used by IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) to encrypt VPN (Virtual Private Network) traffic.

whyNot.A: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is a hashing algorithm and does not encrypt data.
whyNot.C: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is a transport protocol and not an encryption algorithm.
whyNot.D: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is a framework for managing certificates and keys, not an encryption algorithm.

cards.front:
A security administrator is evaluating three different services: radius, diameter, and Kerberos. Which of the following is a feature that is UNIQUE to Kerberos?
A. It provides authentication services
B. It uses tickets to identify authenticated users
C. It provides single sign-on capability
D. It uses XML for cross-platform interoperability
cards.back: B. It uses tickets to identify authenticated users
cards.why: Kerberos uses tickets issued by a Key Distribution Center (KDC) to identify and authenticate users without resending passwords, which is the feature unique among RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service), Diameter, and Kerberos.

whyNot.A: Providing authentication services is common to RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service), Diameter, and Kerberos, so it is not unique to Kerberos.
whyNot.C: Single sign-on (SSO) is not unique to Kerberos, since other federated and directory-based systems also provide single sign-on.
whyNot.D: Kerberos does not use XML (Extensible Markup Language); XML-based interoperability is associated with SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language).

cards.front:
Which of the following can affect electrostatic discharge in a network operations center?
A. Fire suppression
B. Environmental monitoring
C. Proximity card access
D. Humidity controls
cards.why: Humidity controls affect electrostatic discharge (ESD) because low humidity lets static charge build up on people and equipment, while proper humidity levels dissipate it and protect network hardware.

whyNot.A: Fire suppression protects against fire damage and does not influence static charge buildup in a network operations center.
whyNot.B: Environmental monitoring only observes and reports conditions like temperature and humidity, so it does not itself change electrostatic discharge (ESD) risk.
whyNot.C: Proximity card access controls physical entry and has no effect on electrostatic discharge (ESD).

cards.front:
A malicious attacker has intercepted HTTP traffic and inserted an ASCII line that sets the referrer URL. Which of the following is the attacker most likely utilizing?
A. Header manipulation
B. Cookie hijacking
C. Cross-site scripting
D. Xml injection
cards.why: Header manipulation alters HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) header fields, such as the Referer value, in intercepted traffic, which matches an attacker inserting a line that sets the referrer URL (Uniform Resource Locator).

whyNot.B: Cookie hijacking steals or reuses session cookies and does not involve inserting a referrer header line.
whyNot.C: Cross-site scripting (XSS) injects malicious script into web pages viewed by users, not a header line in intercepted traffic.
whyNot.D: XML (Extensible Markup Language) injection inserts malicious XML content into an application and does not set HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) referrer headers.

cards.front:
A company would like to prevent the use of a known set of applications from being used on company computers. Which of the following should the security administrator implement?
A. Whitelisting
B. Anti-malware
C. Application hardening
D. Blacklisting
E. Disable removable media
cards.why: Blacklisting (a deny list) blocks a known set of unwanted applications while allowing everything else, which fits a requirement to prevent specific known applications from running.

whyNot.A: Whitelisting (an allow list) permits only approved applications and blocks everything else, which is broader than blocking just a known set.
whyNot.B: Anti-malware detects malicious software and does not block a specific list of otherwise legitimate applications.
whyNot.C: Application hardening reduces the attack surface of an application and does not stop chosen applications from running.
whyNot.E: Disabling removable media blocks external storage devices and does not prevent specific installed applications from running.

cards.front:
A new hire wants to use a personally owned phone to access company resources. The new hire expresses concern about what happens to the data on the phone when they leave the company. Which of the following portions of the company's mobile device management configuration would allow the company data to be removed from the device without touching the new hire's data?
A. Asset control
B. Device access control
C. Storage lock out
D. Storage segmentation
cards.why: Storage segmentation in MDM (Mobile Device Management) separates corporate data from personal data in containers, so the company can remotely wipe only its own data without affecting the user's personal data.

whyNot.A: Asset control tracks and inventories devices and does not separate corporate data from personal data.
whyNot.B: Device access control restricts who or what can use the device or resources and does not enable selective removal of company data.
whyNot.C: Storage lock out locks the device or storage after failed attempts and does not partition corporate data for selective removal.

cards.front:
A consultant has been tasked to assess a client's network. The client reports frequent network outages. Upon viewing the spanning tree configuration, the consultant notices that an old and law performing edge switch on the network has been elected to be the root bridge. Which of the following explains this scenario?
A. The switch also serves as the DHCP server
B. The switch has the lowest MAC address
C. The switch has spanning tree loop protection enabled
D. The switch has the fastest uplink port
cards.back: B. The switch has the lowest MAC address
cards.why: In STP (Spanning Tree Protocol), the root bridge is elected by the lowest bridge ID (priority plus MAC, Media Access Control, address); with default priorities, the switch with the lowest MAC address wins, even if it is old and slow.

whyNot.A: Acting as a DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) server has no bearing on STP (Spanning Tree Protocol) root bridge election.
whyNot.C: Loop protection features like root guard or BPDU (Bridge Protocol Data Unit) guard prevent unwanted root elections rather than cause them.
whyNot.D: Uplink speed affects path cost calculations but is not a criterion for electing the STP (Spanning Tree Protocol) root bridge.

cards.front:
An organization is trying to decide which type of access control is most appropriate for the network. The current access control approach is too complex and requires significant overhead. Management would like to simplify the access control and provide user with the ability to determine what permissions should be applied to files, document, and directories. The access control method that BEST satisfies these objectives is:
A. Rule-based access control
B. Role-based access control
C. Mandatory access control
D. Discretionary access control
cards.why: DAC (Discretionary Access Control) lets the data owner decide who gets permissions on files, documents, and directories, which is simple and removes central administrative overhead.

whyNot.A: Rule-based access control applies centrally defined rules, such as time or network conditions, and does not let users set permissions.
whyNot.B: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) assigns permissions by job role through central administration, which adds overhead and does not let users decide.
whyNot.C: MAC (Mandatory Access Control) uses central labels and clearances enforced by the system, which is complex and removes user discretion.

cards.front:
While reviewing the security controls in place for a web-based application, a security controls assessor notices that there are no password strength requirements in place. Because of this vulnerability, passwords might be easily discovered using a brute force attack. Which of the following password requirements will MOST effectively improve the security posture of the application against these attacks? (Select two)
A. Minimum complexity
B. Maximum age limit
C. Maximum length
D. Minimum length
E. Minimum age limit
F. Minimum re-use limit
cards.back:
A. Minimum complexity
D. Minimum length
cards.why: Minimum complexity and minimum length raise the number of possible password combinations, making brute force attacks take far longer and therefore most effectively improving resistance to them.

whyNot.B: A maximum age limit forces periodic password changes and does not make an individual password harder to brute force.
whyNot.C: A maximum length limit would restrict password strength rather than improve it against brute force attacks.
whyNot.E: A minimum age limit prevents rapid password changes and does not increase the difficulty of brute force attacks.
whyNot.F: A re-use limit stops people from recycling old passwords and does not make a new password harder to brute force.

cards.front:
A security administrator determined that users within the company are installing unapproved software. Company policy dictates that only certain applications may be installed or ran on the user's computers without exception. Which of the following should the administrator do to prevent all unapproved software from running on the user's computer?
A. Deploy antivirus software and configure it to detect and remove pirated software
B. Configure the firewall to prevent the downloading of executable files
C. Create an application whitelist and use OS controls to enforce it
D. Prevent users from running as administrator so they cannot install software.
cards.back: C. Create an application whitelist and use OS controls to enforce it
cards.why: Application whitelisting, enforced with operating system controls, permits only approved software to run and blocks everything else, which meets a policy of no exceptions for unapproved applications.

whyNot.A: Antivirus detects known malicious or pirated software but does not block all unapproved applications from running.
whyNot.B: A firewall blocking executable downloads cannot stop software arriving through other means such as USB (Universal Serial Bus) drives or approved channels.
whyNot.D: Removing administrator rights limits installation but does not prevent unapproved portable applications from running.

cards.front:
A security administrator is tasked with implementing centralized management of all network devices. Network administrators will be required to logon to network devices using their LDAP credentials. All command executed by network administrators on network devices must fall within a preset list of authorized commands and must be logged to a central facility. Which of the following configuration commands should be implemented to enforce this requirement?
A. LDAP server 10.55.199.3
B. CN=company, CN=com, OU=netadmin, DC=192.32.10.233
C. SYSLOG SERVER 172.16.23.50
D. TACAS server 192.168.1.100
cards.why: The question asks for authorized commands and central logging of administrator activity, which is the job of TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus), providing authentication, command authorization, and accounting. The keyed LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) distinguished name only handles directory lookup.

whyNot.A: An LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) server entry only handles authentication and cannot restrict commands or log them.
whyNot.C: A SYSLOG (System Logging) server provides central logging but does not authenticate users or authorize commands.
whyNot.D: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) provides command authorization and accounting, but it is misspelled here; however it is not the keyed answer.

cards.keyDoubt: D, because TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) alone provides per-command authorization and accounting for network devices, while the keyed option is only an LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) distinguished name string.

cards.front:
A website administrator has received an alert from an application designed to check the integrity of the company's website. The alert indicated that the hash value for a particular MPEG file has changed. Upon further investigation, the media appears to be the same as it was before the alert. Which of the following methods has MOST likely been used?
A. Cryptography
B. Time of check/time of use
C. Man in the middle
D. Covert timing
E. Steganography
cards.why: Steganography hides data inside a media file such as an MPEG (Moving Picture Experts Group) video, changing the file's hash value while the content looks and plays the same.

whyNot.A: Cryptography protects data confidentiality through encryption and would not by itself explain a changed hash on media that looks unchanged.
whyNot.B: Time of check/time of use (TOCTOU) is a race condition between validating and using a resource and does not alter a file's hash invisibly.
whyNot.C: A man in the middle (MITM) attack intercepts communications and does not specifically explain hidden changes inside a media file.
whyNot.D: Covert timing is a covert channel that signals information through timing and does not modify the file's contents.

cards.front:
An attacker captures the encrypted communication between two parties for a week, but is unable to decrypt the messages. The attacker then compromises the session key during one exchange and successfully compromises a single message. The attacker plans to use this key to decrypt previously captured and future communications, but is unable to. This is because the encryption scheme in use adheres to:
A. Asymmetric encryption
B. Out-of-band key exchange
C. Perfect forward secrecy
D. Secure key escrow
cards.why: PFS (Perfect Forward Secrecy) generates a unique session key for each exchange, so compromising one session key cannot decrypt earlier or later captured communications.

whyNot.A: Asymmetric encryption uses public and private key pairs and does not by itself guarantee that each session uses an independent key.
whyNot.B: Out-of-band key exchange delivers keys through a separate channel but does not ensure that one compromised key is isolated from other sessions.
whyNot.D: Secure key escrow stores copies of keys with a trusted party for recovery and does not protect other sessions from a compromised key.

cards.front:
Many employees are receiving email messages similar to the one shown below: From IT department To employee Subject email quota exceeded Pease click on the following link http:www.website.info/email.php?quota=1Gb and provide your username and password to increase your email quota. Upon reviewing other similar emails, the security administrator realized that all the phishing URLs have the following common elements; they all use HTTP, they all come from .info domains, and they all contain the same URI. Which of the following should the security administrator configure on the corporate content filter to prevent users from accessing the phishing URL, while at the same time minimizing false positives?
A. BLOCK http://www.*.info/"
B. DROP http://"website.info/email.php?*
C. Redirect http://www,*. Info/email.php?quota=*TOhttp://company.com/corporate_polict.html
D. DENY http://*.info/email.php?quota=1Gb
cards.why: The rule must match the shared HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) scheme, .info domain, and specific URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) path and query, while keeping false positives low; the keyed option is the most specific pattern, blocking only that path and query on .info domains.

whyNot.A: Blocking every http .info URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is too broad and would block many legitimate sites, causing false positives.
whyNot.B: Dropping the specific website.info domain misses phishing URLs on other .info domains that share the same URI (Uniform Resource Identifier).
whyNot.C: Redirecting rather than blocking still lets users reach a modified page, and the pattern contains typos that would not match correctly.

cards.front:
