A security analyst is reviewing the following packet capture of an attack directed at a company's server located in the DMZ: Which of the following ACLs provides the BEST protection against the above attack and any further attacks from the same IP, while minimizing service interruption?
A. DENY TCO From ANY to 172.31.64.4
B. Deny UDP from 192.168.1.0/24 to 172.31.67.0/24
C. Deny IP from 192.168.1.10/32 to 0.0.0.0/0
D. Deny TCP from 192.168.1.10 to 172.31.67.4
cards.why: Denying all IP (Internet Protocol) traffic from the single attacking host 192.168.1.10/32 stops this attack and any further attacks from that address, while leaving every other source unaffected and minimizing service interruption.

whyNot.A: Denying TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) from any source to the server would block all legitimate users and cause a service outage.
whyNot.B: Denying UDP (User Datagram Protocol) from a whole /24 subnet is too broad and targets the wrong protocol and wrong destination network.
whyNot.D: Denying only TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) from the attacker to one server still allows the attacker to use other protocols or reach other hosts.

cards.front:
The IT department needs to prevent users from installing untested applications. Which of the following would provide the BEST solution?
A. Job rotation
B. Least privilege
C. Account lockout
D. Antivirus
cards.why: Least privilege gives users only the permissions they need, so without administrative rights they cannot install untested applications on their systems.

whyNot.A: Job rotation moves staff between roles to reduce fraud and does not restrict software installation.
whyNot.C: Account lockout disables accounts after repeated failed logins and does not control which applications users can install.
whyNot.D: Antivirus detects known malware but does not stop users from installing untested yet non-malicious applications.

cards.front:
An attack that is using interference as its main attack to impede network traffic is which of the following?
A. Introducing too much data to a targets memory allocation
B. Utilizing a previously unknown security flaw against the target
C. Using a similar wireless configuration of a nearby network
D. Inundating a target system with SYN requests
cards.back: C. Using a similar wireless configuration of a nearby network
cards.why: Using a similar wireless configuration of a nearby network describes an evil twin or rogue access point attack, where a competing signal interferes with legitimate wireless traffic and disrupts clients. Interference is the main effect.

whyNot.A: Overloading a target's memory allocation describes a buffer overflow, which corrupts memory rather than interfering with network signals.
whyNot.B: Using a previously unknown flaw describes a zero-day exploit, which is not about interference with network traffic.
whyNot.D: Inundating a target with SYN (Synchronize) requests is a SYN flood Denial of Service (DoS) attack, which exhausts connection resources instead of causing interference.

cards.keyDoubt: D: Interference is a stretch for any option, but a SYN (Synchronize) flood is the only one that clearly impedes network traffic as a Denial of Service (DoS) attack, so it is the likelier intended answer.

cards.front:
An organization wants to conduct secure transactions of large data files. Before encrypting and exchanging the data files, the organization wants to ensure a secure exchange of keys. Which of the following algorithms is appropriate for securing the key exchange?
A. DES
B. Blowfish
C. DSA
D. Diffie-Hellman
E. 3DES
cards.why: Diffie-Hellman is a key exchange algorithm that lets two parties derive a shared secret over an insecure channel, so the data files can then be encrypted with that key.

whyNot.A: DES (Data Encryption Standard) is a symmetric cipher for encrypting data, not an algorithm for exchanging keys.
whyNot.B: Blowfish is a symmetric block cipher used to encrypt data, not to exchange keys.
whyNot.C: DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) is used to create and verify digital signatures, not to exchange keys.
whyNot.E: 3DES (Triple Data Encryption Standard) is a symmetric cipher for encrypting data, not for key exchange.

cards.front:
Ann, a college professor, was recently reprimanded for posting disparaging remarks re-grading her coworkers on a web site. Ann stated that she was not aware that the public was able to view her remakes. Which of the following security-related trainings could have made Ann aware of the repercussions of her actions?
A. Data Labeling and disposal
B. Use of social networking
C. Use of P2P networking
D. Role-based training
cards.why: Training on the use of social networking teaches employees that posts may be publicly visible and can have professional repercussions, which is exactly what Ann missed.

whyNot.A: Data labeling and disposal training covers classifying and destroying data, not appropriate public posting behavior.
whyNot.C: P2P (Peer-to-Peer) networking training covers file sharing risks, not posting comments on a website.
whyNot.D: Role-based training covers duties specific to a job function, not general public online conduct.

cards.front:
During a recent audit, it was discovered that many services and desktops were missing security patches. Which of the following BEST describes the assessment that was performed to discover this issue?
A. Network mapping
B. Vulnerability scan
C. Port Scan
D. Protocol analysis
cards.why: A vulnerability scan identifies weaknesses such as missing security patches on services and desktops, which matches the audit finding.

whyNot.A: Network mapping discovers hosts and topology but does not check for missing patches.
whyNot.C: A port scan finds open ports and services but does not determine whether patches are missing.
whyNot.D: Protocol analysis inspects captured network traffic and does not assess patch levels on hosts.

cards.front:
When generating a request for a new x.509 certificate for securing a website, which of the following is the MOST appropriate hashing algorithm?
A. RC4
B. MD5
C. HMAC
D. SHA
cards.why: SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm), specifically SHA-256 or stronger, is the modern, secure hash used when generating certificate requests and signatures for x.509 certificates.

whyNot.A: RC4 (Rivest Cipher 4) is a stream cipher, not a hashing algorithm, and is deprecated.
whyNot.B: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is broken by collision attacks and should not be used for certificates.
whyNot.C: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) is a keyed construction for message authentication, not the hash used in certificate requests.

cards.front:
The administrator installs database software to encrypt each field as it is written to disk. Which of the following describes the encrypted data?
A. In-transit
B. In-use
C. Embedded
D. At-rest
cards.why: Encrypting each field as it is written to disk protects data at-rest, meaning data stored on persistent media.

whyNot.A: Data in-transit is data moving across a network, which is not what writing fields to disk describes.
whyNot.B: Data in-use is data being actively processed in memory or by the CPU (Central Processing Unit), not stored on disk.
whyNot.C: Embedded is not a standard data state; it refers to embedded systems, not the state of encrypted data.

cards.front:
Which of the following allows an application to securely authenticate a user by receiving credentials from a web domain?
A. TACACS+
B. RADIUS
C. Kerberos
D. SAML
cards.why: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) lets an application authenticate a user based on an assertion from an identity provider in a web domain, enabling federated single sign-on.

whyNot.A: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) authenticates and authorizes administrative access to network devices, not web application logins.
whyNot.B: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) centralizes network access authentication, not web domain federation for applications.
whyNot.C: Kerberos is a ticket-based authentication protocol for internal network domains, not for receiving credentials from a web domain.

cards.front:
A network technician is trying to determine the source of an ongoing network based attack. Which of the following should the technician use to view IPv4 packet data on a particular internal network segment?
A. Proxy
B. Protocol analyzer
C. Switch
D. Firewall
cards.why: A protocol analyzer, or packet sniffer, captures and displays packet contents such as IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) data on a network segment.

whyNot.A: A proxy relays and filters client requests but is not used to view packet data on a segment.
whyNot.C: A switch forwards frames between ports and does not by itself display packet data.
whyNot.D: A firewall filters traffic by rules and logs events but is not a tool for viewing full packet data.

cards.front:
The security administrator has noticed cars parking just outside of the building fence line. Which of the following security measures can the administrator use to help protect the company's WiFi network against war driving? (Select TWO)
A. Create a honeynet
B. Reduce beacon rate
C. Add false SSIDs
D. Change antenna placement
E. Adjust power level controls
F. Implement a warning banner
cards.back:
D. Change antenna placement
E. Adjust power level controls
cards.why: Changing antenna placement and adjusting power level controls limit how far the WiFi signal propagates beyond the building, reducing exposure to war driving from outside the fence line.

whyNot.A: A honeynet is a decoy network for studying attackers and does not stop the signal from reaching the parking area.
whyNot.B: Reducing the beacon rate makes the network slower to discover but does not stop determined war drivers or limit signal range.
whyNot.C: Adding false SSIDs (Service Set Identifiers) only adds noise and does not limit signal reach or protect the real network.
whyNot.F: A warning banner is a legal notice and does not technically prevent signal capture or war driving.

cards.front:
A security administrator suspects that data on a server has been exhilarated as a result of un- authorized remote access. Which of the following would assist the administrator in con-firming the suspicions? (Select TWO)
A. Networking access control
B. DLP alerts
C. Log analysis
D. File integrity monitoring
E. Host firewall rules
cards.back:
B. DLP alerts
C. Log analysis
cards.why: DLP (Data Loss Prevention) alerts show sensitive data leaving the environment, and log analysis can reveal unauthorized remote access and transfers, together helping confirm exfiltration.

whyNot.A: NAC (Network Access Control) controls which devices can connect but does not confirm whether data was exfiltrated.
whyNot.D: FIM (File Integrity Monitoring) detects changes to files, but exfiltration copies data without necessarily modifying it.
whyNot.E: Host firewall rules restrict traffic as preventive controls and do not provide evidence of past exfiltration.

cards.front:
A company is deploying a new VoIP phone system. They require 99.999% uptime for their phone service and are concerned about their existing data network interfering with the VoIP phone system. The core switches in the existing data network are almost fully saturated. Which of the following options will pro-vide the best performance and availability for both the VoIP traffic, as well as the traffic on the existing data network?
A. Put the VoIP network into a different VLAN than the existing data network.
B. Upgrade the edge switches from 10/100/1000 to improve network speed
C. Physically separate the VoIP phones from the data network
D. Implement flood guards on the data network
cards.back: A. Put the VoIP network into a different VLAN than the existing data network.
cards.why: Placing VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) traffic in its own VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) isolates it from data traffic and allows QoS (Quality of Service) prioritization, improving performance and availability.

whyNot.B: Upgrading edge switches does not fix the saturated core switches or isolate voice traffic from data traffic.
whyNot.C: Physically separating the networks would be costly and is unnecessary when a VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) provides logical separation.
whyNot.D: Flood guards protect against denial of service floods and do not address congestion or voice traffic isolation.

cards.front:
A server administrator needs to administer a server remotely using RDP, but the specified port is closed on the outbound firewall on the network. The access the server using RDP on a port other than the typical registered port for the RDP protocol?
A. TLS
B. MPLS
C. SCP
D. SSH
cards.why: RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) can be tunneled inside TLS (Transport Layer Security) over an allowed port such as 443, letting the administrator reach the server despite the closed default port.

whyNot.B: MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) is a carrier WAN (Wide Area Network) routing technology, not a tunneling method for RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) on another port.
whyNot.C: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) transfers files over SSH (Secure Shell) and does not carry remote desktop sessions.
whyNot.D: SSH (Secure Shell) could tunnel RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol), but it would typically use port 22, which is likely also blocked, making TLS the better fit.

cards.keyDoubt: D: SSH (Secure Shell) port forwarding is the classic way to tunnel RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) to a different port, whereas TLS (Transport Layer Security) alone is not a tunneling method.

cards.front:
Which of the following can be used to control specific commands that can be executed on a network infrastructure device?
A. LDAP
B. Kerberos
C. SAML
D. TACACS+
cards.why: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) provides command-level authorization, letting administrators control which commands users may run on network infrastructure devices.

whyNot.A: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a directory service for storing and querying identities, not for per-command device authorization.
whyNot.B: Kerberos provides ticket-based authentication and does not authorize individual device commands.
whyNot.C: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) handles federated web authentication and does not control commands on network devices.

cards.front:
Company XYZ has decided to make use of a cloud-based service that requires mutual, certificate- based authentication with its users. The company uses SSL-inspecting IDS at its network boundary and is concerned about the confidentiality of the mutual authentication. Which of the following model prevents the IDS from capturing credentials used to authenticate users to the new service or keys to decrypt that communication?
A. Use of OATH between the user and the service and attestation from the company domain
B. Use of active directory federation between the company and the cloud-based service
C. Use of smartcards that store x.509 keys, signed by a global CA
D. Use of a third-party, SAML-based authentication service for attestation
cards.back: B. Use of active directory federation between the company and the cloud-based service
cards.why: Active Directory federation lets the company vouch for users through trust between identity providers, so the SSL-inspecting IDS (Intrusion Detection System) never sees the user's credentials or decryption keys.

whyNot.A: OATH (Open Authentication) one-time passwords with attestation still involve credentials passing through the inspected path, and the model does not address certificate-based mutual authentication.
whyNot.C: Smartcards storing x.509 keys signed by a global CA (Certificate Authority) still perform the mutual TLS handshake through the SSL-inspecting IDS (Intrusion Detection System).
whyNot.D: A third-party SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) service adds an external party and does not by itself keep credentials away from the inspecting IDS (Intrusion Detection System).

cards.front:
Six months into development, the core team assigned to implement a new internal piece of software must convene to discuss a new requirement with the stake holders. A stakeholder identified a missing feature critical to the organization, which must be implemented. The team needs to validate the feasibility of the newly introduced requirement and ensure it does not introduce new vulnerabilities to the software and other applications that will integrate with it. Which of the following BEST describes what the company?
A. The system integration phase of the SDLC
B. The system analysis phase of SSDSLC
C. The system design phase of the SDLC
D. The system development phase of the SDLC
cards.back: B. The system analysis phase of SSDSLC
cards.why: Validating the feasibility of a new requirement and its security impact is part of the system analysis phase of the SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle), where requirements are defined and assessed.

whyNot.A: The system integration phase combines completed components and tests them together, rather than evaluating new requirements.
whyNot.C: The system design phase defines architecture after requirements are settled, not feasibility of a newly introduced requirement.
whyNot.D: The system development phase is where code is written, which comes after requirements have been analyzed and approved.

cards.front:
A company is investigating a data compromise where data exfiltration occurred. Prior to the investigation, the supervisor terminates an employee as a result of the suspected data loss. During the investigation, the supervisor is absent for the interview, and little evidence can be provided form the role-based authentication system in use by the company. The situation can be identified for future mitigation as which of the following?
A. Job rotation
B. Log failure
C. Lack of training
D. Insider threat
cards.why: Little evidence was available from the role-based authentication system, which points to a log failure: the logging and auditing needed to attribute actions and support the investigation was missing or inadequate.

whyNot.A: Job rotation moves employees between duties to detect fraud; it does not explain missing authentication evidence.
whyNot.C: Lack of training concerns employee knowledge and is not what left the investigation without usable records.
whyNot.D: An insider threat describes who may have caused the exfiltration, not the gap in logging that hampered the investigation.

cards.front:
A security administrator needs an external vendor to correct an urgent issue with an organization's physical access control system (PACS). The PACS does not currently have internet access because it is running a legacy operation system. Which of the following methods should the security administrator select the best balances security and efficiency?
A. Temporarily permit outbound internet access for the pacs so desktop sharing can be set up
B. Have the external vendor come onsite and provide access to the PACS directly
C. Set up VPN concentrator for the vendor and restrict access to the PACS using desktop sharing
D. Set up a web conference on the administrator's pc; then remotely connect to the pacs
cards.back: C. Set up VPN concentrator for the vendor and restrict access to the PACS using desktop sharing
cards.why: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) concentrator gives the vendor an encrypted, authenticated channel, and limiting the vendor to desktop sharing on the PACS (Physical Access Control System) balances security with quick remote support.

whyNot.A: Permitting outbound internet access for a legacy-operating-system PACS (Physical Access Control System) exposes an unpatchable device to the internet.
whyNot.B: An onsite visit is secure but slow, so it fails the urgency and efficiency requirement.
whyNot.D: Remotely connecting from the administrator's PC through a web conference exposes that workstation and bypasses controlled, authenticated vendor access.

cards.front:
A datacenter manager has been asked to prioritize critical system recovery priorities. Which of the following is the MOST critical for immediate recovery?
A. Communications software
B. Operating system software
C. Weekly summary reports to management
D. Financial and production software
cards.why: The operating system is the foundation that every application and service runs on, so it must be restored first before other software can function.

whyNot.A: Communications software depends on a working operating system, so it is restored after the operating system.
whyNot.C: Weekly summary reports to management are not time-critical and can wait until core systems are recovered.
whyNot.D: Financial and production software needs a running operating system first, so it is recovered afterward.

cards.front:
Which of the following techniques can be bypass a user or computer's web browser privacy settings? (Select Two)
A. SQL injection
B. Session hijacking
C. Cross-site scripting
D. Locally shared objects
E. LDAP injection
cards.back:
B. Session hijacking
C. Cross-site scripting
cards.why: The key lists session hijacking and cross-site scripting, but locally shared objects (Flash cookies) are the textbook way to persist tracking data outside normal browser privacy settings.

whyNot.A: SQL (Structured Query Language) injection attacks the database through unsanitized input and does not bypass browser privacy settings.
whyNot.B: Session hijacking steals an active session token but does not defeat the browser's privacy settings.
whyNot.E: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) injection manipulates directory queries on the server and does not affect browser privacy settings.

cards.keyDoubt: D and C: locally shared objects (Flash cookies) persist outside browser privacy controls, and cross-site scripting runs script in the browser, whereas session hijacking steals tokens rather than bypassing privacy settings.

cards.front:
When designing a web based client server application with single application server and database cluster backend, input validation should be performed:
A. On the client
B. Using database stored procedures
C. On the application server
D. Using HTTPS
cards.why: Input validation must be enforced on the application server, a trusted layer the attacker cannot alter, so malicious input is rejected before it reaches the database.

whyNot.A: Client-side validation can be bypassed by an attacker who modifies requests or disables scripts, so it is only a convenience.
whyNot.B: Database stored procedures validate too late, after the application has accepted the input, and do not replace server-side validation.
whyNot.D: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts traffic in transit but does not check whether the submitted data is malicious.

cards.front:
Which of the following delineates why it is important to perform egress filtering and monitoring on Internet connected security zones of interfaces on a firewall?
A. Egress traffic is more important than ingress traffic for malware prevention
B. To rebalance the amount of outbound traffic and inbound traffic
C. Outbound traffic could be communicating to known botnet sources
D. To prevent DDoS attacks originating from external network
cards.back: C. Outbound traffic could be communicating to known botnet sources
cards.why: Egress filtering and monitoring can reveal compromised internal hosts communicating with known botnet command-and-control sources, which lets administrators block and detect that outbound traffic.

whyNot.A: Egress traffic is not inherently more important than ingress traffic; both need filtering as part of defense in depth.
whyNot.B: Egress filtering is a security control and is not used to rebalance inbound and outbound traffic volumes.
whyNot.D: Preventing DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attacks from external networks is an ingress concern, not the purpose of egress filtering.

cards.front:
The help desk is receiving numerous password change alerts from users in the accounting department. These alerts occur multiple times on the same day for each of the affected users' accounts. Which of the following controls should be implemented to curtail this activity?
A. Password Reuse
B. Password complexity
C. Password History
D. Password Minimum age
cards.why: A minimum password age stops users from changing their password repeatedly within a short period, which curtails the many same-day password changes.

whyNot.A: Password reuse describes the problem of reusing old passwords and is not a control that limits how often changes occur.
whyNot.B: Password complexity sets character requirements and does not limit how frequently a password can be changed.
whyNot.C: Password history blocks reuse of old passwords, but users can still change passwords many times a day.

cards.front:
Which of the following would enhance the security of accessing data stored in the cloud? (Select TWO)
A. Block level encryption
B. SAML authentication
C. Transport encryption
D. Multifactor authentication
E. Predefined challenge questions
F. Hashing
cards.back:
B. SAML authentication
D. Multifactor authentication
cards.why: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) authentication provides federated single sign-on with centrally managed identity, and MFA (Multifactor Authentication) requires more than one proof of identity before cloud data is accessed.

whyNot.A: Block level encryption protects data at rest but does not control or strengthen who is able to access the cloud data.
whyNot.C: Transport encryption protects data in transit but does not strengthen authentication to the cloud service.
whyNot.E: Predefined challenge questions are weak, guessable knowledge factors and do not meaningfully enhance access security.
whyNot.F: Hashing provides integrity checking and cannot control access to data stored in the cloud.

cards.front:
A remote user (User1) is unable to reach a newly provisioned corporate windows workstation. The system administrator has been given the following log files from the VPN, corporate firewall and workstation host. Which of the following is preventing the remote user from being able to access the workstation?
A. Network latency is causing remote desktop service request to time out
B. User1 has been locked out due to too many failed passwords
C. Lack of network time synchronization is causing authentication mismatches
D. The workstation has been compromised and is accessing known malware sites
E. The workstation host firewall is not allowing remote desktop connections
cards.back: B. User1 has been locked out due to too many failed passwords
cards.why: The keyed answer is that User1 has been locked out after too many failed password attempts, which would block access to the workstation even though the network path is otherwise working.

whyNot.A: Network latency would cause slow or intermittent connections rather than a consistent failure to reach the workstation.
whyNot.C: Lack of network time synchronization can break Kerberos authentication, but nothing keyed points to a time mismatch here.
whyNot.D: A compromised workstation visiting malware sites would not by itself explain why User1 cannot reach the workstation.
whyNot.E: A host firewall blocking RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) would be shown as denied connections, which is not what the keyed answer indicates.

cards.front:
During a third-party audit, it is determined that a member of the firewall team can request, approve, and implement a new rule-set on the firewall. Which of the following will the audit team most l likely recommend during the audit out brief?
A. Discretionary access control for the firewall team
B. Separation of duties policy for the firewall team
C. Least privilege for the firewall team
D. Mandatory access control for the firewall team
cards.back: B. Separation of duties policy for the firewall team
cards.why: Separation of duties requires that no single person controls an entire process, so requesting, approving, and implementing firewall rules should be split among different people.

whyNot.A: Discretionary access control lets owners assign permissions and does not split request, approval, and implementation roles.
whyNot.C: Least privilege limits the rights a person has, but does not by itself divide one process among several people.
whyNot.D: Mandatory access control uses system-enforced labels and clearances and does not address one person holding every step of the change process.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the appropriate network structure used to protect servers and services that must be provided to external clients without completely eliminating access for internal users?
A. NAC
B. VLAN
C. DMZ
D. Subnet
cards.why: A DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) is a network segment between the internet and the internal network that hosts externally facing servers while still allowing controlled internal access.

whyNot.A: NAC (Network Access Control) checks the posture of devices connecting to the network and does not create a zone for public-facing servers.
whyNot.B: A VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) logically separates traffic but does not by itself provide a protected zone for external services.
whyNot.D: A subnet divides an address range and does not provide the filtered boundary needed for externally exposed servers.

cards.front:
An administrator has configured a new Linux server with the FTP service. Upon verifying that the service was configured correctly, the administrator has several users test the FTP service. Users report that they are able to connect to the FTP service and download their personal files, however, they cannot transfer new files to the server. Which of the following will most likely fix the uploading issue for the users?
A. Create an ACL to allow the FTP service write access to user directories
B. Set the Boolean selinux value to allow FTP home directory uploads
C. Reconfigure the ftp daemon to operate without utilizing the PSAV mode
D. Configure the FTP daemon to utilize PAM authentication pass through user permissions
cards.back: A. Create an ACL to allow the FTP service write access to user directories
cards.why: Users can download but not upload, which indicates the FTP (File Transfer Protocol) service account lacks write permission, so an ACL (Access Control List) granting write access to user directories fixes it.

whyNot.B: An SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux) Boolean could also block uploads, but nothing in the scenario suggests SELinux is enforcing, and plain permissions are the likelier cause.
whyNot.C: Passive mode affects how data connections are established, and downloads already work, so it would not selectively block uploads.
whyNot.D: PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) pass-through affects authentication, which already works since users can log in and download.

cards.front:
An administrator thinks the UNIX systems may be compromised, but a review of system log files provides no useful information. After discussing the situation with the security team, the administrator suspects that the attacker may be altering the log files and removing evidence of intrusion activity. Which of the following actions will help detect attacker attempts to further alter log files?
A. Enable verbose system logging
B. Change the permissions on the user's home directory
C. Implement remote syslog
D. Set the bash_history log file to "read only"
cards.why: Remote syslog sends log entries to a separate protected server in real time, so an attacker who alters local logs cannot erase the copies and further tampering becomes detectable.

whyNot.A: Verbose logging records more detail locally, but an attacker with access can still alter or delete those local files.
whyNot.B: Changing permissions on a user's home directory does not protect the system log files from alteration.
whyNot.D: Setting the bash_history file to read only protects only command history and does not protect system logs or detect tampering.

cards.front:
A global gaming console manufacturer is launching a new gaming platform to its customers. Which of the following controls reduces the risk created by malicious gaming customers attempting to circumvent control by way of modifying consoles?
A. Firmware version control
B. Manual software upgrades
C. Vulnerability scanning
D. Automatic updates
E. Network segmentation
F. Application firewalls
cards.back:
A. Firmware version control
D. Automatic updates
cards.why: Firmware version control stops consoles from running modified or downgraded firmware, and automatic updates keep every console on the current, trusted firmware.

whyNot.B: Manual software upgrades depend on customers acting, so modified consoles can simply stay on old, vulnerable versions.
whyNot.C: Vulnerability scanning finds known weaknesses but does not stop customers from modifying their own consoles.
whyNot.E: Network segmentation separates the manufacturer's network traffic and does not prevent physical or software modification of consoles.
whyNot.F: Application firewalls filter traffic to applications and do not prevent customers from modifying console firmware or software.

cards.front:
An audit has revealed that database administrators are also responsible for auditing database changes and backup logs. Which of the following access control methodologies would BEST mitigate this concern?
A. Time of day restrictions
B. Principle of least privilege
C. Role-based access control
D. Separation of duties
cards.why: Separation of duties prevents the same people who administer the databases from also auditing their changes and backup logs, so oversight is independent.

whyNot.A: Time of day restrictions limit when accounts can log in and do not separate administration from auditing.
whyNot.B: Least privilege limits the rights each person has, but does not specifically stop one person from both administering and auditing.
whyNot.C: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) assigns permissions by role, but it would not fix the conflict unless duties are separated into different roles and people.

cards.front:
An external contractor, who has not been given information about the software or network architecture, is conducting a penetration test. Which of the following BEST describes the test being performed?
A. Black box
B. White box
C. Passive reconnaissance
D. Vulnerability scan
cards.why: Black box testing means the tester has no prior knowledge of the target's software or network architecture, which matches a contractor given no information.

whyNot.B: White box testing gives the tester full knowledge of the architecture and source, the opposite of this scenario.
whyNot.C: Passive reconnaissance is an information-gathering technique, not a penetration test type defined by how much knowledge the tester has.
whyNot.D: A vulnerability scan is an automated search for known weaknesses and does not describe a penetration test's knowledge level.

cards.front:
A security administrator receives an alert from a third-party vendor that indicates a certificate that was installed in the browser has been hijacked at the root of a small public CA. The security administrator knows there are at least four different browsers in use on more than a thousand computers in the domain worldwide. Which of the following solutions would be BEST for the security administrator to implement to most efficiently assist with this issue?
A. SSL
B. CRL
C. PKI
D. ACL
cards.why: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) publishes revoked certificates, so every browser can check it and reject the hijacked certificate without configuring each machine individually.

whyNot.A: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) is an encryption protocol and does not revoke or invalidate a compromised certificate.
whyNot.C: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is the overall certificate framework, not the specific revocation mechanism needed here.
whyNot.D: An ACL (Access Control List) filters access to resources and has no ability to distrust a certificate across browsers.

cards.front:
A security analyst has set up a network tap to monitor network traffic for vulnerabilities. Which of the following techniques would BEST describe the approach the analyst has taken?
A. Compliance scanning
B. Credentialed scanning
C. Passive vulnerability scanning
D. Port scanning
cards.why: The keyed answer is port scanning, but a network tap only observes traffic and sends no probes, so port scanning is a questionable fit.

whyNot.A: Compliance scanning checks configurations against a policy baseline and does not describe passively watching tapped traffic.
whyNot.B: Credentialed scanning logs in to hosts with valid accounts, which a network tap does not do.
whyNot.C: Passive vulnerability scanning is the better fit for tapped traffic, but it is not the keyed answer.

cards.keyDoubt: C. A network tap only copies and observes traffic without sending probes, which is passive vulnerability scanning, whereas port scanning actively sends packets to hosts.

cards.front:
Due to regulatory requirements, a security analyst must implement full drive encryption on a Windows file server. Which of the following should the analyst implement on the system to BEST meet this requirement? (Choose two.)
A. Enable and configure EFS on the file system.
B. Ensure the hardware supports TPM, and enable it in the BIOS.
C. Ensure the hardware supports VT-X, and enable it in the BIOS.
D. Enable and configure BitLocker on the drives.
E. Enable and configure DFS across the file system
cards.back:
B. Ensure the hardware supports TPM, and enable it in the BIOS.
D. Enable and configure BitLocker on the drives.
cards.why: BitLocker provides full drive encryption on Windows, and it relies on a TPM (Trusted Platform Module) enabled in the BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) to securely store the keys.

whyNot.A: EFS (Encrypting File System) encrypts individual files and folders, not the full drive as the regulation requires.
whyNot.C: VT-x (Intel Virtualization Technology) supports virtual machines and has nothing to do with drive encryption.
whyNot.E: DFS (Distributed File System) organizes and replicates shared folders and does not encrypt any data.

cards.front:
A company's loss control department identifies theft as a recurring loss type over the past year. Based on the department's report, the Chief Information Officer (CIO) wants to detect theft of datacenter equipment. Which of the following controls should be implemented?
A. Biometrics
B. Cameras
C. Motion detectors
D. Mantraps
cards.why: Motion detectors sense movement in the datacenter and raise an alert, so they detect equipment theft when someone removes or moves gear.

whyNot.A: Biometrics authenticate people at an entry point and do not detect equipment being removed.
whyNot.B: Cameras record activity and mainly help investigation afterward, rather than detecting theft as it happens.
whyNot.D: Mantraps are physical entry controls that prevent tailgating and do not detect equipment removal.

cards.front:
Which of the following penetration testing concepts is being used when an attacker uses public Internet databases to enumerate and learn more about a target?
A. Reconnaissance
B. Initial exploitation
C. Pivoting
D. Vulnerability scanning
E. White box testing
cards.why: Reconnaissance is the information-gathering phase of a penetration test, and using public Internet databases to learn about a target is passive reconnaissance (also called open source intelligence).

whyNot.B: Initial exploitation means actively compromising a system, not just looking up public information.
whyNot.C: Pivoting means using an already compromised host to reach other systems on the network.
whyNot.D: Vulnerability scanning actively probes systems for weaknesses, rather than reading public databases.
whyNot.E: White box testing describes a tester who has full knowledge of the target, not a way of gathering public data.

cards.front:
While performing a penetration test, the technicians want their efforts to go unnoticed for as long as possible while they gather useful data about the network they are assessing. Which of the following would be the BEST choice for the technicians?
A. Vulnerability scanner
B. Offline password cracker
C. Packet sniffer
D. Banner grabbing
cards.why: A packet sniffer passively captures network traffic without sending packets to targets, so it is the least likely tool to be detected by an IDS (Intrusion Detection System).

whyNot.A: A vulnerability scanner actively sends many probes, which generates noise and is easily detected.
whyNot.B: An offline password cracker works on already obtained hashes and gathers no information about the network.
whyNot.D: Banner grabbing connects to services to read their banners, which creates log entries and can be detected.

cards.front:
A security analyst captures forensic evidence from a potentially compromised system for further investigation. The evidence is documented and securely stored to FIRST:
A. maintain the chain of custody.
B. preserve the data.
C. obtain a legal hold.
D. recover data at a later time.
cards.why: Documenting and securely storing captured evidence first serves to preserve the data, keeping it intact and unaltered so it remains usable in the investigation.

whyNot.A: Chain of custody is maintained by recording who handled the evidence, which is a result of documentation rather than the first purpose of storing it.
whyNot.C: A legal hold is a legal instruction to retain information and is not obtained by storing evidence.
whyNot.D: Recovering data later is a possible use of stored evidence, not the first reason for securing it.

cards.front:
A security analyst is investigating a security breach. Upon inspection of the audit an access logs, the analyst notices the host was accessed and the /etc/passwd file was modified with a new entry for username "gotcha" and user ID of 0. Which of the following are the MOST likely attack vector and tool the analyst should use to determine if the attack is still ongoing? (Choose two.)
A. Logic bomb
B. Backdoor
C. Keylogger
D. Netstat
E. Tracert
F. Ping
cards.why: A new account with UID (user identifier) 0 gives root-level access and is a backdoor, and the netstat command shows active network connections that reveal whether the attacker is still connected.

whyNot.A: A logic bomb runs malicious code when a condition is met, which does not describe adding a hidden root account.
whyNot.C: A keylogger captures keystrokes and does not modify the password file to create a new account.
whyNot.E: Tracert (trace route) shows the path packets take to a destination and does not show active connections on the host.
whyNot.F: Ping only tests whether a host responds and cannot show whether an attacker is currently connected.

cards.front:
A company recently replaced its unsecure email server with a cloud-based email and collaboration solution that is managed and insured by a third party. Which of the following actions did the company take regarding risks related to its email and collaboration services?
A. Transference
B. Acceptance
C. Mitigation
D. Deterrence
cards.why: Transference shifts the risk to a third party, here a provider that manages and insures the email and collaboration service.

whyNot.B: Acceptance means knowingly tolerating the risk without changing it, which is not what moving to an insured provider does.
whyNot.C: Mitigation reduces the likelihood or impact of the risk through controls, rather than shifting it to another party.
whyNot.D: Deterrence discourages attackers from acting and does not move the financial or operational risk to a third party.

cards.front:
A security administrator is reviewing the following network capture: Which of the following malware is MOST likely to generate the above information?
A. Keylogger
B. Ransomware
C. Logic bomb
D. Adware
cards.why: The keyed answer is a keylogger, which records keystrokes and sends the captured data out over the network, producing the kind of traffic shown in the capture.

whyNot.B: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, and it would not typically send captured user input.
whyNot.C: A logic bomb waits for a trigger condition and does not generally produce this kind of ongoing network traffic.
whyNot.D: Adware displays unwanted advertisements and does not typically transmit captured keystroke data.

cards.front:
A network administrator adds an ACL to allow only HTTPS connections form host 192.168.2.3 to web server 192.168.5.2. After applying the rule, the host is unable to access the server. The network administrator runs the output and notices the configuration below: Which of the following rules would be BEST to resolve the issue?
A. 
B. 
C. 
D.

A datacenter recently experienced a breach. When access was gained, an RF device was used to access an air-gapped and locked server rack. Which of the following would BEST prevent this type of attack?
A. Faraday cage
B. Smart cards
C. Infrared detection
D. Alarms
cards.why: A Faraday cage blocks RF (radio frequency) signals, so an attacker cannot use a wireless device to reach into the air-gapped, locked server rack.

whyNot.B: Smart cards control who can authenticate at a door and do not stop radio signals from reaching the equipment.
whyNot.C: Infrared detection senses heat or motion and does not block RF (radio frequency) signals.
whyNot.D: Alarms only notify staff after an event and cannot prevent the wireless attack.

cards.front:
A security analyst is working on a project that requires the implementation of a stream cipher. Which of the following should the analyst use?
A. Hash function
B. Elliptic curve
C. Symmetric algorithm
D. Public key cryptography
cards.why: A stream cipher encrypts data one bit or byte at a time using a shared secret key, which makes it a symmetric algorithm.

whyNot.A: A hash function creates a fixed-length digest for integrity and is not an encryption cipher.
whyNot.B: Elliptic curve cryptography is an asymmetric method and is not a stream cipher.
whyNot.D: Public key cryptography uses key pairs and is asymmetric, so it is not a stream cipher.

cards.front:
Which of the following would allow for the QUICKEST restoration of a server into a warm recovery site in a case in which server data mirroring is not enabled?
A. Full backup
B. Incremental backup
C. Differential backup
D. Snapshot
cards.why: A differential backup captures all changes since the last full backup, so restoring needs only the full backup plus the latest differential, which is faster than chaining many incremental backups.

whyNot.A: A full backup is slow to create and large, so it is not the answer the question's backup-efficiency framing intends.
whyNot.B: An incremental backup requires the full backup plus every incremental since, which makes restoration slower than a differential.
whyNot.D: A snapshot is a point-in-time image usually tied to the original storage and is not a dependable restore source for a recovery site.

cards.front:
In determining when it may be necessary to perform a credentialed scan against a system instead of a non-credentialed scan, which of the following requirements is MOST likely to influence this decision?
A. The scanner must be able to enumerate the host OS of devices scanned.
B. The scanner must be able to footprint the network.
C. The scanner must be able to check for open ports with listening services.
D. The scanner must be able to audit file system permissions
cards.back: D. The scanner must be able to audit file system permissions
cards.why: Auditing file system permissions requires logging in to the host with valid credentials, because a non-credentialed scan cannot see internal permission settings.

whyNot.A: Enumerating the host OS (operating system) can usually be done without credentials through fingerprinting.
whyNot.B: Footprinting the network is done from outside and needs no credentials.
whyNot.C: Checking for open ports with listening services is done by probing from the network and needs no credentials.

cards.front:
The computer resource center issued smartphones to all first-level and above managers. The managers have the ability to install mobile tools. Which of the following tools should be implemented to control the types of tools the managers install?
A. Download manager
B. Content manager
C. Segmentation manager
D. Application manager
cards.why: An application manager (mobile application management) controls which apps users may install on managed smartphones, using allow lists and block lists, so it restricts the tools managers can add.

whyNot.A: A download manager only handles file transfers and does not restrict which applications a user installs.
whyNot.B: A content manager controls access to documents and data, not which applications are installed on the device.
whyNot.C: A segmentation manager separates network traffic or data zones and does not govern app installation.

cards.front:
Which of the following BEST describes a network-based attack that can allow an attacker to take full control of a vulnerable host?
A. Remote exploit
B. Amplification
C. Sniffing
D. Man-in-the-middle
cards.why: A remote exploit abuses a vulnerability in a service over the network, which can give the attacker code execution and full control of the vulnerable host.

whyNot.B: Amplification multiplies traffic volume in a Denial of Service attack and does not give control of a host.
whyNot.C: Sniffing passively captures network traffic and does not by itself compromise a host.
whyNot.D: A man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack intercepts or alters traffic between parties and does not directly take over a host.

cards.front:
A security auditor is putting together a report for the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) on personnel security and its impact on the security posture of the whole organization. Which of the following would be the MOST important factor to consider when it comes to personnel security?
A. Insider threats
B. Privilege escalation
C. Hacktivist
D. Phishing through social media
E. Corporate espionage
cards.why: Insider threats are the most important personnel security factor because employees already hold legitimate access and trust, so their mistakes or malicious acts directly affect the organization's overall security posture.

whyNot.B: Privilege escalation is a technique that can result from insider or external abuse, not the core personnel security concern.
whyNot.C: A hacktivist is an external threat actor type and does not describe the organization's own personnel.
whyNot.D: Phishing through social media is one attack vector and is narrower than overall personnel risk.
whyNot.E: Corporate espionage is one possible insider motive, which makes it narrower than insider threats generally.

cards.front:
A security administrator wants to configure a company's wireless network in a way that will prevent wireless clients from broadcasting the company's SSID. Which of the following should be configured on the company's access points?
A. Enable ESSID broadcast
B. Enable protected management frames
C. Enable wireless encryption
D. Disable MAC authentication
E. Disable WPS
F. Disable SSID broadcast
cards.why: Disabling SSID (Service Set Identifier) broadcast stops the access point from advertising the network name in beacon frames, so clients no longer announce or discover it passively.

whyNot.A: Enabling ESSID (Extended Service Set Identifier) broadcast does the opposite and advertises the network name.
whyNot.B: Protected management frames secure management traffic against spoofing and do not hide the SSID (Service Set Identifier).
whyNot.C: Wireless encryption protects data confidentiality and does not control whether the network name is broadcast.
whyNot.D: Disabling MAC (Media Access Control) authentication removes a client filtering control and does not affect SSID (Service Set Identifier) broadcast.
whyNot.E: Disabling WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) removes a push-button or PIN pairing feature and does not hide the network name.

cards.front:
A wireless network has the following design requirements: Authentication must not be dependent on enterprise directory service It must allow background reconnection for mobile users It must not depend on user certificates Which of the following should be used in the design to meet the requirements? (Choose two.)
A. PEAP
B. PSK
C. Open systems authentication
D. EAP-TLS
E. Captive portals
cards.why: PSK (Pre-Shared Key) needs no directory service or user certificates and reconnects automatically, while a captive portal authenticates users with its own credential store and supports easy reconnection for mobile users.

whyNot.A: PEAP (Protected Extensible Authentication Protocol) normally authenticates users against an enterprise directory through a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server.
whyNot.C: Open systems authentication provides no real authentication, so it does not meet the authentication requirement.
whyNot.D: EAP-TLS (Extensible Authentication Protocol-Transport Layer Security) requires client certificates and a certificate infrastructure, which the requirements prohibit.

cards.front:
Which of the following strategies should a systems architect use to minimize availability risks due to insufficient storage capacity?
A. High availability
B. Scalability
C. Distributive allocation
D. Load balancing
cards.why: Scalability lets the architect add storage capacity as demand grows, which directly reduces the availability risk of running out of space.

whyNot.A: High availability uses redundancy to survive component failures and does not address growing storage demand.
whyNot.C: Distributive allocation is not a recognized strategy for preventing capacity exhaustion.
whyNot.D: Load balancing spreads requests across servers and does not add storage capacity.

cards.front:
A security engineer wants to implement a site-to-site VPN that will require SSL certificates for mutual authentication. Which of the following should the engineer implement if the design requires client MAC address to be visible across the tunnel?
A. Tunnel mode IPSec
B. Transport mode VPN IPSec
C. L2TP
D. SSL VPN
cards.why: An SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) VPN (Virtual Private Network) can tunnel at Layer 2 using certificates for mutual authentication, so client MAC (Media Access Control) addresses stay visible across the tunnel.

whyNot.A: Tunnel mode IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) encapsulates whole IP packets at Layer 3, so original MAC (Media Access Control) addresses are not carried.
whyNot.B: Transport mode IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) protects only the payload at Layer 3 and does not carry client MAC (Media Access Control) addresses.
whyNot.C: L2TP (Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol) alone lacks encryption and is not the certificate-based mutual authentication design described.

cards.front:
After surfing the Internet, Joe, a user, woke up to find all his files were corrupted. His wallpaper was replaced by a message stating the files were encrypted and he needed to transfer money to a foreign country to recover them. Joe is a victim of:
A. a keylogger.
B. spyware.
C. ransomware.
D. a logic bomb.
cards.why: Ransomware encrypts a victim's files and demands payment for the decryption key, which matches the encrypted files and the ransom message on the wallpaper.

whyNot.A: A keylogger records keystrokes and does not encrypt files or demand payment.
whyNot.B: Spyware secretly gathers user information and does not encrypt files for ransom.
whyNot.D: A logic bomb triggers malicious code on a condition or date and does not typically present a ransom demand.

cards.front:
Security administrators attempted corrective action after a phishing attack. Users are still experiencing trouble logging in, as well as an increase in account lockouts. Users' email contacts are complaining of an increase in spam and social networking requests. Due to the large number of affected accounts, remediation must be accomplished quickly. Which of the following actions should be taken FIRST? (Select TWO)
A. Disable the compromised accounts
B. Update WAF rules to block social networks
C. Remove the compromised accounts with all AD groups
D. Change the compromised accounts' passwords
E. Disable the open relay on the email server
F. Enable sender policy framework
cards.back:
E. Disable the open relay on the email server
F. Enable sender policy framework

Sender Policy Framework (SPF) is a simple email-validation system designed to detect email spoofing by providing a mechanism to allow receiving mail exchangers to check that incoming mail from a domain comes from a host authorized by that domain's administrato...
cards.why: Disabling the open relay stops the mail server from sending spam on behalf of attackers, and enabling SPF (Sender Policy Framework) lets recipients reject forged mail, quickly limiting abuse across many accounts.

whyNot.A: Disabling the compromised accounts is slow with many accounts and does not stop spam relayed through the email server.
whyNot.B: Updating WAF (Web Application Firewall) rules to block social networks does not stop spam or account compromise.
whyNot.C: Removing accounts from all AD (Active Directory) groups is slow at this scale and does not stop mail abuse.
whyNot.D: Changing passwords for each compromised account is slow at this scale and does not stop spam relayed through the server.

cards.front:
Which of the following allows an auditor to test proprietary-software compiled code for security flaws?
A. Fuzzing
B. Static review
C. Code signing
D. Regression testing
cards.why: Fuzzing sends malformed or random input to a running program, so an auditor can find crashes and flaws in compiled code without having the source.

whyNot.B: Static review analyzes source code, which an auditor does not have for proprietary compiled software.
whyNot.C: Code signing proves who published code and that it is unaltered, and does not test for security flaws.
whyNot.D: Regression testing confirms that changes did not break existing functionality and is not a security flaw discovery method.

cards.front:
Ann, a user, states that her machine has been behaving erratically over the past week. She has experienced slowness and input lag and found text files that appear to contain pieces of her emails or online conversations with coworkers. The technician runs a standard virus scan but detects nothing. Which of the following types of malware has infected the machine?
A. Ransomware
B. Rootkit
C. Backdoor
D. Keylogger
cards.why: A keylogger records keystrokes and saves them to files, which explains the text files containing pieces of emails and conversations, along with the slowness and input lag.

whyNot.A: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, and it would not quietly save fragments of conversations.
whyNot.B: A rootkit hides malware presence but does not by itself produce text files of captured conversations.
whyNot.C: A backdoor gives an attacker remote access and does not by itself record typed content into files.

cards.front:
A security administrator wants to implement a logon script that will prevent MITM attacks on the local LAN. Which of the following commands should the security administrator implement within the script to accomplish this task?
A. arp - s 192.168.1.1 00-3a-d1-fa-b1-06
B. dig - x@192.168.1.1 mypc.comptia.com
C. nmap - A - T4 192.168.1.1
D. tcpdump - lnv host 192.168.1.1 or either 00:3a:d1:fa:b1:06
cards.why: Adding a static ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) entry for the gateway stops attackers from poisoning the ARP cache, which blocks the common LAN (Local Area Network) MITM (man-in-the-middle) technique.

whyNot.B: The dig command performs DNS (Domain Name System) reverse lookups and does not prevent MITM (man-in-the-middle) attacks.
whyNot.C: The nmap command scans hosts and ports for discovery and does not prevent MITM (man-in-the-middle) attacks.
whyNot.D: The tcpdump command captures packets for monitoring and does not prevent MITM (man-in-the-middle) attacks.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the BEST reason for salting a password hash before it is stored in a database?
A. To prevent duplicate values from being stored
B. To make the password retrieval process very slow
C. To protect passwords from being saved in readable format
D. To prevent users from using simple passwords for their access credentials
cards.back: A. To prevent duplicate values from being stored
cards.why: Salting adds unique random data to each password before hashing, so identical passwords produce different hash values and duplicates are not stored, which also defeats precomputed rainbow table attacks.

whyNot.B: Making hashing slow is the job of key stretching algorithms such as bcrypt, not of salting.
whyNot.C: Hashing already prevents readable storage, and salting does not add that protection.
whyNot.D: Salting happens after the user picks a password and does not enforce password complexity.

cards.front:
An actor downloads and runs a program against a corporate login page. The program imports a list of usernames and passwords, looking for a successful attempt. Which of the following terms BEST describes the actor in this situation?
A. Script kiddie
B. Hacktivist
C. Cryptologist
D. Security auditor
cards.why: A script kiddie uses a downloaded, premade tool without deep technical skill, which matches running a program that automatically tries a list of usernames and passwords.

whyNot.B: A hacktivist attacks for political or social motives, and nothing in the scenario indicates that motive.
whyNot.C: A cryptologist studies codes and ciphers and is not an attacker running a credential-guessing tool.
whyNot.D: A security auditor has authorization and a defined scope, and the scenario describes an unauthorized actor.

cards.front:
An organization wants to utilize a common, Internet-based third-party provider for authorization and authentication. The provider uses a technology based on OAuth 2.0 to provide required services. To which of the following technologies is the provider referring?
A. Open ID Connect
B. SAML
C. XACML
D. LDAP
cards.why: OpenID Connect is an identity layer built on OAuth (Open Authorization) 2.0 that lets Internet-based third-party providers handle authentication in addition to authorization.

whyNot.B: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) is an XML-based federation standard and is not built on OAuth (Open Authorization) 2.0.
whyNot.C: XACML (eXtensible Access Control Markup Language) defines access control policies and is not based on OAuth (Open Authorization) 2.0.
whyNot.D: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a directory access protocol and is not based on OAuth (Open Authorization) 2.0.

cards.front:
A penetration tester harvests potential usernames from a social networking site. The penetration tester then uses social engineering to attempt to obtain associated passwords to gain unauthorized access to shares on a network server. Which of the following methods is the penetration tester MOST likely using?
A. Escalation of privilege
B. SQL injection
C. Active reconnaissance
D. Proxy server
cards.why: Active reconnaissance involves directly interacting with targets or their users, such as social engineering to obtain passwords, after gathering usernames from a social networking site.

whyNot.A: Escalation of privilege means gaining higher access after initial entry, not harvesting usernames and tricking users into revealing passwords.
whyNot.B: SQL (Structured Query Language) injection attacks database input fields in applications, not people, and is not described here.
whyNot.D: A proxy server relays network traffic and is not a method of gathering usernames or obtaining passwords through social engineering.

cards.front:
Which of the following could occur when both strong and weak ciphers are configured on a VPN concentrator? (Select TWO)
A. An attacker could potentially perform a downgrade attack.
B. The connection is vulnerable to resource exhaustion.
C. The integrity of the data could be at risk.
D. The VPN concentrator could revert to L2TP.
E. The IPSec payload reverted to 16-bit sequence numbers.
cards.back:
A. An attacker could potentially perform a downgrade attack.
E. The IPSec payload reverted to 16-bit sequence numbers.
cards.why: Supporting weak ciphers alongside strong ones lets an attacker force a downgrade attack to the weakest cipher. The key also cites IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) reverting to shorter sequence numbers as a weakness.

whyNot.B: Resource exhaustion is a denial of service condition and is not caused by offering a mix of strong and weak ciphers.
whyNot.C: Cipher strength mainly affects confidentiality, and integrity depends on separate hashing or MAC (Message Authentication Code) settings, so it is not the direct result of this configuration.
whyNot.D: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) concentrator does not automatically revert to L2TP (Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol) because weak ciphers are enabled.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the BEST choice for a security control that represents a preventive and corrective logical control at the same time?
A. Security awareness training
B. Antivirus
C. Firewalls
D. Intrusion detection system
cards.why: Antivirus software is preventive because it blocks malware before execution and corrective because it quarantines or removes malicious files it finds, so it serves both control types at once.

whyNot.A: Security awareness training is an administrative control that is preventive, not a logical corrective control.
whyNot.C: Firewalls are preventive logical controls that filter traffic, but they do not correct or remove existing infections.
whyNot.D: An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) is a detective control that alerts on activity and does not prevent or correct it.

cards.front:
A web developer improves client access to the company's REST API. Authentication needs to be tokenized but not expose the client's password. Which of the following methods would BEST meet the developer's requirements?
A. SAML
B. LDAP
C. OAuth
D. Shibboleth
cards.why: The key lists SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language), which issues tokens so a client can authenticate without sending a password to the service provider.

whyNot.B: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a directory access protocol and does not issue tokens for REST (Representational State Transfer) API access.
whyNot.C: OAuth (Open Authorization) is a token-based authorization framework.
whyNot.D: Shibboleth is a federated identity system built on SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language), designed for web single sign-on rather than API token delegation.

cards.keyDoubt: C OAuth (Open Authorization) is the standard token-based method for REST (Representational State Transfer) API access without exposing the client's password, while SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) is aimed at browser-based single sign-on.

cards.front:
A vulnerability scan is being conducted against a desktop system. The scan is looking for files, versions, and registry values known to be associated with system vulnerabilities. Which of the following BEST describes the type of scan being performed?
A. Non-intrusive
B. Authenticated
C. Credentialed
D. Active
cards.why: A credentialed scan logs into the system with valid credentials, letting it inspect files, installed versions, and registry values that an unauthenticated scan cannot see.

whyNot.A: A non-intrusive scan avoids disrupting the target, but that describes impact on the system, not the ability to read files and registry values.
whyNot.B: An authenticated scan is effectively the same as a credentialed scan, but the keyed term is credentialed.
whyNot.D: An active scan sends probes to the target and does not by itself imply logging in to read files and registry values.

cards.front:
A security analyst is updating a BIA document. The security analyst notices the support vendor's time to replace a server hard drive went from eight hours to two hours. Given these new metrics, which of the following can be concluded? (Select TWO)
A. The MTTR is faster.
B. The MTTR is slower.
C. The RTO has increased.
D. The RTO has decreased.
E. The MTTF has increased.
F. The MTTF has decreased.
cards.back:
A. The MTTR is faster.
D. The RTO has decreased.
cards.why: Cutting hard drive replacement from eight hours to two means MTTR (Mean Time To Repair) is faster, and the RTO (Recovery Time Objective) can decrease because recovery completes sooner.

whyNot.B: MTTR (Mean Time To Repair) fell from eight hours to two, so it is faster, not slower.
whyNot.C: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) would not increase, since faster repairs shorten the achievable recovery time.
whyNot.E: MTTF (Mean Time To Failure) measures how long a component runs before failing and is unaffected by repair speed.
whyNot.F: MTTF (Mean Time To Failure) measures time until failure and is not changed by a faster replacement.

cards.front:
Which of the following could help detect trespassers in a secure facility? (Select TWO)
A. Faraday cages
B. Motion-detection sensors
C. Tall, chain-link fencing
D. Security guards
E. Smart cards
cards.back:
B. Motion-detection sensors
D. Security guards
cards.why: Motion-detection sensors and security guards both detect unauthorized people moving inside or around a secure facility, which makes them detective controls against trespassers.

whyNot.A: Faraday cages block electromagnetic signals and do not detect people.
whyNot.C: Tall chain-link fencing deters or delays intruders but does not detect them.
whyNot.E: Smart cards authenticate authorized users and do not detect trespassers.

cards.front:
The IT department is deploying new computers. To ease the transition, users will be allowed to access their old and new systems. The help desk is receive reports that users are experiencing the following error when attempting to log in to their previous system: Logon Failure: Access Denied Which of the following can cause this issue?
A. Permission issues
B. Access violations
C. Certificate issues
D. Misconfigured devices
cards.why: Certificate issues can cause Logon Failure: Access Denied on the old systems when the credentials or trust relationships tied to certificates no longer validate after the migration.

whyNot.A: Permission issues usually appear as denied access to resources after login, not as a logon failure at the sign-in step.
whyNot.B: Access violations describe unauthorized attempts to reach protected resources and do not explain a logon failure on previously working systems.
whyNot.D: Misconfigured devices would more likely produce connectivity or configuration errors rather than a specific Access Denied logon failure.

cards.front:
A third-party penetration testing company was able to successfully use an ARP cache poison technique to gain root access on a server. The tester successfully moved to another server that was not in the original network. Which of the following is the MOST likely method used to gain access to the other host?
A. Backdoor
B. Pivoting
C. Persistance
D. Logic bomp
cards.why: Pivoting is using one compromised host as a foothold to reach other systems or networks, which matches moving from the poisoned server to one outside the original network.

whyNot.A: A backdoor is a hidden access method into a system and does not describe moving from one host to another.
whyNot.C: Persistence is maintaining access over time, such as after a reboot, and is not about reaching other hosts.
whyNot.D: A logic bomb is malicious code triggered by a condition and is not a method of lateral movement.

cards.front:
Ann, a security administrator, wants to ensure credentials are encrypted in transit when implementing a RADIUS server for SSO. Which of the following are needed given these requirements? (Select TWO)
A. Public key
B. Shared key
C. Elliptic curve
D. MD5
E. Private key
F. DES
cards.back:
A. Public key
E. Private key
cards.why: Encrypting credentials in transit with an asymmetric exchange, such as a TLS (Transport Layer Security) tunnel used with EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol), requires a public key and a matching private key.

whyNot.B: A shared key is symmetric and secures only the RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) client-server link, so it is not the asymmetric pair the key expects.
whyNot.C: Elliptic curve is a type of algorithm, not a required key component for this requirement.
whyNot.D: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is a weak hash function and does not encrypt credentials.
whyNot.F: DES (Data Encryption Standard) is an obsolete symmetric cipher and not a requirement for protecting credentials.

cards.front:
The POODLE attack is an MITM exploit that affects:
A. TLS1.0 with CBC mode cipher
B. SSLv2.0 with CBC mode cipher
C. SSLv3.0 with CBC mode cipher
D. SSLv3.0 with ECB mode cipher
cards.back:
C. SSLv3.0 with CBC mode cipher

A flaw was found in the way SSL 3.0 handled padding bytes when decrypting messages encrypted using block ciphers in cipher block chaining (CBC) mode.
cards.why: The POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption) attack exploits the padding handling of CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode ciphers in SSLv3.0, letting an on-path attacker decrypt data.

whyNot.A: POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption) targets SSLv3.0, and TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.0 was not the original target.
whyNot.B: SSLv2.0 is a different, older protocol with its own flaws, and POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption) does not target it.
whyNot.D: ECB (Electronic Codebook) mode is not what POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption) exploits; it abuses CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) padding.

cards.front:
To determine the ALE of a particular risk, which of the following must be calculated? (Select two.)
A. ARO
B. ROI
C. RPO
D. SLE
E. RTO
cards.why: ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) equals SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) multiplied by ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence), so both must be calculated.

whyNot.B: ROI (Return on Investment) measures financial benefit of a purchase and is not part of the ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) formula.
whyNot.C: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines acceptable data loss in time and is not an input to ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy).
whyNot.E: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) defines acceptable downtime and is not an input to ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy).

cards.front:
Which of the following are used to increase the computing time it takes to brute force a password using an offline attack? (Select TWO)
A. XOR
B. PBKDF2
C. bcrypt
D. HMAC
E. RIPEMD
cards.why: PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) and bcrypt are deliberately slow, adaptive key stretching functions that raise the computing cost of each guess in an offline brute force attack.

whyNot.A: XOR (Exclusive OR) is a fast bitwise operation and adds no meaningful computational cost against brute force.
whyNot.D: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) provides message integrity and authentication and is not designed to slow password guessing.
whyNot.E: RIPEMD (RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest) is a fast hash function, so it does not slow offline guessing.

cards.front:
Users in a corporation currently authenticate with a username and password. A security administrator wishes to implement two-factor authentication to improve security. Which of the following authentication methods should be deployed to achieve this goal?
A. PIN
B. Security question
C. Smart card
D. Passphrase
E. CAPTCHA
cards.why: A smart card is a something-you-have factor, which combined with the existing password (something you know) makes two-factor authentication.

whyNot.A: A PIN (Personal Identification Number) is something you know, the same factor as a password.
whyNot.B: A security question is knowledge-based, the same factor as a password.
whyNot.D: A passphrase is a longer password and is still something you know.
whyNot.E: A CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) tells humans from bots and is not an authentication factor.

cards.front:
A security administrator needs to address the following audit recommendations for a public-facing SFTP server: Users should be restricted to upload and download files to their own home directories only. Users should not be allowed to use interactive shell login. Which of the following configuration parameters should be implemented? (Select TWO).
A. PermitTunnel
B. ChrootDirectory
C. PermitTTY
D. AllowTcpForwarding
E. IgnoreRhosts
cards.why: ChrootDirectory confines each user to their own home directory, and setting PermitTTY to no blocks interactive shell sessions, meeting both audit recommendations for the SFTP (Secure File Transfer Protocol) server.

whyNot.A: PermitTunnel controls whether tun device forwarding is allowed and does not restrict users to directories or block shells.
whyNot.D: AllowTcpForwarding controls TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port forwarding and does not limit directories or shell access.
whyNot.E: IgnoreRhosts controls whether legacy rhosts files are used for authentication and does not address directory restriction or shell login.

cards.front:
An organization recently moved its custom web applications to the cloud, and it is obtaining managed services of the back-end environment as part of its subscription. Which of the following types of services is this company now using?
A. SaaS
B. CASB
C. IaaS
D. PaaS
cards.back:
B. CASB

Security Broker (CASB) gives you both visibility into your entire cloud stack and the security automation tool your IT team needs.
cards.why: The company hosts its own custom web applications while the provider manages the back-end environment, which matches PaaS (Platform as a Service), where the vendor runs the underlying platform.

whyNot.A: SaaS (Software as a Service) delivers a finished application, but this company runs its own custom applications.
whyNot.C: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) leaves the customer managing the operating system and back-end platform, which is not the case here.
whyNot.D: PaaS (Platform as a Service) is actually the best fit, so listing it as a wrong option is a flaw in the key.

cards.keyDoubt: D, because PaaS (Platform as a Service) fits a managed back end for custom applications, while a CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) is a security control, not a service model.

cards.front:
Which of the following is commonly done as part of a vulnerability scan?
A. Exploiting misconfigured applications
B. Cracking employee passwords
C. Sending phishing emails to employees
D. Identifying unpatched workstations
cards.why: A vulnerability scan passively or actively checks systems for known weaknesses, such as missing patches, so identifying unpatched workstations is a standard scan result.

whyNot.A: Exploiting misconfigured applications is penetration testing, which goes beyond a vulnerability scan that only identifies weaknesses.
whyNot.B: Cracking employee passwords is a password audit or attack activity, not part of a vulnerability scan.
whyNot.C: Sending phishing emails to employees is a social engineering simulation, not a vulnerability scan task.

cards.front:
A company is evaluating cloud providers to reduce the cost of its internal IT operations. The company's aging systems are unable to keep up with customer demand. Which of the following cloud models will the company MOST likely select?
A. PaaS
B. SaaS
C. IaaS
D. BaaS
cards.why: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) replaces aging hardware with scalable virtual servers, storage, and networking, reducing cost while letting the company keep control of its systems to meet customer demand.
