cards.back: A. Confiscate the media and dispose of it in a secure manner as per company policy.
cards.why: Unlabeled media of unknown origin may carry malware, so the most immediate safe action is to confiscate it and dispose of it securely under company policy without ever inserting it into a computer.

whyNot.B: Inserting unknown media into a computer risks executing malware and infecting the system, and returning it leaves the threat in place.
whyNot.C: Holding unclaimed media for a month keeps a possible threat on site and delays the immediate response that is needed.
whyNot.D: Copying the disc requires inserting it into a computer, which risks infection, and returning the original leaves the hazard on the desk.

cards.front:
A company has noticed multiple instances of proprietary information on public websites. It has also observed an increase in the number of email messages sent to random employees containing malicious links and PDFs. Which of the following changes should the company make to reduce the risks associated with phishing attacks? (Select TWO)
A. Install an additional firewall
B. Implement a redundant email server
C. Block access to personal email on corporate systems
D. Update the X.509 certificates on the corporate email server
E. Update corporate policy to prohibit access to social media websites
F. Review access violation on the file server
cards.back:
C. Block access to personal email on corporate systems
E. Update corporate policy to prohibit access to social media websites
cards.why: Blocking personal email on corporate systems and prohibiting social media access reduce the channels through which employees receive phishing messages and leak proprietary information publicly.

whyNot.A: An additional firewall filters network traffic by rules and does not stop users from opening malicious links or PDFs (Portable Document Format files) in email.
whyNot.B: A redundant email server improves availability of email and does nothing to reduce phishing risk.
whyNot.D: Updating X.509 certificates on the email server maintains encryption and server identity, but it does not stop malicious messages from reaching users.
whyNot.F: Reviewing access violations on the file server may help investigate the leak, but it does not reduce the phishing messages employees receive.

cards.front:
A security analyst is investigating a potential breach. Upon gathering, documenting, and securing the evidence, which of the following actions is the NEXT step to minimize the business impact?
A. Launch an investigation to identify the attacking host
B. Initiate the incident response plan
C. Review lessons learned captured in the process
D. Remove malware and restore the system to normal operation
cards.back: D. Remove malware and restore the system to normal operation
cards.why: After evidence is gathered and secured, eradication and recovery come next: removing malware and restoring systems returns the business to normal operation and limits ongoing impact.

whyNot.A: Identifying the attacking host is attribution work and does not restore business operations or reduce downtime.
whyNot.B: The IRP (Incident Response Plan) should already have been initiated before evidence was collected, so it is not the next step.
whyNot.C: Lessons learned is the final phase of incident response and happens after eradication and recovery.

cards.front:
Joe, a salesman, was assigned to a new project that requires him to travel to a client site. While waiting for a flight, Joe, decides to connect to the airport wireless network without connecting to a VPN, and the sends confidential emails to fellow colleagues. A few days later, the company experiences a data breach. Upon investigation, the company learns Joe's emails were intercepted. Which of the following MOST likely caused the data breach?
A. Policy violation
B. Social engineering
C. Insider threat
D. Zero-day attack
cards.why: Joe broke the company's policy requiring a VPN (Virtual Private Network) on untrusted public wireless, so a policy violation exposed the emails to interception.

whyNot.B: Social engineering manipulates a person through deception, and no attacker tricked Joe in this scenario.
whyNot.C: An insider threat implies malicious intent or deliberate harm, while Joe acted carelessly without malice.
whyNot.D: A zero-day attack exploits an unknown software vulnerability, and intercepting unencrypted traffic on open wireless needs no such flaw.

cards.front:
A company is performing an analysis of the corporate enterprise network with the intent of identifying what will cause losses in revenue, referrals, and/or reputation when out of commission. Which of the following is an element of a BIA that is being addressed?
A. Mission-essential function
B. Single point of failure
C. backup and restoration plans
D. Identification of critical systems
cards.back:
A. Mission-essential function

The BIA is composed of the following three steps: Determine mission/business processes and recovery criticality.
cards.why: A mission-essential function is a business function whose outage causes losses in revenue, referrals, or reputation, which is what the BIA (Business Impact Analysis) is examining here.

whyNot.B: A single point of failure is a component whose loss stops a service, not the analysis of business losses from an outage.
whyNot.C: Backup and restoration plans are recovery measures, not the identification of what causes business loss when unavailable.
whyNot.D: Identification of critical systems maps functions to technology, whereas the question describes the business functions and their loss impact.

cards.front:
A company wants to ensure confidential data from storage media is sanitized in such a way that the drive cannot be reused. Which of the following method should the technician use?
A. Shredding
B. Wiping
C. Low-level formatting
D. Repartitioning
E. Overwriting
cards.why: Shredding physically destroys the storage media, so data cannot be recovered and the drive cannot be reused, which meets the stated requirement.

whyNot.B: Wiping erases the data but leaves the drive intact and reusable.
whyNot.C: Low-level formatting resets the drive structure, and the drive remains usable afterward.
whyNot.D: Repartitioning only changes the partition table, leaving data recoverable and the drive reusable.
whyNot.E: Overwriting replaces the stored data but the drive remains functional and reusable.

cards.front:
A forensic expert is given a hard drive from a crime scene and is asked to perform an investigation. Which of the following is the FIRST step the forensic expert needs to take the chain of custody?
A. Make a forensic copy
B. Create a hash of the hard rive
C. Recover the hard drive data
D. Update the evidence log
cards.why: Chain of custody begins by documenting receipt of the evidence, so updating the evidence log is the first step before any handling or analysis.

whyNot.A: Making a forensic copy is a handling step that should only occur after custody has been recorded in the evidence log.
whyNot.B: Creating a hash verifies integrity but comes after the evidence receipt is documented in the log.
whyNot.C: Recovering data is analysis work that happens after custody is established and a forensic copy exists.

cards.front:
An incident response manager has started to gather all the facts related to a SIEM alert showing multiple systems may have been compromised. The manager has gathered these facts: The breach is currently indicated on six user PCs One service account is potentially compromised Executive management has been notified In which of the following phases of the IRP is the manager currently working?
A. Recovery
B. Eradication
C. Containment
D. Identification
cards.why: The Identification phase of the IRP (Incident Response Plan) is where the responder confirms an incident and determines its scope, such as affected PCs, accounts, and who has been notified.

whyNot.A: Recovery restores systems to normal operation after eradication, and nothing is being restored yet.
whyNot.B: Eradication removes the threat from systems, but the manager is still gathering facts about scope.
whyNot.C: Containment isolates affected systems to stop spread, but the manager has only collected facts so far.

cards.front:
A stock trading company had the budget for enhancing its secondary datacenter approved. Since the main site is a hurricane-affected area and the disaster recovery site is 100 mi (161 km) away, the company wants to ensure its business is always operational with the least amount of man hours needed. Which of the following types of disaster recovery sites should the company implement?
A. Hot site
B. Warm site
C. Cold site
D. Cloud-based site
cards.why: A cloud-based disaster recovery site is geographically distributed, scales automatically, and is always available with the least staff effort, which fits the always-operational and low man-hours goal.

whyNot.A: A hot site is ready to run but requires staff to maintain duplicate hardware and data, using more man hours than a cloud site.
whyNot.B: A warm site needs staff time and effort to bring systems fully online, so it is not always operational.
whyNot.C: A cold site has only space and power with no equipment, so it takes the longest and most labor to activate.

cards.front:
User from two organizations, each with its own PKI, need to begin working together on a joint project. Which of the following would allow the users of the separate PKIs to work together without connection errors?
A. Trust model
B. Stapling
C. Intermediate CA
D. Key escrow
cards.why: A trust model, such as cross-certification between the two PKIs (Public Key Infrastructures), lets each organization's certificates be trusted by the other and prevents certificate errors.

whyNot.B: OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) stapling delivers revocation status quickly but does not establish trust between separate PKIs.
whyNot.C: An intermediate CA (Certificate Authority) sits inside one hierarchy and does not by itself make two independent PKIs trust each other.
whyNot.D: Key escrow stores copies of keys for recovery and has nothing to do with cross-organization certificate trust.

cards.front:
A security analyst is mitigating a pass-the-hash vulnerability on a Windows infrastructure. Given the requirement, which of the following should the security analyst do to MINIMIZE the risk?
A. Enable CHAP
B. Disable NTLM
C. Enable Kerebos
D. Disable PAP
cards.why: Pass-the-hash abuses captured NTLM (New Technology LAN Manager) password hashes to authenticate, so disabling NTLM removes the mechanism and minimizes the risk.

whyNot.A: CHAP (Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol) is not the Windows hash-based authentication being abused in pass-the-hash.
whyNot.C: Enabling Kerberos alone leaves NTLM available as a fallback, so pass-the-hash attacks remain possible.
whyNot.D: PAP (Password Authentication Protocol) is unrelated to Windows NTLM hashes, so disabling it does not stop pass-the-hash.

cards.front:
A security analyst is reviewing an assessment report that includes software versions, running services, supported encryption algorithms, and permission settings. Which of the following produced the report?
A. Vulnerability scanner
B. Protocol analyzer
C. Network mapper
D. Web inspector
cards.why: A vulnerability scanner reports software versions, running services, supported encryption algorithms, and permission settings while checking systems for known weaknesses.

whyNot.B: A protocol analyzer captures and inspects network packets and does not report installed software versions or permission settings.
whyNot.C: A network mapper discovers hosts and open ports but does not assess permission settings or supported encryption algorithms in depth.
whyNot.D: A web inspector examines page code and requests in a browser and does not produce an assessment of services and permissions.

cards.front:
A Chief Information Officer (CIO) asks the company's security specialist if the company should spend any funds on malware protection for a specific server. Based on a risk assessment, the ARO value of a malware infection for a server is 5 and the annual cost for the malware protection is $2500. Which of the following SLE values warrants a recommendation against purchasing the malware protection?
A. $500
B. $1000
C. $2000
D. $2500
cards.why: ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) equals SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) times ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence). With an ARO of 5, an SLE of $500 gives an ALE of $2500, which does not exceed the $2500 protection cost.

whyNot.B: An SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) of $1000 gives an ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) of $5000, which exceeds the $2500 cost, so buying protection is justified.
whyNot.C: An SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) of $2000 gives an ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) of $10000, far above the $2500 cost, so protection is justified.
whyNot.D: An SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) of $2500 gives an ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) of $12500, far above the cost, so protection is justified.

cards.front:
A recent internal audit is forcing a company to review each internal business unit's VMs because the cluster they are installed on is in danger of running out of computer resources. Which of the following vulnerabilities exist?
A. Buffer overflow
B. End-of-life systems
C. System sprawl
D. Weak configuration
cards.why: System sprawl is the uncontrolled growth of VMs (Virtual Machines) across business units, which consumes cluster resources and leaves unmanaged systems, matching the audit finding.

whyNot.A: A buffer overflow is a memory-handling flaw in software code and does not describe a cluster running out of compute resources.
whyNot.B: End-of-life systems are no longer supported by the vendor, which is unrelated to running low on cluster resources.
whyNot.D: Weak configuration refers to insecure settings, not to excess VMs (Virtual Machines) exhausting cluster capacity.

cards.front:
A security analyst is attempting to identify vulnerabilities in a customer's web application without impacting the system or its data. Which of the following BEST describes the vulnerability scanning concept performed?
A. Aggressive scan
B. Passive scan
C. Non-credentialed scan
D. Compliance scan
cards.back:
B. Passive scan

Passive scanning is a method of vulnerability detection that relies on information gleaned from network data that is captured from a target computer without direct interaction.
cards.why: A passive scan observes traffic and system information without sending probes, so it identifies vulnerabilities without impacting the web application or its data.

whyNot.A: An aggressive scan sends intensive probes and tests that can disrupt the system or alter its data.
whyNot.C: A non-credentialed scan lacks login access but still actively probes the target, so it can still impact the system.
whyNot.D: A compliance scan checks configuration against a standard and does not describe avoiding impact on the system.

cards.front:
Two users must encrypt and transmit large amounts of data between them. Which of the following should they use to encrypt and transmit the data?
A. Symmetric algorithm
B. Hash function
C. Digital signature
D. Obfuscation
cards.why: A symmetric algorithm uses one shared key and is fast, making it the right choice for encrypting large amounts of data between two parties.

whyNot.B: A hash function is one-way and cannot be reversed, so the receiver could never decrypt the data.
whyNot.C: A digital signature proves authenticity and integrity but does not provide confidentiality for bulk data.
whyNot.D: Obfuscation only makes data harder to read and is not strong encryption, so it does not protect transmitted data.

cards.front:
A new Chief Information Officer (CIO) has been reviewing the badging and decides to write a policy that all employees must have their badges rekeyed at least annually. Which of the following controls BEST describes this policy?
A. Physical
B. Corrective
C. Technical
D. Administrative
cards.why: A policy requiring employees to have badges rekeyed annually is a written rule governing behavior and procedure, which makes it an administrative control.

whyNot.A: A physical control is the tangible barrier itself, such as a lock or badge reader, while this item is a policy about it.
whyNot.B: A corrective control repairs damage after an incident, and an annual rekeying policy is not a response to an event.
whyNot.C: A technical control is enforced by technology such as software or hardware logic, and this item is a policy decision.

cards.front:
A software developer is concerned about DLL hijacking in an application being written. Which of the following is the MOST viable mitigation measure of this type of attack?
A. The DLL of each application should be set individually
B. All calls to different DLLs should be hard-coded in the application
C. Access to DLLs from the Windows registry should be disabled
D. The affected DLLs should be renamed to avoid future hijacking
cards.back: B. All calls to different DLLs should be hard-coded in the application
cards.why: Hard-coding the full path to each DLL (Dynamic Link Library) in the application stops Windows from searching other directories, so an attacker cannot plant a malicious DLL earlier in the search order.

whyNot.A: Setting each application's DLL individually is vague and does not control the search path an attacker exploits to load a malicious DLL (Dynamic Link Library).
whyNot.C: Disabling DLL (Dynamic Link Library) access from the Windows registry would break applications and does not address the search-order weakness that hijacking abuses.
whyNot.D: Renaming DLLs (Dynamic Link Libraries) is security through obscurity; an attacker can still place a malicious file with the expected name or discover the new name.

cards.front:
An application was recently compromised after some malformed data came in via web form. Which of the following would MOST likely have prevented this?
A. Input validation
B. Proxy server
C. Stress testing
D. Encoding
cards.why: Input validation checks and rejects malformed or unexpected data before the application processes it, which directly prevents attacks that arrive through web form fields.

whyNot.B: A proxy server filters and forwards traffic but does not validate the content of form fields inside the application's own processing logic.
whyNot.C: Stress testing measures how an application performs under heavy load and does not stop malformed data from being accepted.
whyNot.D: Encoding transforms output so it is rendered safely, but it does not reject malformed input the way input validation does before processing.

cards.front:
While working on an incident, Joe, a technician, finished restoring the OS and applications on a workstation from the original media. Joe is about to begin copying the user's files back onto the hard drive. Which of the following incident response steps is Joe working on now?
A. Recovery
B. Eradication
C. Containment
D. Identification
cards.why: Recovery is the incident response phase where systems are restored to normal operation, including rebuilding from original media and returning user data to the machine.

whyNot.B: Eradication removes the threat, such as malware or attacker access, from the environment; restoring user files comes after that work is already done.
whyNot.C: Containment limits the spread or impact of an incident by isolating affected systems, which happens before rebuilding and restoring data.
whyNot.D: Identification is the phase of detecting and confirming that an incident occurred, which takes place well before restoring a workstation.

cards.front:
A systems administrator found a suspicious file in the root of the file system. The file contains URLs, usernames, passwords, and text from other documents being edited on the system. Which of the following types of malware would generate such a file?
A. Keylogger
B. Rootkit
C. Bot
D. RAT
cards.why: A keylogger records keystrokes, which explains a file holding URLs, usernames, passwords, and text from documents the user was typing or editing.

whyNot.B: A rootkit hides malicious processes and files with privileged access, but its main purpose is concealment rather than capturing typed text into a file.
whyNot.C: A bot (compromised host in a botnet) takes remote commands for tasks like attacks or spam, and does not typically log typed credentials and document text.
whyNot.D: A RAT (Remote Access Trojan) gives an attacker remote control, but the file of captured typed content is characteristic of keylogging functionality.

cards.front:
A computer emergency response team is called at midnight to investigate a case in which a mail server was restarted. After an initial investigation, it was discovered that email is being exfiltrated through an active connection. Which of the following is the NEXT step the team should take?
A. Identify the source of the active connection
B. Perform eradication of active connection and recover
C. Performance containment procedure by disconnecting the server
D. Format the server and restore its initial configuration
cards.back: A. Identify the source of the active connection
cards.why: During an active exfiltration, the team must first identify the source of the connection, which is the identification step of incident response, before choosing containment or eradication actions.

whyNot.B: Eradication and recovery come after the incident is understood and contained, so performing them first would skip scoping and could destroy evidence.
whyNot.C: Disconnecting the server is containment, which follows identification of the connection; acting blindly could lose volatile evidence and miss other compromised systems.
whyNot.D: Formatting and restoring the server destroys forensic evidence and skips identification, containment, and proper eradication, so it is not the next step.

cards.front:
A remote intruder wants to take inventory of a network so exploits can be researched. The intruder is looking for information about software versions on the network. Which of the following techniques is the intruder using?
A. Banner grabbing
B. Port scanning
C. Packet sniffing
D. Virus scanning
cards.why: Banner grabbing retrieves service banners that reveal software names and version numbers, which an intruder can then match against known exploits during reconnaissance.

whyNot.B: Port scanning finds open ports and running services but does not by itself reliably reveal the specific software versions in use.
whyNot.C: Packet sniffing captures traffic passing on a network segment and is passive eavesdropping, not an inventory technique for software versions across the network.
whyNot.D: Virus scanning looks for malware on a system and does not enumerate software versions on remote hosts for exploit research.

cards.front:
A security technician is configuring an access management system to track and record user actions. Which of the following functions should the technician configure?
A. Accounting
B. Authorization
C. Authentication
D. Identification
cards.why: Accounting, the last part of AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting), tracks and records user actions through logging and auditing so activity can be reviewed later.

whyNot.B: Authorization determines which resources and actions an authenticated user is permitted to use, not the recording of what the user did.
whyNot.C: Authentication verifies a user's claimed identity using credentials such as passwords or tokens and does not record the user's later actions.
whyNot.D: Identification is the user claiming an identity, such as providing a username, and does not track or log subsequent activity.

cards.front:
A security administrator installed a new network scanner that identifies new host systems on the network. Which of the following did the security administrator install?
A. Vulnerability scanner
B. Network-based IDS
C. Rogue system detection
D. Configuration compliance scanner
cards.why: Rogue system detection discovers unauthorized or unknown hosts that appear on the network, which matches a scanner built to identify new host systems.

whyNot.A: A vulnerability scanner looks for known weaknesses on hosts it already targets, rather than focusing on detecting new unknown hosts joining the network.
whyNot.B: A NIDS (Network-based Intrusion Detection System) inspects traffic for malicious patterns and does not primarily inventory newly connected host systems.
whyNot.D: A configuration compliance scanner checks whether known systems match a security baseline and does not find new or unauthorized hosts.

cards.front:
A Chief Information Officer (CIO) has decided it is not cost effective to implement safeguards against a known vulnerability. Which of the following risk responses does this BEST describe?
A. Transference
B. Avoidance
C. Mitigation
D. Acceptance
cards.why: Risk acceptance means knowingly taking on a risk without added controls, which fits a decision that safeguards are not cost effective for a known vulnerability.

whyNot.A: Transference shifts the risk to another party, such as through insurance or outsourcing, and nothing in the scenario moves the risk elsewhere.
whyNot.B: Avoidance eliminates the risk by stopping the risky activity altogether, whereas the CIO (Chief Information Officer) is continuing operations with the vulnerability present.
whyNot.C: Mitigation reduces likelihood or impact by implementing safeguards, which the CIO (Chief Information Officer) explicitly decided not to do.

cards.front:
A technician is investigating a potentially compromised device with the following symptoms: Browser slowness Frequent browser crashes Hourglass stuck New search toolbar Increased memory consumption Which of the following types of malware has infected the system?
A. Man-in-the-browser
B. Spoofer
C. Spyware
D. Adware
cards.why: Adware displays unwanted advertisements and installs things like new search toolbars, and it commonly causes browser slowness, crashes, and high memory use.

whyNot.A: A man-in-the-browser attack intercepts and alters web transactions such as banking, and typically stays hidden rather than adding visible toolbars and slowing the browser.
whyNot.B: A spoofer impersonates another identity, address, or system, and does not explain the toolbar and resource-consumption symptoms described.
whyNot.C: Spyware secretly gathers user information and usually tries to remain unnoticed, so it would not typically add a visible new search toolbar.

cards.front:
A penetration tester has written an application that performs a bit-by-bit XOR 0xFF operation on binaries prior to transmission over untrusted media. Which of the following BEST describes the action performed by this type of application?
A. Hashing
B. Key exchange
C. Encryption
D. Obfusication
cards.why: XORing bytes with a fixed value like 0xFF is trivially reversible without a secret key, so it only obscures the data rather than securing it, which is obfuscation.

whyNot.A: Hashing is a one-way function producing a fixed-length digest, whereas an XOR (exclusive OR) with a constant can be directly reversed to recover the original data.
whyNot.B: Key exchange securely establishes a shared secret between parties, such as with Diffie-Hellman, and a fixed XOR operation does not do that.
whyNot.C: Encryption relies on a secret key and a strong algorithm; a fixed XOR (exclusive OR) with 0xFF has no key secrecy and offers no real confidentiality.

cards.front:
An audit reported has identifies a weakness that could allow unauthorized personnel access to the facility at its main entrance and from there gain access to the network. Which of the following would BEST resolve the vulnerability?
A. Faraday cage
B. Air gap
C. Mantrap
D. Bollards
cards.why: A mantrap is an access control vestibule with two interlocking doors that allows only one person through at a time, preventing tailgating at the main entrance.

whyNot.A: A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic signals to prevent wireless eavesdropping or emanation leaks and does not control physical entry by people.
whyNot.B: An air gap isolates a network from other networks physically, which does not stop unauthorized people from walking into the building's entrance.
whyNot.D: Bollards stop vehicles from ramming into a building and do not prevent unauthorized people from entering on foot.

cards.front:
When attempting to secure a mobile workstation, which of the following authentication technologies rely on the user's physical characteristics? (Select TWO)
A. MAC address table
B. Retina scan
C. Fingerprint scan
D. Two-factor authentication
E. CAPTCHA
F. Password string
cards.back:
B. Retina scan
C. Fingerprint scan
cards.why: Retina scans and fingerprint scans are biometric factors, which authenticate users based on physical characteristics, the 'something you are' factor.

whyNot.A: A MAC (Media Access Control) address table maps device addresses to switch ports and is not a user authentication method based on physical traits.
whyNot.D: Two-factor authentication combines two different factor types and is not itself a physical characteristic; it could include non-biometric factors only.
whyNot.E: CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) distinguishes humans from bots and does not authenticate a user by physical characteristics.
whyNot.F: A password string is something you know, a knowledge factor, and not a physical characteristic of the user.

cards.front:
Systems administrator and key support staff come together to simulate a hypothetical interruption of service. The team updates the disaster recovery processes and documentation after meeting. Which of the following describes the team's efforts?
A. Business impact analysis
B. Continuity of operation
C. Tabletop exercise
D. Order of restoration
cards.why: A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based simulation where staff walk through a hypothetical disruption and then update the disaster recovery plan and documentation.

whyNot.A: A BIA (Business Impact Analysis) identifies critical functions and the impact of their loss, and is not a group simulation of an interruption.
whyNot.B: Continuity of operations is the broader planning goal of keeping essential functions running, not the specific act of simulating an event in a meeting.
whyNot.D: Order of restoration defines the sequence in which systems are brought back online and is not a simulated exercise by the team.

cards.front:
A company has two wireless networks utilizing captive portals. Some employees report getting a trust error in their browsers when connecting to one of the networks. Both captive portals are using the same server certificate for authentication, but the analyst notices the following differences between the two certificate details: Certificate 1 Certificate Path: Geotrust Global CA *company.com Certificate 2 Certificate Path: *company.com Which of the following would resolve the problem?
A. Use a wildcard certificate.
B. Use certificate chaining.
C. Use a trust model.
D. Use an extended validation certificate.
cards.why: Certificate 1 includes the intermediate Geotrust CA in its path while Certificate 2 lacks it, so certificate chaining, which installs the full chain on the server, lets browsers validate trust.

whyNot.A: Both portals already use the same wildcard certificate for *company.com, so a wildcard certificate does not address the missing intermediate CA (Certificate Authority) in one path.
whyNot.C: A trust model describes how trust is structured among certificate authorities in general and is not a specific fix for a server missing its intermediate certificate.
whyNot.D: An EV (Extended Validation) certificate changes the identity vetting level and does not fix a missing intermediate certificate causing browser trust errors.

cards.front:
Company A has acquired Company B. Company A has different domains spread globally, and typically migrates its acquisitions infrastructure under its own domain infrastructure. Company B, however, cannot be merged into Company A's domain infrastructure. Which of the following methods would allow the two companies to access one another's resources?
A. Attestation
B. Federation
C. Single sign-on
D. Kerberos
cards.why: Federation (a trust relationship between separate identity systems) lets two organizations keep independent domains while still accepting each other's authentication, so users can reach resources across both companies.

whyNot.A: Attestation (proving a system's state or identity) does not establish cross-domain authentication between two separate organizations.
whyNot.C: SSO (Single Sign-On) reduces repeated logins within one trust realm and does not by itself join two unmergeable domains.
whyNot.D: Kerberos is an authentication protocol that operates within or between Kerberos realms and is not the cross-organization trust method asked about.

cards.front:
A technician is configuring a load balancer for the application team to accelerate the network performance of their applications. The applications are hosted on multiple servers and must be redundant. Given this scenario, which of the following would be the BEST method of configuring the load balancer?
A. Round-robin
B. Weighted
C. Least connection
D. Locality-based
cards.why: Locality-based load balancing sends each request to the server closest to the client, which reduces latency and speeds up application performance while still spreading traffic across multiple redundant servers.

whyNot.A: Round-robin rotates through servers in order without considering distance or speed, so it does not specifically accelerate network performance.
whyNot.B: Weighted balancing favors servers by assigned capacity, which helps uneven hardware but does not target network proximity or performance.
whyNot.C: Least connection sends traffic to the server with the fewest active sessions, which balances load rather than shortening the network path.

cards.front:
An organization's employees currently use three different sets of credentials to access multiple internal resources. Management wants to make this process less complex. Which of the following would be the BEST option to meet this goal?
A. Transitive trust
B. Single sign-on
C. Federation
D. Secure token
cards.why: SSO (Single Sign-On) lets users authenticate once and access multiple internal resources, replacing three separate sets of credentials with one and making the process less complex.

whyNot.A: Transitive trust extends trust between domains automatically but does not reduce the number of credentials a user must manage.
whyNot.C: Federation links identities across separate organizations, which is more than needed for internal resources within one company.
whyNot.D: A secure token is a single authentication factor or device and does not consolidate multiple credential sets by itself.

cards.front:
An external attacker can modify the ARP cache of an internal computer. Which of the following types of attacks is described?
A. Replay
B. Spoofing
C. DNS poisoning
D. Client-side attack
cards.why: Modifying a computer's ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache with false address mappings is ARP spoofing (also called poisoning), where the attacker impersonates another host on the local network.

whyNot.A: A replay attack resends previously captured valid traffic and does not alter an ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache.
whyNot.C: DNS (Domain Name System) poisoning corrupts name-to-address records in DNS caches, not ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) caches.
whyNot.D: A client-side attack exploits software on the user's device, such as a browser, and does not describe forging ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) entries.

cards.front:
A systems administrator has isolated an infected system from the network and terminated the malicious process from executing. Which of the following should the administrator do NEXT according to the incident response process?
A. Restore lost data from a backup.
B. Wipe the system.
C. Document the lessons learned.
D. Determine the scope of impact.
cards.back: A. Restore lost data from a backup.
cards.why: After containment (isolating the system) and eradication (terminating the malicious process), the incident response process moves to recovery, which includes restoring lost data from a backup.

whyNot.B: Wiping the system is a heavier eradication step and is not the next stage once the malicious process has already been stopped.
whyNot.C: Documenting lessons learned is the final phase of incident response and happens after recovery is complete.
whyNot.D: Determining the scope of impact belongs to the earlier identification and analysis phase, which precedes containment and eradication.

cards.front:
A new security administrator ran a vulnerability scanner for the first time and caused a system outage. Which of the following types of scans MOST likely caused the outage?
A. Non-intrusive credentialed scan
B. Non-intrusive non-credentialed scan
C. Intrusive credentialed scan
D. Intrusive non-credentialed scan
cards.why: An intrusive scan actively tests vulnerabilities and can crash services, and a non-credentialed scan probes from outside without login access, so an intrusive non-credentialed scan is most likely to cause an outage.

whyNot.A: A non-intrusive credentialed scan only reads configuration with valid logins and does not exploit anything, so it rarely disrupts systems.
whyNot.B: A non-intrusive non-credentialed scan only observes exposed services without exploiting them, so it is unlikely to crash a system.
whyNot.C: An intrusive credentialed scan can cause disruption, but credentials let it gather information directly, making it less likely than an uncredentialed intrusive scan to trigger crashes.

cards.front:
A security analyst is hardening a WiFi infrastructure. The primary requirements are the following: The infrastructure must allow staff to authenticate using the most secure method. The infrastructure must allow guests to use an "open" WiFi network that logs valid email addresses before granting access to the Internet. Given these requirements, which of the following statements BEST represents what the analyst should recommend and configure?
A. Configure a captive portal for guests and WPS for staff.
B. Configure a captive portal for staff and WPA for guests.
C. Configure a captive portal for staff and WEP for guests.
D. Configure a captive portal for guest and WPA2 Enterprise for staff
cards.back: D. Configure a captive portal for guest and WPA2 Enterprise for staff
cards.why: A captive portal can collect and log guest email addresses on an open network, and WPA2 Enterprise (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 with 802.1X authentication) is the most secure of the listed methods for staff.

whyNot.A: WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) uses a weak PIN-based process and is not the most secure staff authentication method.
whyNot.B: A captive portal is not a secure staff authentication method, and WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) on guests conflicts with the open network requirement.
whyNot.C: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) is broken and insecure, and an open guest network should not use it.

cards.front:
A security administrator is trying to eradicate a worm, which is spreading throughout the organization, using an old remote vulnerability in the SMB protocol. The worm uses Nmap to identify target hosts within the company. The administrator wants to implement a solution that will eradicate the current worm and any future attacks that may be using zero-day vulnerabilities. Which of the following would BEST meet the requirements when implemented?
A. Host-based firewall
B. Enterprise patch management system
C. Network-based intrusion prevention system
D. Application blacklisting
E. File integrity checking
cards.why: A NIPS (Network-based Intrusion Prevention System) can block worm traffic inline, including exploits of unknown zero-day vulnerabilities through anomaly detection, and stops spreading across the network.

whyNot.A: A host-based firewall protects only the individual host it runs on and would need configuration on every system to stop the worm.
whyNot.B: Enterprise patch management fixes known vulnerabilities such as the old SMB (Server Message Block) flaw but cannot protect against future zero-day vulnerabilities.
whyNot.D: Application blacklisting blocks known bad programs and does not stop network-based exploitation or unknown zero-day attacks.
whyNot.E: File integrity checking detects changes to files after the fact and neither eradicates the worm nor prevents zero-day exploitation.

cards.front:
Which of the following is a deployment concept that can be used to ensure only the required OS access is exposed to software applications?
A. Staging environment
B. Sandboxing
C. Secure baseline
D. Trusted OS
cards.why: Sandboxing runs applications in an isolated environment with limited access, so software only gets the OS (Operating System) resources it needs and cannot affect the wider system.

whyNot.A: A staging environment is a pre-production copy used for testing releases and does not restrict which OS (Operating System) access an application gets.
whyNot.C: A secure baseline is a standard hardened configuration and does not isolate an application's access to the OS (Operating System).
whyNot.D: A trusted OS (Operating System) enforces strong access controls system-wide, but it is not a deployment concept for exposing only required access to an application.

cards.front:
A procedure differs from a policy in that it:
A. is a high-level statement regarding the company's position on a topic.
B. sets a minimum expected baseline of behavior.
C. provides step-by-step instructions for performing a task.
D. describes adverse actions when violations occur.
cards.back: C. provides step-by-step instructions for performing a task.
cards.why: A procedure is a detailed, step-by-step set of instructions for carrying out a specific task, whereas a policy states high-level management direction.

whyNot.A: A high-level statement of the company's position on a topic describes a policy, not a procedure.
whyNot.B: Setting a minimum expected baseline of behavior describes a standard or baseline, not a procedure.
whyNot.D: Describing adverse actions for violations describes the enforcement or sanctions portion of a policy, not a procedure.

cards.front:
Ann, a user, reports she is unable to access an application from her desktop. A security analyst verifies Ann's access and checks the SIEM for any errors. The security analyst reviews the log file from Ann's system and notices the following output: Which of the following is MOST likely preventing Ann from accessing the application from the desktop?
A. Web application firewall
B. DLP
C. Host-based firewall
D. UTM
E. Network-based firewall
cards.why: The log comes from Ann's own desktop and the user's access was verified, so a host-based firewall on that machine is the most likely control blocking the application's traffic.

whyNot.A: A WAF (Web Application Firewall) protects web servers and would not appear in a log from Ann's desktop.
whyNot.B: DLP (Data Loss Prevention) blocks sensitive data leaving the organization and does not typically prevent a user from reaching an application.
whyNot.D: A UTM (Unified Threat Management) device is a network appliance, so its blocks would be logged on that device and not on Ann's desktop.
whyNot.E: A network-based firewall logs on the network device, not in a log file from Ann's own system.

cards.front:
Which of the following types of penetration test will allow the tester to have access only to password hashes prior to the penetration test?
A. Black box
B. Gray box
C. Credentialed
D. White box
cards.why: A gray box penetration test gives the tester partial knowledge, such as password hashes, before testing begins, which sits between no knowledge and full knowledge.

whyNot.A: A black box test gives the tester no prior information, so the tester would not have password hashes in advance.
whyNot.C: A credentialed test uses valid login accounts, which is more than only password hashes and describes access level rather than knowledge level.
whyNot.D: A white box test gives the tester full knowledge of the environment, which is more than access to password hashes alone.

cards.front:
Which of the following threats has sufficient knowledge to cause the MOST danger to an organization?
A. Competitors
B. Insiders
C. Hacktivists
D. Script kiddies
cards.why: Insiders already have legitimate access and detailed knowledge of systems, data, and security controls, so they can cause the most damage to an organization.

whyNot.A: Competitors are external and usually lack detailed internal knowledge unless they recruit an insider.
whyNot.C: Hacktivists are motivated by ideology and typically attack from outside with limited knowledge of internal systems.
whyNot.D: Script kiddies use prebuilt tools with little technical understanding, so they have the least knowledge and capability.

cards.front:
While troubleshooting a client application connecting to the network, the security administrator notices the following error: Certificate is not valid. Which of the following is the BEST way to check if the digital certificate is valid?
A. PKI
B. CRL
C. CSR
D. IPSec
cards.why: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) published by the certificate authority lists revoked certificates, so checking it shows whether a certificate is still valid or has been revoked.

whyNot.A: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is the overall framework for managing certificates and is not itself the way to check one certificate's validity.
whyNot.C: A CSR (Certificate Signing Request) is submitted to request a new certificate and does not verify an existing one.
whyNot.D: IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) encrypts and authenticates network traffic and does not check certificate validity.

cards.front:
A business sector is highly competitive, and safeguarding trade secrets and critical information is paramount. On a seasonal basis, an organization employs temporary hires and contractor personnel to accomplish its mission objectives. The temporary and contract personnel require access to network resources only when on the clock. Which of the following account management practices are the BEST ways to manage these accounts?
A. Employ time-of-day restrictions.
B. Employ password complexity.
C. Employ a random key generator strategy.
D. Employ an account expiration strategy.
E. Employ a password lockout policy
cards.why: Time-of-day restrictions limit logins to the hours personnel are on the clock, reducing exposure of trade secrets by blocking access outside scheduled work times.

whyNot.B: Password complexity strengthens passwords but does not limit when temporary and contract personnel can access network resources.
whyNot.C: A random key generator strategy creates unpredictable keys and does not restrict access to working hours.
whyNot.D: Account expiration disables accounts on a set end date, but it does not stop access outside daily working hours.
whyNot.E: A password lockout policy blocks accounts after failed attempts and does not control when users may log in.

cards.front:
Which of the following locations contain the MOST volatile data?
A. SSD
B. Paging file
C. RAM
D. Cache memory
cards.why: Cache memory sits closest to the CPU (Central Processing Unit) and loses its contents the instant power is removed, so it is the most volatile item in the order of volatility.

whyNot.A: An SSD (Solid State Drive) is non-volatile storage and keeps its data without power.
whyNot.B: A paging file lives on disk and persists across power loss, so it is less volatile than cache memory.
whyNot.C: RAM (Random Access Memory) is volatile, but data in CPU cache is lost even faster, so RAM is not the most volatile.

cards.front:
Ann, a customer, is reporting that several important files are missing from her workstation. She recently received communication from an unknown party who is requesting funds to restore the files. Which of the following attacks has occurred?
A. Ransomware
B. Keylogger
C. Buffer overflow
D. Rootkit
cards.why: Missing files combined with a demand for payment to restore them is the signature of ransomware, which encrypts or locks data and extorts the victim.

whyNot.B: A keylogger records keystrokes to steal information and does not remove files or demand payment.
whyNot.C: A buffer overflow is a memory-corruption exploit and does not itself produce a ransom demand.
whyNot.D: A rootkit hides malicious activity at a deep level of the OS (Operating System) and is not tied to extortion for file recovery.

cards.front:
Every morning, a systems administrator monitors failed login attempts on the company's log management server. The administrator notices the DBAdmin account has five failed username and/or password alerts during a ten-minute window. The systems administrator determines the user account is a dummy account used to attract attackers. Which of the following techniques should the systems administrator implement?
A. Role-based access control
B. Honeypot
C. Rule-based access control
D. Password cracker
cards.why: A dummy account that exists only to attract attackers is a honeypot (or honeytoken) decoy, and failed logins against it reveal attacker activity.

whyNot.A: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) assigns permissions by job role and does not lure attackers.
whyNot.C: Rule-based access control applies fixed rules such as time-of-day limits and is not a decoy.
whyNot.D: A password cracker is an attacker tool for recovering passwords and is not a defensive decoy.

cards.front:
Joe, a user, has been trying to send Ann, a different user, an encrypted document via email. Ann has not received the attachment but is able to receive the header information. Which of the following is MOST likely preventing Ann from receiving the encrypted file?
A. Unencrypted credentials
B. Authentication issues
C. Weak cipher suite
D. Permission issues
cards.why: The message header arrives but the encrypted attachment does not, which suggests Ann cannot be authenticated or validated to receive or decrypt the protected content.

whyNot.A: Unencrypted credentials would expose passwords but would not block delivery of an attachment.
whyNot.C: A weak cipher suite reduces encryption strength and does not stop a file from being delivered.
whyNot.D: Permission issues affect file or folder access on a system, which is less likely to block an email attachment in transit.

cards.front:
A systems administrator is configuring a system that uses data classification labels. Which of the following will the administrator need to implement to enforce access control?
A. Discretionary access control
B. Mandatory access control
C. Role-based access control
D. Rule-based access control
cards.why: MAC (Mandatory Access Control) enforces access by comparing data classification labels, such as Confidential or Secret, against user clearance levels set by the system.

whyNot.A: DAC (Discretionary Access Control) lets the data owner grant access and does not depend on classification labels.
whyNot.C: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) grants access by job role, not by data classification label.
whyNot.D: Rule-based access control applies administrator-defined rules such as time or location limits and does not use classification labels.

cards.front:
An analyst is using a vulnerability scanner to look for common security misconfigurations on devices. Which of the following might be identified by the scanner? (Select TWO).
A. The firewall is disabled on workstations.
B. SSH is enabled on servers.
C. Browser homepages have not been customized.
D. Default administrator credentials exist on networking hardware.
E. The OS is only set to check for updates once a day.
cards.back:
A. The firewall is disabled on workstations.
B. SSH is enabled on servers.
cards.why: A vulnerability scanner checks configuration against a baseline, so a disabled firewall on workstations is a typical misconfiguration finding.

whyNot.C: Browser homepages are cosmetic preferences and not a security misconfiguration a scanner would flag.
whyNot.D: Default administrator credentials are a classic misconfiguration finding, so this is arguably correct even though the key omits it.
whyNot.E: Checking for updates once a day is an acceptable setting and not a security misconfiguration.

cards.keyDoubt: D: Default administrator credentials on networking hardware are a textbook scanner misconfiguration finding, while SSH (Secure Shell) being enabled on servers is normal and not inherently a misconfiguration.

cards.front:
A security analyst is reviewing patches on servers. One of the servers is reporting the following error message in the WSUS management console: The computer has not reported status in 30 days. Given this scenario, which of the following statements BEST represents the issue with the output above?
A. The computer in question has not pulled the latest ACL policies for the firewall.
B. The computer in question has not pulled the latest GPO policies from the management server.
C. The computer in question has not pulled the latest antivirus definitions from the antivirus program.
D. The computer in question has not pulled the latest application software updates.
cards.back: D. The computer in question has not pulled the latest application software updates.
cards.why: WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) distributes operating system and Microsoft application patches, so a client that has not reported in 30 days has not pulled the latest updates.

whyNot.A: ACL (Access Control List) firewall rules are not delivered or tracked through WSUS (Windows Server Update Services).
whyNot.B: GPO (Group Policy Object) settings come from Active Directory, not from the WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) status report.
whyNot.C: Antivirus definitions are normally updated by the antivirus vendor's own management console, not by WSUS (Windows Server Update Services).

cards.front:
A security administrator is reviewing the following PowerShell script referenced in the Task Scheduler on a database server: Which of the following did the security administrator discover?
A. Ransomeware
B. Backdoor
C. Logic bomb
D. Trojan
cards.why: A script scheduled in Task Scheduler on a database server that performs a harmful action at a set time or condition is a logic bomb, malicious code triggered by an event.

whyNot.A: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, which a scheduled trigger script alone does not indicate.
whyNot.B: A backdoor provides hidden remote access and is not defined by a scheduled trigger.
whyNot.D: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software to get installed, which is not what a scheduled script shows.

cards.front:
A bank is experiencing a DoS attack against an application designed to handle 500 IP-based sessions. in addition, the perimeter router can only handle 1Gbps of traffic. Which of the following should be implemented to prevent a DoS attacks in the future?
A. Deploy multiple web servers and implement a load balancer
B. Increase the capacity of the perimeter router to 10 Gbps
C. Install a firewall at the network to prevent all attacks
D. Use redundancy across all network devices and services
cards.back: D. Use redundancy across all network devices and services
cards.why: Redundancy across all network devices and services removes single points of failure, such as the 1 Gbps (gigabit per second) router and the session-limited application, so DoS (Denial of Service) load does not take everything down.

whyNot.A: Web servers with a load balancer help the application but leave the router as a single point of failure.
whyNot.B: Raising the router to 10 Gbps (gigabits per second) only moves the bottleneck and leaves the application session limit unaddressed.
whyNot.C: A firewall cannot prevent all attacks, and a DoS (Denial of Service) flood can still overwhelm it.

cards.front:
A malicious system continuously sends an extremely large number of SYN packets to a server. Which of the following BEST describes the resulting effect?
A. The server will be unable to server clients due to lack of bandwidth
B. The server's firewall will be unable to effectively filter traffic due to the amount of data transmitted
C. The server will crash when trying to reassemble all the fragmented packets
D. The server will exhaust its memory maintaining half-open connections
cards.back: D. The server will exhaust its memory maintaining half-open connections
cards.why: A SYN (Synchronize) flood leaves many half-open TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections waiting for the final ACK (Acknowledgment), which exhausts the server's connection table and memory.

whyNot.A: SYN (Synchronize) packets are small, and the damage comes from half-open state rather than bandwidth consumption.
whyNot.B: The firewall is not the main target, and the attack works by exhausting server connection resources.
whyNot.C: SYN (Synchronize) floods do not involve fragmented packets that must be reassembled.

cards.front:
A systems administrator is deploying a new mission essential server into a virtual environment. Which of the following is BEST mitigated by the environment's rapid elasticity characteristic?
A. Data confidentiality breaches
B. VM escape attacks
C. Lack of redundancy
D. Denial of service
cards.why: Rapid elasticity lets a cloud or virtual environment quickly add resources under heavy load, which absorbs traffic spikes and mitigates DoS (Denial of Service) conditions.

whyNot.A: Elasticity scales resources and does not protect the confidentiality of data.
whyNot.B: A VM (Virtual Machine) escape is a hypervisor vulnerability issue, which elasticity does not address.
whyNot.C: Redundancy comes from replication and failover design, not from elasticity, which only adds or removes capacity.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the proper order for logging a user into a system from the first step to the last step?
A. Identification, authentication, authorization
B. Identification, authorization, authentication
C. Authentication, identification, authorization
D. Authentication, identification, authorization
E. Authorization, identification, authentication
cards.why: Login proceeds by identification (claiming an identity), then authentication (proving it), and finally authorization (granting permissions).

whyNot.B: Authorization cannot come before authentication because permissions require a verified identity.
whyNot.C: Authentication cannot come before identification because there must be a claimed identity to verify.
whyNot.D: This repeats option C and has the same wrong order, with authentication before identification.
whyNot.E: Authorization comes last, since access rights are granted only after identity is proven.

cards.front:
A company stores highly sensitive data files used by the accounting system on a server file share. The accounting system uses a service account named accounting-svc to access the file share. The data is protected will a full disk encryption, and the permissions are set as follows: File system permissions: Users = Read Only Share permission: accounting-svc = Read Only Given the listed protections are in place and unchanged, to which of the following risks is the data still subject?
A. Exploitation of local console access and removal of data
B. Theft of physical hard drives and a breach of confidentiality
C. Remote exfiltration of data using domain credentials
D. Disclosure of sensitive data to third parties due to excessive share permissions
cards.back: A. Exploitation of local console access and removal of data
cards.why: Full disk encryption protects data at rest only when the drive is offline, so someone with local console access to the running server can read and copy the decrypted data.

whyNot.B: Full disk encryption specifically protects against stolen physical drives, so this risk is mitigated.
whyNot.C: Remote access is limited by the Read Only share permission for accounting-svc, and the question stresses local risk.
whyNot.D: The share permissions are restrictive, with only a single service account having Read Only access, so excess exposure is not the main risk.

cards.front:
A bank uses a wireless network to transmit credit card purchases to a billing system. Which of the following would be MOST appropriate to protect credit card information from being accessed by unauthorized individuals outside of the premises?
A. Air gap
B. Infrared detection
C. Faraday cage
D. Protected distributions
cards.why: A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic signals from leaving the premises, which stops outsiders from capturing wireless transmissions of credit card data.

whyNot.A: An air gap isolates a network physically and would not allow a wireless network to function.
whyNot.B: Infrared detection senses heat or light and does not stop radio signals from leaking.
whyNot.D: Protected distribution secures physical cabling, not wireless transmissions.

cards.front:
A help desk technician receives a phone call from an individual claiming to be an employee of the organization and requesting assistance to access a locked account. The help desk technician asks the individual to provide proof of identity before access can be granted. Which of the following types of attack is the caller performing?
A. Phishing
B. Shoulder surfing
C. Impersonation
D. Dumpster diving
cards.why: The caller falsely claims to be an employee to gain access to an account, which is impersonation, a social engineering technique that exploits trust.

whyNot.A: Phishing uses deceptive email or messages at scale, and this is a direct phone call.
whyNot.B: Shoulder surfing means watching someone enter sensitive information in person.
whyNot.D: Dumpster diving means searching discarded materials for sensitive information.

cards.front:
Confidential emails from an organization were posted to a website without the organization's knowledge. Upon investigation, it was determined that the emails were obtained from an internal actor who sniffed the emails in plain text. Which of the following protocols, if properly implemented, would have MOST likely prevented the emails from being sniffed? (Select TWO)
A. Secure IMAP
B. DNSSEC
C. S/MIME
D. SMTPS
E. HTTPS
cards.why: S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) encrypts the message body end to end, and SMTPS (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts mail in transit, so a sniffer would see only ciphertext instead of plain text.

whyNot.A: Secure IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) also protects mail retrieval in transit, but it was not one of the two keyed answers and does not protect messages sent between servers.
whyNot.B: DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) signs DNS records to prove authenticity but does not encrypt email content, so sniffed emails would still be readable.
whyNot.E: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) protects web traffic, not email protocols such as SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), so it would not stop email sniffing.

cards.front:
A company wants to implement an access management solution that allows employees to use the same usernames and passwords for multiple applications without having to keep multiple credentials synchronized. Which of the following solutions would BEST meet these requirements?
A. Multifactor authentication
B. SSO
C. Biometrics
D. PKI
E. Federation
cards.why: SSO (Single Sign-On) lets a user authenticate once and use the same credentials across multiple applications without keeping separate credentials synchronized.

whyNot.A: MFA (Multifactor Authentication) adds extra proof of identity but does not let one set of credentials work across multiple applications.
whyNot.C: Biometrics verify identity using physical traits, but they do not provide one credential set shared across applications.
whyNot.D: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) manages certificates and keys, and it is not designed to let users reuse one username and password across applications.
whyNot.E: Federation shares identity across separate organizations or domains, which is broader than the single-organization need for one set of credentials.

cards.front:
An external auditor visits the human resources department and performs a physical security assessment. The auditor observed documents on printers that are unclaimed. A closer look at these documents reveals employee names, addresses, ages, and types of medical and dental coverage options each employee has selected. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate actions to take?
A. Flip the documents face down so no one knows these documents are PII sensitive
B. Shred the documents and let the owner print the new set
C. Retrieve the documents, label them with a PII cover sheet, and return them to the printer
D. Report to the human resources manager that their personnel are violating a privacy policy
cards.back: D. Report to the human resources manager that their personnel are violating a privacy policy
cards.why: Unclaimed printouts containing PII (Personally Identifiable Information) and medical data are a privacy policy violation, so reporting it to the human resources manager lets the owner fix the process and address the exposure.

whyNot.A: Flipping documents face down only hides them briefly and leaves sensitive PII (Personally Identifiable Information) exposed and unaddressed.
whyNot.B: Shredding the documents destroys them without reporting the violation, and it does not fix the underlying policy failure.
whyNot.C: Adding a PII (Personally Identifiable Information) cover sheet and returning the documents to the printer leaves the sensitive data unattended and exposed.

cards.front:
Which of the following authentication concepts is a gait analysis MOST closely associated?
A. Somewhere you are
B. Something you are
C. Something you do
D. Something you know
cards.why: Gait analysis measures how a person walks, which is a behavior, so it falls under the something you do authentication factor.

whyNot.A: Somewhere you are relies on location, such as GPS (Global Positioning System) or network address, not on how a person moves.
whyNot.B: Something you are covers static physical traits such as fingerprints or retina patterns, while gait is a learned behavior.
whyNot.D: Something you know covers secrets such as passwords or PINs (Personal Identification Numbers), which gait does not involve.

cards.front:
Which of the following metrics are used to calculate the SLE? (Select TWO)
A. ROI
B. ARO
C. ALE
D. MTBF
E. MTTF
F. TCO
cards.why: SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) is asset value times exposure factor, and it relates to ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) and ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) because ALE equals SLE times ARO, so SLE equals ALE divided by ARO.

whyNot.A: ROI (Return on Investment) measures the financial benefit of a purchase and is not used to calculate SLE (Single Loss Expectancy).
whyNot.D: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) measures reliability of repairable systems and is not an input to SLE (Single Loss Expectancy).
whyNot.E: MTTF (Mean Time To Failure) measures expected lifespan of non-repairable items and is not an input to SLE (Single Loss Expectancy).
whyNot.F: TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) measures lifetime cost of an asset and is not used to calculate SLE (Single Loss Expectancy).

cards.front:
Due to regulatory requirements, server in a global organization must use time synchronization. Which of the following represents the MOST secure method of time synchronization?
A. The server should connect to external Stratum 0 NTP servers for synchronization
B. The server should connect to internal Stratum 0 NTP servers for synchronization
C. The server should connect to external Stratum 1 NTP servers for synchronization
D. The server should connect to external Stratum 1 NTP servers for synchronization
cards.back: B. The server should connect to internal Stratum 0 NTP servers for synchronization
cards.why: Using an internal Stratum 0 NTP (Network Time Protocol) source keeps time synchronization inside the organization, so it avoids exposure to spoofed or tampered external time sources.

whyNot.A: External Stratum 0 NTP (Network Time Protocol) sources are not reachable over the network, and relying on external sources exposes the servers to spoofing.
whyNot.C: External Stratum 1 NTP (Network Time Protocol) servers depend on outside sources over the internet, which is less secure than an internal reference clock.
whyNot.D: External Stratum 1 NTP (Network Time Protocol) servers depend on outside sources over the internet, which is less secure than an internal reference clock.

cards.front:
When sending messages using symmetric encryption, which of the following must happen FIRST?
A. Exchange encryption key
B. Establish digital signatures
C. Agree on an encryption method
D. Install digital certificates
cards.back: C. Agree on an encryption method
cards.why: Both parties must first agree on which encryption method, such as the algorithm, they will use before they can exchange keys or send encrypted messages.

whyNot.A: Exchanging the encryption key comes after the parties agree on the method, because the key format depends on the chosen algorithm.
whyNot.B: Digital signatures provide authenticity and non-repudiation, and they are not required before symmetric encryption can begin.
whyNot.D: Digital certificates support asymmetric encryption and identity validation, and they are not required to start symmetric encryption.

cards.front:
Which of the following scenarios BEST describes an implementation of non-repudiation?
A. A user logs into a domain workstation and access network file shares for another department
B. A user remotely logs into the mail server with another user's credentials
C. A user sends a digitally signed email to the entire finance department about an upcoming meeting
D. A user access the workstation registry to make unauthorized changes to enable functionality within an application
cards.back: C. A user sends a digitally signed email to the entire finance department about an upcoming meeting
cards.why: A digitally signed email proves who sent it and that it was not altered, so the sender cannot later deny sending it, which is non-repudiation.

whyNot.A: Logging into a workstation and accessing file shares shows authentication and access, and it does not prove who sent or approved an action.
whyNot.B: Using another user's credentials is impersonation, which undermines non-repudiation because actions cannot be tied to the true person.
whyNot.D: Making unauthorized registry changes is a policy violation and does not provide proof of origin or prevent denial.

cards.front:
An office manager found a folder that included documents with various types of data relating to corporate clients. The office manager notified the data included dates of birth, addresses, and phone numbers for the clients. The office manager then reported this finding to the security compliance officer. Which of the following portions of the policy would the security officer need to consult to determine if a breach has occurred?
A. Public
B. Private
C. PHI
D. PII
cards.why: Dates of birth, addresses, and phone numbers are PII (Personally Identifiable Information), so the officer should consult the PII portion of the policy to decide whether a breach occurred.

whyNot.A: Public data is intended for open release, and client dates of birth and addresses are not public information.
whyNot.B: Private is a general classification label and does not specifically address personal identifiers that trigger breach rules.
whyNot.C: PHI (Protected Health Information) covers health-related data, and the folder contained no medical details.

cards.front:
Which of the following is an asymmetric function that generates a new and separate key every time it runs?
A. RSA
B. DSA
C. DHE
D. HMAC
E. PBKDF2
cards.why: DHE (Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral) is an asymmetric key exchange that generates a new, separate key pair for each session, which provides forward secrecy.

whyNot.A: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) uses a long-term key pair and does not generate a new separate key every time it runs.
whyNot.B: DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) creates digital signatures using a long-term key pair, not a fresh key each time.
whyNot.D: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) is a symmetric integrity function that uses a shared key and does not generate new keys.
whyNot.E: PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) stretches passwords into keys and is not an asymmetric function.

cards.front:
Which of the following would be considered multifactor authentication?
A. Hardware token and smart card
B. Voice recognition and retina scan
C. Strong password and fingerprint
D. PIN and security questions
cards.why: A strong password is something you know and a fingerprint is something you are, so together they combine two different authentication factors.

whyNot.A: A hardware token and a smart card are both something you have, so they are the same factor.
whyNot.B: Voice recognition and a retina scan are both something you are, so they are the same factor.
whyNot.D: A PIN (Personal Identification Number) and security questions are both something you know, so they are the same factor.

cards.front:
A user receives an email from ISP indicating malicious traffic coming from the user's home network is detected. The traffic appears to be Linux-based, and it is targeting a website that was recently featured on the news as being taken offline by an Internet attack. The only Linux device on the network is a home surveillance camera system. Which of the following BEST describes what is happening?
A. The camera system is infected with a bot.
B. The camera system is infected with a RAT.
C. The camera system is infected with a Trojan.
D. The camera system is infected with a backdoor.
cards.back: A. The camera system is infected with a bot.
cards.why: A bot is a compromised device controlled remotely to join a botnet, and a hacked surveillance camera sending attack traffic at a website matches a botnet used for a DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack.

whyNot.B: A RAT (Remote Access Trojan) gives an attacker remote control of a device, but the scenario describes coordinated attack traffic typical of a bot.
whyNot.C: A Trojan is malware disguised as legitimate software, and that does not specifically explain participation in an attack on another website.
whyNot.D: A backdoor is a hidden way to bypass authentication, and it does not itself describe the camera sending attack traffic.

cards.front:
A security auditor is testing perimeter security in a building that is protected by badge readers. Which of the following types of attacks would MOST likely gain access?
A. Phishing
B. Man-in-the-middle
C. Tailgating
D. Watering hole
E. Shoulder surfing
cards.why: Tailgating means following an authorized person through a badge-controlled door without presenting a badge, which directly bypasses badge readers.

whyNot.A: Phishing uses deceptive messages to steal information and does not defeat a physical badge reader.
whyNot.B: A man-in-the-middle attack intercepts network communication and does not help someone get through a physical door.
whyNot.D: A watering hole attack compromises websites visited by targets and is not a physical entry method.
whyNot.E: Shoulder surfing observes someone entering secrets, and it does not by itself get a person past a badge reader.

cards.front:
An organization wants to upgrade its enterprise-wide desktop computer solution. The organization currently has 500 PCs active on the network. the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) suggests that the organization employ desktop imaging technology for such a large scale upgrade. Which of the following is a security benefit of implementing an imaging solution?
A. it allows for faster deployment
B. it provides a consistent baseline
C. It reduces the number of vulnerabilities
D. It decreases the boot time
cards.back: B. it provides a consistent baseline
cards.why: An imaging solution deploys the same hardened, approved configuration to every PC, which creates a consistent security baseline across all 500 machines.

whyNot.A: Faster deployment is an efficiency benefit, not a security benefit.
whyNot.C: Imaging does not reduce the number of vulnerabilities by itself, because the image can include vulnerable software unless it is patched.
whyNot.D: Decreased boot time is a performance benefit and has no direct security value.

cards.front:
An organization has implemented an IPSec VPN access for remote users. Which of the following IPSec modes would be the MOST secure for this organization to implement?
A. Tunnel mode
B. Transport mode
C. AH-only mode
D. ESP-only mode
cards.back:
A. Tunnel mode

In both ESP and AH cases with IPSec Transport mode, the IP header is exposed. The IP header is not exposed in IPSec Tunnel mode.
cards.why: IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) tunnel mode encrypts and encapsulates the entire original packet, including the header, which makes it the most secure choice for remote user VPN (Virtual Private Network) access.

whyNot.B: Transport mode protects only the payload and leaves the original IP (Internet Protocol) header visible, so it is less secure for remote access.
whyNot.C: AH (Authentication Header) provides integrity and authentication but no encryption, so the data would remain readable.
whyNot.D: ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) alone does not specify tunnel encapsulation of the full packet, so it is less complete than tunnel mode.

cards.front:
Several workstations on a network are found to be on OS versions that are vulnerable to a specific attack. Which of the following is considered to be a corrective action to combat this vulnerability?
A. Install an antivirus definition patch
B. Educate the workstation users
C. Leverage server isolation
D. Install a vendor-supplied patch
E. Install an intrusion detection system
cards.why: A vendor-supplied patch fixes the flaw in the vulnerable OS (Operating System) versions. Removing the vulnerability itself is a corrective control, because it repairs the weakness after it was found.

whyNot.A: An antivirus definition update only improves malware signature detection and does not fix a vulnerability in the OS (Operating System) itself.
whyNot.B: User education is a preventive administrative measure and does not correct the unpatched OS (Operating System) weakness on the workstations.
whyNot.C: Server isolation is a compensating containment measure for servers, and it does not repair the vulnerable workstation OS (Operating System) versions.
whyNot.E: An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) only detects attacks and cannot remove the underlying vulnerability, so it is detective rather than corrective.

cards.front:
A security administrator suspects that a DDoS attack is affecting the DNS server. The administrator accesses a workstation with the hostname of workstation01 on the network and obtains the following output from the ipconfig command: The administrator successfully pings the DNS server from the workstation. Which of the following commands should be issued from the workstation to verify the DDoS attack is no longer occuring?
A. dig www.google.com
B. dig 192.168.1.254
C. dig workstation01.com
D. dig 192.168.1.26
cards.why: Querying the workstation's own hostname with dig sends a fresh lookup to the DNS (Domain Name System) server. A prompt, correct answer shows the server is responding normally and no longer overwhelmed by the DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack.
