whyNot.A: Looking up www.google.com may be answered from cache or forwarded externally, so it does not clearly prove the local DNS (Domain Name System) server is healthy after the DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack.
whyNot.B: Running dig against an IP (Internet Protocol) address as the query name is not a valid forward lookup and would not test DNS (Domain Name System) resolution of a host.
whyNot.D: Running dig against an IP (Internet Protocol) address as the query name is not a proper lookup without a reverse option, so it does not verify DNS (Domain Name System) recovery.

cards.front:
A security administrator has configured a RADIUS and a TACACS+ server on the company's network. Network devices will be required to connect to the TACACS+ server for authentication and send accounting information to the RADIUS server. Given the following information: RADIUS IP: 192.168.20.45 TACACS+ IP: 10.23.65.7 Which of the following should be configured on the network clients? (Select two.)
A. Accounting port: TCP 389
B. Accounting port: UDP 1812
C. Accounting port: UDP 1813
D. Authentication port: TCP 49
E. Authentication port: TCP 88
F. Authentication port: UDP 636
cards.back:
C. Accounting port: UDP 1813
D. Authentication port: TCP 49
cards.why: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) authenticates over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 49, and RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) accounting uses UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 1813.

whyNot.A: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) 389 is LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), not RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) accounting.
whyNot.B: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) 1812 is the RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) authentication port, not the accounting port.
whyNot.E: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) 88 is Kerberos, not TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus), which uses TCP port 49.
whyNot.F: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) 636 is not a TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) port, since LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol over SSL) uses TCP 636.

cards.front:
A number of employees report that parts of an ERP application are not working. The systems administrator reviews the following information from one of the employee workstations: Execute permission denied: financemodule.dll Execute permission denied: generalledger.dll Which of the following should the administrator implement to BEST resolve this issue while minimizing risk and attack exposure?
A. Update the application blacklist
B. Verify the DLL's file integrity
C. Whitelist the affected libraries
D. Place the affected employees in the local administrator's group
cards.why: The execute denials show application whitelisting is blocking the legitimate ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) DLL (Dynamic Link Library) files. Whitelisting only those libraries restores function with minimal added risk and attack exposure.

whyNot.A: Updating the blacklist would block more items rather than allow the blocked ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) DLL (Dynamic Link Library) files to run.
whyNot.B: Verifying DLL (Dynamic Link Library) file integrity checks for tampering but does not lift the execute permission denial caused by the application control policy.
whyNot.D: Adding users to the local administrators group grants excessive privilege and greatly increases attack exposure, violating least privilege.

cards.front:
A security analyst receives a notification from the IDS after working hours, indicating a spike in network traffic. Which of the following BEST describes this type of IDS?
A. Anomaly-based
B. Stateful
C. Host-based
D. Signature-based
cards.why: An anomaly-based IDS (Intrusion Detection System) compares activity against a learned baseline and alerts on deviations, such as an unexpected spike in network traffic after working hours.

whyNot.B: Stateful describes tracking connection state, as in firewalls, and does not describe alerting on a traffic spike from baseline deviation.
whyNot.C: A host-based IDS (Intrusion Detection System) monitors activity on a single endpoint, whereas a network traffic spike points to network-level monitoring.
whyNot.D: A signature-based IDS (Intrusion Detection System) matches known attack patterns and would not alert on a general traffic volume increase with no known signature.

cards.front:
An active/passive configuration has an impact on:
A. confidentiality
B. integrity
C. availability
D. Non-repudiation
cards.why: An active/passive configuration keeps a standby system ready to take over if the active one fails, so services stay up. That is availability, one part of the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad.

whyNot.A: Confidentiality is about preventing unauthorized disclosure, and a standby failover node does not control who can read data.
whyNot.B: Integrity is about preventing unauthorized changes to data, and failover pairing does not verify or protect data accuracy.
whyNot.D: Non-repudiation means a sender cannot deny an action, usually through digital signatures, and has nothing to do with failover design.

cards.front:
Which of the following physical security controls can be implemented as a secondary authentication factor that cannot be lost or misplaced but would allowed authorized entry into a controlled area?
A. Key Management
B. Biometrics
C. Hardware Token
D. Password
cards.why: Biometrics, such as fingerprints or iris scans, use a physical trait of the person, so they cannot be lost or misplaced. They work as an additional authentication factor for entry into a controlled area.

whyNot.A: Key management is the process of handling cryptographic or physical keys, and physical keys can be lost or misplaced.
whyNot.C: A hardware token is a physical device that can be lost, stolen, or left behind, which the question rules out.
whyNot.D: A password is a knowledge factor, not a physical security control, and it can be forgotten or shared.

cards.front:
When sending messages using symmetric encryption, which of the following must happen FIRST?
A. Exchange Encryption keys
B. Establish digital signature
C. Agree on an encryption method
D. Install digital certificates
cards.why: Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key, so both parties must securely exchange that key before they can encrypt or decrypt any messages. Without the shared key, no protected communication can start.

whyNot.B: A digital signature relies on asymmetric cryptography and provides authentication and non-repudiation, so it is not a prerequisite for symmetric encryption.
whyNot.C: Agreeing on a method matters, but the key must be shared before the encrypted message exchange can actually begin, which is the keyed first step.
whyNot.D: Digital certificates bind public keys to identities in asymmetric systems, and symmetric encryption does not require them to function.

cards.front:
A system administrator is attempting to recover from a catastrophic failure in a datacenter. To recover the domain controller, the systems administrator needs to provide the domain administrator credentials. Which of the following account types is the systems administrator using?
A. Shared Account
B. Guest Account
C. Service Account
D. User Account
cards.why: A service account is a non-interactive account that systems and recovery tooling run under, often holding elevated rights. The key treats the credentials used during domain controller recovery as this type of account.

whyNot.A: A shared account is used by multiple people with the same credentials, which does not describe a single administrator performing a recovery.
whyNot.B: A guest account has minimal, restricted access and could never hold domain administrator rights.
whyNot.D: A user account belongs to one individual for day-to-day work, though a named domain administrator could arguably fit here.

cards.keyDoubt: D. A domain administrator login used by a named systems administrator is a privileged user account, and nothing in the question describes an application or service running under it.

cards.front:
Which of the following BEST describes an important security advantage yielded by implementing vendor diversity?
A. Sustainability
B. Homogeneity
C. Resiliency
D. Configurability
cards.why: Vendor diversity means using products from multiple vendors, so a single vendor flaw or outage does not take down everything. This improves resiliency, the ability to keep operating and recover.

whyNot.A: Sustainability concerns long-term environmental or operational viability, not the security benefit of using multiple vendors.
whyNot.B: Homogeneity means using the same product everywhere, which is the opposite of vendor diversity and increases shared-vulnerability risk.
whyNot.D: Configurability describes how adjustable a product is, and vendor diversity does not provide it as a security advantage.

cards.front:
A stock trading company had the budget for enhancing its secondary datacenter approved. Since the main site is in a hurricane-affected area and the disaster recovery site is a 100mi (161km) away, the company wants to ensure its business is always operational with the least amount of man hours needed. Which of the following types of disaster recovery sites should the company implements?
A. Hot site
B. Warm Site
C. Cold site
D. Cloud-based site
cards.why: A cloud-based disaster recovery site can replicate and fail over automatically, keeping the business always operational with minimal staff effort. It also sits outside the hurricane-affected region without a company-run facility.

whyNot.A: A hot site is a fully equipped duplicate facility that works, but it requires ongoing staff effort to maintain and operate.
whyNot.B: A warm site has partial equipment and needs time and manual work to bring online, so the business is not always operational.
whyNot.C: A cold site is an empty space with little or no equipment, requiring the most time and labor to restore operations.

cards.front:
A security analyst is investigating a potential breach. Upon gathering, documenting, and securing the evidence, which of the following actions is the NEXT step to minimize the business impact?
A. Launch an investigation to identify the attacking host
B. Initiate the incident response plan
C. Review lessons learned captured in the process
D. Remove malware and restore the systems to normal operation
cards.back: B. Initiate the incident response plan
cards.why: After evidence is gathered, documented, and secured, the next step is to initiate the incident response plan, which coordinates containment and recovery in an organized way and limits business impact.

whyNot.A: Identifying the attacking host is an investigative task that can follow, but it does not directly reduce business impact first.
whyNot.C: Reviewing lessons learned is the final phase of incident response, done after eradication and recovery are complete.
whyNot.D: Removing malware and restoring systems comes later in the process, and doing it before the plan is initiated risks uncoordinated action.

cards.front:
In determining when it may be necessary to perform a credentialed scan against a system instead of a non-credentialed scan, which of the following requirements is MOST likely to influence this decision?
A. The scanner must be able to enumerate the host OS of devices scanned
B. The scanner must be able to footprint the network.
C. The scanner must be able to check for open ports with listening services
D. The scanner must be able to audit the file system permissions.
cards.back: D. The scanner must be able to audit the file system permissions.
cards.why: A credentialed scan logs into the host, so it can inspect internal settings such as file system permissions that a non-credentialed scan seen from the network cannot reach. That requirement most likely forces a credentialed scan.

whyNot.A: A non-credentialed scan can often fingerprint the host Operating System (OS) remotely from network responses.
whyNot.B: Footprinting the network is done from the outside using discovery techniques and needs no login credentials.
whyNot.C: Checking for open ports with listening services is a standard network-level check that works without credentials.

cards.front:
An analyst is reviewing a simple program for potential security vulnerabilities before being deployed to a windows server. Given the following code Void foo (char *bar) { Char random_user_input {12}; Strcpy    {random_user_input, bar}; } Which of the following vulnerability is present?
A. Bad memory Pointer
B. Buffer overflow
C. Integer overflow
D. Backdoor
cards.why: The code copies user-controlled input into a 12-byte array with strcpy, which does no length checking. Longer input overruns the buffer and overwrites adjacent memory, which is a buffer overflow.

whyNot.A: A bad memory pointer involves dereferencing an invalid or uninitialized pointer, which is not what this fixed-size array copy does.
whyNot.C: An integer overflow happens when arithmetic exceeds a numeric type's range, and the code shows no such calculation.
whyNot.D: A backdoor is a hidden access mechanism intentionally placed in software, and nothing in this code provides secret access.

cards.front:
A member of the admins group reports being unable to modify the “changes” file on a server. The permissions on the file are as follows: Permissions             User              Group              File -rwxrw-r--+              Admins        Admins            changes Based on the output above, which of the following BEST explains why the user is unable to modify the “changes” file?
A. The SELinux mode on the server is set to “enforcing”
B. The SELinux mode on the server is set to “Permissive”
C. An FACL has been added to the permissions for the file
D. The admins group does not have adequate permissions to access the file.
cards.back: A. The SELinux mode on the server is set to “enforcing”
cards.why: The owner and group permissions would normally allow modification, so an extra control must be denying access. SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux) in enforcing mode can block actions even when standard file permissions allow them.

whyNot.B: SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux) permissive mode only logs policy violations without blocking them, so it would not stop the modification.
whyNot.C: A plus sign does indicate an FACL (File Access Control List) exists, but nothing shows it restricts this user, so it is only a possible cause.
whyNot.D: The Admins group has read and write permission in the group field, so the group does have adequate permissions to modify the file.

cards.keyDoubt: C. The plus sign at the end of the permissions shows an FACL (File Access Control List) is attached, which can override the displayed group permissions and block this user.

cards.front:
A company wants to ensure confidential data from storage media is sanitized in such a way that drive cannot be reused. Which of the following methods should the technician use?
A. Shredding
B. Wiping
C. Low-level formatting
D. Repartitioning
E. Overwriting
cards.why: Shredding physically destroys the storage media, so the data cannot be recovered and the drive cannot be reused. That matches the requirement for confidential data on media that must not be reused.

whyNot.B: Wiping erases data with software so the drive can be reused, which fails the requirement that the drive cannot be reused.
whyNot.C: Low-level formatting rewrites the drive structure for reuse, and the drive remains usable afterward.
whyNot.D: Repartitioning only changes the partition layout, leaving data recoverable, and the drive stays reusable.
whyNot.E: Overwriting replaces existing data with new patterns so the drive can be reused, which contradicts the requirement.

cards.front:
A technician is investigating a potentially compromised device with the following symptoms:  Browser slowness  Frequent browser crashes  Hourglass stuck  New search toolbar  Increased memory consumption Which of the following types of malwares has infected the system?
A. Man-in-the-browser
B. Spoofer
C. Spyware
D. Adware
cards.why: Adware displays unwanted advertising and often installs unwanted browser toolbars. Slowness, browser crashes, and high memory use are typical symptoms of it.

whyNot.A: A man-in-the-browser attack intercepts and alters web transactions quietly, and it does not typically add visible toolbars.
whyNot.B: A spoofer impersonates another identity or address, and that is an attack technique, not a type of malware causing these symptoms.
whyNot.C: Spyware secretly collects user information and tries to stay hidden, so it would not usually add a visible search toolbar.

cards.front:
When attackers use a compromised host as a platform for launching attackers deeper into a company’s network, it is said that they are:
A. Escalating privilege
B. Becoming persistent
C. Fingerprinting
D. Pivoting
cards.why: Pivoting is when attackers use a compromised host as a platform to launch further attacks deeper into a network, reaching systems they could not access directly from outside.

whyNot.A: Escalating privilege means gaining higher access rights on a system, not using one host to attack other systems.
whyNot.B: Becoming persistent means maintaining long-term access, such as through a backdoor, and does not describe attacking inward from a compromised host.
whyNot.C: Fingerprinting identifies operating systems or services through reconnaissance and does not involve launching attacks from a compromised host.

cards.front:
Which of the following threat actors is MOST likely to steal a company’s proprietary information to gain a market edge and reduce time to market?
A. Competitor
B. Hacktivist
C. Insider
D. Organized crime.
cards.why: A competitor has a clear business motive to steal proprietary information, because it can gain a market edge and shorten its own time to market without doing the research and development.

whyNot.B: A hacktivist is driven by political or social causes, not by gaining a market advantage.
whyNot.C: An insider may steal data for several reasons, but the stated goal of a market edge fits a rival company best.
whyNot.D: Organized crime is typically motivated by direct financial gain, such as ransom or selling data, and not by speeding up a product launch.

cards.front:
A security engineer must install the same x.509 certificate on three different servers. The client application that connects to the server performs a check to ensure the certificate matches the host name. Which of the following should the security engineer use?
A. Wildcard certificate
B. Extended validation certificate
C. Certificate chaining D Certificate utilizing the SAN field.
cards.why: A wildcard certificate covers every subdomain of a domain, such as *.example.com, so one certificate can be installed on multiple servers and still match each hostname the client checks.

whyNot.B: An Extended Validation certificate indicates stricter identity vetting of the organization, and it does not address matching multiple hostnames.
whyNot.C: Certificate chaining describes the path of trust from a certificate up to a root authority, not hostname coverage across servers.
whyNot.D: A certificate using the SAN (Subject Alternative Name) field can also list multiple hostnames, but the keyed wildcard approach is the intended answer here.

cards.front:
A forensic expert is given a hard drive from a crime scene and asked to perform an investigation. Which of the following is the FIRST step the forensic expert needs to take to protect the chain of custody?
A. Make a forensic copy
B. Create a hash of the hard drive
C. Recover the hard drive data
D. Update the evidence log
cards.why: Making a forensic copy (bit-for-bit image) lets the expert analyze a duplicate while the original drive stays untouched, which preserves the evidence and supports the chain of custody (the documented trail of evidence handling).

whyNot.B: Hashing proves integrity but is normally done on the original and the copy together, so the key treats imaging as the first protective step.
whyNot.C: Recovering data directly from the original drive risks altering the evidence and breaking the chain of custody.
whyNot.D: Updating the evidence log is necessary documentation but does not itself protect the original evidence from alteration.

cards.keyDoubt: B: Creating a hash of the original drive first, ideally behind a write blocker, fixes its integrity before any copy is made, so the copy can later be verified against it.

cards.front:
A compromised server has been isolated and analyzed for anomalies. Data was exfiltrated from the server by embedding it into .jpg files. This concept is known as:
A. MITM
B. Covert channel
C. Hashing
D. Steganography
cards.why: Steganography hides data inside another file, such as embedding stolen information in a .jpg image, so the exfiltration looks like normal image traffic.

whyNot.A: MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) is an interception attack on communications, not a method of hiding data inside image files.
whyNot.B: A covert channel is a broader hidden communication path, but hiding data inside image files specifically is steganography.
whyNot.C: Hashing creates a fixed-length digest for integrity checking and does not conceal data inside files.

cards.front:
Which of the refers to the term used to restore a system to its operational state?
A. MTBF
B. MTTR
C. RTO
D. RPO
cards.why: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the target amount of time within which a system must be restored to its operational state after a disruption.

whyNot.A: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) measures the average time a system runs between failures, not restoration time.
whyNot.B: MTTR (Mean Time To Repair) is the average repair duration, whereas the objective for restoring operations is set by the RTO (Recovery Time Objective).
whyNot.D: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines how much data loss is acceptable, measured back from the failure, not how fast service returns.

cards.front:
Which of the following BEST describes a network-based attack that can allow an attacker to take full control of vulnerability host?
A. Remote exploit
B. Amplification
C. Sniffing
D. Man-in-the-middle
cards.why: A remote exploit abuses a vulnerability in a host across the network, which can give the attacker full control of the vulnerable system.

whyNot.B: Amplification multiplies traffic volume in denial-of-service attacks and does not give control of a host.
whyNot.C: Sniffing passively captures network traffic and does not by itself give an attacker control of a host.
whyNot.D: MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) intercepts or alters communications between parties and does not directly take over a vulnerable host.

cards.keyDoubt: A: Remote exploit is the network-based attack that gives full control of a vulnerable host, while sniffing only captures traffic passively.

cards.front:
A security analyst receives an alert from a WAF with the following payload Var data = “<test test test> ++ < - - / - - / - - / - - / - - / - - /etc/passwd>” Which of the following types of attacks is this?
A. Cross-site request forgery
B. Buffer overflow
C. SQL injection
D. JavaScript data insertion
E. Firewall evasion script
cards.why: The payload uses odd spacing and repeated dash patterns around a path to /etc/passwd, an obfuscated input crafted to slip past the WAF (Web Application Firewall) filtering, which fits a firewall evasion script.

whyNot.A: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending unwanted requests, which this payload does not do.
whyNot.B: A buffer overflow sends oversized input to overwrite memory, not obfuscated strings referencing a file path.
whyNot.C: SQL (Structured Query Language) injection would contain database syntax such as quotes, UNION or OR clauses, which are absent here.
whyNot.D: JavaScript data insertion would include script content that runs in a browser, but this payload is not a working script.

cards.front:
A computer emergency response team is called at midnight to investigate a case in which a mail server was restarted. After an initial investigation, it was discovered that email is being exfiltrated through an active connection. Which of the following is the NEXT step the team should take?
A. Identify the source of the active connection
B. Perform eradication of the active connection and recover
C. Perform a containment procedure by disconnecting the server.
D. Format the server and restore its initial configuration
cards.back: A. Identify the source of the active connection
cards.why: After detection, the team should first identify the source of the active connection so the response is informed and the scope of the exfiltration is understood before acting on the server.

whyNot.B: Eradication and recovery come after the incident is contained and understood, so doing them now is premature.
whyNot.C: Containment by disconnecting is a valid response step, but the key places identifying the connection source first.
whyNot.D: Formatting the server destroys forensic evidence and skips the identification and containment phases of incident response.

cards.keyDoubt: C: With data actively leaving, the next incident response step after detection is containment, such as disconnecting the server, before further investigation.

cards.front:
Two users must encrypt and transmit large amounts of data between them. Which of the following should they use to encrypt and transfer data?
A. Symmetric algorithm
B. Hash Function
C. Digital signature
D. Obfuscation
cards.why: A symmetric algorithm uses one shared key and is fast, so it is the right choice for encrypting large amounts of data between two users.

whyNot.B: A hash function produces a one-way digest and cannot be reversed to recover the original encrypted data.
whyNot.C: A digital signature provides authentication and non-repudiation, not bulk data encryption.
whyNot.D: Obfuscation only makes data harder to read and does not provide real cryptographic protection.

cards.front:
An analyst receives an alert from the SIEM showing an IP address that does not belong to the assigned network can be seen sending packets to the wrong gateway. Which of the following network devices is misconfigured and which should be done to remediate the issue?
A. Firewall, implement an ACL on the interface
B. Router, place the correct subnet on the interface
C. Switch, modify the access port to trunk port
D. Proxy, add the correct transparent interface
cards.back: A. Firewall, implement an ACL on the interface
cards.why: The key treats the problem as unauthorized traffic from an address outside the assigned network, so a firewall ACL (Access Control List) on the interface would filter packets from addresses that do not belong.

whyNot.B: A router with the wrong subnet on its interface could cause this, but the key points to filtering with a firewall instead.
whyNot.C: Changing an access port to a trunk port carries multiple VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) and would not fix a misplaced IP (Internet Protocol) address.
whyNot.D: A proxy mediates application requests and adding a transparent interface does not address an address outside the assigned network.

cards.keyDoubt: B: A host with an address outside the network sending to the wrong gateway points to a router interface with the wrong subnet, fixed by placing the correct subnet on it.

cards.front:
A security technician is configuring an access management system to track and record user actions. Which of the following should the technician configure?
A. Accounting
B. Authorization
C. Authentication
D. Identification
cards.why: Accounting tracks and records user actions, such as logins and resource usage, which is the third part of AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting).

whyNot.B: Authorization decides what resources an authenticated user may access and does not record what they did.
whyNot.C: Authentication verifies a user's claimed identity and does not log subsequent actions.
whyNot.D: Identification is the user claiming an identity, such as a username, and does not track actions.

cards.front:
An external attacker can modify the ARP cache of an internal computer. Which of the following types of attacks is described?
A. Replay
B. Spoofing
C. DNS Poisoning
D. Client-side attack
cards.why: Modifying a computer's ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache with false address mappings is ARP spoofing, a form of spoofing in which the attacker impersonates another device.

whyNot.A: A replay attack resends previously captured valid transmissions and does not alter an ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache.
whyNot.C: DNS (Domain Name System) poisoning corrupts name-to-address records in DNS, not the local ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache.
whyNot.D: A client-side attack exploits software on the user's device, such as a browser, rather than forging network address mappings.

cards.front:
A Chief Information Officer (CIO) asks the company’s security specialist if the company should spend any funds on malware protection from a specific server. Based on a risk assessment, the ARO value of a malware infection for the server is 5 and the annual cost for the malware protection is $2500. Which of the following SLE values warrants a recommendation against purchasing the malware protection?
A. $500
B. $1000
C. $2000
D. $2500
cards.why: ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) equals SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) times ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence). With an ARO of 5, an SLE of $500 gives $2500, which does not exceed the $2500 protection cost.

whyNot.B: An SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) of $1000 times an ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) of 5 is $5000, which exceeds the $2500 cost and justifies buying protection.
whyNot.C: An SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) of $2000 times an ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) of 5 is $10000, far above the $2500 cost, so protection is warranted.
whyNot.D: An SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) of $2500 times an ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) of 5 is $12500, far above the $2500 cost, so protection is warranted.

cards.front:
Which of the following differentiates a collision attack from a rainbow table attack?
A. A rainbow table attack performs a hash lookup
B. A rainbow table attack uses the hash as a password
C. In a collision attack, the hash and the input data are equivalent
D. In a collision attack, the same input results in different hashes.
cards.back: A. A rainbow table attack performs a hash lookup
cards.why: A rainbow table attack looks up a captured hash in precomputed tables to find the matching plaintext, while a collision attack finds two different inputs that produce the same hash.

whyNot.B: A rainbow table attack does not use the hash itself as a password; it uses the hash to find the original plaintext.
whyNot.C: In a collision attack, the hash values match but the input data differ, so they are not equivalent.
whyNot.D: A hash function gives the same output for the same input, so a collision attack involves different inputs producing one hash.

cards.front:
A security analyst is mitigating a pass-the-hash vulnerability on a windows infrastructure. Given the requirement, which of the following should the security analyst do to MINIMIZE the risk?
A. Enable CHAP
B. Disable NTLM
C. Enable Kerberos
D. Disable PAP
cards.why: Pass-the-hash relies on NTLM (New Technology LAN Manager) authentication accepting a stolen password hash, so disabling NTLM removes the mechanism and minimizes the risk.

whyNot.A: CHAP (Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol) is a remote access protocol and does not stop Windows NTLM (New Technology LAN Manager) hash reuse.
whyNot.C: Enabling Kerberos helps, but NTLM (New Technology LAN Manager) remains available for fallback unless it is disabled, so the risk persists.
whyNot.D: PAP (Password Authentication Protocol) is an unrelated legacy protocol, and disabling it does not address pass-the-hash on Windows.

cards.front:
Joe, a salesman, was assigned to a new project that requires him to travel to a client site. While waiting for a flight, Joe decides to connect to the airport wireless network without connecting to a VPN, and then sends confidential emails to follow colleagues. A few days later, the company experiences a data breach. Upon investigation, the company learns joe’s email were intercepted. Which of the following MOST likely caused the data breach?
A. violation Policy
B. Social engineering
C. Insider threat
D. Zero-day attack
cards.why: Joe knowingly sent confidential email over public wireless without a VPN (Virtual Private Network), which breaks company security policy, so a policy violation most likely caused the breach.

whyNot.B: Social engineering manipulates people into revealing information, and nothing here shows an attacker tricking Joe.
whyNot.C: An insider threat involves intentional or malicious misuse of access, but Joe was careless rather than malicious.
whyNot.D: A zero-day attack exploits an unknown software vulnerability, and the interception here resulted from unprotected public wireless use.

cards.front:
A security Technician has been receiving alerts from several servers that indicate load balancers have had a significant increase in traffic. The technician initiates a system scan. The scan results illustrate that the desk space on several servers has reached capacity. The scan also indicates that incoming internet traffic to the servers has increased. Which of the following is the MOST likely cause of the decreased disk space?
A. Misconfigured devices
B. Logs and events anomalies
C. Authentication issues
D. Unauthorized software
cards.why: The key attributes the full disks and rising load balancer traffic to misconfigured devices, such as servers or balancers set up in a way that causes excess data to accumulate.

whyNot.B: Logs and events anomalies are the key's alternative explanation, but the key treats the cause as device configuration rather than log content.
whyNot.C: Authentication issues involve failed or abused logins and do not typically fill disk space or raise load balancer traffic.
whyNot.D: Unauthorized software could consume disk space, but the scan results give no sign of unapproved programs.

cards.keyDoubt: B: Rising traffic filling disks most likely comes from logs and events growing rapidly, which is a logs and events anomaly rather than a device misconfiguration.

cards.front:
A security engineer wants to implement a site-to-site VPN that will require SSL certificates for mutual authentication. Which of the following should the engineer implement if the design requires client MAC addresses to be visible across the tunnel?
A. Tunnel Mode IPSec
B. Transport mode VPN IPSec
C. L2TP
D. SSL VPN
cards.why: An SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) VPN (Virtual Private Network), such as one running in bridged Layer 2 mode, authenticates both ends with certificates and can carry Ethernet frames, so client MAC (Media Access Control) addresses stay visible.

whyNot.A: Tunnel mode IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) encapsulates Layer 3 IP packets, so the original MAC (Media Access Control) addresses are not carried across the tunnel.
whyNot.B: Transport mode IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) protects only the packet payload between two hosts and does not build a tunnel that exposes MAC (Media Access Control) addresses.
whyNot.C: L2TP (Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol) has no encryption or SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) certificate authentication of its own and normally relies on IPSec (Internet Protocol Security).

cards.front:
An application was recently compromised recently after some malformed data came in via a web form. Which of the following would MOST likely have prevented this?
A. Input validation
B. Proxy server
C. Stress testing
D. Encoding
cards.why: Input validation checks and rejects malformed or unexpected data from a web form before the application processes it, which blocks injection and similar data-driven attacks.

whyNot.B: A proxy server filters and forwards traffic but does not fix an application's failure to check the data it receives.
whyNot.C: Stress testing measures behavior under heavy load and does not stop malformed input from being processed.
whyNot.D: Encoding changes how data is represented for output and is a secondary defense, not the primary control against malformed form input.

cards.front:
After a user reports slow computer performance, a system administrator detects a suspicious file, which was installed as part of a freeware software package. The systems administrator reviews the output below: Based on the above information, which of the following types of malware was installed on the user’s computer?
A. RAT
B. Keylogger
C. Spyware
D. Worm
E. Bot
cards.why: A bot is malware installed with freeware that quietly makes the system slow while it takes part in a botnet and talks to a remote command and control server.

whyNot.A: A RAT (Remote Access Trojan) gives an attacker interactive control of one host, and nothing here points to that kind of manual remote control.
whyNot.B: A keylogger only records keystrokes and would not usually cause the network activity and slowdown described.
whyNot.C: Spyware gathers user information and browsing habits and does not typically enroll the machine in a command and control network.
whyNot.D: A worm self-replicates across the network without user action, but this file arrived through a freeware package.

cards.front:
A cybersecurity analyst is looking into the payload of a random packet capture file that was selected for analysis. The analyst notices that an internal host had a socket established with another internal host over a non-standard port. Upon investigation, the origin host that initiated the socket shows this output: usera@host>history mkdir  /local/user/bin/somedirectory nc -1 192.168.5.1 –p 9856 ping –c 30 8.8.8.8 –a 600 rm /etc/dir2/somefile rm   -rm  /etc/dir2/ traceroute 8.8.8.8 pskill pid 9487 usera@host> Given the above output, which of the following commands would have established the questionable socket?
A. Traceroute 8.8.8.8
B. Ping -1      30        8.8.8.8     -s   600
C. Nc     -1  192.169.5.1 –p  9856
D. Pskill   pid  9487
cards.why: The command nc -l with a port opens a netcat listener, which creates the unexpected socket on non-standard port 9856 that the capture showed.

whyNot.A: Traceroute only maps the network hops to 8.8.8.8 and does not open a listening socket.
whyNot.B: Ping sends ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo requests and does not establish a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) socket on a port.
whyNot.D: Pskill terminates a process by its process ID and does not create any network connection.

cards.front:
A security administrator receives an alert from a third-party vendor that indicates a certificate that was installed in the browser has been hijacked at the root of a small public CA. The security administrator knows there are at least four different browsers in use on more than a thousand computers in the domain worldwide. Which of the following solutions would be BEST for the security administrator to most efficiently assist with this issue?
A. SSL
B. CRL
C. PKI
D. ACL
cards.why: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) lets the administrator revoke the hijacked certificate so every browser that checks revocation stops trusting it, which is more efficient than touching each machine.

whyNot.A: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) is an encryption protocol and offers no way to revoke a compromised certificate across many browsers.
whyNot.C: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is the overall certificate framework and is not the specific mechanism that revokes one hijacked certificate.
whyNot.D: An ACL (Access Control List) filters traffic or permissions and cannot invalidate a certificate stored in browsers.

cards.keyDoubt: B: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) revokes the compromised certificate for all browsers, whereas SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) is only a protocol and cannot fix this.

cards.front:
A security administrator has written a script that will automatically upload binary and text-based configuration files into a remote server using a scheduled task. The configuration sensitive information. Which of the following should the administrator use? (Select Two).
A. TOTP
B. SCP
C. FTP over a non-standard port
D. SRTP
E. Certificate-based authentication
F. SNMP V3
cards.back:
B. SCP
C. FTP over a non-standard port
cards.why: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) sends both binary and text files over SSH (Secure Shell) encryption, which protects sensitive configuration data during an automated transfer. FTP (File Transfer Protocol) on a non-standard port only obscures the service and does not encrypt it.

whyNot.A: TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) needs a user to supply a changing code, which does not suit an unattended scheduled script.
whyNot.D: SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) protects voice and video streams and is not used for file transfer.
whyNot.E: Certificate-based authentication would let the unattended script authenticate securely without a stored password, so it is arguably the better second answer.
whyNot.F: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) version 3 secures device monitoring and management traffic and is not a file transfer method.

cards.keyDoubt: E: Certificate-based authentication secures the unattended script's login, while FTP (File Transfer Protocol) on a non-standard port still sends the sensitive data unencrypted.

cards.front:
A penetration tester has written an application that performs a bit-by-bit XOR 0Xff operation on binaries prior to transmission over untrusted media. Which of the following BEST describes the action performed by this type of application?
A. Hashing
B. Key exchange
C. Encryption
D. Obfuscation
cards.why: XOR (exclusive OR) with a fixed constant 0xff is a trivially reversible scramble with no secret key, so it hides content without providing real cryptographic protection. That is obfuscation.

whyNot.A: Hashing is a one-way function that cannot be reversed, but an XOR (exclusive OR) with a constant is fully reversible.
whyNot.B: Key exchange is the process of securely sharing cryptographic keys, and this operation shares no key.
whyNot.C: Encryption depends on a secret key and a strong algorithm, but a fixed XOR (exclusive OR) constant offers no real secrecy.

cards.keyDoubt: D: XOR (exclusive OR) with a fixed 0xff value uses no secret key and is trivially reversible, so it is obfuscation rather than encryption.

cards.front:
Which of the following solutions should as administrator use to reduce the risk from an unknown vulnerability in a third-party software application?
A. Sandboxing
B. Encryption
C. Code signing
D. Fuzzing
cards.why: Sandboxing isolates the third-party application so that an unknown vulnerability, if exploited, is contained and cannot easily reach the rest of the system.

whyNot.B: Encryption protects data confidentiality and does not stop an exploit of a flaw in the application.
whyNot.C: Code signing proves who published the software and that it was not altered, but it does not address flaws inside it.
whyNot.D: Fuzzing is a testing technique that helps developers find vulnerabilities, and an administrator cannot use it to fix an unknown flaw in third-party code.

cards.keyDoubt: A: Sandboxing contains the impact of an unknown flaw in third-party software, while fuzzing only helps discover flaws and the administrator cannot patch the code.

cards.front:
Which of the following attack types BEST describes a client-side attack that is used to manipulate an HTML iframe with JavaScript code via a web browser?
A. Buffer overflow
B. MITM
C. XSS
D. SQLi
cards.why: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) injects JavaScript into a page, such as through an HTML iframe, so it runs in the victim's browser. This is a client-side attack.

whyNot.A: A buffer overflow overwrites memory in a running program and is not carried out by manipulating an HTML iframe with JavaScript.
whyNot.B: MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) intercepts traffic between two parties and does not rely on scripts running in the browser.
whyNot.D: SQLi (Structured Query Language injection) targets the back-end database, so it is a server-side attack.

cards.front:
Which of the following is used to validate the registry of data?
A. CBC
B. Blowfish
C. MD5
D. RSA
cards.why: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is a hashing algorithm that produces a digest used to check that data has not changed, which is how data integrity is validated.

whyNot.A: CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) is a block cipher mode of operation for encryption and does not validate data integrity.
whyNot.B: Blowfish is a symmetric encryption cipher that protects confidentiality and does not validate data integrity.
whyNot.D: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) is an asymmetric algorithm used for encryption and signatures, not a simple integrity check of data.

cards.keyDoubt: C: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is a hash function that validates data integrity, whereas Blowfish is an encryption cipher.

cards.front:
An organization is expanding its network team. Currently, it has local accounts on all network devices, but with growth, it wants to move to centrally managed authentication. Which of the following are the BEST solutions for the organization? (Select Two)
A. TACAC+
B. CHAP
C. LDAP
D. RADIUS
E. MSCHAPv2
cards.why: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) centralizes authentication for network devices, and LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) provides a central directory of accounts that can back that authentication.

whyNot.A: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) is actually a strong fit for centralized network device authentication and arguably belongs in the answer.
whyNot.B: CHAP (Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol) is a challenge-response method between a client and server and does not centralize account management.
whyNot.E: MSCHAPv2 (Microsoft Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol version 2) is a credential exchange method, not a centralized authentication service.

cards.keyDoubt: A: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) is purpose-built for centralized network device administration, while LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is only a directory protocol.

cards.front:
A security administrator installed a new network scanner that identifies new host systems on the network. Which of the following did the security administrator installed?
A. Vulnerability scanner
B. Network-based IDS
C. Rogue system detection
D. Configuration compliance scanner
cards.why: Rogue system detection finds new or unauthorized hosts that appear on the network, which matches a scanner that identifies new host systems.

whyNot.A: A vulnerability scanner looks for weaknesses on known hosts and does not mainly flag newly appearing systems.
whyNot.B: A network-based IDS (Intrusion Detection System) monitors traffic for malicious activity and does not inventory new hosts.
whyNot.D: A configuration compliance scanner checks settings against a baseline and does not detect new hosts.

cards.front:
A system administrator wants to provide for and enforce wireless access accountability during events where external speakers are invited to make presentations to a mixed audience of employees and non-employees. Which of the following should the administrator implement?
A. Shared Accounts
B. Preshared passwords
C. Least privilege
D. Sponsored guest
cards.why: A sponsored guest account is created and vouched for by an employee, which ties each guest's wireless use to a named account and so enforces accountability.

whyNot.A: Shared accounts hide who did what, so they remove accountability.
whyNot.B: Preshared passwords are known by everyone who has them, so individual guest activity cannot be traced.
whyNot.C: Least privilege limits the access rights granted but does not by itself identify or track individual wireless users.

cards.front:
A recent internal audit is enforcing a company to review each internal business unit’s VMs because the cluster they are installed on is in danger of running out of computer resources. Which of the following vulnerabilities exists?
A. Buffer overflow
B. End-of-life systems
C. System sprawl
D. Weak configuration
cards.why: System sprawl is the uncontrolled growth of virtual machines that consume cluster resources, which is why a review of each business unit's VMs is needed.

whyNot.A: A buffer overflow is a memory handling flaw in software and has nothing to do with a cluster running low on compute resources.
whyNot.B: End-of-life systems no longer receive vendor support, but the problem described is resource exhaustion from too many VMs (Virtual Machines).
whyNot.D: A weak configuration is an insecure setting, but the problem here is the number of VMs (Virtual Machines) using up resources.

cards.front:
A company is looking for an authentication protocol that uses tickets and time stamps to ensure the validity of requests and prevent against replay attacks. Which of the following would be BEST suited to meet this requirement?
A. TACACS+
B. Kerberos
C. RADIUS
D. MSCHAP
cards.why: Kerberos uses tickets issued by a key distribution center together with time stamps to validate requests and block replay attacks.

whyNot.A: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) handles authentication, authorization, and accounting but does not use tickets and time stamps.
whyNot.C: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) uses shared secrets and challenge-response, not tickets with time stamps.
whyNot.D: MSCHAP (Microsoft Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol) uses a challenge-response exchange and has no ticket system.

cards.front:
An organization requires users to provide their fingerprints to access an application. To improve security, the application developer intends to implement multifactor authentication. Which of the following should be implemented?
A. Use a camera for facial recognition
B. Have users sign their name naturally
C. Require a palm geometry scan
D. Implement Iris recognition
cards.back: B. Have users sign their name naturally
cards.why: A fingerprint is a biometric (something you are) factor, so MFA (Multifactor Authentication) needs a different factor type. A natural signature is a behavioral (something you do) characteristic, which adds a distinct factor.

whyNot.A: Facial recognition is another biometric (something you are) factor, so it repeats the fingerprint's factor type instead of adding a new one for MFA (Multifactor Authentication).
whyNot.C: A palm geometry scan is a biometric (something you are) factor, the same category as fingerprints, so it does not create true MFA (Multifactor Authentication).
whyNot.D: Iris recognition is a biometric (something you are) factor, so it duplicates the fingerprint's category and does not add a second factor to MFA (Multifactor Authentication).

cards.front:
A new Chief Information Officer (CIO) has been reviewing the badging procedures and decides to write a policy that all employees must have their badges rekeyed at least annually. Which of the following controls BEST describes this policy?
A. Physical
B. Corrective
C. Technical
D. Administrative
cards.why: Rekeying badges is a physical security control because it changes the physical credentials and locks that restrict entry to facilities. The annual rekeying requirement is carried out on physical access hardware.

whyNot.B: A corrective control repairs damage after an incident, and an annual scheduled rekeying is not a response to an event.
whyNot.C: A technical control uses software or system mechanisms such as encryption or firewalls, while badge rekeying deals with physical access hardware.
whyNot.D: An administrative control is a policy or procedure, and although the CIO (Chief Information Officer) writes a policy, the rekeyed badges themselves are a physical control.

cards.front:
The computer resource center issued smartphones to all first-level and above managers. The managers have the ability to install mobile tools. Which of the following tools should be implemented to control the types of tools the managers install?
A. Download manager
B. Content manager
C. Segmentation manager
D. Application Manager
cards.why: An application manager, as in MAM (Mobile Application Management), controls which apps can be installed or run on managed smartphones, using allow lists or deny lists for the managers' devices.

whyNot.A: A download manager only handles file transfers and does not control which applications users are allowed to install.
whyNot.B: A content manager controls documents and data on a device, not which applications users can install.
whyNot.C: A segmentation manager separates network or data zones and does not restrict application installation on mobile devices.

cards.front:
A company has a data classification system with definitions for “Private” and “Public.” The company’s security policy outlines how data should be protected based on type. The company recently added the data type “Proprietary.” Which of the following is the MOST likely reason the company added this data type?
A. Reduced Cost
B. More searchable data
C. Better Data classification
D. Expanded authority of the privacy officer
cards.why: Adding a more granular Proprietary type gives the organization better data classification, so each kind of data gets handling and protection rules that match its sensitivity.

whyNot.A: Adding a classification type adds administrative work and does not reduce cost.
whyNot.B: Classification labels do not make data more searchable; they define handling and protection requirements.
whyNot.D: A new data type does not expand the authority of the privacy officer, whose role is set by policy and law.

cards.keyDoubt: C, because the purpose of adding a more specific Proprietary level is better data classification, and searchability is not what classification is for.

cards.front:
A recent audit contained significant findings for several servers, including: Server Name Audit findings Server A  Missing 26 critical OS patches  Missing five third vendor patches  Expired SSL certificate Server B  Missing 15 critical OS patches  Missing three third-party patches  Out-of-date antivirus Server C  Missing three important OS Patches Server D  Out-of-date antivirus  SSH static connections allowed In the future, which of the following capabilities would enable administrators to detect these issues proactively?
A. Credentialed vulnerability scan
B. Non- Credentialed vulnerability scan
C. Automatic file integrity checking
D. Manual file integrity checking
E. Log collection and correlation
cards.why: A credentialed vulnerability scan logs in to each server and can see missing OS (operating system) patches, third-party patches, expired SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) certificates, outdated antivirus and insecure SSH (Secure Shell) settings, so scheduling it finds these issues proactively.

whyNot.B: A non-credentialed vulnerability scan sees only what is exposed over the network and usually misses installed patch levels, antivirus signature age and local configuration.
whyNot.C: Automatic file integrity checking detects changed files and does not report missing patches, expired certificates or outdated antivirus.
whyNot.D: Manual file integrity checking is slow and reactive, and it detects file changes rather than missing patches or weak configuration.
whyNot.E: Log collection and correlation, as in SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), shows events after they occur and does not audit patch levels or configuration.

cards.front:
Which of the following would provide additional security by adding another factor to a smart card?
A. Token
B. Proximity Badge
C. Physical key
D. PIN
cards.why: A smart card is something you have, so adding a PIN (Personal Identification Number), which is something you know, creates two-factor authentication.

whyNot.A: A token is also something you have, so it does not add a different factor to a smart card.
whyNot.B: A proximity badge is something you have, the same factor type as a smart card.
whyNot.C: A physical key is something you have, so it duplicates the smart card's factor type.

cards.front:
A security analyst is attempting to solve compatibility issues between the company’s ERP software and application whitelisting controls. The organization uses application whitelisting to ensure only tested and approved applications are able to run within the organization. In the current configuration, only executables installed in C:\program files\ are able to be executed by the user. The following information is logged by the ERP software: ERP Corp Application V1.2 Date: 1/22/2017 5:00 AM Running scheduled task processdata1 Copying file C:\program files\ERPCorp\processdata.exe to \c:\temp\processdata-1-22-2017- 0500.exe Error: could not execute c:\temp\processdata-a-22-2017-0500.exe – Access Denied Fault in application 0x00f4bc01 – Shutting Down Which of the following would BEST resolve the issue without allowing for any potentially untested or unapproved software to be executed?
A. Create a path rule that permits C:\temp\processdata-1-22-2017-0500.exe to be executed.
B. Create a hash rule that permits the application processdata.exe to be executed
C. Create a path rule that permits c:\temp\*.exe to be executed
D. Create a rule that allows all software digitally signed by ERP Corp to be executed.
E. Contact the software’s publisher and request a patch be made to change the behavior of the software.
cards.back: D. Create a rule that allows all software digitally signed by ERP Corp to be executed.
cards.why: A rule allowing software digitally signed by ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) Corp permits the copied processdata executable wherever it runs, while still blocking any unsigned or untested software.

whyNot.A: A path rule for one filename fails because the timestamped filename changes with every scheduled run.
whyNot.B: A hash rule for the original file would match the copy, but it breaks whenever the vendor updates the file, which makes it less maintainable than a publisher signature rule.
whyNot.C: A path rule allowing every executable in the temp folder lets any user or malware run untested software from a writable location.
whyNot.E: Waiting for a vendor patch does not resolve the problem now and may never change the behavior.

cards.front:
A network administrator needs to allocate a new network for the R&D group. The network must not be accessible from the internet regardless of the network firewall or other internal misconfigurations. Which of the following settings should the network administrator implement to accomplish this?
A. Configure the OS default TTL to 1
B. Use NAT on the R&D network
C. Implement a router ACL
D. Enable protected ports on the switch
cards.why: Setting the operating system default TTL (Time To Live) to 1 means packets from the R&D (research and development) hosts expire at the first router, so they cannot reach the internet even if a firewall is misconfigured.

whyNot.B: NAT (Network Address Translation) hides internal addresses but is not a security control, and misconfigured rules or port forwards can still expose the network.
whyNot.C: A router ACL (Access Control List) is a filtering rule that can itself be misconfigured, so it does not guarantee isolation regardless of misconfigurations.
whyNot.D: Protected ports on a switch only stop layer 2 traffic between ports on the same switch and do not stop internet access.

cards.keyDoubt: A, because TTL (Time To Live) of 1 prevents packets from crossing a router regardless of firewall or ACL (Access Control List) misconfigurations, while a router ACL is itself a configuration that can be wrong.

cards.front:
An information security specialist is reviewing the following output from a Linux server: user@server:~$ crontab -1 5 * * * *  /user/local/bin/backup.sh user@server:~$ cat /user/local/bin/backup.sh #!/bin/bash If ! grep –quiet joeuser      /etc/passwd Then rm   -rf   / Fi Based on the above information, which of the following types of malware was installed on the server?
A. Logic bomb
B. Trojan
C. Backdoor
D. Ransomware
E. Rootkit
cards.why: The script runs rm -rf on the whole filesystem when the account joeuser no longer exists in /etc/passwd, so it is a logic bomb that triggers on a condition, here an employee's departure.

whyNot.B: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software to get installed, and this script is a scheduled job with a destructive condition.
whyNot.D: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment, while this script simply deletes files and has no ransom component.
whyNot.E: A rootkit hides its presence by modifying the operating system, and this plain script does not conceal itself.

cards.keyDoubt: A, because the script runs a destructive payload only when a condition is met (joeuser missing from /etc/passwd), which defines a logic bomb, and it creates no remote access, so it is not a backdoor.

cards.front:
A systems administrator wants to provide balance between the security of a wireless network and usability. The administrator is concerned with wireless encryption compatibility of the older devices used by some employees. Which of the following would provide strong security and background compatibility when accessing the wireless network?
A. Open wireless network and SSL VPN
B. WPA using a preshared key
C. WPA2 using a RADIUS back-end for 802.1x authentication
D. WEP with a 40-bit key
cards.back:
B. WPA using a preshared key
C. WPA2 using a RADIUS back-end for 802.1x authentication
cards.why: WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) with a preshared key runs on older hardware via TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol), and WPA2 with RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) and 802.1X gives strong per-user authentication, so both balance security and compatibility.

whyNot.A: An open wireless network has no encryption at the wireless layer, and a Secure Sockets Layer VPN (Virtual Private Network) leaves the wireless link itself exposed.
whyNot.D: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) with a 40-bit key is easily cracked and does not provide strong security.

cards.front:
A security administrator has found a hash in the environment known to belong to malware. The administrator then finds this file to be in in the preupdate area of the OS, which indicates it was pushed from the central patch system. File: winx86_adobe_flash_upgrade.exe Hash: 99ac28bede43ab869b853ba62c4ea243 The administrator pulls a report from the patch management system with the following output: Given the above outputs, which of the following MOST likely happened?
A. The file was corrupted after it left the patch system.
B. The file was infected when the patch manager downloaded it.
C. The file was not approved in the application whitelist system.
D. The file was embedded with a logic bomb to evade detection.
cards.back: D. The file was embedded with a logic bomb to evade detection.
cards.why: A logic bomb is malicious code embedded in a legitimate-looking update that activates on a later condition, which fits a malicious file arriving through the trusted patch system without being flagged.

whyNot.A: Corruption after leaving the patch system would not make the file match a known malware hash that came through the central patch channel.
whyNot.B: Infection when the patch manager downloaded it would be possible, but the report does not show that the download itself was altered.
whyNot.C: Missing application whitelist approval would not explain why the file was pushed by the central patch system with a known malicious hash.

cards.front:
After attempting to harden a web server, a security analyst needs to determine if an application remains vulnerable to SQL injection attacks. Which of the following would BEST assist the analyst in making this determination?
A. Tracert
B. Fuzzer
C. Nslookup
D. Nmap
E. Netcat
cards.why: A fuzzer sends malformed and unexpected input to an application, so it can test input fields for SQL (Structured Query Language) injection weaknesses after hardening.

whyNot.A: Tracert (trace route) only shows the network path to a host and says nothing about application vulnerabilities.
whyNot.C: Nslookup queries DNS (Domain Name System) records and cannot test application input handling.
whyNot.D: Nmap (Network Mapper) discovers hosts and open ports, but it does not test application input for SQL (Structured Query Language) injection.
whyNot.E: Netcat opens raw network connections and can send data manually, but it does not systematically test for SQL (Structured Query Language) injection.

cards.front:
An administrator is replacing a wireless router. The configuration of the old wireless router was not documented before it stopped functioning. The equipment connecting to the wireless network uses older legacy equipment that was manufactured prior to the release of the 802.11i standard. Which of the following configuration options should the administrator select for the new wireless router?
A. WPA+CCMP
B. WPA2+CCMP
C. WPA+TKIP
D. WPA2+TKIP
cards.why: Hardware made before the 802.11i standard cannot run WPA2, so it needs WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) with TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol), which was designed to run on old WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) hardware through firmware updates.

whyNot.A: WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) with CCMP (Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol) is not a standard pairing, and CCMP needs hardware older devices lack.
whyNot.B: WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) with CCMP (Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol) requires AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) hardware that devices predating 802.11i do not have.
whyNot.D: WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) is based on the 802.11i standard, so devices manufactured before that standard generally cannot use it.

cards.keyDoubt: C, because WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) with TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol) is the combination legacy devices from before 802.11i support, while WPA2 is defined by 802.11i.

cards.front:
Users from two organizations, each with its own PKI, need to begin working together on a joint prospect. Which of the following would allow the users of their separate PKIs to work together without connection errors?
A. Trust model
B. Stapling
C. Intermediate CA
D. Key escrow
cards.why: Stapling lets a server attach a signed certificate status response, as in OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) stapling, so clients can check validity without separately contacting the issuing certificate authority.

whyNot.A: A trust model, such as cross-certification, defines how separate PKIs (Public Key Infrastructures) trust each other, and it is what lets users of different PKIs work together.
whyNot.C: An intermediate CA (Certificate Authority) issues certificates beneath a root and does not by itself connect two separate PKIs (Public Key Infrastructures).
whyNot.D: Key escrow stores copies of private keys for recovery and does not establish trust between two PKIs (Public Key Infrastructures).

cards.keyDoubt: A, because connecting two separate PKIs (Public Key Infrastructures) without connection errors requires an agreed trust model such as cross-certification or a bridge CA (Certificate Authority), while stapling only delivers certificate status.

cards.front:
To help prevent one job role from having sufficient access to create, modify, and approve payroll data, which of the following practices should be employed?
A. Least privilege
B. Job rotation
C. Background checks
D. Separation of duties
cards.why: Separation of duties splits critical tasks across different people, so no single role can create, modify and approve payroll data alone.

whyNot.A: Least privilege limits each user to the access needed for the job, but it does not by itself divide one process's steps among different people.
whyNot.B: Job rotation moves employees between roles periodically to help detect fraud, but it does not stop one role from holding conflicting permissions at the same time.
whyNot.C: Background checks screen employees before hiring and do not limit what access a role holds.

cards.front:
An organization wants to ensure servers and applications can be deployed rapidly, in a consistent manner, and allow for flexible configuration changes. Which of the following should the organization use to make process repeatable across multiple locations?
A. Redundancy
B. Templates
C. Snapshots
D. Elasticity
E. Configuration validation
cards.why: Templates (preconfigured server and application images or infrastructure-as-code definitions) let an organization deploy the same consistent configuration repeatedly in many locations while still allowing flexible changes. Snapshots can also copy a state, but templates are the standard repeatable method.

whyNot.A: Redundancy adds duplicate components for availability and does not make deployments repeatable or consistent.
whyNot.D: Elasticity automatically scales resources up or down with demand and does not standardize how systems are deployed.
whyNot.E: Configuration validation checks that settings are correct after the fact and does not provide a repeatable deployment method.

cards.front:
An audit takes place after company-wide restructuring, in which several employees changed roles. The following deficiencies are found during the audit regarding access to confidential data: Employee Job Function Audit Finding Ann Sales Manager Access to confidential payroll shares Access to payroll processing program Access to marketing shares Jeff Marketing Director Access to human resources annual review folder Access to shared human resources mailbox John Sales Manager (Terminated) Access account Access to human resources annual review folder Access to confidential payroll shares Which of the following would be the BEST method to prevent similar audit findings in the future?
A. Implement separation of duties for the payroll department
B. Implement a DLP solution on the payroll and human resources servers
C. Implement rule-based access controls on the human resources server
D. Implement regular permission auditing and reviews
cards.back: A. Implement separation of duties for the payroll department
cards.why: Separation of duties splits critical tasks, such as payroll processing, among different people so no single role holds excessive access, which limits the damage when employees change roles.

whyNot.B: DLP (Data Loss Prevention) monitors and blocks data leaving the network and does not fix excessive permissions left over after role changes.
whyNot.C: Rule-based access control applies fixed rules on one server and does not address permissions accumulating across employee role changes and terminations.
whyNot.D: Regular permission auditing and reviews is detective rather than structural, so the key prefers separation of duties.

cards.keyDoubt: D: Findings were stale permissions after role changes and a termination, which regular permission auditing and reviews (access recertification) directly prevents, while separation of duties does not.

cards.front:
A remote intruder wants to take inventory of a network so exploits can be researched. The intruder is looking for information about software versions on the network. Which of the following techniques is the intruder using?
A. Banner grabbing
B. Port scanning
C. Packet sniffing
D. Virus scanning
cards.why: Banner grabbing connects to services and reads their identification banners, which reveal software names and versions that an intruder can then match against known exploits.

whyNot.B: Port scanning finds open ports and services, but it does not by itself reveal specific software versions.
whyNot.C: Packet sniffing passively captures traffic on a network and is not a technique to inventory software versions on remote hosts.
whyNot.D: Virus scanning looks for malware on a system and does not enumerate network software versions for exploit research.

cards.front:
A security analyst conducts a manual scan on a known hardened host that identifies many non- compliant configuration items. Which of the following BEST describe why this has occurred? (Select Two).
A. Privileged-user credentials were used to scan the host
B. Non-applicable plugins were selected in the scan policy
C. The output audit file was used
D. The output of the report contains false positives
E. The target host has been compromise
cards.back:
A. Privileged-user credentials were used to scan the host
B. Non-applicable plugins were selected in the scan policy
cards.why: Selecting plugins (scan checks) that do not apply to the target can report many items as non-compliant, and a credentialed scan with privileged credentials can also surface many configuration findings on a hardened host.

whyNot.C: An output audit file records scan results and does not cause a hardened host to be reported as non-compliant.
whyNot.D: False positives are a possible symptom, but the key treats scan setup choices as the cause of the many findings.
whyNot.E: A compromised host would show signs of tampering, and nothing in the scenario suggests the hardened host was compromised.

cards.keyDoubt: D: Non-applicable plugins (option B) and false positives in the report best explain many non-compliant items on a known hardened host, while privileged credentials would make results more accurate.

cards.front:
A home invasion occurred recently in which an intruder compromised a home network and accessed a WIFI-enabled baby monitor while the baby’s parents were sleeping. Which of the following BEST describes how the intruder accessed the monitor?
A. Outdated antivirus
B. WiFi signal strength signal strength
C. Social engineering
D. Default configurations
cards.why: Many consumer Internet of Things devices such as baby monitors ship with default usernames, passwords, and settings that owners never change, so an intruder can log in directly.

whyNot.A: Outdated antivirus does not apply because baby monitors do not run antivirus, and the attack was simple unauthorized access.
whyNot.B: Wireless signal strength affects range and connection quality and does not give an intruder access to the device.
whyNot.C: Social engineering manipulates people, and nothing in the scenario shows the parents were tricked into giving access.

cards.front:
A security analyst observes the following events in the logs of an employee workstation: 1/23 1:07:16 865 Access to C:\Users\user\temp\oasdfkh.hta has been restricted by your administrator by the default restriction policy level. 1/23 1:07:09 1034 The scan completed. No detections were found The security analyst reviews the file system and observes the following: C:\>dir C:\Users\user\temp 1/23 1:07:02 oasdfkh.hta 1/23 1:07:02 update.bat 1/23 1:07:02 msg.txt Given the information provided, which of the following MOST likely occurred on the workstation?
A. Application whitelisting controls blocked an exploit payload from executing
B. Antivirus software found and quarantined three malware files
C. Automatic updates were initiated but failed because they had not been approved
D. The SIEM log agent was not tuned properly and reported a false positive.
cards.back: A. Application whitelisting controls blocked an exploit payload from executing
cards.why: The log says the file was restricted by the default restriction policy level while the antivirus scan found nothing, which indicates application whitelisting (software restriction policy) blocked the .hta (HTML Application) payload from running.

whyNot.B: The antivirus log states the scan completed with no detections, so nothing was found or quarantined.
whyNot.C: The restriction message refers to a policy blocking the .hta file, not to failed update approval.
whyNot.D: The log entries show a real policy block on a specific file, so nothing indicates a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) tuning false positive.

cards.front:
A system administrator has isolated an infected system from the network and terminated the malicious process from executing. Which of the following should the administrator do NEXT according to the incident response process?
A. Restore lost data from backup
B. Wipe the system
C. Document the lessons learned
D. Determined the scope of impact.
cards.back: A. Restore lost data from backup
cards.why: After containing an infection and stopping the malicious process, the key treats restoring lost data from backup as the next recovery step in the incident response process.

whyNot.B: Wiping the system is part of eradication and recovery and normally follows determining scope and preserving evidence.
whyNot.C: Documenting lessons learned is the final incident response phase, performed after recovery is complete.
whyNot.D: Determining the scope of impact is a valid step, but the key places data restoration next.

cards.keyDoubt: D: After containment and ending the process, the administrator should next determine the scope of impact before eradication and recovery steps such as restoring data.

cards.front:
Which of the following specifically describes the exploitation of an interactive process to access otherwise restricted areas of the OS?
A. Privilege escalation
B. Pivoting
C. Process affinity
D. Buffer overflow
cards.why: Privilege escalation exploits a flaw or misconfiguration in a running interactive process to gain higher permissions and reach restricted areas of the OS (Operating System).

whyNot.B: Pivoting uses a compromised host to attack other systems on a network and is not exploitation of a process for higher privileges.
whyNot.C: Process affinity binds a process to specific CPU (Central Processing Unit) cores for performance and is not an attack.
whyNot.D: A buffer overflow is a specific memory flaw that may enable escalation, but the question asks for the general exploitation described.

cards.front:
A security administrator is developing controls for creating audit trails and tracking if a PHI data breach is to occur. The administrator has been given the following requirements:  All access must be correlated to a user account  All user accounts must be assigned to a single individual  User access to the PHI data must be recorded  Anomalies in PHI data access must be reported.  Logs are records cannot be detected or modified. Which of the following should the administrator implement to meet the above requirements? (Select three.)
A. Eliminate shared accounts.
B. Create a standard naming convention for accounts.
C. Implement usage auditing and review.
D. Enable account lockout thresholds.
E. Copy logs in real time to a secured WORM drive.
F. Implement time-of-day restrictions.
G. Perform regular permission audits and reviews.
cards.back:
A. Eliminate shared accounts.
C. Implement usage auditing and review.
G. Perform regular permission audits and reviews.
cards.why: Eliminating shared accounts ties every action to one person, usage auditing and review records and reports anomalies in PHI (Protected Health Information) access, and permission audits and reviews keep access tied to the right individuals.

whyNot.B: A naming convention organizes accounts but does not record access, report anomalies, or protect logs.
whyNot.D: Account lockout thresholds limit failed logins and do not create audit trails of PHI access.
whyNot.E: Copying logs in real time to a WORM (Write Once Read Many) drive does meet the requirement that logs cannot be modified, though the key omits it.
