whyNot.F: Time-of-day restrictions limit when users can log in and do not meet any listed audit trail requirement.

cards.keyDoubt: E: Copying logs in real time to a WORM (Write Once Read Many) drive is the only option that meets the requirement that logs cannot be deleted or modified.

cards.front:
A security administrator is diagnosing a server where the CPU utilization is at 100% for 24 hours. The main culprit of CPU utilization is the antivirus program. Which of the following issues could occur if left unresolved? (Select Two).
A. MITM attack
B. DoS attack
C. DLL injection
D. Buffer overflow
E. Resource exhaustion
cards.back:
B. DoS attack
E. Resource exhaustion
cards.why: A server pinned at full CPU (Central Processing Unit) usage for a day is suffering resource exhaustion, which can leave legitimate requests unserved and amount to a DoS (Denial of Service) condition.

whyNot.A: A MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attack intercepts traffic and is not caused by high CPU use from antivirus.
whyNot.C: DLL (Dynamic Link Library) injection forces malicious code into a process and is not a result of CPU load.
whyNot.D: A buffer overflow is a memory handling flaw in code and is not caused by sustained CPU utilization.

cards.front:
Joe, a senior systems administrator, must leave for a family emergency. While Joe is absent, another systems administrator discovers Joe stole confidential company information. Which of the following organizational procedures would have detected this breach sooner?
A. Background check
B. Separation of duties
C. Job rotation
D. Rules of behavior
E. Non-disclosure agreement
cards.why: Rules of behavior set expected conduct and acceptable use for privileged staff, and the key treats them as the control that would have flagged Joe's improper handling of confidential information earlier.

whyNot.A: A background check screens people before hiring and cannot detect misconduct that happens later.
whyNot.B: Separation of duties limits what one person can do but does not rotate someone out so a colleague can discover fraud.
whyNot.C: Job rotation is the control that would have detected this breach sooner, since another administrator taking over would have exposed the theft.
whyNot.E: A non-disclosure agreement is a legal deterrent and does not detect a breach.

cards.keyDoubt: C: Job rotation puts another administrator into Joe's role, which exposes misconduct sooner without waiting for an emergency absence.

cards.front:
A security administrator is reviewing the following PowerShell script referenced in the Task Scheduler on a database server: $members = GetADGroupMember – Identity “Domain Admins” - recursive I Select - ExpandProperty Name If  ($members -notcontains “JohnDoe”) ( Remove-Item -path C:\Database -recurse  -force } Which of the following did the security administrator discover?
A. Ransomware
B. Backdoor
C. Logic bomb
D. Trojan
cards.why: The script runs from Task Scheduler and deletes the C:\Database folder if a specific user is no longer in the Domain Admins group, which is a condition-triggered malicious payload, a logic bomb.

whyNot.A: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, whereas this script simply deletes data and makes no ransom demand.
whyNot.B: A backdoor provides covert remote access, and this script does not open any access path.
whyNot.D: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software, while this scheduled script triggers on a condition and is not a disguised program.

cards.keyDoubt: C: The script destroys the database only when JohnDoe is missing from the Domain Admins group, which is a trigger-based logic bomb.

cards.front:
A security analyst is reviewing an assessment report that includes software versions, running services, supported encryption algorithms, and permission settings. Which of the following produced the report?
A. Vulnerability scanner
B. Protocol Analyzer
C. Network mapper
D. Web inspector
cards.why: A vulnerability scanner reports software versions, running services, supported encryption algorithms, and permission settings, and then flags weaknesses, which matches the assessment report described.

whyNot.B: A protocol analyzer captures and decodes network traffic and does not assess permission settings or installed software versions.
whyNot.C: A network mapper discovers hosts and open services, but it does not typically report permission settings or configuration weaknesses.
whyNot.D: A web inspector examines web page elements and traffic in a browser and does not produce a network-wide assessment.

cards.keyDoubt: A: A vulnerability scanner produces reports covering software versions, services, encryption algorithms, and permission settings, while a network mapper focuses on host and port discovery.

cards.front:
A security administrator wants to install a AAA server to centralize the management of network devices, such as routers and switches. The server must reauthorize each individual command on a network device. Which of the following should be implemented?
A. RADIUS
B. Kerberos
C. SAML
D. TACACS+
cards.why: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is a widely used AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) protocol for centralizing network device access, and the key selects it.

whyNot.B: Kerberos is a ticket-based authentication protocol and does not authorize individual commands on network devices.
whyNot.C: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) provides web single sign-on federation and is not used for network device command authorization.
whyNot.D: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) is the usual choice for per-command authorization on network devices, but the key selects another option.

cards.keyDoubt: D: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) separates authentication from authorization and can reauthorize each individual command on routers and switches, which RADIUS does not do.

cards.front:
An audit report has identified a weakness that could allow unauthorized personnel access to the facility at its main entrance and from there gain access to the network. Which of the following would BEST resolve the vulnerability?
A. Faraday cage
B. Air gap
C. Mantrap
D. Bollards
cards.why: Bollards are posts that block vehicles from reaching or ramming a main entrance, which is the control the key selects for protecting that entrance.

whyNot.A: A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic signals and does not control physical entry through a door.
whyNot.B: An air gap isolates a network from other networks and does not stop people entering the building.
whyNot.C: A mantrap is a double-door vestibule that stops tailgating and unauthorized entry at the entrance, which better fits the scenario.

cards.keyDoubt: C: A mantrap controls who walks through the main entrance and prevents tailgating, while bollards only stop vehicles.

cards.front:
A user typically works remotely over the holidays, using a web-based VPN to access corporate resources. The user reports getting untrusted host error and being unable to connect. Which of the following is MOST likely the cause??
A. The certificate has expired
B. The browser does not support SSL
C. The user’s account is locked out
D. The VPN software has reached the seat license maximum.
cards.why: An expired certificate makes the browser report an untrusted host, because the VPN (Virtual Private Network) gateway's TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificate can no longer be validated. This is the most likely cause of an untrusted host error.

whyNot.B: A browser that lacked SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) support would fail to negotiate a connection, not report an untrusted host, and this user has connected before.
whyNot.C: A locked-out account produces an authentication failure after the secure session is established, not a certificate trust error.
whyNot.D: Reaching the seat license maximum produces a license or capacity error, not a certificate trust warning.

cards.front:
When it comes to cloud computing, if one of the requirements for a project is to have the most control over the systems in the cloud, which of the following is a service model that would be BEST suited?
A. Infrastructure
B. Platform
C. Software
D. Virtualization
cards.why: The keyed answer, Software as a Service, gives the customer the least control, because the provider manages the application and everything beneath it.

whyNot.A: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) is actually the model that gives the most control over operating systems and configuration, which is why it fits this requirement best.
whyNot.B: PaaS (Platform as a Service) lets the customer control applications but not the underlying operating system or servers.
whyNot.D: Virtualization is a technology used to build cloud services, not a cloud service model.

cards.keyDoubt: A, because IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) gives the customer control of operating systems, storage and networking, whereas SaaS (Software as a Service) gives the least control.

cards.front:
Multiple organizations operating in the same vertical want to provide seamless access for their employees as they visit the other organizations. Which of the following should be implemented if all the organizations use the native 802.1x client on their mobile devices?
A. Shibboleth
B. RADIUS federation
C. SAML
D. OAuth
E. OpenID connect
cards.why: A RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) federation lets organizations trust each other's authentication servers, so employees from one organization can use 802.1X wireless access at another with their home credentials.

whyNot.A: Shibboleth is a web single sign-on system and does not work with the native 802.1X network client.
whyNot.C: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) federates web application logins, not 802.1X network access.
whyNot.D: OAuth (Open Authorization) delegates authorization to applications and is not used for 802.1X network authentication.
whyNot.E: OpenID Connect handles web application identity and is not used by native 802.1X wireless clients.

cards.front:
A company was recently audited by a third party. The audit revealed the company’s network devices were transforming files in the clear. Which of the following protocols should the company use to transfer files?
A. HTTPS
B. LDAPS
C. SCP
D. SNMPv3
cards.why: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) transfers files over an SSH (Secure Shell) encrypted channel, which fixes the audit finding that network devices moved files in cleartext.

whyNot.A: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) is encrypted but is designed for web traffic, not for device file transfers.
whyNot.B: LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol over SSL) secures directory queries, not file transfers.
whyNot.D: SNMPv3 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 3) secures device management and monitoring, not file transfers.

cards.front:
Which of the following technologies would be MOST appropriate to utilize when testing a new software patch before a company-wide deployment
A. Cloud computing
B. Virtualization
C. Redundancy
D. Application control
cards.why: Virtualization lets the company run a patch in an isolated virtual machine that mirrors production, so problems can be found and the machine reverted before company-wide deployment.

whyNot.A: Cloud computing is a hosting model and does not by itself provide an isolated copy of production for patch testing.
whyNot.C: Redundancy provides availability through duplicate components and does not test patches safely.
whyNot.D: Application control restricts which programs may run and does not provide a patch test environment.

cards.front:
Which of the following types of cloud Infrastructures would allow several organizations with similar structures and interests to realize shared storage and resources?
A. Private
B. Hybrid
C. Public
D. Community
cards.why: A community cloud is shared by several organizations with similar structures, interests or compliance needs, so they can share storage and resources.

whyNot.A: A private cloud serves a single organization, not several organizations.
whyNot.B: A hybrid cloud combines private and public clouds, and does not target organizations with shared interests.
whyNot.C: A public cloud is open to the general public and is not limited to organizations with similar interests.

cards.front:
Which of the following implements two-factor authentication?
A. A phone system requiring a PIN to make a call
B. An ATM requiring a credit card and PIN
C. A computer requiring username and password
D. A datacenter mantrap requiring fingerprint and iris scan
cards.back: B. An ATM requiring a credit card and PIN
cards.why: An ATM (Automated Teller Machine) requires a card, which is something you have, and a PIN (Personal Identification Number), which is something you know. These are two different factor types, so it is two-factor authentication.

whyNot.A: A PIN alone is a single factor, something you know.
whyNot.C: A username and password together are a single factor, something you know.
whyNot.D: A fingerprint and an iris scan are both something you are, so they are two instances of one factor type.

cards.front:
A company is terminating an employee for misbehavior. Which of the following steps is MOST important in the process of disengagement from this employee?
A. Obtain a list of passwords used by the employee.
B. Generate a report on outstanding projects the employee handled
C. Have the employee surrender company identification.
D. Have the employee sign an NDA before departing
cards.back: D. Have the employee sign an NDA before departing
cards.why: A signed NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement) legally obligates the departing employee to keep confidential information private after leaving, which protects company data once the employee no longer has access.

whyNot.A: Employees should not know or hand over a list of passwords, and accounts should simply be disabled or reset.
whyNot.B: A project report helps with continuity of work but does not reduce security risk.
whyNot.C: Surrendering identification is a useful step, but it does not address the confidential information the employee still knows.

cards.keyDoubt: C, because collecting company identification removes physical access immediately, which is the most urgent step when terminating an employee for misbehavior.

cards.front:
A company's loss control department identifies theft as a recurring loss type over the past year. Based on the department's report, the Chief information Office (CIO) wants to detect theft of datacenter equipment. Which of the following controls should be implemented?
A. Biometrics
B. Motion detectors
C. Mantraps
D. Cameras
cards.why: Motion detectors can detect movement in a datacenter at times when no one should be present, which alerts staff to equipment being removed.

whyNot.A: Biometrics authenticate people at an entry point and do not detect equipment being stolen.
whyNot.C: A mantrap controls entry and exit, which is preventive and does not detect theft.
whyNot.D: Cameras mainly record events for later review, and they do not alert on theft as it occurs without someone watching.

cards.front:
A security analyst reviews the following output: The analyst loads the hash into the SIEM to discover if this hash is seen in other parts of the network. After inspecting a large number of files, the SIEM reports the following. File hash: E289F21CD33E4F57890DDEA5CF267ED2 File found: somestuff.xls, somefile.pdf, nofile.doc Which of the following is the MOST likely cause of the hash being found in other areas?
A. The file is encrypted.
B. Shadow copies are present.
C. There are MD5 has collisions
D. Jan Smith is an insider threat.
cards.why: Shadow copies are duplicate versions of the same file, so they would share one hash and could appear in several locations on the network.

whyNot.A: Encryption would change the file contents and hash, and would not make different files share a hash.
whyNot.C: An MD5 (Message Digest 5) collision is actually the better fit, because files of different types sharing one hash indicates different content producing the same hash.
whyNot.D: Nothing in the output points to Jan Smith being an insider threat.

cards.keyDoubt: C, because an xls, a pdf and a doc cannot be copies of one file, so identical MD5 (Message Digest 5) hashes indicate a hash collision.

cards.front:
An analyst wants to implement a more secure wireless authentication for office access points. Which of the following technologies allows for encrypted authentication of wireless clients over TLS?
A. WPA2
B. PEAP
C. EAP
D. RADIUS
cards.why: The keyed answer, WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2), secures wireless links with AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) encryption but does not itself tunnel authentication over TLS (Transport Layer Security).

whyNot.B: PEAP (Protected Extensible Authentication Protocol) is actually the better fit, because it wraps authentication inside a TLS tunnel.
whyNot.C: EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) is a framework and does not itself provide a TLS tunnel.
whyNot.D: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is the authentication server protocol and does not create the TLS tunnel with the client.

cards.keyDoubt: B, because PEAP (Protected Extensible Authentication Protocol) encapsulates the authentication exchange in a TLS (Transport Layer Security) tunnel.

cards.front:
A security analyst receives a notification from the IDS after working hours, indicating a spike in network traffic. Which of the following BEST describes this type of IDS?
A. Stateful
B. Host-based
C. Signature-based
D. Anomaly-based
cards.why: The keyed answer, signature-based, matches traffic against known attack patterns, so it does not describe an alert triggered by a general traffic spike.

whyNot.A: Stateful describes a firewall that tracks connection state and is not a type of IDS (Intrusion Detection System) detection.
whyNot.B: Host-based describes where the IDS (Intrusion Detection System) runs, and the alert here concerns network traffic.
whyNot.D: Anomaly-based is actually the better fit, because it alerts when traffic deviates from the normal baseline.

cards.keyDoubt: D, because a spike in traffic is a deviation from baseline, which is how an anomaly-based IDS (Intrusion Detection System) detects activity.

cards.front:
A datacenter recently experienced a breach. When access was gained, an RF device was used to access an air-gapped and locked server rack. Which of the following would Best prevent this type of attack?
A. Faraday cage
B. infrared detection
C. Smart cards
D. Alarms
cards.why: A Faraday cage blocks radio frequency signals, so an RF (radio frequency) device cannot reach or communicate with equipment inside the shielded rack.

whyNot.B: Infrared detection senses heat or motion and does not block radio frequency signals.
whyNot.C: Smart cards control authentication at doors and do not stop radio frequency attacks.
whyNot.D: Alarms notify staff after an event and do not prevent a radio frequency attack.

cards.front:
A network technician is setting up a segmented network that will utilize a separate ISP to provide wireless access to the public area for a company. Which of the following wireless security methods should the technician implement to provide basic accountability for access to the public network?
A. Enterprise
B. Wi-Fi Protected Setup
C. Pre-shared key
D. Captive Portal
cards.why: The keyed answer, Wi-Fi Protected Setup, simplifies device pairing with a PIN (Personal Identification Number) or button and does not identify individual users for accountability.

whyNot.A: Enterprise authentication gives individual accountability but is more than the basic accountability needed for a public area.
whyNot.C: A PSK (Pre-Shared Key) is shared by everyone, so it provides no accountability for individual users.
whyNot.D: A captive portal is actually the better fit, because it makes users accept terms or register before they get access.

cards.keyDoubt: D, because a captive portal makes users accept a policy or register before connecting, which gives basic accountability for public network access.

[Sim: FIM log] File integrity monitoring on a busy server that has never been updated since install. Which log entry is the FIRST instance of compromise?
/etc/passwd hashes change at 1/1/2017 1:20, 1:22, 1:23, 1:23
/etc/iptables/iptables-save: 12/30 1:00 ...cc3, 12/31 2:00 ...co3, 1/1 3:00 ...co3
/boot/initrd.img: 12/30 and 12/31 ...ca02, 1/1/2017 3:30 7813a8...
A. /etc/passwd 1/1/2017 1:20:34
B. /etc/iptables/iptables-save 12/30/2016 1:00:00
C. /etc/iptables/iptables-save 12/31/2016 2:00:00
D. /boot/initrd.img 1/1/2017 3:30:00
cards.why: File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) on a server never updated since install should show no changes, so the first hash difference is the first compromise indicator. The key treats the 12/30 iptables-save entry as that first instance.

whyNot.A: The /etc/passwd hash changes at 1:20 on 1/1/2017 come after the iptables-save entry, so they are not the first instance.
whyNot.C: The 12/31 iptables-save entry is later than the 12/30 entry the key selects as first.
whyNot.D: The /boot/initrd.img hash change at 3:30 on 1/1/2017 is the latest of the listed changes, so it cannot be the first.

cards.keyDoubt: C. The iptables-save hash is the same on 12/30 and changes on 12/31 at 2:00, so the first change from the baseline is the 12/31/2016 2:00:00 entry.

cards.front:

cards.front:

cards.front:
[Sim: Device controls] Drag and drop: where does the control "Device Encryption" go?
A. Company Managed Smart Phone
B. Data Center Terminal Server
cards.why: Device encryption protects data at rest on a company managed smartphone, so a lost or stolen phone does not expose stored corporate data.

cards.front:
[Sim: Device controls] Drag and drop: where does the control "Remote Wipe" go?

whyNot.B: A hoax is a false warning or claim meant to deceive or waste time, not a targeted theft of executive information.
whyNot.C: Vishing (voice phishing) uses phone calls, and the scenario does not describe a voice-based attack on executives.
whyNot.D: Spam is unsolicited bulk messaging sent to many recipients, not aimed specifically at executives.
whyNot.E: Pharming redirects users to fake websites by tampering with name resolution, and it is not targeted at executives.

whyNot.G: Generic phishing casts a wide net at many victims, while this scenario targets only the Chief Executive Officer and board.
whyNot.H: Spear phishing targets specific individuals or groups generally, but the executive-only target makes whaling the more precise answer.

cards.front:
[Sim: RAID] Drag and drop: which RAID level matches the Media Streaming Server profile?
A. RAID-0 (striping)
B. RAID-1 (mirroring)
C. RAID-5 (striping + 1 parity)
D. RAID-6 (striping + 2 parity)
cards.why: A media streaming server needs maximum read speed and capacity. Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 0 (RAID-0) stripes data across disks for performance, and the media can be re-created if a disk fails.

whyNot.B: Mirroring halves usable capacity and adds redundancy that a streaming workload does not need as much as speed.
whyNot.C: Striping with single parity adds write overhead and capacity cost that a speed-focused streaming server does not need.
whyNot.D: Striping with double parity has the highest write overhead and capacity cost, which is unnecessary for replaceable media.

cards.front:
[Sim: RAID] Drag and drop: which RAID level matches the Authentication Server profile?
A. RAID-0 (striping)
B. RAID-1 (mirroring)
C. RAID-5 (striping + 1 parity)
D. RAID-6 (striping + 2 parity)
cards.why: An authentication server needs high availability and simple, fast recovery. Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 1 (RAID-1) mirrors data to a second disk, so one disk can fail without downtime or data loss.

whyNot.A: Striping with no redundancy means one disk failure destroys all authentication data and takes the server down.
whyNot.C: Single parity striping needs at least three disks and has slower writes, which is not the expected match for a small authentication server.
whyNot.D: Double parity striping needs at least four disks and has heavy write overhead, which is more than an authentication server's profile calls for.

cards.front:
[Sim: RAID] Drag and drop: which RAID level matches the Email Archive profile?
A. RAID-0 (striping)
B. RAID-1 (mirroring)
C. RAID-5 (striping + 1 parity)
D. RAID-6 (striping + 2 parity)
cards.why: An email archive is read often and written less often, and it needs capacity efficiency with fault tolerance. Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 5 (RAID-5) stripes data with distributed single parity and survives one disk failure.

whyNot.A: Striping with no parity gives no fault tolerance, so one disk failure would lose the archive.
whyNot.B: Mirroring survives a disk failure but wastes half the capacity, which is costly for a large archive.
whyNot.D: Striping with double parity survives two failures but costs more capacity and write speed than an archive requires.

cards.front:
[Sim: RAID] Drag and drop: which RAID level matches the Identity Management Server profile?
A. RAID-0 (striping)
B. RAID-1 (mirroring)
C. RAID-5 (striping + 1 parity)
D. RAID-6 (striping + 2 parity)
cards.why: An identity management server holds critical data and warrants the strongest protection. Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 6 (RAID-6) uses double distributed parity and survives two simultaneous disk failures.

whyNot.A: Striping with no parity provides no fault tolerance for critical identity data.
whyNot.B: Mirroring tolerates only one disk failure in a pair, which is less resilient than double parity.
whyNot.C: Single parity striping survives only one disk failure, so it is less protective than double parity for critical identity data.

cards.front:
[Sim: RAID] RAID-5 on 4 disks: how is it built?
A. 3 stripe data + 1 parity box checked
B. 2 mirror data, no parity
C. 4 stripe data + 2 parity boxes checked
D. 2 stripe data, no parity
cards.back: A. 3 stripe data + 1 parity box checked
cards.why: Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 5 (RAID-5) on four disks stripes data across all of them with distributed parity, giving the capacity of three data disks and one disk's worth of parity.

whyNot.B: Mirroring with no parity describes Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 1 (RAID-1), not level 5.
whyNot.C: Two parity boxes describes Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 6 (RAID-6), and four data stripes would leave no room for parity.
whyNot.D: Two data stripes with no parity describes striping without redundancy and does not match level 5 on four disks.

cards.front:
[Sim: RAID] RAID-6 on 4 disks: how is it built?
A. 3 stripe data + 1 parity box checked
B. 2 mirror data, no parity
C. 4 stripe data + 2 parity boxes checked
D. 2 stripe data, no parity
cards.back: C. 4 stripe data + 2 parity boxes checked
cards.why: Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 6 (RAID-6) uses two parity blocks. On four disks, the parity boxes are checked and the array tolerates two disk failures.

whyNot.A: One parity box describes Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 5 (RAID-5), which tolerates only one disk failure.
whyNot.B: Mirroring with no parity describes Redundant Array of Independent Disks level 1 (RAID-1), not level 6.
whyNot.D: Two data stripes with no parity gives no fault tolerance, which does not match level 6.

cards.front:
[Sim: Ports] Drag and drop the default port for FTP.
A. 21
B. 22
C. 23
D. 25

F. 161
cards.why: File Transfer Protocol (FTP) uses TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 21 for its control connection, which is the default port for FTP.

whyNot.B: Port 22 is used by Secure Shell (SSH), not File Transfer Protocol (FTP).
whyNot.C: Port 23 is used by Telnet (Teletype Network), not File Transfer Protocol (FTP).
whyNot.D: Port 25 is used by Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), not File Transfer Protocol (FTP).
whyNot.E: Port 69 is used by Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP), a different protocol from File Transfer Protocol (FTP).
whyNot.F: Port 161 is used by Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), not File Transfer Protocol (FTP).

[Sim: Ports] Drag and drop the default port for Telnet.
A. 21
B. 22
C. 23
D. 25
E. 69
F. 161
cards.why: Telnet (Teletype Network) provides unencrypted remote terminal access and uses TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 23 by default.

whyNot.A: Port 21 is the control port for File Transfer Protocol (FTP), not Telnet (Teletype Network).
whyNot.B: Port 22 is used by Secure Shell (SSH), the encrypted replacement for Telnet (Teletype Network).
whyNot.D: Port 25 is used by Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), not Telnet (Teletype Network).
whyNot.E: Port 69 is used by Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP), not Telnet (Teletype Network).
whyNot.F: Port 161 is used by Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), not Telnet (Teletype Network).

[Sim: Ports] Drag and drop the default port for SMTP.
A. 21
B. 22
C. 23
D. 25
E. 69
F. 161
cards.why: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) uses TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 25 by default to send and relay email between mail servers.

whyNot.A: Port 21 is the control port for FTP (File Transfer Protocol), not SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol).
whyNot.B: Port 22 is used by SSH (Secure Shell) and tools built on it, such as SCP (Secure Copy Protocol).
whyNot.C: Port 23 is used by Telnet, an unencrypted remote terminal protocol.
whyNot.E: Port 69 is used by TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) over UDP (User Datagram Protocol).
whyNot.F: Port 161 is used by SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) over UDP (User Datagram Protocol).

cards.front:
[Sim: Ports] Drag and drop the default port for SNMP.
A. 21
B. 22
C. 23
D. 25
E. 69
F. 161
cards.why: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) uses UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 161 by default for managers to query and monitor network devices.

whyNot.A: Port 21 is the control port for FTP (File Transfer Protocol), not network device management.
whyNot.B: Port 22 is used by SSH (Secure Shell) for encrypted remote administration and file transfer.
whyNot.C: Port 23 is used by Telnet, an unencrypted remote terminal protocol.
whyNot.D: Port 25 is used by SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) for email relay.
whyNot.E: Port 69 is used by TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol), a simple file transfer service.

cards.front:
[Sim: Ports] Drag and drop the default port for SCP.
A. 21
B. 22
C. 23
D. 25
E. 69
F. 161
cards.why: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) runs over SSH (Secure Shell), so it uses TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 22 by default for encrypted file transfer.

whyNot.A: Port 21 is the control port for FTP (File Transfer Protocol), which does not encrypt traffic.
whyNot.C: Port 23 is used by Telnet, an unencrypted remote terminal protocol.
whyNot.D: Port 25 is used by SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) for email relay.
whyNot.E: Port 69 is used by TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol), which has no encryption or authentication.
whyNot.F: Port 161 is used by SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) for device monitoring.

cards.front:
[Sim: Ports] Drag and drop the default port for TFTP.
A. 21
B. 22
C. 23
D. 25
E. 69
F. 161
cards.why: TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) uses UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 69 by default for simple, unauthenticated file transfers such as network device boot images.

whyNot.A: Port 21 is the control port for FTP (File Transfer Protocol), a different and more full-featured protocol.
whyNot.B: Port 22 is used by SSH (Secure Shell) and SCP (Secure Copy Protocol).
whyNot.C: Port 23 is used by Telnet, an unencrypted remote terminal protocol.
whyNot.D: Port 25 is used by SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) for email relay.
whyNot.F: Port 161 is used by SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) for device monitoring.

cards.front:
[Sim: Order of volatility] Order of volatility, most to least volatile: what is #1?
A. CPU cache
B. RAM
C. Swap
D. Hard drive
cards.why: CPU (Central Processing Unit) cache is the most volatile evidence source because it holds data for nanoseconds and changes constantly, so it is collected first in the order of volatility.

whyNot.B: RAM (Random Access Memory) is volatile but holds data longer than CPU (Central Processing Unit) cache, so it ranks second.
whyNot.C: Swap space lives on disk and survives longer than RAM (Random Access Memory), so it ranks third.
whyNot.D: A hard drive keeps data without power, making it the least volatile of these sources.

cards.front:
[Sim: Order of volatility] Order of volatility, most to least volatile: what is #2?
A. CPU cache
B. RAM
C. Swap
D. Hard drive
cards.why: RAM (Random Access Memory) is the second most volatile source: its contents vanish at power loss, but they persist longer than CPU (Central Processing Unit) cache.

whyNot.A: CPU (Central Processing Unit) cache changes faster than RAM (Random Access Memory), so it is first in the order of volatility.
whyNot.C: Swap space is stored on disk and lasts longer than RAM (Random Access Memory), so it ranks third.
whyNot.D: A hard drive retains data without power, so it is the least volatile of these sources.

cards.front:
[Sim: Order of volatility] Order of volatility, most to least volatile: what is #3?
A. CPU cache
B. RAM
C. Swap
D. Hard drive
cards.why: Swap space is third because it extends RAM (Random Access Memory) onto disk, so it is less volatile than memory but still temporary and rewritten as the system runs.

whyNot.A: CPU (Central Processing Unit) cache is the most volatile source, so it ranks first, not third.
whyNot.B: RAM (Random Access Memory) loses data at power loss and changes faster than swap, so it ranks second.
whyNot.D: A hard drive holds persistent data and is the least volatile, so it ranks fourth.

cards.front:
[Sim: Order of volatility] Order of volatility, most to least volatile: what is #4?
A. CPU cache
B. RAM
C. Swap
D. Hard drive
cards.why: The hard drive is the least volatile of these sources because it stores data persistently without power, so it is collected last in the order of volatility.

whyNot.A: CPU (Central Processing Unit) cache is the most volatile source, so it ranks first.
whyNot.B: RAM (Random Access Memory) is lost at power-off and ranks second, well above a hard drive.
whyNot.C: Swap space is temporary paging data that changes while the system runs, so it ranks third.

cards.front:

cards.why: Phishing is a mass email that lures many recipients to a fake external site to steal their credentials, which matches this scenario.

whyNot.B: Whaling targets senior executives specifically, not a broad group of users.
whyNot.C: Vishing (voice phishing) uses phone calls, not email.
whyNot.D: Spim (Spam over Instant Messaging) is unsolicited messaging sent through instant message platforms, not email.
whyNot.E: Social engineering is the broad category of manipulating people; phishing is the specific technique used here.
whyNot.F: Pharming redirects users to a fake site by corrupting DNS (Domain Name System) resolution, without relying on an emailed link.
whyNot.G: Spoofing means falsifying an identity or address, which is a technique rather than this attack type.
whyNot.H: A hoax is a false warning or story meant to deceive, not a credential-stealing link.

cards.front:
[Sim: Attack type] Choose the attack type: Phone calls made to the CEO asking for various financial data.
A. Phishing
B. Whaling
C. Vishing
D. Spim
E. Social Engineering
F. Pharming
G. Spoofing
H. Hoax
cards.why: Whaling is a social engineering attack aimed at senior executives such as the CEO (Chief Executive Officer) to obtain high-value information like financial data.

whyNot.A: Phishing is a broad email lure aimed at many users, not a targeted call to one executive.
whyNot.C: Vishing is voice phishing aimed at ordinary users; here the high-value executive target defines the attack as whaling.
whyNot.D: Spim (Spam over Instant Messaging) is unsolicited instant messages, not phone calls.
whyNot.E: Social engineering is the general category; whaling is the more specific answer for an executive target.
whyNot.F: Pharming redirects users to fake sites through DNS (Domain Name System) tampering, not phone calls.
whyNot.G: Spoofing means falsifying an identity or address, which is a technique rather than this attack type.
whyNot.H: A hoax is a false warning or story, not a request for financial data.

cards.front:
[Sim: Attack type] Choose the attack type: Phone call to an individual claiming an IT issue and asking for the user's password.
A. Phishing
B. Whaling
C. Vishing
D. Spim
E. Social Engineering
F. Pharming
G. Spoofing
H. Hoax
cards.why: Vishing is voice phishing: the attacker phones the victim, claims an IT (Information Technology) problem, and tricks them into revealing a password.

whyNot.A: Phishing is typically delivered by email or text with a link, not a live phone call.
whyNot.B: Whaling targets senior executives, but this victim is an ordinary individual.
whyNot.D: Spim (Spam over Instant Messaging) uses instant messages, not phone calls.
whyNot.E: Social engineering is the broad category; vishing is the specific phone-based technique here.
whyNot.F: Pharming redirects users to fake sites through DNS (Domain Name System) tampering, not phone calls.
whyNot.G: Spoofing means falsifying an identity or address, which is a technique rather than this attack type.
whyNot.H: A hoax is a false warning or story, not a request for a password.

cards.front:
[Sim: Attack type] Choose the attack type: Instant message on a social media site from a friend with a link to a breakthrough diet.
A. Phishing
B. Whaling
C. Vishing
D. Spim
E. Social Engineering
F. Pharming
G. Spoofing
H. Hoax
cards.why: Spim (Spam over Instant Messaging) is unsolicited or malicious content, here a diet link, delivered through instant messaging or social media message platforms.

whyNot.A: Phishing is usually an email lure aimed at stealing credentials, not an instant message promoting a diet.
whyNot.B: Whaling targets senior executives, not a general social media contact.
whyNot.C: Vishing uses voice phone calls, not instant messages.
whyNot.E: Social engineering is the broad category; spim is the specific message-based form described here.
whyNot.F: Pharming redirects users to fake sites through DNS (Domain Name System) tampering, not a messaged link.
whyNot.G: Spoofing means falsifying an identity or address, which is a technique rather than this attack type.
whyNot.H: A hoax is a false warning or story, while this scenario is a spam message with a link.

cards.front:
[Sim: Attack type] Choose the attack type: A friend/colleague asks personal questions that could be typical password reset questions.
A. Phishing
B. Whaling
C. Vishing
D. Spim
E. Social Engineering
F. Pharming
G. Spoofing
H. Hoax
cards.why: Social engineering manipulates people into revealing information; asking casual personal questions that match password reset answers is a classic elicitation tactic.

whyNot.A: Phishing relies on deceptive email or messages with lures, not friendly in-person questions.
whyNot.B: Whaling targets senior executives, but nothing here points to an executive target.
whyNot.C: Vishing is a voice phone call attack, while this scenario describes a friend or colleague asking questions.
whyNot.D: Spim (Spam over Instant Messaging) is unsolicited instant messages, not personal questions.
whyNot.F: Pharming redirects users to fake sites through DNS (Domain Name System) tampering.
whyNot.G: Spoofing means falsifying an identity or address, which is a technique rather than this attack type.
whyNot.H: A hoax is a false warning or story, not a series of probing questions.

cards.front:
[Sim: Room controls] CEO's office: remove redundancies to deploy THREE-factor authentication while keeping the expensive iris scanner. Which set?
A. Iris Scanner + Smart Card Reader + Pin Pad
B. Iris Scanner + Thumbprint Scanner + Voice Recognition
C. Iris Scanner + Username/Password + Pin Pad
D. Iris Scanner + Smart Card Reader
cards.back: A. Iris Scanner + Smart Card Reader + Pin Pad
cards.why: Iris scanning is something you are, a smart card is something you have, and a PIN (Personal Identification Number) is something you know, giving three distinct factors.

whyNot.B: Iris, thumbprint, and voice recognition are all something you are, so they count as only one factor type.
whyNot.C: A username/password and a PIN (Personal Identification Number) are both something you know, so there is no something you have factor.
whyNot.D: Iris scanner plus smart card reader gives only two factors, missing something you know.

cards.front:
[Sim: Room controls] Data Center: add a "something you know" factor and use the existing smart card reader on the door. Which set?
A. Smart Card Reader + Pin Pad
B. Smart Card Reader + Iris Scanner
C. Smart Card Reader only
D. Mantrap + Thumbprint Scanner
cards.back: A. Smart Card Reader + Pin Pad
cards.why: Adding a PIN (Personal Identification Number) pad supplies something you know, which combines with the smart card reader's something you have for two-factor authentication.

whyNot.B: A smart card (something you have) plus an iris scan (something you are) adds no something you know factor.
whyNot.C: A smart card reader alone provides only a single factor, something you have.
whyNot.D: A mantrap is a physical access control vestibule, and with a thumbprint scanner it lacks both the smart card and a something you know factor.

cards.front:
[Sim: Room controls] Help Desk office: single-factor authentication using physical tokens handed to guests by the receptionist. Which control?
A. Smart Card Reader
B. Pin Pad
C. Thumbprint Scanner
D. Username/Password
cards.why: Physical tokens handed to guests are 'something you have' single-factor authentication, and a smart card reader reads those tokens to grant access to the room.

whyNot.B: A PIN (Personal Identification Number) pad checks a memorized code, which is 'something you know', not a physical token handed out by the receptionist.
whyNot.C: A thumbprint scanner checks a biometric trait ('something you are'), which cannot be handed to guests as a token.
whyNot.D: A username and password pair is 'something you know' and involves no physical token.

cards.front:
[Sim: Room controls] Public Cafe: secure the WAP with WPA and put the passphrase on customer receipts. Which setting?
A. WPA with a pre-shared key (PSK)
B. WPA Enterprise with RADIUS
C. Open network + captive portal
D. WEP with a 40-bit key
cards.back: A. WPA with a pre-shared key (PSK)
cards.why: WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) with a PSK (Pre-Shared Key) lets a cafe print one shared passphrase on receipts, encrypting traffic while keeping setup simple for customers.

whyNot.B: WPA Enterprise with RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) needs per-user accounts and a server, which is impractical for anonymous cafe customers using a printed passphrase.
whyNot.C: An open network with a captive portal does not use a WPA passphrase and leaves wireless traffic unencrypted.
whyNot.D: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) with a 40-bit key is obsolete and easily cracked, and it is not WPA.

cards.front:
[Sim: Firewall] Only allow the Accounting computer (10.4.255.10/24) HTTPS access to Administrative Server 1 (10.4.255.101). Which rule?
A. 10.4.255.10/24 → 10.4.255.101, 443, TCP, Allow
B. 10.4.255.10/24 → 10.4.255.101, 80, TCP, Allow
C. 10.4.255.10/24 → 10.4.255.101, 443, UDP, Allow
D. 10.4.255.10/24 → 10.4.255.102, Any, Any, Allow
cards.why: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) uses TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 443, so allowing that port and protocol from the Accounting computer to Administrative Server 1 permits only HTTPS.

whyNot.B: Port 80 TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is unencrypted HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), not HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure).
whyNot.C: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) runs over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), so UDP (User Datagram Protocol) on port 443 does not match the requirement.
whyNot.D: This rule targets 10.4.255.102, the wrong server, and allows any port and protocol, which violates least privilege.

cards.why: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) runs over SSH (Secure Shell), which uses TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 22, so that rule permits only SCP from the HR computer to Server 2.

whyNot.B: Port 21 TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is FTP (File Transfer Protocol), which is unencrypted and not SCP (Secure Copy Protocol).
whyNot.C: Port 69 UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol), an unencrypted transfer service and not SCP (Secure Copy Protocol).
whyNot.D: Port 443 TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) web traffic, not SCP (Secure Copy Protocol).

cards.front:
[Sim: Firewall] Allow the IT computer (10.4.255.10/25) to reach both Administrative Server 1 (.101) and Administrative Server 2 (.102). Which rules? (Select TWO)
A. 10.4.255.10/25 → 10.4.255.101, Any, Any, Allow
B. 10.4.255.10/25 → 10.4.255.102, Any, Any, Allow
C. 10.4.255.10/25 → 10.4.255.2, 22, TCP, Allow
D. 10.4.255.10/26 → 10.4.255.101, Any, Any, Allow
cards.why: The IT computer needs one allow rule per server, so one rule to 10.4.255.101 and one to 10.4.255.102 using the correct /25 source, give access to both Administrative Servers.

whyNot.C: This rule targets 10.4.255.2 on SSH (Secure Shell) port 22, which is neither Administrative Server 1 nor Administrative Server 2.
whyNot.D: The /26 source mask does not match the IT computer's /25 network, so this rule would not correctly cover the IT computer's address range.

cards.front:
[Sim: Auth factors] Authentication category for: Retina scan?
A. Something you have
B. Something you know
C. Something you are
D. All given authentication categories
cards.why: A retina scan measures a physical biological trait, which is the 'something you are' (inherence) authentication factor, also called biometrics.

whyNot.A: 'Something you have' covers physical items like smart cards or tokens, and a retina is a body trait, not an item.
whyNot.B: 'Something you know' covers memorized secrets like passwords or PINs (Personal Identification Numbers), not body traits.
whyNot.D: A retina scan belongs to only one category, 'something you are', so 'all given categories' is incorrect.

cards.front:
[Sim: Auth factors] Authentication category for: Smart card?
A. Something you have
B. Something you know
C. Something you are
D. All given authentication categories
cards.why: A smart card is a physical object the user carries, which makes it the 'something you have' (possession) authentication factor.

whyNot.B: 'Something you know' covers memorized secrets such as passwords or PINs (Personal Identification Numbers), not a carried card.
whyNot.C: 'Something you are' covers biometric traits such as fingerprints or retina scans, not a physical card.
whyNot.D: A smart card is only a possession factor, so 'all given categories' is incorrect.

cards.front:
[Sim: Auth factors] Authentication category for: Hardware token?
A. Something you have
B. Something you know
C. Something you are
D. All given authentication categories
cards.why: A hardware token is a physical device the user carries to generate or present codes, so it is the 'something you have' (possession) authentication factor.

whyNot.B: 'Something you know' covers memorized secrets such as passwords or PINs (Personal Identification Numbers), and a token is a physical device.
whyNot.C: 'Something you are' covers biometric traits such as fingerprints, not a carried device.
whyNot.D: A hardware token fits only the possession category, so 'all given categories' is incorrect.

cards.front:
[Sim: Auth factors] Authentication category for: Password?
A. Something you have
B. Something you know
C. Something you are
D. All given authentication categories
cards.why: A password is a secret the user memorizes, so it is the 'something you know' (knowledge) authentication factor.

whyNot.A: 'Something you have' covers physical items such as smart cards or tokens, and a password is memorized, not carried.
whyNot.C: 'Something you are' covers biometric traits such as fingerprints, and a password is not a body trait.
whyNot.D: A password fits only the knowledge category, so 'all given categories' is incorrect.

cards.front:
[Sim: Auth factors] Authentication category for: PIN number?
A. Something you have
B. Something you know
C. Something you are
D. All given authentication categories
cards.why: A PIN (Personal Identification Number) is a memorized numeric secret, so it is the 'something you know' (knowledge) authentication factor.

whyNot.A: 'Something you have' covers physical items such as smart cards or tokens, and a PIN (Personal Identification Number) is memorized, not carried.
whyNot.C: 'Something you are' covers biometric traits such as fingerprints, and a PIN (Personal Identification Number) is not a body trait.
whyNot.D: A PIN (Personal Identification Number) fits only the knowledge category, so 'all given categories' is incorrect.

cards.front:
[Sim: Auth factors] Authentication category for: Fingerprint scan?
A. Something you have
B. Something you know
C. Something you are
D. All given authentication categories
cards.why: A fingerprint is a unique physical trait of the user, so scanning it is the 'something you are' (inherence) authentication factor, also called biometrics.

whyNot.A: 'Something you have' covers physical items such as smart cards or tokens, and a fingerprint is a body trait, not an item.
whyNot.B: 'Something you know' covers memorized secrets such as passwords or PINs (Personal Identification Numbers), not body traits.
whyNot.D: A fingerprint fits only the inherence category, so 'all given categories' is incorrect.

cards.front:
[Sim: Auth types] Authentication type for: Fingerprint scan?
A. Biometric authentication
B. One Time Password
C. Multi-factor
D. PAP authentication
cards.why: A fingerprint scan verifies a unique physical characteristic of the user, which is biometric authentication.

whyNot.B: An OTP (One Time Password) is a code valid for a single use, not a physical trait like a fingerprint.
whyNot.C: Multi-factor authentication combines two or more factor categories, and a fingerprint scan alone is only one factor.
whyNot.D: PAP (Password Authentication Protocol) sends a username and password in plain text, which has nothing to do with fingerprints.

cards.front:
[Sim: Auth types] Authentication type for: Hardware token?
A. Biometric authentication
B. One Time Password
C. Multi-factor
D. PAP authentication
cards.why: A hardware token typically displays a code that changes each time or after a short interval, which is an OTP (One Time Password) used once per login.

whyNot.A: Biometric authentication uses body traits like fingerprints or retinas, and a hardware token is a carried device.
whyNot.C: Multi-factor authentication combines two or more factor categories, and a hardware token by itself is only the possession factor.
whyNot.D: PAP (Password Authentication Protocol) is a legacy plain-text password exchange, not a token that generates changing codes.

cards.front:
[Sim: Auth types] Authentication type for: Smart card?
A. Biometric authentication
B. One Time Password
C. Multi-factor
D. PAP authentication
cards.why: A smart card is normally paired with a PIN (Personal Identification Number), combining 'something you have' with 'something you know', which makes it multi-factor authentication.

whyNot.A: Biometric authentication uses body traits like fingerprints, and a smart card is a carried object.
whyNot.B: An OTP (One Time Password) is a single-use code, and a smart card stores a certificate rather than generating a one-time code.
whyNot.D: PAP (Password Authentication Protocol) is a plain-text password exchange, not a smart card method.

cards.front:
[Sim: Auth types] Authentication type for: Password?
A. Biometric authentication
B. One Time Password
C. Multi-factor
D. PAP authentication
cards.why: A password sent as a plain-text username and password pair matches PAP (Password Authentication Protocol), the simple legacy authentication type in this list.

whyNot.A: Biometric authentication uses body traits such as fingerprints, and a password is a memorized secret.
whyNot.B: An OTP (One Time Password) is valid for only one use, while an ordinary password is reused.
whyNot.C: Multi-factor authentication needs two or more factor categories, and a password alone is only one factor.

cards.front:
[Sim: Auth types] Authentication type for: PIN number?
A. Biometric authentication
B. One Time Password
C. Multi-factor
D. PAP authentication
cards.why: PAP (Password Authentication Protocol) sends a simple credential such as a PIN or password in cleartext, so a PIN number maps to PAP authentication as a single knowledge-based secret.

whyNot.A: Biometric authentication uses physical traits such as a fingerprint or retina, not a memorized PIN number.
whyNot.B: A One Time Password (OTP) is a dynamically generated code valid for one use, while a PIN is static.
whyNot.C: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) combines two or more different factor types, and a PIN alone is only one factor.

cards.front:
[Sim: Auth types] Authentication type for: Retina scan?
A. Biometric authentication
B. One Time Password
C. Multi-factor
D. PAP authentication
cards.why: A retina scan measures a unique physical characteristic of the eye, which is the 'something you are' factor and defines biometric authentication.

whyNot.B: A One Time Password (OTP) is a temporary code used once, not a scan of a body feature.
whyNot.C: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires combining two or more factor categories, and a retina scan alone is one factor.
whyNot.D: PAP (Password Authentication Protocol) transmits a password in cleartext and has nothing to do with scanning a retina.

cards.front:
[Sim: Forensics] Logs show an attack completed against one node (web server 10.10.10.10, database server 10.10.10.12, IDS 10.10.10.20, user PC 172.30.0.1). Which node was compromised?
A. Database Server
B. Web Server
C. IDS
D. Users PC
cards.why: The logs show the attack traffic completing against the database server at 10.10.10.12, so that node holds the evidence of compromise, which is the target of the successful attack.

whyNot.B: The web server at 10.10.10.10 appears in the logs as a path or relay, but the attack did not complete against it.
whyNot.C: The IDS (Intrusion Detection System) at 10.10.10.20 only monitors and alerts, so it recorded the attack rather than being compromised.
whyNot.D: The user PC at 172.30.0.1 is on a different network segment and is not where the attack completed.

cards.front:
[Sim: Forensics] Critical production network, LEAST disruptive incident response for the compromised database server. Which actions? (Select TWO)
A. Capture network traffic
B. Chain of custody
C. Shut down the server
D. Reimage the server
E. Disconnect the whole network
cards.back:
A. Capture network traffic
B. Chain of custody
cards.why: Capturing network traffic preserves volatile evidence without interrupting production, and chain of custody documents who handled the evidence, so both support incident response with the least disruption.

whyNot.C: Shutting down the server causes an outage on a critical production network and destroys volatile memory evidence.
whyNot.D: Reimaging the server wipes forensic evidence and causes downtime, so it is a disruptive recovery step, not a least disruptive response.
whyNot.E: Disconnecting the whole network halts all production systems, which is far more disruptive than isolating or monitoring only the affected server.

decks.name: AI Engineering Hub — Roadmap Q&A (math, LLMs, RAG, agents, MCP, fine-tuning)

cards.front: What is AI engineering, and how is it different from classical ML engineering?
cards.back: Building applications on top of pre-trained foundation models (prompting, RAG, agents, fine-tuning, eval, serving) instead of training models from scratch on your own data.

cards.front: What is a vector?
cards.back: An ordered list of numbers; in ML it represents a data point or an embedding in n-dimensional space.

cards.front: What is a dot product and why does it matter in ML?
cards.back: Sum of element-wise products of two vectors; it measures alignment and is the core of similarity search and attention scores.

cards.front: What is cosine similarity?
cards.back: Dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their lengths; measures the angle between them, ignoring magnitude. Used to compare embeddings.

cards.front: What is a matrix multiplication doing in a neural network?
cards.back: Applying a linear transformation: every layer multiplies its input vector by a weight matrix, then adds a bias.

cards.front: What is a gradient?
cards.back: The vector of partial derivatives of the loss with respect to each parameter; it points in the direction of steepest increase of the loss.

cards.front: What is gradient descent?
cards.back: Repeatedly nudging parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient to reduce the loss.

cards.front: What is a learning rate?
cards.back: The step size multiplied against the gradient on every update; too high diverges, too low crawls.

cards.front: What is backpropagation?
cards.back: The chain rule applied layer by layer, from the loss backward to every weight, to compute all gradients in one pass.

cards.front: What is a loss function?
cards.back: A number measuring how wrong the model's output is; training minimizes it. Cross-entropy is the standard loss for language models.

cards.front: What is probability versus likelihood?
cards.back: Probability: how likely an outcome is given fixed parameters. Likelihood: how plausible parameters are given observed data.

cards.front: What is a softmax?
cards.back: Turns a vector of raw scores (logits) into a probability distribution that sums to 1 by exponentiating and normalizing.

cards.front: What is the normal (Gaussian) distribution and why is it everywhere?
cards.back: A bell curve defined by mean and variance; sums of many small random effects tend toward it (central limit theorem).

cards.front: What is overfitting?
cards.back: The model memorizes the training set and performs worse on new data; fix with more data, regularization, dropout, or early stopping.

cards.front: What is a train/validation/test split?
cards.back: Train on one slice, tune hyperparameters on validation, report final numbers once on the untouched test slice.

cards.front: What is a neural network?
cards.back: Stacked layers of weighted sums followed by nonlinear activations, trained by gradient descent to approximate a function.

cards.front: What is an activation function and name three?
cards.back: A nonlinearity applied after each linear layer so the network can model curves; ReLU, GELU, sigmoid.

cards.front: What is a token?
cards.back: The unit an LLM reads and writes: a word piece, character chunk, or symbol produced by a tokenizer (roughly 4 characters of English).

cards.front: What is a tokenizer such as BPE?
cards.back: Byte Pair Encoding merges the most frequent byte pairs into a vocabulary of sub-word tokens so any text can be encoded.

cards.front: What is an embedding?
cards.back: A learned dense vector representing a token, sentence, or document so that similar meanings sit close together.

cards.front: What does an LLM actually predict?
cards.back: A probability distribution over the next token given all previous tokens; text is generated one token at a time.

cards.front: What is a transformer?
cards.back: The neural architecture behind modern LLMs: stacked blocks of self-attention plus feed-forward layers, trained to predict the next token.

cards.front: What is self-attention?
cards.back: Each token builds a query, key, and value; it scores its query against every other token's key and takes a weighted sum of their values to pull in context.

cards.front: What are Q, K, and V in attention?
cards.back: Query (what I am looking for), Key (what I contain), Value (what I pass along). Attention weight = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)).

cards.front: What is multi-head attention?
cards.back: Running several attention heads in parallel so each can learn a different kind of relationship, then concatenating the results.

cards.front: What is a positional encoding?
cards.back: Extra signal added to token embeddings so the transformer knows word order, since attention itself is order-blind. RoPE is the modern version.

cards.front: What is a context window?
cards.back: The maximum number of tokens the model can attend to at once; everything outside it is invisible to the model.

cards.front: What is a KV cache?
cards.back: Storing each token's key and value during generation so earlier tokens are not recomputed; it is why long outputs cost memory.

cards.front: What is temperature in sampling?
cards.back: A divisor on the logits before softmax; low values make output deterministic, high values make it more random.

cards.front: What is top-p (nucleus) sampling?
cards.back: Sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p, cutting off the long tail.

cards.front: What is pretraining?
cards.back: Next-token prediction on trillions of tokens of raw internet text; it gives the model its knowledge and language ability.

cards.front: What is supervised fine-tuning (SFT)?
cards.back: Further training on curated prompt/response pairs so the model follows instructions in a chat format.

cards.front: What is RLHF?
cards.back: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: a reward model trained on human preferences steers the policy toward helpful, safe answers.

cards.front: What is DPO?
cards.back: Direct Preference Optimization: trains on preferred vs rejected answer pairs directly, without a separate reward model.

cards.front: What is GRPO?
cards.back: Group Relative Policy Optimization: samples a group of answers per prompt and rewards those above the group average; used to train reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1.

cards.front: What is a reasoning model?
cards.back: A model trained to emit a long chain of thought before the final answer, trading inference tokens for accuracy on hard problems.

cards.front: What is LoRA?
cards.back: Low-Rank Adaptation: freezes the base weights and trains small rank-r matrices added to them, cutting fine-tuning memory by 10x or more.

cards.front: What is QLoRA?
cards.back: LoRA on top of a 4-bit quantized base model so fine-tuning fits on a single consumer GPU.

cards.front: What is quantization?
cards.back: Storing weights in fewer bits (8, 4) to shrink memory and speed up inference at a small accuracy cost; GGUF is the common local format.

cards.front: What is Unsloth?
cards.back: A library that makes LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning of open models roughly 2x faster and lighter; the hub uses it to fine-tune DeepSeek and Qwen.

cards.front: What is Ollama?
cards.back: A local runtime that downloads and serves open models (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, DeepSeek) behind a simple HTTP API on your own machine.

cards.front: What is knowledge distillation?
cards.back: Training a small student model to imitate a large teacher model's outputs so it keeps most of the quality at a fraction of the cost.

cards.front: What is RAG?
cards.back: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetch relevant documents at query time and put them in the prompt so the model answers from your data instead of memory.

cards.front: What are the stages of a RAG pipeline?
cards.back: Load documents, chunk them, embed each chunk, store in a vector DB, embed the query, retrieve top-k chunks, feed them plus the question to the LLM.

cards.front: What is chunking and why does chunk size matter?
cards.back: Splitting documents into pieces before embedding; too big dilutes the embedding, too small loses context. Overlap keeps sentences intact.

cards.front: What is a vector database and name three?
cards.back: A store optimized for nearest-neighbor search over embeddings; Qdrant, Milvus, Chroma (also pgvector in Postgres).

cards.front: What is hybrid search?
cards.back: Combining dense vector similarity with keyword (BM25) search so exact terms and semantic matches both score.

cards.front: What is a reranker?
cards.back: A cross-encoder that re-scores the retrieved chunks against the query to put the best ones first before they reach the LLM.

cards.front: What is ColBERT (late interaction)?
cards.back: Embeds every token instead of the whole passage and scores by per-token max similarity; more precise retrieval than single-vector embeddings.

cards.front: What is agentic RAG?
cards.back: The model decides when and what to retrieve, can retry with a rewritten query, and can fall back to web search instead of a single fixed retrieve step.

cards.front: What is corrective RAG (CRAG)?
cards.back: Grading retrieved documents for relevance and falling back to web search or query rewriting when they are weak.

cards.front: What is a hallucination?
cards.back: A fluent but false output; mitigated with grounding (RAG), citations, lower temperature, and evaluation.

cards.front: What is an AI agent?
cards.back: An LLM running in a loop that chooses tools, observes results, and keeps going until a goal is met.

cards.front: What is the difference between a workflow and an agent (Anthropic's definition)?
cards.back: Workflow: LLM calls orchestrated by predefined code paths. Agent: the LLM itself directs its own steps and tool use dynamically.

cards.front: What is the ReAct pattern?
cards.back: Reason + Act: the model alternates between a thought, a tool call, and reading the observation until it can answer.

cards.front: What is tool calling (function calling)?
cards.back: The model emits a structured JSON call matching a declared schema; your code runs it and returns the result as the next message.

cards.front: Name five agent workflow patterns from Anthropic's Building Effective Agents.
cards.back: Prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer.

cards.front: What is a multi-agent system?
cards.back: Several specialized agents (researcher, writer, reviewer) coordinated by an orchestrator or handoffs; CrewAI, AutoGen, and LangGraph are frameworks for it.

cards.front: What is CrewAI?
cards.back: A Python framework where agents have a role, goal, and backstory, work on tasks, and run as a Crew (autonomous) or a Flow (event-driven, deterministic).

cards.front: What is agent memory and what are its types?
cards.back: State an agent keeps across turns or sessions: short-term (conversation), long-term (vector or graph store), episodic (past runs). Zep and Graphiti build temporal knowledge graphs for it.

cards.front: What is MCP?
cards.back: Model Context Protocol: an open standard where a client (Claude, Cursor) connects to servers that expose tools, resources, and prompts over JSON-RPC via stdio or HTTP.

cards.front: What are the three primitives an MCP server can expose?
cards.back: Tools (functions the model can call), resources (data it can read), prompts (reusable templates).

cards.front: What is A2A (agent-to-agent protocol)?
cards.back: Google's protocol for agents to discover each other through an agent card and exchange tasks, complementary to MCP's tool connections.

cards.front: What is context engineering?
cards.back: Deliberately deciding what goes into the context window each step: instructions, retrieved facts, memory, tool results, and compaction of history.

cards.front: What is prompt caching?
cards.back: Reusing the processed prefix of a prompt (system prompt, documents) across calls so you pay a fraction of the input cost and get faster responses.

cards.front: What is structured output?
cards.back: Forcing the model to return JSON matching a schema (Pydantic model) so downstream code can parse it reliably.

cards.front: What is LLM-as-a-judge?
cards.back: Using a strong model with a rubric to score another model's outputs at scale when human grading is too slow.

cards.front: What are the main RAG evaluation metrics?
cards.back: Faithfulness (answer grounded in context), answer relevance, context precision, context recall (RAGAS metrics).

cards.front: What is observability for LLM apps?
cards.back: Tracing every call with prompts, tool calls, latency, tokens, and cost (Opik, LangSmith, Langfuse) so failures can be replayed and measured.

cards.front: What is a guardrail?
cards.back: A check before or after the model (input filter, output validator, policy rule) that blocks unsafe or off-policy behavior.

cards.front: What is latency vs throughput in LLM serving?
cards.back: Latency: time to first token and per-token speed for one request. Throughput: tokens served per second across all requests. Batching trades one for the other.

cards.front: What is time to first token (TTFT)?
cards.back: Delay before the first output token appears; dominated by prompt processing (prefill) and the main driver of perceived speed.

cards.front: What is LitServe?
cards.back: A FastAPI-based serving framework from Lightning AI for deploying model and RAG endpoints with batching and autoscaling.

cards.front: What is a multimodal model?
cards.back: A model that accepts more than text (images, audio, video) in its input; Llama 3.2 Vision, Gemma 3, and Qwen 2.5 VL are open examples.

cards.front: What is OCR with a vision LLM?
cards.back: Sending an image to a multimodal model and asking for the text (or structured fields) instead of using a classical OCR engine.

cards.front: What is a knowledge graph in AI apps?
cards.back: Entities and relationships stored as a graph; GraphRAG and Graphiti use it to answer multi-hop questions that vector search misses.

cards.front: What is fine-tuning versus RAG, and when do you pick each?
cards.back: Fine-tune to change style, format, or skill; RAG to inject fresh or private facts. Start with prompting, then RAG, fine-tune last.

cards.front: What is the Zero to Hero series by Karpathy and why do it?
cards.back: Ten videos building micrograd, makemore, and GPT from scratch in Python; it is the fastest way to understand what a transformer really computes.

cards.front: What are the four 3Blue1Brown topics on LLMs?
cards.back: How neural networks learn, how transformers work, attention explained visually, how LLMs store facts in MLP layers.

cards.front: What single book does the hub recommend for AI engineering?

decks.name: AI Engineering — Answer First (name the term)

cards.front: Building applications on top of pre-trained foundation models (prompting, RAG, agents, fine-tuning, eval, serving) instead of training models from scratch on your own data.
cards.back: What is AI engineering, and how is it different from classical ML engineering?

cards.front: An ordered list of numbers; in ML it represents a data point or an embedding in n-dimensional space.
Sum of element-wise products of two vectors; it measures alignment and is the core of similarity search and attention scores.
cards.back: What is a dot product and why does it matter in ML?

cards.front: Dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their lengths; measures the angle between them, ignoring magnitude. Used to compare embeddings.
Applying a linear transformation: every layer multiplies its input vector by a weight matrix, then adds a bias.
cards.back: What is a matrix multiplication doing in a neural network?

cards.front: The vector of partial derivatives of the loss with respect to each parameter; it points in the direction of steepest increase of the loss.
Repeatedly nudging parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient to reduce the loss.
The step size multiplied against the gradient on every update; too high diverges, too low crawls.
The chain rule applied layer by layer, from the loss backward to every weight, to compute all gradients in one pass.
A number measuring how wrong the model's output is; training minimizes it. Cross-entropy is the standard loss for language models.
Probability: how likely an outcome is given fixed parameters. Likelihood: how plausible parameters are given observed data.
Turns a vector of raw scores (logits) into a probability distribution that sums to 1 by exponentiating and normalizing.
A bell curve defined by mean and variance; sums of many small random effects tend toward it (central limit theorem).
cards.back: What is the normal (Gaussian) distribution and why is it everywhere?

cards.front: The model memorizes the training set and performs worse on new data; fix with more data, regularization, dropout, or early stopping.
Train on one slice, tune hyperparameters on validation, report final numbers once on the untouched test slice.
Stacked layers of weighted sums followed by nonlinear activations, trained by gradient descent to approximate a function.
A nonlinearity applied after each linear layer so the network can model curves; ReLU, GELU, sigmoid.
cards.back: What is an activation function and name three?

cards.front: The unit an LLM reads and writes: a word piece, character chunk, or symbol produced by a tokenizer (roughly 4 characters of English).
Byte Pair Encoding merges the most frequent byte pairs into a vocabulary of sub-word tokens so any text can be encoded.
cards.back: What is a tokenizer such as BPE?

cards.front: A learned dense vector representing a token, sentence, or document so that similar meanings sit close together.
A probability distribution over the next token given all previous tokens; text is generated one token at a time.
cards.back: What does an LLM actually predict?

cards.front: The neural architecture behind modern LLMs: stacked blocks of self-attention plus feed-forward layers, trained to predict the next token.
Each token builds a query, key, and value; it scores its query against every other token's key and takes a weighted sum of their values to pull in context.
Query (what I am looking for), Key (what I contain), Value (what I pass along). Attention weight = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)).
cards.back: What are Q, K, and V in attention?

cards.front: Running several attention heads in parallel so each can learn a different kind of relationship, then concatenating the results.
Extra signal added to token embeddings so the transformer knows word order, since attention itself is order-blind. RoPE is the modern version.
The maximum number of tokens the model can attend to at once; everything outside it is invisible to the model.
Storing each token's key and value during generation so earlier tokens are not recomputed; it is why long outputs cost memory.
A divisor on the logits before softmax; low values make output deterministic, high values make it more random.
Sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p, cutting off the long tail.
Next-token prediction on trillions of tokens of raw internet text; it gives the model its knowledge and language ability.
Further training on curated prompt/response pairs so the model follows instructions in a chat format.
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: a reward model trained on human preferences steers the policy toward helpful, safe answers.
Direct Preference Optimization: trains on preferred vs rejected answer pairs directly, without a separate reward model.
Group Relative Policy Optimization: samples a group of answers per prompt and rewards those above the group average; used to train reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1.
A model trained to emit a long chain of thought before the final answer, trading inference tokens for accuracy on hard problems.
Low-Rank Adaptation: freezes the base weights and trains small rank-r matrices added to them, cutting fine-tuning memory by 10x or more.
LoRA on top of a 4-bit quantized base model so fine-tuning fits on a single consumer GPU.
Storing weights in fewer bits (8, 4) to shrink memory and speed up inference at a small accuracy cost; GGUF is the common local format.
A library that makes LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning of open models roughly 2x faster and lighter; the hub uses it to fine-tune DeepSeek and Qwen.
A local runtime that downloads and serves open models (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, DeepSeek) behind a simple HTTP API on your own machine.
Training a small student model to imitate a large teacher model's outputs so it keeps most of the quality at a fraction of the cost.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetch relevant documents at query time and put them in the prompt so the model answers from your data instead of memory.
Load documents, chunk them, embed each chunk, store in a vector DB, embed the query, retrieve top-k chunks, feed them plus the question to the LLM.
